pages.title: Handled for you — the foundation behind your app
pages.body:
Somewhere combines hosting, functions, identity, data, files, and application services in one project. Your agent can use the project's verified user across those services and declare access rules alongside the source. It does not need to assemble a separate account system, file-permission layer, email sender, and deployment pipeline for each app.

This is a reference to the work the platform handles today, with links to the implementation contracts. **Automatic** means no additional protection to implement when using the named platform path. **Declare or configure** means you describe your app's intent; the platform enforces or runs it. **Available service** means your app calls it when needed. Availability and allowances vary by plan; [limits](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/limits.txt) and [pricing](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/pricing.txt) are the current reference.

## Nothing extra to set up

These protections are built into the relevant platform service. You do not add a separate library, server, or security recipe for them.

| Already handled | Where it applies |
|---|---|
| **Password hashing and salting** | Platform password accounts use salted password hashes; the app does not store or compare plaintext passwords. [Auth](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.auth.txt) |
| **Password-guessing protection** | Password sign-in automatically limits attempts per project/source address and per project/account, and locks an account for 15 minutes after 10 consecutive wrong passwords. [Exact limits](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.auth.txt#automatic-password-sign-in-protection) |
| **Generic invalid-login responses** | A missing account and a wrong password receive the same invalid-credentials response; the missing-account path also performs password-hashing work. Your app need not distinguish or expose those cases. [Auth](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.auth.txt) |
| **Browser session cookies** | The starter and cookie auth helpers issue Secure, HttpOnly, host-only session cookies. Page JavaScript cannot read those cookies. Session refresh and logout are provided; hand-written token storage is unnecessary on this path. [Client auth](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/auth-client.txt) |
| **Single-use recovery links** | Password-reset tokens have an expiry and are consumed atomically, so concurrent attempts cannot both use one. A completed reset revokes the user's existing sessions and refresh tokens. [Password recovery](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.auth.txt) |
| **Cross-site request checks (CSRF)** | Cookie-authenticated writes through the platform auth path require an accepted Origin; missing or disallowed origins are refused. The generated data API also checks Origin. This is already part of these paths, not a CSRF package to install. [Auth](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/auth-client.txt) |
| **Outbound address checks (SSRF)** | Deployed function fetches block private, loopback, link-local, and metadata destinations, check DNS answers at request time, and recheck followed redirects. Platform URL-fetching services have their own guarded fetch path. [Outbound requests](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.fetch.txt) |
| **Browser access closed until declared** | A managed table without browser permissions has no browser data access. Only declared operations and permitted columns are available through the generated client and its HTTP endpoint. [Declared data](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/declared-data.txt) |
| **Protected ownership fields** | Structured owner-scoped writes derive ownership from the verified user; browser input cannot nominate another owner or overwrite the platform's author field. [Declared data](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/declared-data.txt) |
| **Private project settings** | New environment values are private by default, including browser-looking names. Publishing a value requires an explicit public choice. Recognized server secrets are refused from public settings, and recognized source-code secret literals are refused at deploy. [Environment](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.env.txt) |
| **Auth email delivery** | Password reset, verification, and magic-link flows use the platform's sender. Auth-email limits and recipient suppression are applied by the platform. [Email](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.email.txt) |
| **Hosted HTTPS and edge delivery** | A project gets an HTTPS address, source compilation, and hosted assets/functions. Network DDoS mitigation comes from the hosting network; it does not replace app-specific abuse rules. [Deploy](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/deploy.txt) · [Network protection](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ddos-protection/about/) |

Cookie protections apply when using the cookie path; a custom token system does not inherit them by name. Likewise, outbound address checks do not decide whether a user is allowed to trigger your business operation.

## Sign-in and account lifecycle

**Declare or configure:** mount the provided auth route or use the working starter; choose the sign-in methods and which actions require a user. The platform supplies:

- Registration, password sign-in, session refresh, logout, email verification, password recovery, and account profile operations.
- Session inventory and revocation, so an app can let someone end other sessions without building a token store.
- Magic-link and supported social sign-in flows (Google, GitHub, Discord). Provider registration remains a configuration decision. App users can sign in with a password and an email code, which the app owner turns on for everyone or for those who choose it (`sw.auth` → `email-sign-in-codes`); authenticator-app codes and passkeys are not available.
- A verified request identity for supported data, file, billing, and other user-bound operations. Derive the user from that verified session, never from a user ID the browser submits.
- An optional SDK and React auth components, so an agent can preserve working session behavior while changing the app's layout and styling.

[Auth API](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.auth.txt) · [Browser setup](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/auth-client.txt) · [SDK](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sdk.txt)

## Database access, from personal notes to teams

**Declare:** tables, relationships, access scope, and browser operations in `db/schema.ts`. The declaration travels with the release. The platform applies supported schema changes and enforces declared access on generated browser requests and ordinary structured database calls inside functions.

| Access pattern | What the platform handles |
|---|---|
| **Owner** | Each signed-in user reads and changes their own rows; ownership is assigned from the verified session. |
| **Shared** | Signed-in users can read the shared rows; only a row's author can change or delete it through generated browser access. |
| **Team membership** | Access follows a membership table you name; operation-specific membership can make team access read-only. |
| **Owner or team** | `anyOf` combines owner access with membership permissions without repeating the checks in every handler. |
| **Inherited from a parent** | Child-row access follows the referenced parent's private scope when explicitly declared with `parent`. A relationship alone does not grant access. |
| **Server-only** | The browser has no direct table operations; an authorized function performs the work. |
| **Public reading** | Explicit read columns and, optionally, a publication condition define what signed-out visitors see. Public read access never grants writes. |

**Field-level access is part of the contract.** Separate read, create, and update lists control returned data and accepted input. A newly added column stays out of the browser when it is absent from an explicit list. `read: true` deliberately selects all supported readable fields; use explicit lists when additions should remain private.

The platform also provides typed browser access, filtering, ordering, pagination, related-record reads, supported aggregates, and transaction operations. A schema diff reports changes before application; supported additive changes apply, while production column removals and renames are refused. These capabilities reduce repeated query plumbing as well as repeated permission code.

Shared-table operations inside server functions have a broader service contract than browser authorship rules; protect those handlers accordingly. Intentional server-authority operations and external SQL require your function to authorize its caller. Choosing a public or shared scope is a product decision, not something a platform can infer from a table's name.

[Declared data](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/declared-data.txt) · [Database operations](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.db.txt) · [SQL capabilities](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sql-compatibility.txt)

## Files and controlled sharing

**Declare:** file collections alongside tables, including permitted operations, ownership or membership, file types, and size limits. The generated file client handles uploads, listing, metadata, download, replacement, and deletion under that contract.

- Owner, shared, team, owner-or-team, and server-only collections reuse the access vocabulary. The platform checks membership and ownership on file requests.
- An operation you omit is refused. Public collections are a deliberate declaration and do not grant public upload or deletion.
- Private collections do not become public because someone guesses a storage path. Original filenames do not have to be globally unique.
- Declared-file share links are expiring bearer links. Replacement, deletion, or loss of the issuer's read access invalidates them. Anyone holding a valid link can use it; these are not recipient-bound invitations, and there is no individual-link revocation control on this surface.
- Large uploads and upload URLs are available through the file service, with the applicable upload and plan limits.

Existing uploads and custom upload endpoints do not automatically join a declared collection; existing files need explicit adoption. Your agent supplies the picker, gallery, document view, or other experience. The platform supplies storage and enforcement. These file links do not automatically authorize a custom endpoint or database-record share.

[Declared files](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/declared-files.txt) · [File service](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.fs.txt)

## Keys, environment values, and external services

**Automatic for built-in services:** database, auth, files, managed AI, and transactional email use project-bound platform access. An app does not need separate provider keys just to call them.

**Configure external integrations:** store a key once in project settings, choose its environment scope, and access it from a function. Stored values are encrypted and not returned by management reads. A private value is not made public merely because its name starts with `VITE_` or `REACT_APP_`.

Public browser configuration has an explicit public setting. Publishable keys still become visible to visitors; storing one in settings does not turn it into a secret. Recognized secret checks catch supported patterns, not every arbitrary string that could be sensitive. After runtime configuration is adopted, production values can change without rebuilding or redeploying the app. New production page loads, and server requests that read settings inside the handler, receive changed values within 60 seconds, including a public value made private or deleted. Existing immutable apps adopt on their next ordinary source deploy; new apps adopt on their first deploy. An already open page does not automatically replace values it has read. Previews keep their captured development configuration, and rollback among adopted releases uses current production configuration rather than restoring old keys.

[Environment settings and request-time reads](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.env.txt#timing) · [Functions](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/functions.txt)

## Email without another account to get started

**Available service:** transactional email uses a built-in sender, with no sender-domain setup required. It can address the project owner and the project's users who have verified their email address, with no reply-to and a daily limit per project. An arbitrary outside recipient is refused; your own verified sender domain enables the broader sending use cases.

The platform also handles:

- A **test inbox for agents**: the project's `*.test.somewhere.site` addresses capture auth and application mail without delivering to a real mailbox. Agents can retrieve the actual link and finish the user journey. Captured application sends do not consume the normal email allowance; retention and capture limits apply.
- Auth emails automatically, including recovery and verification links.
- Idempotent send requests when you supply an idempotency key; send status, history, and delivery-event lookup.
- Bounce and complaint suppression, sending allowances, auth-email rate limits, and project pauses for excessive bounce or complaint rates.
- Received mail for addresses on your custom domain, stored per mailbox and read through the mail API (`/v1/mail`).

The built-in sender limits recipients to people connected to your project. Provider acceptance means the provider took the message; later delivery events (`delivered`, `bounced`, …) report what happened to it next.

[Sending and test inbox](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.email.txt) · [Inbound email](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/inbox.txt)

## AI without distributing provider keys

**Available service:** `sw.ai` calls models using platform-managed credentials. The default path uses the account's included allowance, subject to project spend caps and request/token limits. Explicit model selection supports larger or different workloads with the documented billing rules; optional provider credentials let eligible calls bill your provider account directly.

The service provides streaming, structured outputs, tool-call results, conversation handling, and usage reporting through its documented APIs. The agent-loop primitive adds bounded multi-step execution and tool handling when an app needs it. Your app defines the task, permitted tools, approval decisions, and user-facing behavior.

OpenAI backs the Advisor, AI security reviews, and generated deploy descriptions. Anthropic backs Sprite's AI editor. These features and the corresponding provider-backed calls in `sw.ai` are available where their providers operate. Sign-in, deploys, hosting and database access are separate from AI provider availability. [Somewhere Terms](https://somewhere.cloud/terms) · [OpenAI supported regions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/7947663-chatgpt-and-openai-api-supported-countries-and-territories) · [Anthropic supported regions](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/supported-regions)

[Models and allowances](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.ai.txt) · [Agent loop](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.agent.txt)

## Request validation, rate limits, and safe networking

**Declare:** `sw.endpoint` can combine an auth requirement, a body schema, an action-specific rate limit, and a handler. It is optional; ordinary default-export functions remain supported. Your agent can use the wrapper to avoid repeating the same request checks across routes.

**Available service:** `sw.rateLimit.check(key, max, windowSeconds)` supplies project-scoped counters without deploying a separate counter service. Your app chooses the key and responds when the allowance is exhausted. Use a verified user, an IP, or an operation key as appropriate. These fixed-window throttles are not exact financial quotas.

**Automatic controls already present:** password sign-in throttles, auth-email restrictions, and service/plan admission limits. There is no blanket per-user limit that automatically understands every custom endpoint or the cost of calls made with your own outside-provider key.

The frontend and its functions share an origin, so ordinary same-app requests need no cross-site API setup. External browser origins are a separate CORS configuration. CORS and CSRF protect browser request boundaries; authorization decides who may perform the operation. Outbound fetch helpers add bounded requests, checked redirects, and documented retry behavior; non-idempotent effects need deliberate retry choices.

[Endpoint wrapper](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.endpoint.txt) · [Rate limits](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.rateLimit.txt) · [CORS](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/cors.txt) · [Outbound fetch](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.fetch.txt)

## Payments and feature access

**Configure:** connect payments, define plans and prices, and select the features that require an entitlement. The platform supplies checkout, payment-event processing, the user-plan flow, entitlement lookups, and subscription-management surfaces.

For the user-checkout flow, verified identity ties the payment to the user. Functions can check a feature with `sw.billing.has('export')`; the subject comes from the request, not an ID supplied by the browser. React pricing and billing components are available and can be styled by the app.

Prices, refunds, tax/business obligations, order fulfillment, and custom webhook effects remain app decisions. An ad-hoc payment does not automatically fulfill an order.

[Payments](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/payments.txt) · [Plans and entitlements](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.billing.txt)

## Live updates, background work, and scheduled work

| Capability | Work the platform takes over | App input |
|---|---|---|
| **Live database views** | A declared read produces a subscription; writes invalidate it and clients re-read through the authorized function. The notification channel carries invalidation, not your rows. | Declare the read and connect the UI; this is not an arbitrary public broadcast channel. |
| **Shared live-data polling** | Poll once and fan out results for the configured data source instead of making every browser poll it. | Write the scheduled poller and declare its snapshot table/live view; choose the source, cadence, and audience. |
| **Durable background jobs** | Admission, execution, status, retry/recovery behavior, and supported idempotency-key handling. | Write an idempotent handler and verify each invocation. Inspect job status when work does not finish; [recovery](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/recipe-background-jobs.txt) explains failed and indeterminate outcomes. |
| **Cron** | Schedule and invoke a configured job or endpoint. | Choose when it runs and what it is authorized to do; schedules work on every plan, with plan-specific count and interval limits. |
| **Notifications** | Built-in email, push, and unified notification APIs. | Choose recipients and message content. Each user turns on push in their own browser, and the app decides who gets notified. |

[Live views](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/live.txt) · [Live data](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/live-data.txt) · [Jobs](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.jobs.txt) · [Cron](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/cron.txt) · [Notifications](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.notifications.txt)

## Deployment, previews, verification, and rollback

**Automatic on deploy:** compilation of raw React/TypeScript source, dependency resolution, hosting, and built-in checks. You deploy source, not a locally built `dist` directory. The platform distinguishes recognized blocking checks from advisory findings; on-demand AI review is a separate inspection, not proof that every endpoint is authorized correctly.

**Available tools and workflows:**

- `somewhere verify` can exercise a supplied journey and return browser evidence, screenshots, console/network findings, and expected-refusal checks. It complements an agent's own Playwright tests. Closing a browser does not erase test data.
- Source export, surgical file patches, generated types, inspection, and the CLI/MCP/API surfaces let an agent work on the same project without reconstructing it from compiled output.
- GitHub-connected deployment and custom domains are available after connection/ownership setup. HTTPS provisioning is handled by the hosting service.
- Hosted previews for signed-in accounts on **every plan** create an isolated, populated database copy, keep production-only secrets out, and gate access. Promotion checks whether production changed. Preview writes never merge into production.
- Previews have copy limits and restricted side effects: no outbound function requests, read-only copied identity rather than a full public sign-in flow, email only to the project's test inbox, and Stripe test-mode payments whose callbacks are withheld from the project webhook. Local `somewhere dev` instead uses the deployed backend; local writes can be production writes.
- Rollback selects a retained release and checks whether its managed schema can safely activate. It is a code/release recovery operation, not a point-in-time restoration of customer rows.
- Smoke checks provide on-demand health probes; recurring checks have plan-dependent availability. Logs and inspection provide evidence when an operation fails.

[Deploy](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/deploy.txt) · [Previews](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/dev-environments.txt) · [Verification](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/verify-before-deploy.txt) · [Smoke checks](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/smoke.txt) · [Inspection](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/inspect.txt) · [Logs](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.logs.txt)

## Other services in the same project

These are available primitives, not features silently added to every app. Your agent selects the ones the product needs.

| Need | Built-in service and reference |
|---|---|
| Images, thumbnails, and transformations | [Image service](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.image.txt) |
| PDF generation from a page or template | [Rendering](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/render.txt) |
| Booking availability and reservations | [Calendar](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/calendar.txt) |
| Product events and aggregate reports | [Analytics](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/analytics.txt) |
| File extraction, chunking, indexing, and retrieval after explicit ingestion | [Search](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/search.txt) |
| Reading public web content | [Web](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.web.txt) |
| Notifications to a user's browser, with per-device send history | [Push](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.push.txt) |
| Tickets and work tracking inside a project | [Tasks](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/tasks.txt) |
| Organizing related projects | [Project groups](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/project-groups.txt) |
| Source, table, and database exports | [Portability](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/portability.txt) |
| An external PostgreSQL database | [Postgres connection](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/postgres.txt); provider billing, migrations, and SQL authorization remain with that external database. |

## Privacy: what the platform handles and what to ask your human

The platform already knows the facts a privacy page needs. Call `project_privacy_facts` (or `GET /v1/projects/<id>/privacy`). It reports:
- who signs in to the app and how;
- whether the app sends email, takes payments or uses AI, and through which providers;
- the cookies the platform sets on the app;
- how long things are kept;
- the outside services that handle the app's users' data;
- the tables and files that hold personal data, and the outside domains its source loads.

Write or check the app's privacy page from these facts instead of guessing. Stored files and storage are private by default. Fonts from Google are served from the app's own address. Unsubscribe is added to mail sent from the app's free address. For optional analytics in Europe, `analytics_consent: { mode: "auto" }` makes the platform ask visitors there with its own small prompt and honour browser privacy signals ([Analytics](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/analytics.txt)).

Ask your human only what the platform cannot know:
- who runs the app and how people reach them (the name and contact on the privacy page);
- whether the app is aimed at children;
- whether it sends marketing email (which needs a postal address in each message);
- what the app keeps outside the platform, such as a raw SQL table or another service.

Never tell anyone the app "is compliant"; describe what it does.

### Publishing the privacy page

The platform can publish the page for you at `https://<app>/__sw/privacy`. The page is drawn from the live facts each time it is read, so it stays current as the app changes. Link to it from the app as "Privacy".

- `GET /v1/projects/<id>/privacy` returns `privacy_page`: whether it is published, its `url`, the stored `owner` and `contact`, and `suggested` values from the account. It also returns `collects`, the sentences of the page's "What we collect" section.
- `PUT /v1/projects/<id>/privacy/page` with `{ "owner": "...", "contact": "..." }` publishes it. `owner` is the person or business that runs the app, 1 to 120 characters. `contact` is an email address or an `https://` address. Calling it again replaces both and the date.
- `DELETE /v1/projects/<id>/privacy/page` unpublishes it. The address then returns 404.

Both need owner or editor access, and both return the page's `url` and `markdown`. The public page can take up to a minute to show a change.

The name and contact are shown to the public. Ask your human before publishing them, even the suggested ones.

### The person's own data page

`https://<app>/__sw/my-data` lets a person signed in to your app download a copy of their data or delete their account with the records and files that belong only to them. Before either action, the platform emails a 6-digit code to the account's own address, and the page acts only after the person enters it. The code lasts 10 minutes, works once, and works only for that sign-in and that action. The page makes exactly the person's own calls to `GET /v1/auth/users/me/export` and `DELETE /v1/auth/users/me?erase=owned`, which your app can also make for them.

Scripts on your app's pages act as the signed-in person: they can read and change whatever that person can. Load only scripts you trust.

## What you still decide

You choose the product behavior: who belongs to a team, what is public, what an administrator may do, what a purchase delivers, and which outside systems are allowed to act. The platform can enforce a declared rule consistently; it cannot choose the right rule from a description like “invoice” or “customer.”

Test signed-out, owner, wrong-user, and team-membership journeys for the rules you choose. Authorize privileged functions and deliberate server-mode operations. Treat public values and valid bearer links as readable by their holders. Keep recovery/export plans appropriate to the data you hold, and check actual allowances rather than assuming any metered service is unlimited.

Agents can request `somewhere docs handled-for-you --full` for this whole reference or use `--section <heading-id>` for one area. The [documentation index](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/llms.txt) links the complete topic catalog; [getting started](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/getting-started.txt) provides the shortest build path.

pages.title: Database — SQL support, capabilities, and limits
pages.body:
Each project has its own SQL database. Declare each table in `db/schema.ts`
together with who may reach its rows; `somewhere deploy` creates the table and
the platform applies that rule on every structured call:

- `owner()` — each signed-in user reads and changes only their own rows.
- `shared()` — any signed-in user reads every row and changes only the rows
  they wrote.
- `serverOnly()` — use it from server functions; the generated browser
  client has no access. Authorize the caller in your handler.

In the browser, import the generated `data` client from `somewhere:data`; it
has exactly the operations you granted. Inside a function, use `sw.db.from`,
`insert`, `update` and `remove`. Deploy, sign in with two accounts, and each
sees only its own `owner()` rows.

Next: `declared-data` for the schema and the generated client, `sw.db` for
server queries and transactions, `sql-compatibility` for the SQL dialect, and
`postgres` to attach a PostgreSQL database you own.

## Short answer

A fully managed relational database, one database per project. It supports
foreign keys, joins, indexes, transactions, triggers, JSON operators,
full-text search, and math functions.

## Built on Cloudflare D1

Each app's rows live in its own Cloudflare D1 database. Your functions run
on Cloudflare Workers.

- **Regional read replicas shorten read paths.** New project databases are
  created with D1 read replication on. A deployed function's reads go through a
  D1 session, so a replica closer to the request can answer them instead of
  the primary.
- **Writes use one primary.** Every write goes to the database's single
  primary, in the region chosen when the project was created.
- **Read-your-writes travels with the session bookmark.** Within one request,
  a read after a write sees that write. Across requests, it holds while the
  client carries the session bookmark the platform returns; a request without
  it may be answered by a replica that is briefly behind.
- Developer tools that query the database directly (`db_query`, the CLI's
  SQL commands) read the primary.

Replica regions and status:
https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/best-practices/read-replication/

## How storage grows

Managed data grows with your app. Somewhere handles storage as it grows.
Database storage is measured across your account under your plan (see the
storage section of `sw.db`). File contents, platform logs, analytics
events, sign-in credentials and search vectors already live in separate stores
and do not count toward it. App rows and indexes do, along with internal data
such as persisted AI conversations and file-search text. Keep large values in
`sw.fs`.

Growth handling covers data read and written through the managed API. Very
large tables queried with raw SQL stay in one database; use the managed API
for datasets that need to grow.

## Starting a new app? Start here

Start with the managed project database. It comes with the parts of a data
layer you would otherwise build and maintain yourself:

- **Row permissions are declared once and enforced automatically.** A table
  declares who may reach it, and every structured call carries that rule into
  the statement — so the authorization plumbing that usually repeats in every
  handler is written in one place and applied for you.
- **A typed browser client, generated from that declaration.** The operations
  you granted exist and are typed; the ones you did not are absent.
- **The schema is context an agent can use.** `db/schema.ts` is a file it
  reads and changes, so the thing building your app already knows the shape of
  your data — no separate migration tool, no drift between what the code
  believes and what the database holds.
- **Nothing to operate.** No connection string to hold, no pool to size, no
  migration runner, no second bill.

Its SQL surface is narrower than PostgreSQL's; the next section covers
when to attach a database you own.

## When PostgreSQL fits

Attach one PostgreSQL database per project when you already have Postgres data,
need a specific extension or type, or rely on existing Postgres tools.
Use the managed project database for the app data you want the platform to
scope automatically. An app can use both.

The attachment connects to Neon on every plan, including Free. You own the
account, bill, region, credentials, migrations, authorization and recovery.
Queries run through the provider's driver; declared row permissions and the
generated browser client apply to the managed database, not those queries.
See `postgres` for connecting and authorizing access.

Neon references: https://neon.com/docs/reference/compatibility and
https://neon.com/docs/serverless/serverless-driver

## What you get vs Postgres

Supported syntax and capabilities:
- Standard SQL: SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE / JOIN / GROUP BY / HAVING / window functions
- Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY (with ON DELETE/UPDATE), UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK
- Indexes (B-tree), partial indexes, expression indexes
- Triggers (BEFORE / AFTER / INSTEAD OF)
- Transactions with full ACID, savepoints
- JSON columns + JSON operators (`json_extract`, `->`, `->>`)
- Full-text search
- Common Table Expressions, recursive CTEs
- `RETURNING` on INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE

Differences to account for in SQL:
- No `ENUM` types — use CHECK constraints + TEXT.
- No `UUID` type — use TEXT, generate via `crypto.randomUUID()` in your function.
- No stored procedures / PL/pgSQL — write logic in your server function.
- No materialized views — cache results in a regular table refreshed via cron.
- Ordinary writes are direct. The per-project database engine schedules writes
  one at a time; there is no additional platform write queue. Concurrent reads
  may overlap, but placement and database load still affect latency.
- Default-engine semantics apply. Division by zero returns `NULL`,
  ascending order places `NULL` first by default, and `LIKE` is
  case-insensitive for ASCII unless the query makes its intent explicit.

## What the platform compensates for

- **Schema as source** — declare tables in `db/schema.ts` and deploy; the
  platform creates them and arms per-user scoping in the same step, and the
  file stays the only schema writer for those tables. Hand-managed tables keep
  `db_migrate`; their access rules come from `db/schema.ts` too. See the two-worlds section in
  docs({ topic: 'sw.db' }).
- **Vector search** — `sw.search.*` gives you embeddings + similarity queries over your tables without bolting on a separate vector database.
- **Database change events** — the developer-side `db_webhook_set/get/delete`
  tools register a webhook on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Cleaner than LISTEN/NOTIFY
  for typical app use.
- **Per-user row scoping** — the structured builder
  `sw.db.from/count/insert/update/remove` on a declared user-owned table injects the
  owner filter from the request's verified user automatically. Explicit
  `sw.db.server` reads bypass that scope only when selected by the function.
- **Atomic batches** — `sw.db.tx` and `sw.db.server.tx` commit related
  declared operations together; ordinary single writes remain direct.
- **Database storage** — read your plan’s account total in the
  [live pricing catalog](https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/pricing). It is summed
  across your projects.
  This is not a combined cap on database, files, logs
  and analytics: those primitives use separate stores and limits. Internal
  conversation history and file-search text indexes can still occupy project
  database space; see the size boundaries in docs({ topic: 'sw.db' }). Storage
  is enforced; reads are unmetered. The live values are returned by
  `GET /v1/pricing`.

## Choosing for your workload

Use the managed database for relational app data: accounts, content, orders
and messages, with the row rules and typed client declared in your project.
Keep request-path queries bounded and batch related writes. Storage is
measured in GB under your plan; see the database storage notes above.

For large analytical scans, evaluate a warehouse. For Postgres-specific
extensions or existing SQL and tooling, use an attached database. Measure
your own query shapes and write concurrency when choosing between them.

Developer-side `db_dump` gives you a SQL file when another database better
fits the workload. It restores directly into the source database engine;
Postgres requires the two-step conversion in `portability`.

Related: `sw.db`, `portability`, `security-model`.

pages.title: Security model — who can read/write what
pages.body:
The platform runs sign-in, sessions and the data boundary; your functions
decide what each signed-in user may do.

Handled for you: sessions travel in HttpOnly cookies, `sw.auth.fromRequest(req)`
returns the verified user, and browser sessions reach data only through your
functions and the generated data client, never through raw SQL. On a declared
`owner()` table, `sw.db.from`, `insert`, `update` and `remove` are scoped to
that user automatically. Secrets stay on the server in `sw.env`.

Yours to decide: which user may take which action. Check it in the function
before the work runs — `await sw.auth.requireUser(req, { role: 'admin' })`
answers 401 to a signed-out caller and 403 to anyone who isn't an admin. A raw
read through `sw.db.server.query` runs exactly as written, so authorize the
caller first and take the user from the session, never from the request body.

Next: `security-model` → `your-part-the-seven-app-security-rules` has a block
to paste into your project instructions; `sw.auth`, `sw.db` and `cors` cover
each boundary in depth.

## Three actor classes

1. **End users** of your app — sign up via `sw.auth`. Get a JWT in
   cookies or `Authorization: Bearer …`. Identified by
   `sw.auth.fromRequest(req)`. Cannot run raw SQL from the browser.
2. **Your server functions** — code you deploy under `api/*`. Run with
   project-level credentials. Can hit any `sw.*` method and read env
   vars. On managed projects (the default), ordinary raw SQL is refused:
   raw reads go through `sw.db.server.query` / `sw.db.server.batch`
   after your code authorizes the caller, and raw writes are refused.
   SQL-mode projects can run raw SQL.
3. **You (the developer)** — somewhere.cloud account, smt_ API key.
   Can deploy, change settings, query the database, and access logs.

## Data access via the CLI, MCP server & API

The somewhere MCP server and `somewhere` CLI are clients for your own control plane. They let an agent or developer manage YOUR account — create projects, deploy code, run database queries, manage files, secrets, and domains.

- Authentication: OAuth 2.0 (MCP) or interactive browser login (`somewhere auth login`, CLI). The session token is stored locally in `~/.somewhere/config.json` and sent only to the Somewhere API and MCP hosts over HTTPS. We never request, read, or store third-party passwords. A revocable `smt_` API key is offered for CI; it is the only long-lived credential.
- Scope: the token acts as your developer identity — it can perform any action your account can (read/write your projects' source, databases, stored files, environment variables/secrets, deploys, billing config) and ONLY for resources your account owns, never another user's. During `somewhere deploy` the CLI reads the project source in the working directory to upload it and reads nothing outside that directory.
- What it does not do: it does not read arbitrary files on your machine, harvest environment variables, touch other applications' credentials, or contact any host other than the Somewhere API. Secret VALUES are write-only through these tools — they cannot be read back.
- Disconnect a connected agent on the [Agents page](https://somewhere.cloud/app/agents). Revoke a developer key with `DELETE /v1/keys/<id>`.

## Per-user data access

For data scoped to an end-user (notes, orders, messages, etc.), declare the
table with `scope: owner()` in `db/schema.ts` and use the structured
builder — it scopes to the request's verified user automatically, with no user
argument:

```js
// auto-scoped to the signed-in user
const mine = await sw.db.from('notes');
await sw.db.insert('notes', { body }); // owner column set by the platform
```

On managed projects, ordinary `sw.db.query` / `sw.db.batch` are refused.
For an intentional raw read, authorize the caller first and use
`sw.db.server.query` / `sw.db.server.batch`; those calls are never scoped or
rewritten for you.

## Can raw SQL bypass scoping?

- **From browser code:** no. App-user database access is structured table
  access; raw SQL endpoints refuse app-user credentials.
- **From your own server code:** only deliberately. A trusted server function
  must authorize the caller and select `sw.db.server.query` or
  `sw.db.server.batch` for an intentional raw read. Options on ordinary raw
  calls do not grant server authority in managed mode.
- **Via the MCP `db_query` tool:** yes — but only with your developer
  key (smt_), never with an end-user JWT.

## Deploy-time + on-demand review

- **Every deploy** runs a pattern scanner that catches the obvious shapes
  (auth bypass, raw SQL, payment metadata spoof, env leakage, eval,
  RCE). Its hits surface as `warnings[]` in the deploy response and do not
  block the deploy.
- **Deterministic refusals.** A deploy is refused, and nothing is
  published, for a recognized secret key in source (`SECRET_IN_SOURCE`),
  for browser code reading a `VITE_`/`REACT_APP_` variable whose value is a
  secret key (`BROWSER_ENV_SECRET`), and for an uploaded private credential
  file such as `.env`, `.pem`/`.key` or a service-account key
  (`DEPLOY_PATH_REJECTED`).
- **On-demand** (`security_review` MCP tool) runs
  an LLM over the deployed code and returns a Markdown report with
  WHAT/WHERE/IMPACT/FIX per finding. Every plan runs the same reviewer;
  plans that include the deep review (`tier_unlocks_deep_review: true`)
  allow a longer report. Per-run cost is at /v1/pricing.

## Server-side secrets

- `sw.env.SECRET_NAME` — server-side. Reading it inside a handler is
  fine. Returning it in a response (`Response.json(sw.env)`) is a leak;
  the security review flags this shape.
- `VITE_*` / `REACT_APP_*` names remain server-only until you explicitly
  mark them public. A public value with one of those names is visible in
  the browser to every visitor. Use this for an API
  base URL or a publishable key, never a service secret.
- Service keys: set via `somewhere env set KEY --stdin` or the dashboard.
  Stored encrypted; read with `sw.env.KEY` in a server function.
  Do not return the value to the browser.

## Admin paths

- `sw.auth.admin` (privileged auth ops — delete user, list all users)
  is not callable inside deployed functions — any call throws
  `AUTH_ADMIN_REMOVED_FROM_RUNTIME`. Use the developer-key surface
  instead (auth_user_update, auth_user_delete, auth_users_list) from your
  own tooling. A developer cannot sign in as an app user (410
  `IMPERSONATION_RETIRED`).
- `sw.db.migrate` is removed from deployed functions; run schema changes with
  developer credentials through `db_migrate`, the CLI, or dashboard.
- `sw.keys.*` / `sw.deploy.*` are developer-key only.

## Runtime function key scope

Your deployed functions share one server credential
(`PROJECT_API_KEY`) that lives inside the `sw.*` helpers and is never
exposed to your code. On deploy it is scoped to exactly the
surfaces your functions use: a function that only calls `sw.db` and
`sw.payments` gets a key that can reach the database and payments
areas and nothing else — a call to an unused area is refused. This is
derived from your code automatically (no config), and every `sw.*`
surface keeps working unchanged. If you reach the platform only through the
documented `sw.*` methods (the normal case), there is nothing to do.

## Auth token lifecycle

- Access tokens: 1 minute. Auto-refreshed inline — if expired and the
  refresh is valid, the response includes `X-New-Access-Token` +
  `X-New-Refresh-Token` headers (CORS exposes them).
- Refresh tokens rotate on every refresh; store the replacement pair. A
  just-rotated token is briefly accepted so concurrent refreshes don't sign
  the user out. A replay after that window revokes every session and refresh
  token the user has in the project. Lifetimes and current windows:
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.auth', section: 'token-types' })`.
- Revoke a session: `auth_revoke_session` (MCP) or
  `DELETE /v1/auth/sessions/:id` with a developer key.

## Your part — the seven app-security rules

The platform owns the boundaries above. Which of your users may do what —
application-level authorization — is yours. These seven rules are the whole of
it; on somewhere most are the floor, not homework. Paste the block into the
project's CLAUDE.md (or equivalent) so every session starts with it:

```md
# Security rules (the browser is untrusted)
1. NEVER trust the client for identity: the user is who the SERVER says (verified session), never a user_id from a body, query param, or localStorage.
2. SCOPE EVERY QUERY to the signed-in user, server-side; default deny. Declare each table user-owned / shared / server-only (unsure = user-owned). Use sw.db.from / insert / update / remove for user-owned tables; any raw SQL carries its own WHERE user_id = ?.
3. THE BROWSER MAY NEVER WRITE PRIVILEGE FIELDS (role, is_admin, permissions, plan, balance, credits): server-set only; whitelist client-writable columns.
4. NO SECRETS IN CLIENT CODE: keys and tokens live in server env only and are read with sw.env inside a function; public keys are fine; if a secret reaches the page, rotate it.
5. AUTHORIZE ON THE SERVER, not in the UI: a hidden button is not a control; re-check the caller on every endpoint.
6. LOCK DOWN CORS: same-origin by default, explicit allowed origins only; never reflect an arbitrary Origin with credentials.
7. PARAMETERIZE EVERYTHING: no concatenated SQL; validate every input; treat every client field as hostile.
Server code stays free to do anything intended. These rules constrain the untrusted browser and the end-user credential only.
```

The block is written for any coding agent, on any stack. Here, the platform
verifies the session and scopes structured queries on user-owned tables to that
user (rules 1 and 2). In a handler that uses `sw.db.server.*` or raw SQL, take
the user from `sw.auth.requireUser(req)`, never from a request field. The
deploy review flags the most common slips on 3, 4 and 5 — the block keeps you
honest about the rest.

Related: `sw.auth`, `sw.db`, `common-mistakes`.

pages.title: Built-in protections — what the platform handles
pages.body:
Owner tables keep each person's rows separate. Private collections check file
access. Sessions use HttpOnly cookies, and background handlers can verify
signed deliveries with one call. These protections are built into the app
interfaces below.

Start with a table declared using `owner()` and an upload collection scoped to
its user; their ordinary reads and writes apply the access rules for you.
Use explicit server operations only inside a handler that has checked the
caller's permission. Open `declared-data` and `declared-files` for working
examples, or use the table below to find a specific protection.

## Security

| Protection | What the platform enforces | Your part | Details |
|---|---|---|---|
| Owner-scoped data | On a table declared with `scope: owner()`, the ordinary structured calls `sw.db.from`, `insert`, `update`, `remove` and `tx` act only on the verified user's rows. Without a signed-in user, they fail with `AUTH_REQUIRED`. Once a project declares tables, ordinary `sw.db.query` and `sw.db.batch` are refused. `sw.db.server.query` and `sw.db.server.batch` run reads only. | Write through the structured calls. Server operations, both reads and writes, skip the owner scope, so authorize the caller first. | `declared-data`, `sw.db` → `managed-mode-what-a-dbschemats-does-to-raw-sql` |
| Private files | A declared file collection lets each user list, download and share only the files its `scope` and `client.read` allow, checked on every request. A share link opens one file for anyone holding it until it expires. It stops working when the file is replaced or deleted, or when the person who made it can no longer read the file. In a collection declared `public: true`, anyone can read the files at their public URL, while uploads, replacements and deletions still follow `scope` and `client`. A file written with `sw.fs.write` is private unless you write it public. | Declare a collection for user files, and keep share links short. | `declared-files` |
| Signed background calls | Job, queue and cron deliveries are signed for each attempt, and `sw.jobs.verifyInvocation` accepts a signature once. Only a row-bound job may use managed data as its initiating user, within that row grant. | Call `verifyInvocation(request)` before reading the payload, and answer 403 when it returns `false`. | `sw.jobs` → `job-handler-function` |
| Cookie sessions and origins | A write authenticated by a session cookie must carry the app's `Origin` header, or it fails with `ORIGIN_REQUIRED`. In safe CORS mode, a browser request from an unapproved origin that carries a cookie or `Authorization` is refused with 403 `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED` before your code runs. | Add third-party origins to the project's allowlist. | `cors` → `what-is-refused-and-what-reaches-your-function` |
| Per-project signing keys | Each project's app-user tokens are signed with a key derived for that project. A token issued for one project does not verify in another. | Nothing to configure. | `sw.auth` |
| Single-use credentials | A password-reset token or magic link works once, including under concurrent requests. Refresh tokens rotate. Presenting a rotated one after the grace window revokes that user's refresh tokens and sessions everywhere. | Nothing to configure. With manual tokens, keep the newest refresh token after each refresh. | `sw.auth` → `token-refresh` |
| Checkout | Only server code with the project's credentials creates a checkout. A catalog plan takes its price from the project's billing catalog. A deployed app's success and cancel URLs are accepted on its own addresses and attached custom domains, and other public hosts are refused. | Name a catalog plan. An amount you pass in line items is your handler's to validate. | `payments`, `sw.billing` |
| Outbound requests | `fetch` in a deployed function refuses private and cloud-metadata addresses, checks every redirect, and applies a timeout. The platform's own calls to webhook URLs and to job, queue and cron handlers also refuse those addresses and check each redirect. | Make outbound calls with `fetch`. | `sw.fetch` |
| Platform API access | Every platform API route declares which credentials may call it, and an undeclared route is refused. An app user's token reaches only the routes declared for app users. | Keep developer keys out of browser code. | `security-model` |

## Reliability

We never pause free apps for idleness or paid apps because of a platform change;
our [breaking-change policy](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/changes.txt#how-we-handle-breaking-changes)
explains notice, prepared fixes and the safety exception.

After each deploy, the after-deploy check loads your public home page in a
browser. A blank page, or one that throws while loading, is warned about,
not rolled back: the release stays live. When the version before it worked,
the warning names it and gives the exact call that puts it back:
`somewhere restore <version> --project <project_id> --yes`, or over MCP `project_rollback({ project_id, version })`. Server code that fails to start is refused before it goes live.
Details: `deploy` → `reliability-guarantees-on-every-deploy`.

## Security tools

Two advisory tools read your function source and report risky code. A finding
from either one never changes or blocks a deploy. Platform checks apply
regardless: the deterministic refusals of a
secret key in source (`SECRET_IN_SOURCE`), a secret in a browser-exposed
variable (`BROWSER_ENV_SECRET`) and a private credential file
(`DEPLOY_PATH_REJECTED`); each refuses the deploy before anything is
published.

- **`security_review`** (MCP tool): an AI review of the project's deployed
  functions. It returns each finding with its severity and a fix. Run it after
  a deploy; the review depth and any automatic runs depend on the plan.
- **Deploy scanner:** every deploy checks public handlers for risky shapes, such
  as admin calls, a caller-supplied user id or evaluated code. It lists each hit
  under `warnings` in the deploy response.

Both tools in detail: `deploy-intelligence`.

pages.title: Portability — getting your data out
pages.body:
Your data and code are yours. There are four exits, each in an ordinary format:

1. **Source:** `somewhere pull <project-id-or-subdomain>` or
   `project_export({ project_id })` returns the live release's files.
2. **SQL dump:** `somewhere db dump --output backup.sql` or `db_dump({ project_id })`
   writes the raw SQL database's schema and rows as one `.sql` file, up to
   1,000,000 rows per table.
3. **CSV export:** `db_export` returns one raw SQL table as CSV, up to
   100,000 rows per response; filter to collect more.
4. **Your own PostgreSQL:** attach a database in your own Neon account and
   query it as `sw.postgres` (`postgres` topic); attaching moves no existing data.

For a managed table, use `db_browse` with `plane: "managed"` or run
`somewhere db rows <table>`.
Uploaded files come out through `fs_read`, and app users through
`GET /v1/auth/users/inventory`. Password credentials cannot be exported; users
set a password in the new app.

To host elsewhere, keep your React and TypeScript source and replace each
platform service and generated browser client your code calls — auth, data, files, email, AI and the rest
— with the service you choose. Exporting the database moves your rows; it
does not replace `sw.*`.

## Full database dump

In an MCP client, call `db_dump({ project_id: "my-app" })`. For a local
backup, start in a new directory so existing backups remain untouched.

```bash
# In a new backup directory, via the CLI
somewhere db dump --output backup.sql

# Via curl — -D keeps the response headers, which carry the capture receipt
curl --fail --show-error -X POST https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/db/dump \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SOMEWHERE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"project_id":"my-app"}' \
  -D dump-headers.txt -o backup.sql
```

The file holds the schema (CREATE TABLE / INDEX / TRIGGER), every row as
INSERT statements, sequence state, and a transaction wrapper. Schema, rows and
sequence state come from the same captured read.

**Check the file.** When the API returns a capture receipt, `db_dump` checks it for you: it recomputes the SQL hash
over the bytes it received and the policy hash over the labels it parsed, and
on any mismatch returns `DUMP_INTEGRITY_UNCONFIRMED` (502) and no SQL. With
curl, compare `sql_sha256` in the `X-Dump-Capture` header with
`shasum -a 256 backup.sql`. On Linux use `sha256sum backup.sql`. The CLI writes the SQL without the
receipt; use MCP or curl when you need to compare the downloaded bytes with
the capture. Treat a failed or interrupted download as incomplete.

**Restore.** The file restores directly into the source database engine:

```bash
sqlite3 backup.db < backup.sql
```

For another database engine, convert the schema and data for that destination.
Review the dialect differences in `sql-compatibility`, then verify queries
and access rules as described in https://somewhere.cloud/migration.txt.

**Re-declare access.** Table-access declarations and sensitive-column marks
are platform policy, not SQL. Their labels travel as comment lines in the SQL
preamble, and `db_dump` returns them as `excluded_security_policy.policies`
(a warning appears only when the list is non-empty). A SQL restore never
applies them. Re-declare them in the destination system. For a managed Somewhere project,
declare them in `db/schema.ts` and deploy, then inspect them with `db_scope_list`. An empty list means this capture found no table-access
declarations. Member join definitions and handler authorization need separate
configuration and checks.

**Limits.** Each table can hold up to 1,000,000 rows in a dump.
A table over the limit stops the whole dump; there is no option to skip it.
Export tables individually as CSV, filter large tables into smaller ranges,
and recreate their schema from `db/schema.ts` or `db_describe`. Full-text (FTS5) tables with internally stored content — including
the platform's file search index — are captured with their declared options,
configuration and contents and restore into a fresh database with MATCH
intact. `sw.db.dump()` is not available inside a deployed function;
exporting the whole database requires developer credentials. 

### If the dump is refused

A refused capture returns an error instead of SQL. Check the command exit
status before using a downloaded file.

- **Retry** — the database moved or could not be read during the capture:
  `DUMP_SCHEMA_CHANGED` (409), `DUMP_SOURCE_CHANGED` (409, the owner or
  database changed), `DUMP_CAPTURE_UNCONFIRMED` (503),
  `DUMP_SCHEMA_UNAVAILABLE` (503, table metadata could not be verified),
  `DUMP_POLICY_UNAVAILABLE` (503, table-access declarations could not be read).
- **Too large for one dump** — the whole dump is refused; export tables
  individually as CSV and recreate their schema:
  `DUMP_ROW_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (413, a table above 1,000,000 rows),
  `DUMP_CAPTURE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (413, the capture exceeds the supported query size or column count).
- **Fix first** — `DATABASE_NOT_INITIALIZED` (409: the project has no
  database yet; the dump never creates one), `DUMP_POLICY_INVALID` (422:
  table-access declarations are invalid), `DUMP_UNSUPPORTED_SCHEMA` (422:
  external-content or contentless full-text tables, other virtual-table
  modules, or sequence state the dump cannot preserve).

### The capture receipt

The receipt lets you prove later which bytes this capture produced. The REST
response carries it in the `X-Dump-Capture` header and `db_dump` returns it
as `excluded_security_policy.capture` (v1). It holds identity, hashes and
times only — never the labels: the canonical `project_id` and
`database_id`, `sql_sha256` / `schema_sha256` / `policy_sha256`, and
`policy_observed_at`, `data_observation_started_at`,
`data_observation_completed_at`, `binding_checked_at`.

`sql_sha256` covers the SQL bytes, `schema_sha256` the schema statements,
and `policy_sha256` the policy labels. The times are separate observations:
the database and the policy were each captured at their recorded time, and
matching binding checks before and after mean the same project, owner and
database were observed twice; they do not exclude a change between the
observations. An absent receipt (an older API during a rolling release) means
no capture-integrity evidence; the policy labels may still be present. A dump
restores data and schema. Reapply and test the destination's access rules
before serving users.

## Attaching PostgreSQL instead of leaving

You do not have to move OUT to run PostgreSQL. A project can attach one
external PostgreSQL database — a Neon database in your own Neon account, paid
for by you — and query it from your functions as `sw.postgres`.
`docs({ topic: 'postgres' })` is the contract.

You own the account, billing and authorization decisions. Declared row
permissions apply to the managed database; queries through the external
driver use the permissions you implement. Attaching a database does not
move existing data into it.

## One table as CSV

Call `db_export({ project_id: "my-app", table: "orders" })` with the full MCP
tool set, or use `POST /v1/db/export` with developer credentials. The hosted
connectors do not include this tool.

Each response contains up to 100,000 rows. A response at
the cap is marked `truncated`; narrow `filters` (the `db_browse` shape)
until it is clear. Use disjoint ranges to collect a large table. Rows have no
guaranteed order, so an unfiltered capped response is not the first page of a
complete export.

## File storage

Call `fs_read({ project_id: "my-app", path: "/" })` to list a directory.
Pass a file path to read that file.

## Source code

```bash
somewhere pull <project-id-or-subdomain> --out my-app   # Use a new folder
```

`pull` downloads the live release's source and adds a `tsconfig.json` and
`package.json` (only where absent) for local typechecking. Edit and run
`somewhere deploy` to publish again.

The source is TypeScript with no required framework. To run it elsewhere,
replace `sw.*` services, generated `somewhere:data`, `somewhere:files` and
`somewhere:api` clients, and the access rules in `db/schema.ts` with your
own services and checks. Add a build for the destination, such as Vite. https://somewhere.cloud/migration.txt lists what to provide for each service
on the destination.

## App-user inventory and profiles

Use `GET /v1/auth/users/inventory?project_id=<project>` with a developer
key and follow `next_cursor` through every page. Compare the collected IDs
with `total`; each page also carries its own checksum. The project's
`auth_users` table is a copy for joins and can be incomplete.

For profiles, pass those IDs to `GET /v1/auth/users` in batches of up to
200, using its `ids` query parameter. It returns
roles, display names and metadata as well as account identity.

## End-user accounts

For a signed-in user's own data export, use `GET /v1/auth/users/me/export`.
The old `POST /v1/auth/export/request` and `POST /v1/auth/export/download`
routes both return 501 `AUTH_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE`.

Passwords do not move with the app. Users set a password in the new app.

## What does not move

- The somewhere.site subdomain (`<your-app>.somewhere.site`). Custom domains
  do (you own the DNS).
- The dashboard and security-review surfaces — they are platform
  features; your data and code move.

Related: `sw.db`, `security-model`, `sql-compatibility`, `postgres`.

pages.title: Start an app
pages.body:
## Start an app The generated AGENTS.md holds the call shapes and access patterns for a typical app. Teams are built-in groups: `somewhere docs sw.groups --section team-example`. To run an existing public repo in your own account, use `somewhere docs adopt`. Somewhere's product and documentation live at somewhere.cloud. Deployed apps use their own *.somewhere.site address or an attached custom domain. Build a React app with sign-in, server functions and its own SQL database in one project. Somewhere compiles and hosts the source, manages sessions, and enforces the access rules you declare. [How Somewhere works](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/api-reference.txt#how-somewhere-works) explains the whole platform; this page gets your first screen online. Start with the screen people will use, then connect each feature to real data. Build the core action first: for a reading list, save a book and find it again. Keep extra feeds, admin views and settings screens as follow-ups unless the user asked for them. You deploy TypeScript and React source. Somewhere compiles it and serves the app and its functions together. Your data and code are yours: `somewhere pull` returns the source, `somewhere db dump` writes the raw SQL database as one `.sql` file, `db_export` returns one table as CSV, and a project can attach PostgreSQL in your own Neon account. Managed-database tables are not in the dump or CSV export yet; the `portability` topic lists what each path covers and its limits. ### Choose your starting point **Working on an app already live on Somewhere?** Start with `somewhere pull ` in a fresh folder. In a connected chat, read the live source with `project_export` before editing. **Publishing a first app with plain HTTP?** [Deploy with two HTTP calls](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/start.txt) gives you a live app, claim link and expiry without an account. **Building in Claude or ChatGPT without a terminal?** Connect Somewhere through [MCP](https://somewhere.cloud/mcp). Ask your agent to create a project with `project_create`: it starts live with the same starter as `somewhere init`, and your agent changes it with `project_patch`. The [MCP guide](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/setup.txt) shows the tool flow. Use the same design-first approach below; your agent handles the files and checks through the connected tools. **Working in an editor or terminal?** Use the starter below. It includes the auth route, React hooks, design tokens and UI components. ### Create your project In an empty folder, the starter needs no account. Ask before destructive or paid actions unless the user already authorized them. Importing CSV? Use `somewhere docs recipe-csv-import --full` for an upload, a background job and retry-safe batch writes. ```bash mkdir reading-list cd reading-list npx -y @somewhere-cloud/cli@latest init --name reading-list ``` Init writes the starter and installs its pinned dependencies. If you are signed in, it also creates a project and links this folder. If you are signed out, deploy publishes a temporary app and prints its live URL, claim link and expiry. ```bash npx -y @somewhere-cloud/cli@latest deploy ``` The `setup` guide covers remote environments. Keep `.somewhere.json` in Git. It records which project this folder deploys to and holds no credentials. To publish your own copy of someone else's app: Run `npx -y @somewhere-cloud/cli@latest deploy --new` from the clone. It creates a project in your account, or a temporary project when signed out, and updates the clone's link. Use a folder name suitable for the new app's address. The CLI uses that name to generate the address. The starter's `package.json` pins the CLI version that wrote it in the `@somewhere-cloud/cli` devDependency. A newer CLI reports a pin mismatch in one line and keeps control of deploy. Other commands can use the installed pin. `somewhere upgrade` moves the project to the running version and lists what changed. The starter gives you one working sign-in path. Keep it while you build: | Start here | What to change | |---|---| | `src/pages/HomePage.tsx` | The first signed-in screen. | | `src/styles/tokens.css` | Colors, typography, spacing and shape. | | `src/styles/app.css` | Shared classes such as `.panel`, `.field`, `.button` and `.muted`. | | `src/ui/` | Views: `AppShell` (the app's frame; it shows at once, before the session is known), `AuthCard`, and `Alert` and `EmptyState` in `feedback.tsx`. | | `src/services/` | Calls between your UI and its backend. | | `api/` | Server functions. The starter's auth route already lives here. | ### Design the screen Choose a visual direction before adding features, with one distinctive idea rather than "clean and modern". For a reading list, try a library card: cream paper, an oxblood accent and a serif display face. Set it in the starter's tokens so the screen and every component share it: ```css /* src/styles/tokens.css — change these values inside :root */ --color-bg: #f6f0e4; --color-accent: #7a1f2b; --color-focus: #7a1f2b; --font-display: "Iowan Old Style", "Palatino Linotype", Palatino, Georgia, serif; ``` The file also defines `--color-surface`, `--color-text`, `--color-muted`, `--color-border`, `--font-body`, the `--text-*` sizes, the `--space-*` scale and two radii. `app.css` reads them all. The `design-system` guide covers palettes, type and layout. Replace the starter's home page with a small first screen: ```tsx // src/pages/HomePage.tsx import type { User } from '../../types/auth'; import { SignedInLayout } from './SignedInLayout'; const sampleBooks = [ { id: 'earthsea', title: 'A Wizard of Earthsea', author: 'Ursula K. Le Guin' }, { id: 'piranesi', title: 'Piranesi', author: 'Susanna Clarke' }, ]; export function HomePage({ user }: { user: User }) { return (

Your next good book

A small shelf of things you want to read.

    {sampleBooks.map((book) => (
  • {book.title} — {book.author}
    • ))}
); } ``` `SignedInLayout` puts the screen inside `AppShell`, which has the app name and the sign-out button. The two books are sample content, visible to every signed-in account. ### Put it online ```bash npx somewhere typecheck npx somewhere deploy ``` Deploy publishes the source in this folder and prints the live URL. Open it, create an account or sign in, and check the reading-list screen on a phone and on a desktop. Don't bundle the source yourself; the platform runs the frontend build. Share the live URL now so the user can react to the screen. For a static site, the page may already do the whole job; verify it and stop there. For this reading-list app, the next step is to make the shelf personal. ### Connect one feature at a time Use **Data** next: declare a books table in `db/schema.ts` with `owner()` and a `client` block, and replace the sample array with calls to the generated `somewhere:data` client. Those calls return the signed-in user's rows, with no API file. A public enquiry form uses declared `client.intake` to write for a published profile's owner (`declared-data` → `send-an-enquiry-to-a-public-profile`). Read **Functions** for an authorized write the declaration cannot express, or for a side effect such as email. Keep `owner()`/`group()` and the client for everything else. The default `somewhere init` starter has no `db/schema.ts`: create it at the project root, or run `somewhere init --name my-app --features private-data` to start with a schema. `recipe-signed-in-app` shows a validated server write, email and a reminder. | Schema reference | Contract | |---|---| | Columns | `id`, `text`, `number`, `integer`, `boolean`, `timestamp`, `json`, `blob`; options: `nullable`, `default`, `unique`, `references`, `onDelete`. | | Tables | `scope`, `indexes`, `unique: [['org_id','email']]`, `client`. | | Scopes | `owner`, `group`, `appRole`, `shared`, `member`, `anyOf`, `parent`, `serverOnly`. | | Operations | Browser: `list`, `get`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, `aggregate`. Functions: `from(table, { where })`, `insert(table, values)`, `update(table, { where, set })`, `remove(table, { where })`, `count`, `aggregate`; plain objects, not fluent chains. | Keep the screen, auth and shared components you already have. Add one working data path, check it with two separate accounts, and then move on to the next feature. If the feature needs an external service key, see **Env vars and secrets**. Read server secrets inside the handler. After the first production deploy, changes reach new requests within 60 seconds without another deploy. Older apps need one source deploy to enable this behavior; the CLI tells you when that is needed. ### Work locally and verify the result After the first deploy, install Vite with `npm install -D vite` if the frontend doesn't already have it. `somewhere dev` serves the frontend at `http://localhost:8787` with hot reload. Its API requests go to your deployed project, so data you save during local development is written to that project's database. Server-function changes take effect when you deploy. Deploy the schema before using it locally. `somewhere dev` calls the deployed project; it does not apply schema changes. As you connect the screen: - Reuse the starter's components and styles. Extract a helper or component when it removes real duplication; keep server handlers separate from browser code. - Show loading, empty and error states. After a mutation, update the affected view; clear user-specific cached data on sign-out or account change. - For shared data that changes live, use a live view instead of adding a polling loop; see `live-data`. - Put service keys in project secrets, not source files or app tables. Set them through the dashboard or CLI as shown in **Env vars and secrets**, not through chat. Use `somewhere verify` for the browser checks, and inspect failures with `somewhere logs` and `somewhere errors`. Check the real user action too: sign in, save a book, reload, and confirm that another account sees only its own shelf. Once the requested flow works, share what you checked and let the user try it before adding more features. ## Instructions for connecting an agent `GET /v1/agent/instructions` (no key needed) returns the one copy of the text a person pastes into their agent, per place it runs (`hosted`, `local`, `connector`): `{ instructions: [{ id, label, blurb, paste, next }], start_url, connector: { url, claude_url, chatgpt_url, claude_directory_url } }`. Show it as it is rather than writing your own version. ## Available docs topics The complete topic index lists every topic: https://somewhere.cloud/docs/llms.txt.

Declared data — the schema file is the contract
pages.body:
## Data

Application tables are declared in db/schema.ts. sw.db.from reads them with caller-scoped access, and sw.db.server.from reads them once the caller is authorized for server access. The corresponding structured methods, such as sw.db.server.insert, change them. Raw query and batch go to the separate raw SQL database on current projects.

Each project has its own managed database. You describe its tables, and who may
reach each row, in `db/schema.ts`. That file ships with your source, and deploy
creates or updates the tables to match it. The platform generates a typed
browser client and applies the same access rules in your functions. Raw SQL
uses a separate raw database; it never reaches managed tables. To keep an
existing dataset in Postgres, attach it instead (see `postgres`).

A row is private to its owner with `owner()`, as below. To let an owner share
their existing rows with specific people, use `anyOf(owner(), grant(...))`.
Every existing caller-scoped read then includes shared rows. For an
owner-only read, filter by `where: { user_id: me.id }` in a function, using
the signed-in user's ID. See `per-owner-sharing` for the deploy warning.

For one club whose organiser manages the whole app, declare the organiser's
read/create/update/delete permissions with `appRole()`. For 'my rows or the
organiser', combine `owner()` and `appRole()` with `anyOf`. `shared()`
alone keeps writes with each row's creator. See `sw.groups` → `app-wide-roles`
and `sw.db` → `owner-or-member-and-parent-access`.

### Declare a table and use it

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { id, owner, schema, table, text, timestamp } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  notes: table(
    {
      id: id(),
      title: text(),
      body: text({ default: '' }),
      created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }),
    },
    {
      scope: owner(),
      client: {
        read: ['id', 'title', 'body', 'created_at'],
        create: ['title', 'body'],
        update: ['title', 'body'],
        delete: true,
      },
    },
  ),
});
```

`owner()` makes each row belong to the signed-in user who created it. The
platform adds and fills in the owner column itself. The `client` block is the
browser's entire grant: these columns can be read, `title` and `body` can be
set, and rows can be deleted. A table without a `client` block can't be reached
from the browser at all.

`id()` gives a new table a random text key, so `id` is a string. A table
that already has integer ids keeps them under a bare `id()`: the deploy
changes neither the table nor its ids. `id({ uuid: false })` declares an
integer key; the opt-in private-data starter uses it because its safe create retry
needs one. `id({ uuid: true })` over existing integer ids is refused.

Use the generated client from your app:

```ts
// src/services/notes.ts
import { data, DataError } from 'somewhere:data';

export interface Note {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  body: string;
  created_at: string;
}

// owner() scopes every call to the signed-in user. Send no user ID or filter.
export async function listNotes(): Promise<Note[]> {
  const page = await data.notes.list({ limit: 50 });
  return page.data;
}

export async function addNote(title: string, body = ''): Promise<Note | null> {
  const created = await data.notes.create({ title: title.trim(), body });
  return created.data;
}

export async function updateNote(id: Note['id'], title: string, body: string): Promise<void> {
  await data.notes.update(id, { title: title.trim(), body });
}

export async function deleteNote(id: Note['id']): Promise<void> {
  await data.notes.delete(id);
}

export function notesErrorMessage(reason: unknown): string {
  if (reason instanceof DataError) {
    if (reason.code === 'AUTH_REQUIRED') return 'Your session ended. Sign in again.';
    if (reason.code === 'DATA_CONTRACT_MISMATCH') return 'This app was just updated. Reload the page.';
    if (reason.code === 'DATA_NOT_FOUND') return 'That note was not found.';
  }
  return 'Something went wrong. Try again.';
}
```

Run `somewhere typecheck`, then `somewhere deploy`. The deploy creates the
`notes` table, and `somewhere typecheck` types `somewhere:data` from your
schema locally. Sign in with two accounts: each one lists, adds, edits and
deletes only its own notes.

What the declaration gives you:

- **Ownership comes from the session.** Creates set the owner from the
  verified user, and the browser can't name another owner. List, get, update
  and delete only reach the caller's rows. Updating or deleting someone else's
  note gets the same `DATA_NOT_FOUND` as a missing note, and `get` returns
  `null`.
- **Only granted operations exist.** An operation or column you didn't grant
  isn't on the client. Direct HTTP to the data endpoint has the same limits.
  Browser calls send your app's origin automatically. A script calling the
  endpoint must set the `Origin` header itself.
- **Schema changes ship with the source.** Adding tables and columns applies on
  deploy. Production deploys refuse to remove or rename a column that's already
  deployed. After any table change, pages loaded before the deploy get
  `DATA_CONTRACT_MISMATCH` until they reload, which the example handles.

## Teams

A team people join is a built-in group. Give the team's rows a non-null text
column holding the group id and scope them with `group()`; the platform keeps
the team, its invitations, roster and owners. The complete app, with its
endpoints and spec, is `somewhere docs sw.groups --section team-example`.

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { schema, table, id, text, owner, group, anyOf } from 'somewhere/db';
export default schema({
  tasks: table({ id: id(), team_id: text(), title: text() }, {
    scope: anyOf(owner(), group({ column: 'team_id', roles: {
      read: ['owner', 'admin', 'member'], create: ['owner', 'admin', 'member'],
      update: ['owner', 'admin', 'member'], delete: ['owner'],
    } })),
    client: { read: ['id', 'team_id', 'title'], create: ['team_id', 'title'], update: ['title'], delete: true },
  }),
});
```

```ts
// src/services/tasks.ts
import { data } from 'somewhere:data';
export async function addTask(teamId: string, title: string) {
  return data.tasks.create({ team_id: teamId, title });
}
export async function listTasks(teamId: string) {
  return data.tasks.list({ where: { team_id: teamId }, limit: 100 });
}
```

Members read, create and update tasks; the creator or a team owner deletes one,
and someone removed from the team loses even the tasks they created. Inside
`anyOf()` an operation left out of `roles` allows no group role, so all four
are listed. Starting a team needs a signed-in user; joining one needs a
verified email. For a relationship your app records itself (a booking's
provider, a class's students), use `member()` over your own table:
`sw.groups` → `relationships-that-are-not-teams`.

## The same table in a function

Inside a function, the structured calls `sw.db.from`, `insert`, `update` and
`remove` act as the calling user and follow the same `owner()` rule. Use a
function for anything the browser grant can't express. This one searches
titles:

```ts
// api/notes/search.ts — the signed-in user's notes whose title contains ?q=
export default async function searchNotes(
  request: Request,
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
): Promise<Response> {
  if (request.method !== 'GET') {
    return new Response('Use GET.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'GET' } });
  }

  const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(request);
  if (!user) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Sign in to search your notes.' }, { status: 401 });
  }
```
