`docs({ topic: 'architecture-patterns', section: 'minimal-server-only-app' })`.

```ts
const { data: [note] } = await sw.db.insert('notes', { title: 'Hello' });
if (typeof note?.id !== 'string') throw new Error('Expected the new note to have a text ID.');
const { data: rows } = await sw.db.from('notes', { limit: 20 });
const { data: count } = await sw.db.count('notes');
await sw.db.update('notes', { where: { id: note.id }, set: { title: 'Updated' } });
```

These calls apply the caller's declared row permissions. For a serverOnly()
table or authorized cross-user work, use `sw.db.server.insert/from/count/update`
with the same argument shapes. Server calls bypass row permissions; authorize
private operations yourself. Raw `sw.db.query` never reaches declared tables
and runs unscoped: authorize first.

## Server read paging

sw.db.from and sw.db.server.from accept { where, columns, order, limit, offset,
include, has }. limit and offset are non-negative integers; null/omitted means
unset. Server reads have no browser-style after cursor and no 100-row cap.
Use a deterministic order (including a unique key), advance offset by the rows
received, and stop when data.length is less than the page size. Concurrent writes
can shift offsets; for a stable traversal of an increasing key, filter on that
key instead. The result count describes the returned rows, not the total;
use count(table, { where }) for a separate total. Authorize before server reads.

```ts
async function readServerPage(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, offset: number) {
  return sw.db.server.from('notes', {
    columns: ['id', 'title'], order: [['id', 'asc']], limit: 100, offset,
  });
}
```

## Start with the schema file — db/schema.ts

Declare your tables in one file, `db/schema.ts`, deployed with the rest of
your source. On every live deploy the platform reads the file (it is a
declaration the platform reads — never code that runs), compares it with the
real database, creates whatever is missing, and records each table's access
scope in the same step. No migration calls, no separate scope declarations,
no schema SQL.

**On a new project, deploy the file before you test the database.** A
managed schema changes only with a release: `somewhere deploy` applies
`db/schema.ts` to production, and a preview release applies it to the
preview's isolated copy, with the same planner and safety rules. Additive
changes apply. A deployed table is removed with its `removedTable()` marker
(below); deleting its declaration without the marker, or removing or renaming
a column, is refused on production (explore it on a preview). A later deploy with the same file is a
no-op. There
is no separate schema-apply command. Until a deploy runs,
`sw.db.from('your_table')` fails with `TABLE_INTENT_REQUIRED` because a file
on disk cannot declare the table to the platform by itself.

The file is parsed as a declaration, not executed: use literal values and
supported declaration helpers. Imports from `somewhere/db` are recommended
for editor tooling, but the schema reader does not resolve imports. A missing
`owner` import alone does not invalidate an otherwise valid declaration.
Trailing commas are accepted, inside option objects and after the final
argument of a call. Top-level `const NAME = …;` declarations between the
imports and `export default schema(…)` are accepted and expanded in place,
never evaluated: a constant may hold any part of the declaration (an access
rule, a column, a column group, table options, a whole table), later code
refers to it by name, and an object-literal constant may be spread inside an
object literal (`...sharedColumns`). Anything else — `let`/`var`,
computed values, calls to anything but the schema helpers, a spread of a
non-object constant, a reference to a constant declared below — is refused
with the construct and its line named.

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { schema, table, id, text, integer, boolean, timestamp, json, owner, member, shared, serverOnly } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  todos: table({
    id: id(),                                  // random text key (id({ uuid: false }) for an integer key)
    title: text(),                             // required by default
    done: boolean({ default: false }),
    created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }), // stamped on insert
    meta: json({ nullable: true }),
  }, {
    scope: owner(),                            // per-user rows; owner column is platform-managed
    indexes: [['done']],
  }),
  org_invites: table({
    id: id(), org_id: integer(), email: text(),
  }, {
    scope: serverOnly(),
    unique: [['org_id', 'email']],             // composite uniqueness (junction-table idiom)
  }),
  catalog: table({ id: id(), name: text() }, { scope: shared() }),
});
```

Table and column names start with a letter and use letters, digits and
underscores. Reserved prefixes ignore case:
`app_`, `sqlite_`, `d1_`, and any leading `_` (including `__sw_`)
are reserved. Use `customer_user_id` for an app user reference.

Column types: `id`, `text`, `number`, `integer`, `boolean`, `timestamp`,
`json`, `blob`. Columns are required unless `nullable: true`. Defaults
are literals or `timestamp({ default: 'now' })`. Columns also accept
`unique` and `references: 'other_table'` with `onDelete: 'cascade' | 'restrict'`.
The database applies foreign-key actions to `sw.db.server.remove` and
`remove` intents in `sw.db.server.tx` too.

Table options include required `scope`, `indexes` and `unique`. Indexes
and unique groups are lists of column lists. A one-column unique group on
a non-key column is equivalent to `unique: true`. The platform manages the
owner column and refuses standalone uniqueness on it. For one row per user,
use `kind: text({ default: 'profile' })` with `unique: [['user_id', 'kind']]`.
Keep `kind` out of browser writes and omit it in functions to use the default.
Use `unique: [['user_id', 'key']]` for one row per user and key. Schema values
must be literals or references to earlier top-level constants. A deploy error
names the unsupported construct and its line.

Choose a scope for each table:

- `owner()` — per-user rows. The platform creates and manages the owner
  column (`user_id` by default; `owner({ column: 'other_name' })` names
  it differently at creation), sets it on insert, and scopes every structured
  query to the request's VERIFIED SIGNED-IN USER. A request without a signed-in
  user is refused before transport: `AUTH_REQUIRED` (401). Send the request
  signed in — a session cookie or `Authorization: Bearer <app-user token>`.
  For signed-out ownership, explicitly declare `owner({ visitors: true })`;
  the platform can then use a verified visitor cookie. This is per browser,
  not protection against someone discarding their cookie. For an intentional
  cross-user operation, authorize the caller in your function before using
  `sw.db.server`; it is not a remedy for a missing user session. In a
  function, caller-scoped `sw.db.insert` stamps the owner column from the
  request's signed-in user and refuses it in `values`
  (`OWNER_COLUMN_NOT_ASSIGNABLE`); it may set any other declared column,
  since `client.create` limits only the browser's generated client.
  `sw.db.server.insert` never stamps an owner: the row holds exactly the
  columns you pass, so name the owner in the owner column yourself (the
  column is required on a table born with `owner()`).
- `shared()` — cross-user rows with a recorded author. Structured calls need
  a verified app user: reads return every row to any signed-in user, writes
  stamp the platform's managed author column (`_sw_author_id`, added on
  deploy) with the caller. Browser reads through `somewhere:data` or
  `/__sw/data` never return it, even with `read: true`; `sw.db` reads
  and writes in your functions do, so leave it out of a function's response
  when readers should not see who wrote each row. A request with no signed-in
  user is refused `401 AUTH_REQUIRED` ("Shared tables require a signed-in user."). For
  anonymous browser reads declare `client: { read: ['id', 'title'], publicRead: true }`.
  Anonymous results can be cached for up to 120
  seconds. For fresh pages, read published rows and only public fields with
  `sw.db.server.from` in a page handler returning `Cache-Control: no-store`.
  For a trusted server read pass `{ asServer: true }`. Use
  `sw.db.server.insert` for app-owned rows: omit `_sw_author_id` or set it
  to `null`. Supply a verified user's ID to attribute a server-created row
  to that user. Rows without an author remain readable under the table's read
  rules; ordinary caller writes cannot change or delete them.
- `serverOnly()` — trusted server and developer access only; direct
  app-user access is rejected.
- `member()` — per-group rows, shared through a membership table. Declare
  `member({ group, membership, member_user, member_group })`: `group` is the
  group-key column(s) on this table, `membership` names a sibling managed
  table that lists who belongs to which group, `member_user` is that table's
  user column, and `member_group` is its matching group-key column(s). A group
  key can be a single column or a same-arity list (a composite or polymorphic
  key). The platform scopes every structured query to the groups the signed-in
  user belongs to; an `insert` lands only if the user belongs to the group the
  row names, otherwise `403 MEMBERSHIP_REQUIRED` (`403 POLICY_AUTHORITY_REQUIRED`
  when `member()` is inside `anyOf()` or `allOf()`). A request without a signed-in
  user is refused with `401 AUTH_REQUIRED`. Declare both the scoped table
  and its membership table.

What happens on deploy:

- **First deploy** creates tables and enables access rules together.
  The deploy response's `warnings` list what was created.
- **Additive changes apply**: a new table, a new nullable-or-defaulted
  column, a new index, a new unique group. Unchanged schema is a no-op.
- **Unmarked removals and shape changes refuse** with `409
  SCHEMA_DEPLOY_REFUSED` and a message naming the change.
- **Access-rule changes apply in place**: a later deploy can change an
  existing table's scope, and its rows stay. "Two worlds" below lists what
  the deploy reports and what it still refuses.
- **Removing a table** is `old_table: removedTable()`. The deploy keeps the
  table while your previous version is still serving; once the new version is
  live it retires the table and keeps its data for 30 days. The deploy
  response's `warnings` name the table and the date its data is deleted, and
  `somewhere deploy --dry-run` and `somewhere deploy-check` show the same
  line first. To restore it within the 30 days, declare the table again with
  the same scope and deploy — it comes back with its data. Leave the marker in
  the file; it is a no-op once the table is gone.
  Delete a never-deployed starter table's declaration and references.
  A `removedTable()` marker for it is a no-op.
- **Column removals and renames do not apply to a live database**:
  `removed()` and `renamedFrom` are accepted by the schema file and can be
  explored on a preview copy, but a production deploy or a promotion that
  would remove or rename a column is refused before anything changes, so a
  running release never loses a column it uses. Keep the column declared and
  leave its data in place. Your data download and export are unaffected.
- **Leaving schema management** is `old_table: exported()`: the declaration
  is removed and the table + data stay untouched (structured queries on it then
  need a declared scope again).
- Declaring a table that **already exists** brings it under schema management
  (**adoption**) when the declared entry matches the live table and the table
  is eligible — a base table, no triggers, and (for `owner()`) the owner
  column present. A clean match applies zero DDL, arms scoping, and locks the
  table to the file; an ineligible or mismatched declaration is refused with the
  reason. Use `db_import` to generate the matching entry from a table you
  already have, review it, and deploy. Tables not named in the file are
  untouched.
- A `db/schema.ts` that isn't a somewhere schema declaration (another
  tool's file) deploys as plain source with a warning, as long as the
  project has no managed tables.
- A preview release applies managed `db/schema.ts` to the preview's own
  isolated copy; a production deploy applies it to production. Both use the
  same planner. For raw SQL, see the preview database limits below.

Run `somewhere typecheck` before deploying schema changes.

## Browser list limits

The schema-generated browser client accepts `list({ limit: 100, after: page.next })`:
limit is 1–100; continue while `page.has_more`. There is no `order` option.
Sort the returned rows in the client, or use a server endpoint for ordered queries.
Include the primary key in `client.read`.

## Update shape

`await sw.db.update('notes', { where: { id }, set: { title } })` takes two
arguments. `sw.db.server.update` uses the same shape after server authorization.

## Transaction intents

`await sw.db.server.tx([{ op: 'insert', table: 'notes', values }])` takes an
array of write intents, never a callback. Pre-generate related IDs. Authorize
cross-user writes first. See `swdbservertxintents-authorized-cross-user-writes`
for limits and outcome semantics.

## Browser contracts and constraint errors

A schema with no table `client` block has no browser data contract. Inspect
`data.client.status` in the app description: `not_declared` means there
is no client digest to send, and the app data client's endpoint refuses every
request with 403 `DATA_ACCESS_DENIED`. Add explicit client grants only for the
operations you want a browser to call; ordinary `sw.db` calls in a function do
not need a browser contract digest.

A write that violates a unique column, unique group or primary key
(including a value held by another owner) is a
duplicate, and nothing is written. A declared browser write returns HTTP 409
with `error: 'DATA_CONFLICT'` and the message “A record with these values
already exists.” A function's `sw.db` insert, update or transaction throws
the same: `err.code === 'DATA_CONFLICT'`, `err.status === 409`, with that
message. Catch it and answer as a duplicate (for example "slot taken") rather
than retrying the same write. Other constraint failures, such as a missing
required value or a failed check, keep their own codes.

For typed queries, keep literal keys and column names: `const columns =
['id', 'title'] as const` preserves the selected-column type. A broad
`Record<string, unknown>` discards a table's known columns and value types;
use the generated row/write/where shape or an inferred object literal instead
of casting the whole request to that record type.

## Provider-or-booker and owner-or-staff recipes

Match each table to one of three shapes, then take the recipe for it:

1. **Personal rows.** One person owns the row: `owner()`. Sharing a row with
   named people keeps it `owner()` and adds a grant:
   `anyOf(owner(), grant(...))`
   (`docs({ topic: 'declared-data', section: 'per-owner-sharing' })`).
2. **Team rows.** Everyone in a group reads the row: `member()` over your own
   membership table, `group()` for the built-in groups, `appRole()` for a role
   held across the app, `anyOf(owner(), ...)` when the author keeps extra
   rights (`owner-or-member-and-parent-access` below).
3. **Two parties on one row.** A booking has a booker and a provider; a
   ticket has a customer and staff. One row has one owner, and a rule cannot
   show one reader a column it hides from another. So when two people need
   different rights or different columns on the same row, it is two rows:
   the row each party owns, plus a grant, access row or role for the other
   party. The two recipes below are this shape.

`serverOnly()` is for a table no caller should ever read under their own
name: a membership or access ledger your functions fill, trusted
configuration. It is not the answer to "this needs a function": a function
on a declared table reads with the caller's rule, so the function keeps its
validation and loses its access checks (shown under "Owner or staff" below).
When your brief fixes the JSON routes, that is still what declared rules buy:
the function shrinks to validation, revocation and tests come from the
platform, and the deploy report says who can read what.

**Provider or booker, for one booking.** The booker is the managed owner;
a separate access table grants that booking's provider read access. The group
key is the booking row's `id`, not a provider-wide key that would expose
other bookings. This recipe is for several independent providers, each of
whom may see only their own bookings; there, do not replace it with an
app-wide provider role. One business whose staff all see every booking uses
`appRole()` instead (`declared-data`; `sw.groups` → `app-wide-roles`),
with `anyOf(owner(), appRole(...))` for "my bookings or staff".

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { anyOf, id, member, owner, schema, serverOnly, table, text } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  bookings: table({ id: id({ uuid: true }), slot: text() }, {
    scope: anyOf(owner({ column: 'booker_id' }), member({
      group: 'id', membership: 'booking_access',
      member_user: 'user_id', member_group: 'booking_id', operations: ['read'],
    })),
    client: { read: ['id', 'slot'] },
  }),
  booking_access: table({ id: id(), booking_id: text(), user_id: text() }, {
    scope: serverOnly(), unique: [['booking_id', 'user_id']],
  }),
});
```

The booking function verifies the signed-in booker and availability, resolves
the provider from the selected slot (never a caller-supplied owner), then
atomically creates the booking with `booker_id` and two access rows, one for
the booker and one for the provider, using `sw.db.server.tx` (see
`swdbservertxintents-authorized-cross-user-writes` below). The booker needs
their own row: `bookings` is a team table, so its owner keeps a booking only
while also in that booking's group, and the deploy reports this. The browser
cannot create access rows or grant itself membership. Keep booker email out of the shared booking fields: return it only
from a function that verifies the caller is that booking's provider. This scope
does not itself implement availability or prevent double booking; enforce the
slot's unique/transactional rule when creating the booking.

**Provider publishes slots, customers book one.** The same shape when the
app starts from the provider's calendar: a public page lists a provider's free
slots, a signed-in customer books one, and only that customer and the provider
see the booking. Do not book by writing the customer onto the provider's slot
row; that puts two parties with different rights on one row. The slot stays
the provider's and the booking is the customer's:

```ts
// Slots belong to the provider; each booking belongs to its customer.
import { anyOf, boolean, id, integer, member, owner, schema, serverOnly, table, text } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  // The provider's rows. Visitors read the free ones, with no booker data.
  slots: table({ id: id(), start_ms: integer(), booked: boolean({ default: false }) }, {
    scope: owner(),
    client: { read: ['id', 'start_ms', 'booked'], delete: true, publicRead: { where: { booked: false } } },
  }),
  // The customer's row; the provider reads it through the access row.
  bookings: table({ id: id({ uuid: true }), slot_id: text({ unique: true }), message: text({ default: '' }) }, {
    scope: anyOf(owner({ column: 'booker_id' }), member({
      group: 'id', membership: 'booking_access',
      member_user: 'user_id', member_group: 'booking_id', operations: ['read'],
    })),
    client: { read: ['id', 'slot_id', 'message'] },
  }),
  booking_access: table({ id: id(), booking_id: text(), user_id: text() }, {
    scope: serverOnly(), unique: [['booking_id', 'user_id']],
  }),
});
```

`booked` is the publication field, so the browser cannot create or write it:
a function of the provider's adds slots, and `api/book.ts` verifies the
caller, reads the slot with server authority to
find its provider, then in one `sw.db.server.tx` inserts the booking with
`booker_id`, the two access rows, and sets the slot's `booked`. `slot_id` is
unique, so of two concurrent bookers exactly one succeeds; the other sees the
constraint error. Cancelling is the mirror: delete the booking and clear
`booked` in one transaction. The customer's `message` is read by the customer
and that booking's provider and no one else; the public slot list never
carries booking data.

**Owner or staff.** Staff can read and update tickets; only their owner can
delete them. The customer's email and the assignee stay on the ticket row and
reach staff only: the owner branch lists the columns it reads, and a column
outside a reader's branch is absent from the row (`declared-data` →
`one-row-two-readers-different-columns`). Internal notes use a separate
staff-only table so a customer never reads them at all. Staff replies the customer
reads go in a `parent({ via: 'ticket_id' })` child table instead; then add
`create: ['staff']` to the ticket's `appRole` roles, because creating a child row
needs `create` on its parent (`owner-or-member-and-parent-access` below).

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { anyOf, appRole, id, owner, schema, table, text } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  tickets: table({ id: id(), subject: text(), body: text(), status: text({ default: 'open' }), customer_email: text(), assignee_email: text({ nullable: true }) }, {
    scope: anyOf(owner({ read: ['id', 'subject', 'body', 'status'] }), appRole({ roles: { read: ['staff'], update: ['staff'] } })),
    client: { read: ['id', 'subject', 'body', 'status', 'customer_email', 'assignee_email'], create: ['subject', 'body', 'customer_email'], update: ['subject', 'body', 'status', 'assignee_email'], delete: true },
  }),
  internal_notes: table({ id: id(), ticket_id: text(), body: text() }, {
    scope: appRole({ roles: { read: ['staff'], create: ['staff'], update: ['staff'], delete: ['staff'] } }),
    client: { read: ['id', 'ticket_id', 'body'], create: ['ticket_id', 'body'], update: ['body'], delete: true },
  }),
}, { appRoles: { staff: { grantableBy: [] } } });
```

The same shape serves the booking row when the provider and the booker see
different columns: `anyOf(owner(), grant({ ..., read: ['id', 'start'] }))`
keeps `booker_email` with the provider. Filters, ordering and aggregates may
name only the columns every branch reads.

A function on these tables keeps its validation and drops its access checks.
With `serverOnly()` tables, listing tickets is a role check, a caller-scoped
filter, and a per-row check on every detail route:

```ts
const user = await sw.auth.requireUser(request, { appRoles: true });
const staff = user.appRoles?.includes('staff') ?? false;
const { data } = await sw.db.server.from('tickets', { where: staff ? {} : { customer_id: user.id } });
```

With the rule declared, the same route is the read itself, and so is every
other route on the table:

```ts
const { data } = await sw.db.from('tickets', { order: [['created_at', 'desc']] }); // the caller's own, or all of them for staff
```

Seed staff with your developer key once they have signed up: `somewhere auth
roles grant <address> staff` (MCP `app_role_grant`, REST `POST /v1/auth/app-roles/grant`);
the address need not be verified, you vouch for the person. Never assign staff
from a public form. The in-app path stays: an app admin (made with
`auth_user_update({ project_id, user_id, role: 'admin' })`) calls your endpoint
that runs `sw.groups.appRoles.grant(request, userId, 'staff')`, and holders of a
role named in `grantableBy` grant it onward (`sw.groups` → `app-wide-roles`,
"The first staff member"). To make everyone at your company's domain staff instead, declare
`appRoles: { staff: { emailDomain: 'example.com' } }` (`sw.groups` →
`app-wide-roles`). That role holds only while the address is verified, which
happens when the user enters the sign-up code, follows a magic link, or signs
in with Google, GitHub or Discord. An app whose staff skip verification gives
them no staff role: keep a verification step for staff, or grant staff
explicitly. Do not check an unverified address's domain in a function
instead; anyone can sign up with an address they do not own. Verify as the owner, the intended provider/staff member, an
unrelated signed-in user and signed out. The allowed readers must succeed;
other readers must not receive the row, and a ticket owner must not receive
internal notes. Removing the provider access row or staff role must remove
that branch's access; removing the booker's access row removes the booker's
access too. Run these app tests separately from typechecking.

## Owner-or-member and parent access

### Teams

A team people join is a built-in group: `group()` on its rows and `sw.groups`
calls in small endpoints. The complete app, with its spec, is
`somewhere docs sw.groups --section team-example`. `member()` over your own
server-only membership table, below, is for relationships your app records
itself (`sw.groups` → `relationships-that-are-not-teams`).

### Membership and parent examples

**Sharing your own rows with specific people.** When the rows stay the
owner's and the owner invites specific people (sharing contacts read-only,
co-authors, a shared folder), use `anyOf(owner(), grant({ table: 'shares',
grantee: 'grantee_id', operations: ['read'] }))` with an `owner()` shares
table the owner fills: `docs({ topic: 'declared-data', section: 'per-owner-sharing' })`.
`member()` and `group()` need a group key on every row, with the owner in
that group; `grant()` adds nothing to existing rows, and the owner keeps
access without inviting themselves. Adding the grant widens every existing
caller-scoped read of that table to "mine plus shared with me"; a list that
must stay owner-only filters `where: { user_id: me.id }` in a function
(same section).

Import the helpers you use from `somewhere/db`.

**Owner or moderator** keeps personal rows private while letting an app-wide
moderator help. Declare `moderator` in the schema's `appRoles` and grant it
with your developer key (`somewhere auth roles grant <address> moderator`, or
MCP `app_role_grant`); from inside the app, an app admin grants it through
`sw.groups.appRoles.grant(request, userId, role)`:

```ts
scope: anyOf(owner(), appRole({ roles: {
  read: ['moderator'], update: ['moderator'],
} }))
```

For **owner or team admin**, use the built-in group carried by the row's
`group_id: text()` column:

```ts
scope: anyOf(owner(), group({ roles: {
  read: ['admin'], update: ['admin'],
} }))
```

For **creator or team owner can delete**, list only `owner` under `delete`:

```ts
scope: anyOf(owner(), group({ roles: {
  read: ['owner', 'admin', 'member'], delete: ['owner'],
} }))
```

Every member of the row's group reads it; the creator updates and deletes
their own rows; a group owner deletes any row in the group. The platform
records the creator, so no `created_by` column is needed. A creator who leaves
the group loses access to the rows they created. For app-owned teams, keep member reads/creates/updates declared; a team-owner
delete can use one checked server operation without moving all data to server-only.

The role branch grants only the operations you list. In these examples,
moderators or admins may read and update, while only the owner may delete.
Inside `anyOf`, an omitted group operation grants nobody; standalone
`group()` keeps its usual defaults. Browser `client` grants still decide
which operations and fields are exposed.

An owner-or-group insert requires current membership in the supplied group,
then stamps the signed-in user as owner. An owner-or-app-role insert stamps
any signed-in user as owner. Neither lets the caller choose another owner.
The group column cannot be updated, even to the same value. Removing a role
removes that branch's access. Removing someone from the group removes their
access to its rows, including the rows they own: team rows belong to the team.
Under `anyOf(owner(), appRole())` owners keep their own rows.
For a child using `parent()`, creating a child row needs `create` on the parent
for that person: the parent's owner branch, or a role listed under the parent's
`create`. Read or update roles alone do not let anyone add a child; the insert
is refused with 403 `POLICY_AUTHORITY_REQUIRED`.

**Existing app-owned membership tables** can use `member()` instead:


Use `anyOf(owner(), member({ group: 'team_id', membership: 'team_members',
member_user: 'user_id', member_group: 'team_id' }))` when both a row's
creator and its team members should be able to read, update, and delete the
row. This is collaborative editing, including deletion by other team members.
The membership table is declared separately. Ownership is set by the platform
on create. Team rows belong to the team: the creator keeps their rows only
while a member of the row's group, so leaving the team ends their access to
every team row, the ones they wrote included.

For **team reading with author-only editing**, use
`anyOf(owner(), member({ ..., operations: ['read'] }))` (teammates read,
the author edits their own row while still in the team), or
`allOf(gate, who)` when the gate's own operations must be spelled out:

```ts
scope: allOf(
  member({
    group: 'team_id', membership: 'team_members',
    member_user: 'user_id', member_group: 'team_id',
    operations: ['read', 'create', 'update', 'delete'],
  }),
  anyOf(owner(), member({
    group: 'team_id', membership: 'team_members',
    member_user: 'user_id', member_group: 'team_id',
    operations: ['read'],
  })),
)
```

Both must hold, in the same database statement:

- **read:** any current team member reads every row of the team;
- **create:** any current member adds a row to their team, recorded as its
  author;
- **update / delete:** only the row's author, and only while still a member;
- **leaving the team** removes access to every team row on the next request,
  the author's own rows and their `parent()` children included. Rejoining
  restores it.

The gate is current membership: `member()` with its `operations` listed,
`group({ roles })`, or `appRole({ roles })`. Who is `owner()` (the
author) or `anyOf(owner(), …)`, whose second branch is `appRole()` or the
gate's own membership: the same `group()` column, or the same `member()`
table, keys and member user. With `group()`, for example
`allOf(group({ roles: { read: ['member', 'admin'], create: ['member', 'admin'], update: ['member', 'admin'], delete: ['member', 'admin'] } }), anyOf(owner(), group({ roles: { read: ['member', 'admin'], update: ['admin'], delete: ['admin'] } })))`
lets a group admin edit any team row, and an author edit their own. Inside
`allOf`, every role list and `operations` list must be written out; an
operation left out of a written list grants nobody. Creating a row needs the
gate's create permission. The group key and the author are fixed for the row's
life. Not yet supported on `allOf` tables: live subscriptions,
`client.publicRead`, `client.links`, `client.intake`, payment bindings and
file collections.

`anyOf(owner(), member({ ..., operations: ['read'] }))` is the owner (while
still in the row's group) OR a member: teammates read, only the owner edits,
and someone removed from the team loses every team row, their own included.

`operations` restricts what membership grants: `read`, `create`,
`update`, and `delete`. Omit it for all four. Reading includes list,
get, counts, and related-row reads. The owner's authority does not depend on
`operations` (an owner still in the group edits their own row); a read-only
teammate cannot edit or delete someone else's row. A standalone
`member({ ..., operations: ['read'] })` table is also read-only for members.
An empty list grants members nothing. Create-only membership is supported;
update or delete must also include `read`, because those operations return
row data. Upserts remain unsupported for member and policy scopes.
Browser `client` grants still control exposed operations and fields; they
cannot grant authority that the scope denies. A later deploy can change an
existing table's rule, rows in place; "Two worlds" below lists what that does.

Creating a row requires an explicitly supplied, complete, non-null group key
and membership in that group. Ownership alone cannot authorize placing new
content in someone else's team. The membership check and insert are one
database statement. Group keys cannot be changed or incremented on update.
Creating a new group together with its initial memberships is application
logic in an authenticated function; it is not bootstrapped through an
owner-or-member browser insert.

For existing rows, owner-or-member access is the owner while a member of the
row's group, OR a member: removing the creator's membership removes their
permission to read, edit or delete their own rows on their next request
(team rows belong to the team). The rows stay where they are, with the same
owner and group; adding the person back restores their access. Share links
the person made to those rows stop working too. Three consequences to plan for:

- A row with no group (for example one written before the table gained its
  team rule) stays with its owner only. Teammates see it once your server
  code sets its group.
- A row whose group has no members left, or whose built-in group was deleted,
  is reachable only by your server code until someone is added to that group.
- Rows and their `parent()` children are checked inside the database
  statement; files in a team file collection are checked on each request,
  before the file is served.

For a task that follows its project, declare
`project_id: text({ references: 'projects' })` and
`scope: parent({ via: 'project_id' })`. Use `integer` instead of `text` when
the parent declares an integer key, `id({ uuid: false })`. Access is checked against the referenced
parent's private owner, member, group, app-role, or supported owner-or-role
scope. A parent's public
read grant does not propagate to its tasks. A policy-scoped child declares its
own browser operations and readable fields, and cannot declare `publicRead`.

A create supplies the parent ID explicitly and needs `create` on the parent
for that person: its owner, or a role listed under the parent's `create`.
Read or update authority on the parent is not enough. A staff reply to a
customer's ticket is a child insert, so the ticket's rule lists
`create: ['staff']`; without it the reply is refused with 403
`POLICY_AUTHORITY_REQUIRED`.
A move requires access to both the current and proposed parent, checked in the same database statement;
browser moves also require the linking field in `client.update`. An ordinary
field update keeps the current parent. Use `set` to change the parent ID;
incrementing that linking field is refused. Each child operation checks the
parent's authority for that operation. Browser operation grants can narrow it
further.

This contract supports one parent hop through one scalar foreign key to an
`id()` column. It does not support parent chains, arbitrary policy expressions,
visitor policies, or arbitrary per-operation policy expressions. Live subscriptions
over these policy scopes are refused. `onConflict` inserts follow the same
rule (see Upserts below). `sw.db.tx` works
on them: a child insert the parent does not authorize rolls the whole
transaction back with 403 `POLICY_AUTHORITY_REQUIRED`, and an update reaches
only rows the caller may write. A relationship
declaration alone never inherits access; `parent({ via })` is the explicit
authorization declaration.

## Two worlds: your database and the SQL database

Every table lives in exactly one world.

Tables declared in `db/schema.ts` are **your database** — managed. The
schema file is the only schema writer: schema ships with your code, scoping
is armed the moment a table exists, and destructive surprises are refused at
deploy. Managed tables are locked to the file — `db_migrate` on them
returns `409 SCHEMA_MANAGED`, and raw DDL on them
is refused at query time (`SCHEMA_LOCKED`) — edit `db/schema.ts` and
deploy instead.

An existing managed table can change its access rule in a later deploy, rows
in place: between `owner()`, `shared()`, `serverOnly()`, `member()` and the
composed rules (`anyOf`, `allOf`, `parent`), in production or a preview. The
new rule applies to every request admitted after the release activates, and
admission under the previous release ends within 60 seconds; a request already
running finishes under the rule it started with. A column the new rule needs is added in the same deploy, empty: existing rows
with no owner stay readable only by server code until one is set, and the
deploy says how many there are. The platform never guesses an owner, and an
existing column cannot become the owner column. Group keys and parent links
that rows already hold do decide access under the new rule, and the deploy
says so. A table that stops using its owner column keeps it, declared as an
ordinary column. A `member()` rule cannot rely on a membership table that
accepted browser writes in an earlier version: declare a new `serverOnly()`
membership table and fill it from server code.

On a rule that uses `group()` or `appRole()`, a deploy can change which roles
may read, create, update or delete on a `group()` or `appRole()` the rule
already has: staff gains create, a team owner gains delete, a member loses
update. That is the only change such a rule takes in a deploy. Such a deploy
changes one table's rule (a table that inherits it through `parent()` follows)
and nothing else that decides who may read or write it: the rule's shape (its
`anyOf`/`allOf` branches, group column, owner column and `parent()` links), the
table's columns and `client` permissions, the app's file collections, and the
app's role declarations (the roles, who may grant them, their email domains
and how they are assigned) all stay as deployed. Change those in their own
deploy first, then the roles; to add a role, deploy the role first and use it
in a rule after; to remove one, first deploy the rules without it. A role
change is available only when the app's stored roles and its live version
already carry complete role meaning (the generation, its full history, how
each role is acquired and which email domain holds it, all agreeing). An app
whose stored roles predate that format is refused with
`409 ACCESS_RULE_EDIT_ROLES_NOT_MODERN`: change the rule in a new table, or
handle the operation in a server endpoint. The change is judged against the
rule the live version serves, never against an earlier deploy that failed.
The deploy's `warnings` list, per table, which role gains or loses which
operation, widening first, and the file and room actions that follow: reading
files and joining rooms follow read; uploading, replacing, deleting and moving
files and changing room state follow update. `--json` carries the same entries
as `access_changes` (a `--dry-run` returns them too). The list names roles, not
people: someone whose role loses an operation may still reach a row as its
owner or through another role. In `allOf()`, a role removed from one condition
can deny someone the other condition admits, since both must hold.
Requests admitted under the new release use the new rule; a room ticket keeps
what it was issued with until it expires (at most 5 minutes). If the app's
roles change later, the changed role branch stops granting until a deploy built
for the new roles; other branches of the rule keep working. If the roles
change while the deploy is being built, it is refused with
`409 ACCESS_RULE_EDIT_STALE` before it goes live; deploy again. A preview is
its own copy: a production rule change does not reach a preview that already
exists. Any other change to such a rule, and a table with a checkout that has
not settled, are refused with `409 SCHEMA_DEPLOY_REFUSED` and a message naming
what changed and what to do; nothing changes. Rolling back across an
access-rule change is refused; deploy the previous rule as a new release
instead.
`409 SCOPE_CHANGE_BLOCKED_BY_RELEASE` still protects a takeover or
restoration that would change the posture of retained code.

Everything else is the **SQL database** — you write the SQL. `db_migrate`
applies schema changes (a production target is bookmarked first — a marker
in the database's 30-day history, not an undo, since restoring in place is
not available; keep dumps and exports for recovery). Access rules are set in
`db/schema.ts` and take effect on deploy. On a SQL-mode project, ordinary
`sw.db.query` / `sw.db.batch` run whatever you write. This is a sibling of
the managed database: it is the right world for hand-tuned schemas and external
identity models. A managed project reads and writes its declared tables through
structured operations; cross-user reads of them use `sw.db.server.from`,
`count` and `aggregate`. Raw SQL through the explicit
`sw.db.server.query` / `sw.db.server.batch` namespace reads the SQL
database. Every project created today keeps the two worlds in separate
databases, so its raw SQL never sees a table declared in `db/schema.ts`;
only an older project whose declared and SQL tables share one database can
raw-read declared tables.

Where raw SQL is available, it stays trusted-as-written and unscoped. Managed
projects make that choice explicit through the `sw.db.server` read namespace.

## Managed mode — what a db/schema.ts does to raw SQL

Deploying a `db/schema.ts` that declares at least one table puts the whole
PROJECT into managed mode, not just the declared tables. From that deploy on,
inside deployed function code:

- On an older shared database, ordinary `sw.db.query` / `sw.db.batch` are
  refused with `MANAGED_RAW_SQL_REQUIRES_SERVER_AUTHORITY` (403). With a
  separate SQL database they run there like the server forms, unscoped.
- For a deliberate raw read, authorize the caller first and use
  `sw.db.server.query(sql, params?)` or
  `sw.db.server.batch(statements)`. These calls run as explicit server
  authority, read as written, and do not apply declared row permissions. On a
  project created today they read only the separate SQL database, so a table
  declared in `db/schema.ts` is not found there; read declared tables with
  `sw.db.server.from`, `count` or `aggregate`.
- Raw SQL never writes declared tables. With a separate SQL database, server
  raw writes go to that database; on an older shared database every raw write
  is refused with `MANAGED_RAW_WRITE_FORBIDDEN` (403).
- Writes go through the composed builder: `sw.db.insert`,
  `sw.db.update`, `sw.db.remove`. A composed write needs a declared
  intent, so a table your functions write must be in `db/schema.ts` (or,
  on an older SQL-mode project, carry an access declaration recorded
  through the former scope API).
- It applies to EVERY function, including job, queue, and cron handlers. A
  background handler whose body is a raw INSERT starts returning 403 the
  moment the schema file lands, and on the cron surface the only visible
  symptom is `last_run_status: "failed"` — read the failed run with
  `job_get` to see the code.

An older project that keeps one shared database and runs its own SQL moves to
separate databases with its first `db/schema.ts`, in that deploy. Its existing
database becomes its SQL database, so raw SQL keeps reaching every table it
created; a new managed database holds the declared tables, which start empty,
and the platform's own data (tasks, email history, file search, conversations,
user memory, visitor sessions), copied in the same deploy. Notifications move
to the app's notification inbox. The platform's tables left in the SQL database
are renamed with the prefix `_sw_moved_`, so a raw query that still names one
fails instead of reading old rows. The deploy (and its dry run) refuses, before
anything is created:
- raw SQL in a function that names one of the platform's tables, such as
  `auth_users`: `409 SCHEMA_MIGRATION_RAW_SQL_PLATFORM_TABLE`, naming the file
  and the query. Read app users through `sw.auth` instead.
- a structured call (`sw.db.from`, `insert`, `update`, `remove`, `count`,
  `aggregate`) on a table `db/schema.ts` does not declare, which would answer
  `TABLE_NOT_MANAGED` once the project has moved:
  `409 SCHEMA_MIGRATION_UNDECLARED_TABLE`, naming the file and the call.
- a declared table whose name an existing table with rows already has:
  `409 SCHEMA_MIGRATION_TABLE_EXISTS`. Declare another name, or keep reaching
  the existing table with raw SQL.
- a `_notifications` table with rows that `sw.notifications` did not write:
  `409 SCHEMA_MIGRATION_NOTIFICATIONS_UNSUPPORTED`.
- an open preview: `409 SCHEMA_MIGRATION_PREVIEW_OPEN`, until it is closed.

The check reads the deploy's built function code. It does not see a table name
built at run time, or SQL text assembled from pieces; such a query fails when
it runs, on the renamed table. Versions from before that deploy can no longer
be rolled back to.

Developer authority is untouched: `db_query`, `db_batch`,
`db_migrate`, `db_dump`, the CLI, and the dashboard keep
full raw SQL against the project's raw SQL database. A project that keeps its
tables in the managed database has no raw SQL database, so raw SQL and dumps
answer `RAW_DATABASE_NOT_READY`; read its managed rows with `db_browse`
(`plane: "managed"`) or `somewhere db rows <table>`, and their schema and
row counts with `db_describe`.

Leaving managed mode is possible. There is no flag that flips a project back,
because the transition is deliberate: the owner authorizes it by email FIRST,
and the release that exports every managed table then completes it.

1. `POST /v1/projects/:id/managed-exit/request` — a developer credential for the
   project OWNER. You can request this with managed tables still present; that
   is the point. The platform emails that account's current verified address the
   exact plan: every managed table it would export, and the retained releases
   the exit would override. An account whose email is unverified, or that is
   anonymous, temporary or merged away, is refused. 3 requests per project per
   10 minutes.
2. `GET /v1/managed-exit/review?token=…` — the plan, its digest, the base
   release, the warning, and which stage it is at. Review-only: opening it
   approves nothing and changes nothing.
3. `POST /v1/projects/:id/managed-exit/approve` — the owner submits the token.
   **This records authorization and nothing else.** Your project is exactly as
   managed after approving as before: no authority moves, no table changes, no
   rollback boundary moves. The link is single-use and expires 10 minutes after
   the request.
4. **Deploy the release that marks every managed table `exported()`.** That
   release consumes the authorization and completes the transition. It must
   export exactly the approved set — a partial export, an extra table the
   approval never covered, or a release that adds new managed tables is refused
   and changes nothing.

The dashboard drives the same calls at `/dashboard/managed-exit`.

What the completing deploy does, stated as the warning states it:

- **Your data is preserved.** Existing rows and tables stay as they are.
- The platform **stops enforcing** declared table access and schema-safe composed
  writes. SQL migrations, authorization, validation, and rollback compatibility
  become yours.
- Developer tools, including developer-authorized `run_code`, receive direct SQL
  authority once the transition completes.
- **Already-deployed managed handlers do not change.** They keep their baked
  managed/read-only behavior until you remove the marker-only `db/schema.ts` and
  deploy reviewed SQL source.
- Managed clients for exported tables become unavailable.
- Releases older than the completing release are no longer eligible for rollback.

The completing release therefore ships a marker-only declaration — every
managed table marked, and nothing else in the file:

```ts
import { schema, exported } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  readings: exported(),
  field_notes: exported(),
  audit_log: exported(),
});
```

`exported()` takes no options, and managed search must be removed too.
Downloading a backup does **not** substitute for any of this: `db_dump` or a
data export leaves the declaration exactly as it was, and the transition is
about what the live declaration claims, not about whether you hold a copy.

**Two limits to plan around.** Without an approved exit, `exported()` is refused
while a retained release in the rollback window still queries that table's
declared scope — an approved exit is what authorizes overriding exactly the
releases you were shown. And your app code is not migrated for you: the
`somewhere:data` client is generated from the declaration, so browser code
calling an exported table must change in the SAME release that exports it.

Exiting is a considered migration, not an undo button. If your functions need
raw SQL writes, keep the project in SQL mode. A managed project uses structured
writes, including `sw.db.server.insert / update / remove / tx` after application
authorization for deliberate server-authority writes.

## Managed-schema error codes

- `SCHEMA_READ_FAILED` (503, retryable, at deploy) — the platform could not
  read the project’s prior managed-schema state. Nothing was applied; retry.
- `SCHEMA_APPLY_FAILED` (503, retryable, at deploy) — the declaration was
  valid but its plan could not be applied safely. Nothing changed; retry after
  the message’s rollout or availability condition clears.
- `SCHEMA_DEPLOY_REFUSED` (409, at deploy) — `db/schema.ts` asked for
  something the deploy will not do silently: removing or renaming a column,
  removing a table without its `removedTable()` marker, or changing a
  column's shape. It is also the answer when the database itself refuses the
  declaration: a table with more columns than the database allows (at most
  100 per table, counting the columns the platform keeps), or a rule the rows
  already stored break (a `unique` column over duplicate values). Nothing was
  applied; the message names the exact fix. It is never retried
  automatically: the same declaration is refused the same way.
- `SCHEMA_DECLARATION_INVALID` (400) — on every deploy path (fresh, full,
  patch, deploy-check, preview) the upload's `db/schema.ts` must read as a
  valid declaration and be sent in `files` as text: a syntax error, or the
  file sent under `functions` or as a binary file, is refused before
  anything is published. A full schema application additionally refuses a
  declaration of a platform-reserved table. The message explains the
  problem, with the line for syntax errors. A deploy with no `db/schema.ts`
  is unaffected.
- `SCHEMA_MANAGED` (409) — `db_migrate` targeted a
  managed table. The schema file is that table's only schema writer: edit
  `db/schema.ts` and deploy. Nothing was changed.
- `SCHEMA_LOCKED` (409, at query time) — raw DDL (ALTER / DROP / …)
  targeted a managed table. Same rule, enforced at the query boundary: edit
  `db/schema.ts` and deploy.
- `MANAGED_RAW_SQL_REQUIRES_SERVER_AUTHORITY` (403, before transport) —
  ordinary `sw.db.query` / `sw.db.batch` on an older shared database. Use declared
  structured operations, or authorize the caller and use the matching
  `sw.db.server.query` / `sw.db.server.batch` read.
- `MANAGED_RAW_WRITE_FORBIDDEN` (403, at query time) — raw SQL attempted a
  write on an older shared database, including through `sw.db.server.query` /
  `sw.db.server.batch`. Use structured writes, or run the statement with
  developer authority (`db_query` / `db_batch`).

## What you get out of the box (the industry-standard checklist)

- **Multi-tenant isolation** — one database per project, bindings
  baked at deploy time, no shared schema.
- **Per-user scoping** — the structured builder
  (`sw.db.from/count/insert/update/remove`) auto-scopes a table declared
  user-owned to the request's verified user, with no user argument.
  Explicit `sw.db.server` calls bypass that scope only when chosen. See
  "Per-user scoping" below.
- **ACID transactions** — `sw.db.tx([…])` runs declared operations
  atomically. If statement 3 fails, 1 and 2 roll back. Same shape
  as Postgres `BEGIN; …; COMMIT;`.
- **A documented Postgres-flavored syntax subset** — `$1` placeholders,
  `ILIKE`, `NOW()`, `col->>'key'`, `RETURNING *`, `SERIAL` and
  `BOOLEAN` are translated, outside literals and comments. To move to
  Postgres, `db_dump`, convert the database file and switch clients; a
  managed Postgres adapter is not a selectable backend or migration service.
- **Direct writes** — writes go straight to the project's database, one at a
  time per project, with no extra platform queue. Use `sw.db.tx` for related
  declared operations (`sw.db.batch` for raw SQL in SQL mode). Transient
  backpressure can still be retried.
- **Recovery evidence and exports** — `db_bookmark_create({ project_id, label })` records
  a named marker around a production migration. Projects with SQL tables in a
  separate database get `SPLIT_RESTORE_UNSUPPORTED`. A bookmark records
  operational evidence. In-place database restore is unavailable. Use
  `db_dump` or `db_export` to create a recoverable copy outside the live
  database.
- **Schema introspection** — `db_describe` returns tables +
  columns + row counts + foreign keys in one call.
- **Runaway-query detection** — a query that monopolizes
  database resources is detected and surfaced automatically.

## sw.db.query(sql, params?, options?)
Run raw SQL from a deployed function in a SQL-mode project. In managed mode,
ordinary `sw.db.query` is refused with
`MANAGED_RAW_SQL_REQUIRES_SERVER_AUTHORITY`; use declared structured calls
for ordinary access. The result shape is:

  {
    data: rows[],              // array of row objects (READ + RETURNING)
    error: null,               // never thrown; errors propagate as exceptions
    count: number,             // rows.length
    last_row_id: null,         // use the inserted row in data for its ID
    changes: number,           // every row written, incl. cascades and triggers; test > 0
  }

`changes` counts every row the statement wrote, including child rows removed or cleared by a
foreign key's `ON DELETE CASCADE` / `SET NULL` and rows written by triggers, so a one-row
`UPDATE` or `DELETE` can report more than 1. Test `changes > 0` to know the statement
changed something, never an exact number; use `RETURNING` and `r.data` to know which rows.

Use `r.data` for the rows. The MCP `db_query` tool returns a different
shape (`{ data: { columns, rows, meta } }`) because it surfaces the
raw platform response — don't confuse them. Inside functions it's
always `r.data`.

Raw SQL is never scoped to the caller: authorize in your function. Both
handlers below are in a SQL-mode project and admit only admins.

```ts
// api/admin/active-users.ts — SQL-mode project: raw read
export default async function(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req, { role: 'admin' }) // signed out → 401, not an admin → 403
  const users = await sw.db.query(
    'SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE active = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT ?',
    [1, 20]
  )
  // users.data = [{ id: 1, email: "alice@test.com" }, ...]
  // users.count = users.data.length
  return Response.json(users.data)
}
```

```ts
// api/admin/create-user.ts — writes an app table, not a sign-in account; body { email, name }
export default async function(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Method not allowed', { status: 405 })
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req, { role: 'admin' }) // signed out → 401, not an admin → 403
  const { email, name } = await req.json() as { email?: unknown; name?: unknown }
  if (typeof email !== 'string' || typeof name !== 'string') return Response.json({ error: 'email and name' }, { status: 400 })
  const result = await sw.db.query(
    'INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING *',
    [email, name]
  )
  // result.data = [{ id: 3, email: "bob@test.com", name: "Bob" }]
  // result.data[0].id = 3, result.changes = 1; result.last_row_id = null
  return Response.json(result.data[0])
}
```

## sw.db.server.query(sql, params?) / sw.db.server.batch(statements)

These are the explicit raw-read escape hatch for managed functions. Authorize
the caller before invoking them: the platform does not apply declared owner or
member permissions to the SQL and does not infer your business rule.

They read the SQL database. On every project created today that is a separate
database from your declared tables, so `SELECT … FROM emails` on a table
declared in `db/schema.ts` fails because the table is not there. A report over
declared tables uses the structured server verbs instead:

```ts
// api/admin/email-report.ts — on the emails table from "Per-user scoping" below
export default async function emailReport(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req, { role: 'admin' });
  // Every user's emails, counted together: exactly one row, { count }.
  const report = await sw.db.server.aggregate('emails', { count: true });
  return Response.json(report.data[0]);
}
```

Signatures:

  sw.db.server.query(sql: string, params?: readonly unknown[]): Promise<SomewhereDbResult>
  sw.db.server.batch(statements: readonly SomewhereRawDbStatement[]): Promise<SomewhereRawBatchResult[]>
  type SomewhereRawDbStatement = { sql: string; params?: readonly unknown[] }

Server raw calls accept no options. With a separate SQL database (every
project created today) they read and write that database, never declared
tables; on an older shared database they are read-only. DDL is refused
(`DDL_NOT_ALLOWED_IN_FUNCTION`). Use
`sw.db.server.insert / update / remove / tx` for deliberate server-authority
writes against declared tables.

## Whole numbers wider than JavaScript

Declare ordinary whole numbers, such as counts and cents, with `integer()`.
Generated clients return JavaScript numbers, so arithmetic works directly.
For wider identifiers, declare `bigint()`: values are exact decimal strings
on reads and writes, including the row returned by a structured write.

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { schema, table, id, bigint, boolean, owner } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  events: table({ id: id(), snowflake_id: bigint(), seen: boolean({ default: false }) }, { scope: owner() }),
});
```

```ts
// api/events/by-snowflake.ts — find the signed-in user's event by its 64-bit id
export default async function(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req) // signed out → 401 AUTH_REQUIRED
  const r = await sw.db.from('events', { where: { snowflake_id: '1804000000000000000' } })
  // r.data[0].snowflake_id === "1804000000000000000"   (a string, exactly)
  return Response.json(r.data)
}
```

An `integer()` value outside JavaScript's safe whole-number range is refused
with `DATABASE_VALUE_TOO_LARGE`; use `bigint()` for that column. Safe numeric
strings from URL parameters work as keys and filters. Values written to an
ordinary integer column must be numbers.

For `bigint()`, use canonical decimal text such as `'42'`, without a plus
sign or leading zeros. `min` and `max` work; `sum`, `avg` and
`increment` are refused to prevent overflow. Changing between `integer()`
and `bigint()` leaves stored values unchanged. Changing back to `integer()`
requires those values to fit its range before structured reads can return them.

On a SQL-mode project, raw `sw.db.query` runs exactly as written and is never
rewritten, so cast the column yourself in your own RETURNING clause:

```ts
// api/admin/mark-event-seen.ts — SQL-mode project; body { id }, admins only
export default async function(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Method not allowed', { status: 405 })
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req, { role: 'admin' }) // signed out → 401, not an admin → 403
  const { id } = await req.json() as { id?: unknown }
  if (typeof id !== 'string' || id === '') return Response.json({ error: 'id' }, { status: 400 })
  // RETURNING * over a 64-bit column applies the change, then reports
  // DATABASE_VALUE_TOO_LARGE. The write DID happen — do not retry it. Cast it:
  const marked = await sw.db.query('UPDATE events SET seen = 1 WHERE id = ? RETURNING id, CAST(snowflake_id AS TEXT) AS snowflake_id', [id])
  return Response.json(marked.data)
}
```

A structured write of a number outside the whole-number range the database
stores — below `-9223372036854775808` or above `9223372036854775807` — is
refused before the row is written, naming the column and the range, because the
database cannot hold it as a whole number at all. Store such a value as text.
A whole number past that range bound into a batch statement is refused the same
way, before the batch runs.

That is reading one. WRITING one back has the mirror constraint: a whole number
that wide cannot travel as a JSON number at all, because JSON parsing rounds it
before any platform code runs. A request body
carrying `"params": [9223372036854775807]` is refused with
`NUMBER_PRECISION_LOST` before anything is written, naming the field, the digits
sent and the number that arrived. Send it as a STRING, the same form a read
returns, and the round trip is lossless:

```ts
// api/admin/import-event.ts — SQL-mode project: the raw insert, admins only
export default async function(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Method not allowed', { status: 405 })
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req, { role: 'admin' }) // signed out → 401, not an admin → 403
  // exact: the 64-bit id travels as a string
  await sw.db.query('INSERT INTO events (snowflake_id) VALUES (?)', ['1804000000000000000'])
  return Response.json({ imported: true })
}
```

The structured write in a managed project, on the same `events` schema as the read above:

```ts
// api/events/record.ts — record the signed-in user's event
export default async function(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Method not allowed', { status: 405 })
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req) // signed out → 401 AUTH_REQUIRED
  const created = await sw.db.insert('events', { snowflake_id: '1804000000000000000' })
  return Response.json(created.data)
}
```

And from a developer tool call:

```text
db_query({ project_id, sql: 'UPDATE events SET snowflake_id = ? WHERE id = ?', params: ['1804000000000000000', 7] })
```

The column converts the digits on the way in because it is an integer column, so
the row holds a whole number, not text. A column declared with no type at all
has no affinity to convert it and would keep the text — declare such a column
`INTEGER`, or write it as `CAST(? AS INTEGER)`. A declared `integer` column in
`db/schema.ts` accepts that string too; text that is not a whole number is
still a `TYPE_MISMATCH`, and digits past the storable range are still
`DATABASE_VALUE_TOO_LARGE`.

A request that sends such a value as a bare JSON number is refused before
anything is written, with `NUMBER_PRECISION_LOST` naming the field, the
digits sent and the number that arrived (changed 2026-09-02 — before that it was
stored rounded, silently). Whole numbers up to 9007199254740991, decimals, and
larger whole numbers a JSON number happens to carry exactly are all unaffected.

In JavaScript itself — a deployed function, an SDK call, your own client — the
same limit is the language's: a numeric literal like `9223372036854775807` in
your source is already rounded before any platform code runs, and nothing can
recover it from there. That is why the refusal above can only catch a value
written as JSON text; keep ids of that size in strings end to end.

A database dump writes a value the database stores as a whole number as a bare
numeric literal, so restoring it produces a whole number again whatever the
destination column is declared as — including a column with no declared type.
A text column holding digits stays quoted (changed 2026-09-02 — before that
every wide whole number was quoted, and restored as text into a column with no
type to convert it).

A batch — `db_batch`, `sw.db.batch`, or statements sent together — returns
64-bit whole numbers in the same exact string form as a single query, so the two
paths agree on the same row.

One case a batch cannot return exactly: a batch that WRITES has already
committed every statement by the time its rows are read, so a `RETURNING` row
holding a 64-bit whole number is reported as `DATABASE_VALUE_TOO_LARGE` rather
than rounded. The message says the changes were applied — do not retry the
batch. Cast the column in that statement's own RETURNING list, or read the row
back afterwards:

// exact, in a batch that writes
{ sql: 'INSERT INTO events (name, snowflake_id) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING id, CAST(snowflake_id AS TEXT) AS snowflake_id', params: [name, id] }

## Size boundaries

- SQL text is limited to 100,000 bytes per statement. Bound parameter values
  are separate from that SQL-text count; value, row and request limits still
  apply. Put data in bound parameters instead of expanding it into SQL literals.
  A larger statement returns `STATEMENT_TOO_LARGE`; split bulk statements into batches.
- Treat 2,000,000 bytes as the documented portable maximum for a single string,
  binary value, or complete resulting row. Keep each request within that
  supported maximum: a larger value may be accepted or rejected depending on
  the encoded row, and a rejection returns `DATABASE_VALUE_TOO_LARGE`.
- Large TEXT/BLOB values belong in `sw.fs`, with a path or URL stored in the
  row, before they approach the supported maximum.
## How database storage is measured

- Managed data grows with your app. Somewhere handles storage as it grows.
  Database storage is measured across your account under your plan: the plan
  allowance is your total database storage summed across all of your
  projects, and it scales with the plan.
- Growth handling covers data read and written through the managed API. Very
  large tables queried with raw SQL stay in one database; use the managed API
  for datasets that need to grow.
- **Database storage is not total app storage.** File contents
  use file storage; platform-collected application logs, analytics events,
  sign-in credentials/sessions, and search vectors use separate stores. They
  do not consume this project's database storage and have their own limits.
  Files, logs or events that your code explicitly inserts into an app table
  still count as database storage.
- **What does count:** app rows and indexes, plus internal data kept alongside
  them. Depending on the features used, this includes the sign-in profile
  mirror, anonymous visitor sessions, persisted AI conversations/memory, and
  file-search text indexes. These count toward the project's database size.
  Keep relational records together for joins and transactions; use the file,
  logging, analytics and search primitives for their respective workloads.
- Database usage reporting is warning-only. Successful writes through the
  public database API and deployed functions refresh the byte snapshot when
  post-write size metadata is available. Some internal maintenance writes do
  not refresh usage in the same operation; a complete paginated database
  inventory reconciles every attached project database and remains
  authoritative. An accounting refresh failure never changes an
  already-committed write into an error.

## Per-user scoping — the structured builder, not raw SQL

Per-user scoping lives on the structured builder, never on raw SQL. There is
no `{ user }` option — the platform derives the user from the request's
verified credential and scopes automatically.

On a managed project, ordinary `sw.db.query` / `sw.db.batch` are refused.
When a read must bypass the automatic scoping, choose server authority
explicitly and enforce the caller policy in the function. The examples here use
one `owner()` table, whose owner column is `user_id` (the default):

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { schema, table, id, text, timestamp, owner } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  emails: table({
    id: id(), subject: text(), created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }),
  }, { scope: owner() }),
});
```

```ts
// api/emails/recent.ts — the caller's newest emails, as a server read scoped by hand
export default async function recentEmails(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  const me = await sw.auth.requireUser(req); // signed out → 401 AUTH_REQUIRED
  // Server authority skips the automatic scoping, so the function names the user itself.
  const emails = await sw.db.server.from('emails', {
    where: { user_id: me.id }, order: [['created_at', 'desc']], limit: 20,
  });
  return Response.json(emails.data);
}
```

Passing `{ user }` to ordinary raw SQL is an error
(`RAW_SQL_CANNOT_BE_PLATFORM_SCOPED`, 403 before transport). Passing
`{ unscoped: true }` or `{ asServer: true }` does not opt an ordinary raw
call into server authority; use the `sw.db.server` namespace.

For automatic scoping, use the structured builder on a table declared
user-owned (an `owner()` table in `db/schema.ts`; on an older SQL-mode
project, a `scoped` declaration recorded through the former scope API):

```ts
// api/emails.ts — auto-scoped to the request's verified user; no user argument
export default async function emails(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req);
  if (req.method === 'POST') {
    await sw.db.insert('emails', { subject: 'hi' }); // owner column set by the platform
  }
  const mine = await sw.db.from('emails', { order: [['created_at', 'desc']], limit: 20 });
  return Response.json(mine.data);
}
```

The builder composes the SQL, binds every value, and injects the owner filter
from the verified request identity. Fail-closed:

- A structured query on a table with no declared intent throws
  `TABLE_INTENT_REQUIRED` before transport — declare it `scoped` (owner
  column), `shared`, or `server_only` first.
- A scoped INSERT/UPSERT sets the owner column to the request user; a scoped
  UPDATE cannot reassign it.
- Browser app-user database access uses the structured table API. Raw SQL at
  `/v1/db/query` and `/v1/db/batch` is refused for browser sessions.
- There is no grace interval. Once a serving bundle carries the scope,
  violations are blocked.

`intent: 'server_only'` marks a table for trusted server and developer access
only. Use `{ asServer: true }` for structured reads and `sw.db.server.*` for
structured writes or deliberate raw reads; direct app-user access is rejected.
Platform-managed tables such as `auth_users` are always treated as
`server_only` and cannot be declared `scoped` or `shared`.

### Builder verbs and where-shapes

Verbs take plain objects, not fluent chains. `from(table, options?)` and
`count(table, options?)` take one options object. A signed-in `from` may add
`can: true`: each row then carries `mine` (this caller created it) and
`can.update` / `can.delete` (what this caller may change), never the owner
column itself: `declared-data` → `which-rows-belong-to-the-signed-in-user`. Writes use
`update(table, { set?, increment?, where? })`, `remove(table, { where })`,
and `insert(table, values, { onConflict: 'ignore' | 'update' }?)`.
`sw.db.update(...).set(...).where(...)` does not exist.

Tables for the examples:

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { schema, table, id, text, integer, boolean, timestamp, owner, shared, serverOnly } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  notes: table({
    id: id(), title: text(), done: boolean({ default: false }), created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }),
  }, { scope: owner() }),
  events: table({ id: id(), name: text(), starts_at: timestamp() }, { scope: shared() }),
  signups: table({ id: id(), email: text({ unique: true }) }, { scope: owner() }),
  profiles: table({ id: id(), handle: text({ unique: true }), bio: text({ default: '' }) }, { scope: owner() }),
  counters: table({ id: id(), count: integer({ default: 0 }) }, { scope: owner() }),
  inventory: table({ id: id(), name: text(), stock: integer() }, { scope: serverOnly() }),
});
```

```ts
// src/db-verbs.ts — call these from a handler that has run sw.auth.requireUser(req)
// Call write helpers only from POST handlers. Cookie-authenticated database requests
// (sign-in or visitor) need the app origin or an origin its CORS settings allow.
// Public write handlers still need authorization or abuse controls.

// reads — a bare value in where is equals, so a numeric id is { id: 42 }
export async function readNotes(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  const one  = await sw.db.from('notes', { where: { id: 42 }, limit: 1 });
  const open = await sw.db.from('notes', {
    where: { done: false, title: { contains: 'launch' } },
    order: [['created_at', 'desc']], limit: 20,
  });
  const { data: remaining } = await sw.db.count('notes', { where: { done: false } }); // Result<number>: the count is .data
  return { one: one.data[0] ?? null, open: open.data, remaining };
}

// date/number ranges — an array of single-operator conditions, AND-ed
export async function eventsBetween(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, fromIso: string, toIso: string) {
  const week = await sw.db.from('events', {
    where: { starts_at: [{ gte: fromIso }, { lte: toIso }] },
  });
  return week.data;
}

// idempotent writes — upsert on the table's unique column
export async function saveSignup(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, email: string, handle: string, bio: string) {
  await sw.db.insert('signups', { email }, { onConflict: 'ignore' });   // keep the existing row
  await sw.db.insert('profiles', { handle, bio }, { onConflict: 'update' }); // update it with these values
}

// update — set values, atomically add signed numeric deltas, or both
export async function renameAndCount(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  await sw.db.update('notes', { where: { id: 1 }, set: { title: 'renamed' } });
  const bumped = await sw.db.update('counters', { increment: { count: 1 }, where: { id: 1 } });
  return bumped.data[0]?.count ?? null;
}

// Stock belongs to no single user (serverOnly), so the reservation runs with
// server authority, from a handler that has already authorized the buyer.
export async function reserve(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, itemId: string, qty: number): Promise<Response | null> {
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(qty) || qty <= 0) return Response.json({ error: 'Quantity must be a positive whole number.' }, { status: 400 });
  const reserved = await sw.db.server.update('inventory', {
    increment: { stock: -qty }, where: { id: itemId, stock: { gte: qty } },
  });
  if (reserved.changes === 0) return Response.json({ error: 'not available' }, { status: 409 });
  return null;
}

// remove — ONE options object: { where }
export async function clearDone(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  return sw.db.remove('notes', { where: { done: true } });
  // → { data: [<removed rows>], count: 2, changes: 2 }
}
```

Updates need `set`, `increment`, or both, with no column in both.
Increment deltas are finite, non-zero signed numbers on declared numeric
columns. Addition happens in the scoped UPDATE: don't read then write or
retry an unknown outcome. NULL or integer overflow leaves the row unchanged;
`changes: 0` means scope, `where`, NULL, or overflow excluded it. One case
differs: an ordinary caller's `update` whose only `where` is the primary key
throws `DATA_NOT_FOUND` (404) when no row in their access matches, the answer
a missing row gets. A caller `remove` that matches nothing returns
`changes: 0` like any other zero-change write, the same for a missing row and
one outside the caller's access. Server-authority calls and broader `where`
filters return `changes: 0` too.
`where` uses the same operators as `from`. Omitting it updates every row
in scope. On `shared()` tables, signed-in users read all rows but update
only their own. On `owner()` tables, reads and writes use the signed-in
user's rows; the owner column cannot be reassigned. Update and remove return
`{ data, count, changes }`: `data` contains the touched rows.

Row values from `from`, `insert`, `update`, `remove`, `tx`, and
`aggregate` group keys come back in the types `db/schema.ts` declares: a
`boolean()` column is `true`/`false`, a `json()` column is its parsed value,
a `blob()` column is an array of bytes — the same values the generated
`somewhere:data` client gets for that row, so no conversion code is needed.
Aggregate group keys are typed as `string | number | boolean | null` in
TypeScript. Narrow a text key with `typeof row.link_id === 'string'` before
using it as a string key, for example in `Map<string, string>.get()`.
`sw.db.query` / `sw.db.server.query` rows are exactly as stored (0/1, JSON
text). A stored value that is not its declared type is refused with
`DATA_VALUE_INVALID` naming the column.

## Database rows and app responses

Function-side `sw.db` results hold rows in `.data` (an insert's row is `.data[0]`);
handlers choose their JSON shape. A caller's primary-key update raises
`DATA_NOT_FOUND` (404) for a missing or denied row; remove returns `changes: 0`.
Broader or server-authority writes can return empty `.data`.

For ordinary calls on `owner()` tables, ownership comes from the request,
never browser-supplied `user_id`. Cookie helpers establish browser sessions.
`sw.auth.requireUser(req)` checks sign-in; enforce any additional endpoint
rule separately.
<!-- END START PLATFORM CARD -->

Two argument mistakes are worth naming, because the errors read differently
than the mistake:

- A THIRD argument — the `update(table, values, { where })` shape other
  query builders use — throws `SCOPE_ARGUMENT_REMOVED` (400). Despite the
  wording, it does not mean you passed a scope: it means the verb takes
  exactly two arguments now. Merge your values into `set` and your filter
  into `where` in the ONE options object; do not just delete the extra
  argument, which would leave a table-wide update.
- A wrong option NAME throws `VALIDATION_ERROR` naming the accepted set,
  e.g. `sw.db.update: unknown option "values". Allowed: set, increment, where.`

Where operators, per column: a bare value (equals), `null` (IS NULL),
`{ not: null }` (IS NOT NULL), or a single-operator object — `eq`,
`ne`, `lt`, `lte`, `gt`, `gte`, `like`, `in`, `contains`,
`startsWith`, `endsWith`. One operator per condition object; an array of
condition objects on one column AND-s them (the range form above).

`contains` / `startsWith` / `endsWith` compose the search pattern for
you: the value is data, so `%` and `_` inside it match literally — a
user-typed search string is safe to pass as-is, at any length. `like` takes a
caller-authored pattern instead (its wildcards are your own); the value is
still bound, never spliced into the SQL, and a `like` pattern is limited to
50 bytes (the database refuses longer patterns): search for a text with
`contains`, `startsWith` or `endsWith` instead.

### Related rows in server functions

Two directions, both declared in `db/schema.ts` and both proven at deploy
against a real foreign key:

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { schema, table, id, text, boolean, owner, hasMany, belongsTo } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
```
