`sw.auth.mfa.enrollWithCookie(req)` mails a code and answers `{ challenge_id }`;
`sw.auth.mfa.verifyWithCookie(req, { challenge_id, code })` turns codes on.

**Turning codes off**, signed in, in two steps:
`sw.auth.mfa.unenrollWithCookie(req, { password })` checks the password and mails
a code; `sw.auth.mfa.unenrollWithCookie(req, { challenge_id, code })` turns codes
off. Under `required` this is refused (409 `AUTH_MFA_REQUIRED_BY_APP`).

**A user who cannot receive a code**, with no session:
`sw.auth.mfa.recover({ email, password })` starts a 72-hour wait (202
`{ removal_pending, removes_at }`). It starts only if the app can email the user
right now (otherwise 503 `AUTH_MFA_RECOVERY_NOTICE_UNSENT`). The email carries a
cancel link that works for the whole wait without signing in. The same call after
the wait turns codes off. A code sign-in, a password change or reset, an email
change, or the cancel link stops it.

**The app owner** can turn a user's codes off at once with
`DELETE /v1/auth/users/:id/mfa?project_id=`, or set the user's email address with
`PATCH /v1/auth/users/:id` `{ email }`, for a user who lost their inbox. The new
address is unverified, their codes are turned off, and mail sent to the old address
stops working.

**Limits.** At most one code a minute and 5 an hour per account. Code mail never
counts against the app's email allowance, and mail to a verified address is sent
even while the app's email is paused for bounces. Code mail to unverified addresses
(sign-ups under `required`) is limited to 200 an hour per app and 20 an hour
per network address (429 `AUTH_MFA_NEW_ACCOUNT_LIMITED`).

**Webhooks:** `mfa_factor_removed` (`via`: `self`, `recovery` or `owner`),
`mfa_recovery_started`, `mfa_user_email_changed` and `mfa_policy_changed`.

REST: `POST /v1/auth/mfa/challenge`, `/enroll`, `/verify`, `/unenroll`,
`/recovery`, `/recovery/cancel`; `GET|PUT /v1/auth/mfa/policy`;
`DELETE /v1/auth/users/:id/mfa`. MCP: `auth_mfa_enroll`, `auth_mfa_verify`,
`auth_mfa_challenge`, `auth_mfa_unenroll`.

## Not available

These account features are not available. Their calls answer 501
`AUTH_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE` before anything runs, so they change nothing:

| Feature | Calls that answer 501 |
|---|---|
| Authenticator-app (TOTP) codes | `sw.auth.mfa.reauthenticate`, `verifyReauthentication`, `POST /v1/auth/mfa/activation/reauth*` |
| Passkeys | `/v1/auth/passkey/*` |
| Changing a signed-in user's profile or email address | `sw.auth.updateProfile`, `updateProfileWithCookie`, `verifyEmailChangeWithCookie`, `verifyEmailChangeCurrentWithCookie`, `PATCH /v1/auth/me`, `PATCH /v1/auth/users/me`, `POST /v1/auth/change-email/*` |
| In-app user moderation | `sw.auth.moderation`, `/v1/auth/admin/users` |
| Anonymous-account migration | `POST /v1/auth/migrate-anon` |
| User import and export | `POST /v1/auth/import`, `POST /v1/auth/export/request`, `POST /v1/auth/export/download` |

An account copied from an earlier platform with authenticator-app codes gets
`{ mfa_required: true, mfa_token }` and no session, and cannot complete it.

What works today: password sign-up and sign-in, email sign-in codes, sign-in
links, invitations, Google, GitHub and Discord sign-in, email verification,
password reset and password change, sign-out, account self-delete, and
developer user management with a developer key (list, edit, ban, delete,
sessions, and a user's sign-in codes and address).

## Update password (logged-in user)

```ts
// api/settings/password.ts — POST { current_password?, new_password }
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Use POST.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } });
  const input: unknown = await req.json().catch(() => null);
  const newPassword = typeof input === 'object' && input !== null && 'new_password' in input ? input.new_password : undefined;
  const currentPassword = typeof input === 'object' && input !== null && 'current_password' in input ? input.current_password : undefined;
  if (typeof newPassword !== 'string' || (currentPassword !== undefined && typeof currentPassword !== 'string')) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'new_password is required; current_password must be text.' }, { status: 400 });
  }
  const result = await sw.auth.updatePasswordWithCookie(req, { new_password: newPassword, current_password: currentPassword });
  return Response.json(result);
}
```

Token-mode clients call `sw.auth.updatePassword(token, { current_password, new_password })`.

Wipes ALL active sessions and refresh tokens on success — the user has
to log in again everywhere.

**A bearer token alone cannot set the FIRST password.** An account that
has never had one — magic link, OAuth — is refused here with
`AUTH_PASSWORD_RESET_REQUIRED` (403). Send that user through the existing
`/v1/auth/forgot` and `/v1/auth/reset` pair instead, so the password is set
against a code delivered to their current address rather than against a
token someone may have stolen. On an account that already has a password,
`current_password` is required (`VALIDATION_ERROR` without it, `AUTH_INVALID_CREDS`
if it is wrong), and if the password changes underneath the call it answers
`AUTH_CREDENTIAL_CHANGED` (409) rather than overwriting the newer one.

## Change email (logged-in user)

Not available: see "Not available".

## Update profile (logged-in user)

Not available: see "Not available". A developer key can still edit a
user (see "Admin / test-harness edit").

## Self-service account deletion

```ts
// api/settings/delete-account.ts — POST deletes the signed-in user's own account
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Use POST.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } });
  const result = await sw.auth.deleteUserWithCookie(req);
  return Response.json(result);
}
```

Token-mode clients call `sw.auth.deleteUser(token)`. Both forms end every
session; the cookie form also clears the cookies.

The call removes the sign-in identity, sessions and refresh tokens, password reset
and verification codes, pending email changes, magic links, MFA credentials,
provider links, group memberships, app-role grants, plan selection,
push devices, MCP grants and pending MCP consents. Grants the user gave other
people stay with those people.

Passkey sign-in is not available. Account deletion also clears any
passkey records left by older versions.

The answer keeps `deleted: true` and adds three lists: `removed` names the
categories removed; `kept` names payment records (`accounts_and_disputes`),
the group deletion marker (`prevents_stale_access`), and suppression of a
complained email address (`prevents_unwanted_mail`). These are categories and
reason codes, not a check that such records exist. `not_covered` names rows and
files the person created, AI history, search, mail records, the sign-in mirror,
logs and their archive, and backups. This call does not inspect those stores.
Anything in `not_covered` is yours to delete. The author and bulk deletion
routes return the same lists for each successfully deleted user.

### Delete the person's own data too, and give them a copy

Pass `{ erase: 'owned' }` to `deleteUserWithCookie(req, { erase: 'owned' })` or `deleteUser(token, { erase: 'owned' })`, or add `?erase=owned` to `DELETE /v1/auth/users/me`. The project owner can also use it on `DELETE /v1/auth/users/<id>?project_id=<project>` with their own developer key; editors cannot. The erase also removes:
- rows in tables whose access rule is `owner()` and that hold the person's id;
- files stored as theirs.

The person's own mailbox goes with every deletion. Mail in other people's mailboxes is theirs and is not touched. Rows in shared or policy tables are kept, because the app's own rules decide who keeps them.

Before anything is deleted, the platform checks the app's tables. If a table could reach another person's rows, the request is refused with `ERASE_UNSAFE`, the tables are named and nothing is deleted. Such a table is one that:
- is referenced by another table's foreign key;
- has the app's own triggers;
- has no rowid;
- is declared only in an older release.

Delete without `erase`, or change those tables, and try again. If an option other than `"owned"` is given, nothing is deleted.

The answer's `erasure` has an id, a state and counts. The erase finishes in the background about 15 minutes after the deletion. The owner reads the receipt with `GET /v1/auth/erasures/<id>?project_id=<project>`; it holds counts only.

A person's own copy of their data:
- the signed-in person: `sw.auth.exportUser(token)` or `GET /v1/auth/users/me/export`;
- the owner: `GET /v1/auth/users/<id>/export?project_id=<project>` with their own developer key.

The copy has:
- their profile;
- their rows in `owner()` tables, without columns the app marks sensitive;
- their files by path;
- their passkeys.

Shared and policy tables are named in `not_in_copy`, not copied. A copy over 5,000 rows in one table, or 10 MB in all, is refused with `EXPORT_TOO_LARGE`; nothing is truncated.

When someone asks the app to delete their data or send them a copy, these calls are the answer for what the platform can tell is theirs. Ask your human about anything the answer lists as not covered: raw SQL tables, shared tables, or another service.

A group always keeps an owner. If the account is the only owner of a group,
the call is refused with a 409 `LAST_OWNER` error whose message names the
group, and nothing is deleted. Make another member an owner
(`sw.groups.setRole`), or delete the group, then delete the account again.

An already-admitted sign-in can be honoured for up to 60 seconds after deletion.
An open live-room connection can last until its ticket expires (at most 5 minutes).

## Admin / test-harness deletion (developer key)

```text
auth_user_delete({ project_id: "my-app", user_id: "6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e2a-9c41-8d5e0f7a2b13" })
```

REST: `DELETE /v1/auth/users/:id?project_id=...` with an `smt_` key.

For wiping throwaway test users from your own tooling, when you don't
have the user's JWT. Same cascade and the same `LAST_OWNER` refusal as the
self-service variant. The project must be one you own.

To delete several test users together, with the groups only they belong to:
`POST /v1/auth/users/delete?project_id=...` with an `smt_` key and
`{ "ids": [...], "delete_groups_only_they_belong_to": true }` (1 to 50 exact ids,
never emails). A group whose every member is in `ids` is deleted with them. A user
who is the only owner of a group with any member outside `ids` is kept, and the
group is left alone. The answer gives each id's outcome (`deleted`, `not_found` or
`kept` with the group named) and the groups deleted. `somewhere test` uses this
for the accounts it signed up; in a preview it uses
`POST /v1/preview-tools/signups/delete` with the preview's own credential.

## Admin / test-harness edit (developer key)

```text
auth_user_update({
  project_id: "my-app",
  user_id: "6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e2a-9c41-8d5e0f7a2b13",
  display_name: "Ada Lovelace",
  metadata: { team: "support" },
  role: "admin"
})
```

REST: `PATCH /v1/auth/users/:id?project_id=...` with an `smt_` key.

For admin tooling: edit `display_name`, `metadata`, and/or the
platform-owned `user | admin` role on any end-user in a project you
own. Signup always creates `user`; granting the first `admin` here is
safe because this control-plane call requires the project owner's
developer key and the app-user self-profile route does not accept
`role`. Role changes are audited and invalidate existing access tokens. Email and
password are intentionally NOT here — those have their own verification
and reset flows. `metadata` is REPLACED, not merged; max 16 KB.

Also accepts `banned` and `banned_reason` — see "Ban / suspend" below.

## Server-assigned app roles (setRoles)

Who gets a role is your app's decision; the platform enforces what the role may do.
Require mailbox verification when grant eligibility depends on an email
domain. Anyone can sign up as `anyone@yourco.example` before verifying it.

**First choice: the verified email domain.** When staff are the people with an
address at your domain, declare `appRoles: { staff: { emailDomain: 'yourco.example' } }`.
The role holds as soon as the person verifies that address; there is no grant
code to write or to fail (`sw.groups` → `app-wide-roles`).

**Second choice: an invitation your app issued, granted inside sign-up.** When
staff must hold the role before any verification, grant it only from something
the visitor cannot choose: an invitation code your app created for one address.
The link is a bearer credential for that address. Nothing here verifies the
mailbox, so deliver the link only to that person, over a channel you trust:
whoever holds it can sign up as that address first. Declare the role
`assignedBy: 'server'` and keep the invitations server-only. The invitation row
is the record of who is owed the role: it is claimed once, by one account,
then marked granted.

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { appRole, id, schema, serverOnly, table, text } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  staff_invites: table({
    id: id(), email: text(), code: text(),
    claimed_by: text({ nullable: true }),   // the account that redeemed it; set once
    granted_at: text({ nullable: true }),   // set after the role is held; never grants again
  }, { scope: serverOnly(), unique: [['code']] }),
  staff_notes: table({ id: id(), body: text() }, {
    scope: appRole({ roles: { read: ['staff'], create: ['staff'] } }),
    client: { read: true, create: ['body'] },
  }),
}, { appRoles: { staff: { assignedBy: 'server' } } });
```

```ts
// api/staff-invites.ts — POST { email }: an app admin issues an invitation link
export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'required', body: { email: 'email' },
  handler: async ({ request, body }, sw) => {
    await sw.auth.requireUser(request, { role: 'admin' });
    const code = crypto.randomUUID();
    await sw.db.server.insert('staff_invites', { id: crypto.randomUUID(), email: body.email.toLowerCase(), code });
    return { link: new URL('/api/staff-invite?code=' + code, request.url).href };
  },
});
```

```ts
// api/staff-invite.ts — GET: the invitation link keeps its code for the sign-up route
export const GET = sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'none',
  handler: async ({ request }) => {
    const code = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('code') ?? '';
    if (!/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/.test(code)) return Response.json({ error: 'INVITE_INVALID' }, { status: 400 });
    return new Response(null, { status: 303, headers: {
      location: '/', 'set-cookie': `staff_invite=${code}; Path=/api/auth; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=604800`,
    } });
  },
});
```

```ts
// api/auth/[...path].ts — the starter's auth route, plus: an invited person becomes staff
import { somewhereAuth } from '@somewhere-cloud/sdk/server';
export default async function (request: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  const response = await somewhereAuth(request, sw);
  if (!response.ok || request.method !== 'POST' || !/\/auth\/(signup|login)$/.test(new URL(request.url).pathname)) return response;
  const { user } = await response.clone().json() as { user?: { id?: string; email?: string } };
  if (!user?.id || !user.email) return response; // an emailed sign-in code is still pending
  const code = /(?:^|;\s*)staff_invite=([0-9a-f-]{36})/.exec(request.headers.get('cookie') ?? '')?.[1];
  // 1. Claim: bind an unclaimed invitation for this address to this account. The
  //    condition claimed_by: null makes it single use: of any two attempts, one changes it.
  if (code) {
    await sw.db.server.update('staff_invites', {
      where: { code, email: user.email.toLowerCase(), claimed_by: null }, set: { claimed_by: user.id },
    });
  }
  // 2. Grant what this account is owed: claimed now, or claimed by an earlier sign-in whose grant failed.
  const { data: [owed] } = await sw.db.server.from('staff_invites', { where: { claimed_by: user.id, granted_at: null }, limit: 1 });
  const inviteId = owed?.id;
  if (typeof inviteId !== 'string') return response;
  try {
    await sw.auth.server.setRoles(user.id, { add: ['staff'] }); // idempotent
  } catch {
    // Not granted. The invitation stays bound to this account; its next sign-in grants again.
    sw.auth.clearSessionCookies();
    return Response.json({ error: 'STAFF_SETUP_FAILED', message: 'Your account was created, but staff access could not be set up yet. Sign in again to finish.' }, { status: 503 });
  }
  // 3. Spend it. If this write fails, the person holds the role they were invited to;
  //    their next sign-in finds the row still owed, grants again (a no-op) and spends it.
  await sw.db.server.update('staff_invites', { where: { id: inviteId, claimed_by: user.id, granted_at: null }, set: { granted_at: new Date().toISOString() } })
    .catch((error: unknown) => console.error('staff invite not marked granted; the next sign-in finishes it', String(error)));
  return response;
}
```

```ts
// api/staff-revoke.ts — POST { userId }: an app admin removes staff. The invitation is
// retired first, so no later sign-in can grant the role back.
export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'required', body: { userId: 'string' },
  handler: async ({ request, body }, sw) => {
    await sw.auth.requireUser(request, { role: 'admin' });
    await sw.db.server.remove('staff_invites', { where: { claimed_by: body.userId } });
    await sw.auth.server.setRoles(body.userId, { remove: ['staff'] });
    return { ok: true };
  },
});
```

Every state is safe. Unclaimed, the invitation gives nothing. Claimed, it belongs
to one account and to nobody else, even with the same link. A second account at
that address, or a forwarded link, finds it claimed. Until it is marked granted,
any sign-in of that account (with or without the link) finishes the grant, so a
failed grant is recovered, never lost. Marked granted, it never grants again,
and a revoked role stays revoked. A failed grant signs the person out with the
message above and holds no role. The grant runs before the response is sent, so
the new person's first request already holds the role; a separate setup request
after sign-up would race it. A project that requires emailed sign-in codes
finishes sign-up at the code step, which this route does not intercept; there,
use the verified email domain above.

For a later promotion (an admin, a payment), call setRoles from a POST handler
that first authorizes the caller, for example with
`await sw.auth.requireUser(request, { role: 'admin' })`. Never from a GET:
role changes mutate authentication state, so cookie-authenticated safe methods
are refused.

`setRoles(userId, { add: ['staff'] })` adds; `{ remove: ['staff'] }` removes.
These server methods run in deployed functions, not dev or run_code. In a preview they read and assign roles for that preview's own users in its copy of the data; the live app's users and roles are never reached.
Full declared schema: `somewhere docs declared-data --section server-roles-and-membership-restrictions`.

## Check an app role from a page

For a page that shows owner controls, call a signed-in endpoint that uses
`await sw.auth.requireUser(request, { appRoles: true })` and returns whether
the caller's `appRoles` includes `owner`. The browser auth client's session
contains the built-in auth role. Enforce the required app role again on any
endpoint that reads private data or changes state. See
`somewhere docs sw.groups --section app-wide-roles` for the server-side checks.

## App roles (developer key)

Roles your schema declares (`db/schema.ts` `appRoles`: staff, moderator, …)
are granted here as well, so every `appRole()` rule on your tables applies to
the person at once:

```text
app_role_grant({ project_id: "my-app", email: "ann@example.com", role: "staff" })
app_role_revoke({ project_id: "my-app", user_id: "6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e2a-9c41-8d5e0f7a2b13", role: "staff" })
app_role_list({ project_id: "my-app", role: "staff" })
```

REST: `POST /v1/auth/app-roles/grant`, `POST /v1/auth/app-roles/revoke`,
`GET /v1/auth/app-roles?project_id=…` with an `smt_` key · CLI:
`somewhere auth roles grant|revoke|list`. Name the person by `user_id` or
by the exact address they signed up with; the address need not be verified.
An app role is different from the `user | admin` auth role above: you declare
it and your `appRole()` rules read it; the `admin` auth role is the
platform's. Who holds what, and the in-app grant path: `sw.groups` →
`app-wide-roles`.

## Admin operations are NOT on the runtime

`sw.auth.admin.*` is not callable inside deployed functions — any
call throws `AUTH_ADMIN_REMOVED_FROM_RUNTIME`. A public handler that
accepted a user id from the request body would be an account-takeover
primitive, so admin actions on app users run only from your own
tooling with a developer `smt_` key (MCP tools or REST), never from
a request handler. The sections below are that surface.

## Ban / suspend (developer key)

Block a user from signing in without deleting their data. Bans are
reversible — the row stays put, sessions are wiped, future `login`
returns AUTH_INVALID_CREDS (no enumeration), and any active JWT bounces
with 403 AUTH_BANNED on `/me` so your SPA can log them out.

Ban, then unban (unbanning clears the reason and timestamp):

```text
auth_user_update({ project_id: "my-app", user_id: "6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e2a-9c41-8d5e0f7a2b13", banned: true, banned_reason: "spam" })
auth_user_update({ project_id: "my-app", user_id: "6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e2a-9c41-8d5e0f7a2b13", banned: false })
```

The `banned_reason` is staff-only — never returned to the banned
user. Banning a user invalidates every active session + refresh token.

REST: PATCH /v1/auth/users/:id?project_id=… with `banned` /
`banned_reason` fields  ·  MCP: auth_user_update

## Acting as an app user

The platform does not sign a developer in as one of an app's users.
`POST /v1/auth/users/:id/impersonate` answers **410 IMPERSONATION_RETIRED**
and issues no token. To test your app as a user, use a test identity;
browser_test's `auth: { user_id }` accepts only a test identity of the
project and answers 410 IMPERSONATION_RETIRED for anyone else.

## Test users and the after-deploy check

After every live deploy, Somewhere checks the new release as a stranger and as a
signed-out visitor. It creates two test users in your app, has one of them create
a row in each table the browser may both create in and delete from, tries to read,
change and delete that row as the other test user and as a visitor, and calls each
server function that takes an id in its path (such as `api/notes/[id].ts`) once with
GET, using that test row's id. In the platform's browser it loads the home page and
the pages it links to, signed out and as a test user, on a computer and a phone, and
signs in once through your app's own form with an account it signs up through your
app's sign-up route. It presses no other button. It then deletes that row, any row
your app made for these users, the sign-in account and both test users, by id.
It never changes or deletes anything it did not create; other people's rows are
only read to learn whether a stranger can see them, and their contents are never
stored. The result is one sentence on the deploy log: `GET /v1/deploy/log` field
`access_check`, also linked from the deploy response's `checks`.

A test user's email ends in `.test.somewhere.site`, and `sw.auth` user objects for
managed test users carry `test: true` (the sign-in account is an ordinary sign-up on
that address). Test users are never admins, are not counted in your app's
user totals, and their mail goes to the test inbox. If your code reacts to a new
or first-seen user (notifying the owner, sending a welcome, posting to a channel),
skip users whose email ends in `.test.somewhere.site`:

```ts
const isTestUser = (user: { email?: string | null }) => /\.test\.somewhere\.site$/i.test(user.email ?? '');
```

## Session management (developer key)

List + revoke a user's active sessions. Tokens themselves are never
returned — only session IDs, creation timestamps, and expiries.

`auth_list_sessions` returns `[{ id, created_at, expires_at }, ...]`,
non-expired only, max 100. Revoke one session to log that device out, or all
of them to log every device out:

```text
auth_list_sessions({ project_id: "my-app", user_id: "6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e2a-9c41-8d5e0f7a2b13" })
auth_revoke_session({ project_id: "my-app", session_id: "<id from auth_list_sessions>" })
auth_revoke_all_sessions({ project_id: "my-app", user_id: "6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e2a-9c41-8d5e0f7a2b13" })
```

REST: GET /v1/auth/users/:id/sessions, DELETE /v1/auth/sessions/:id,
DELETE /v1/auth/users/:id/sessions
MCP: auth_list_sessions, auth_revoke_session, auth_revoke_all_sessions

## Lifecycle webhook (clean up your own tables on user delete)

Deleting a user removes their platform account and sessions. Your app must
clean up its own references, such as posts, comments and avatar files.

Configure a project-scoped webhook to handle account events and clean up app data:

  // one-time setup (developer key)
  const { secret } = await auth_webhook_set({
    project_id: 'default',
    url: 'https://yourapp.somewhere.site/api/lifecycle-webhook',
  });
  // store the returned secret in server env (never in the browser bundle):
  //   somewhere env set AUTH_WEBHOOK_SECRET <secret>
  // a URL-only update keeps the secret but does not return it;
  // rotate_secret: true issues a new one (then set the new value).

The tables the handler writes, both `owner()` (the owner column is `user_id`):

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { id, owner, schema, table, text, timestamp } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  profiles: table(
    { id: id(), email: text({ unique: true }), display_name: text({ nullable: true }) },
    { scope: owner() },
  ),
  posts: table(
    { id: id(), title: text(), body: text(), created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }) },
    { scope: owner() },
  ),
});
```

The handler verifies the signature over the exact raw bytes before any write:

```ts
// api/lifecycle-webhook.ts
export default async function lifecycleWebhook(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  const secret = sw.env.AUTH_WEBHOOK_SECRET
  if (!secret) return new Response('webhook secret not configured', { status: 500 })
  const raw = await req.text()   // verify these exact bytes, then parse
  const m = /^t=(\d+),v1=([0-9a-f]{64})$/.exec(req.headers.get('X-Somewhere-Signature') ?? '')
  if (!m || Math.abs(Date.now() - Number(m[1])) > 5 * 60 * 1000) return new Response('forbidden', { status: 403 })
  const sig = new Uint8Array(32)
  for (let i = 0; i < 32; i++) sig[i] = parseInt(m[2].slice(i * 2, i * 2 + 2), 16)
  const key = await crypto.subtle.importKey('raw', new TextEncoder().encode(secret),
    { name: 'HMAC', hash: 'SHA-256' }, false, ['verify'])
  if (!(await crypto.subtle.verify('HMAC', key, sig, new TextEncoder().encode(`${m[1]}.${raw}`)))) {
    return new Response('forbidden', { status: 403 })
  }

  let event: unknown
  try { event = JSON.parse(raw) } catch { return new Response('bad payload', { status: 400 }) }
  const body: object = typeof event === 'object' && event !== null ? event : {}
  const user: object = 'user' in body && typeof body.user === 'object' && body.user !== null ? body.user : {}
  const type = 'type' in body ? body.type : undefined
  const userId = 'id' in user ? user.id : undefined
  // A webhook has no signed-in user, so it writes with explicit server
  // authority and names the owner column (user_id) itself.
  if (type === 'auth.user.created') {
    const email = 'email' in user ? user.email : undefined
    if (typeof userId !== 'string' || typeof email !== 'string') return new Response('bad payload', { status: 400 })
    const displayName = 'display_name' in user && typeof user.display_name === 'string' ? user.display_name : null
    await sw.db.server.insert('profiles', { user_id: userId, email, display_name: displayName },
      { onConflict: 'ignore' })   // a repeated delivery is a no-op: email is unique
  } else if (type === 'auth.user.deleted') {
    if (typeof userId !== 'string') return new Response('bad payload', { status: 400 })
    await sw.db.server.remove('posts', { where: { user_id: userId } })
    await sw.db.server.remove('profiles', { where: { user_id: userId } })
  }
  return Response.json({ ok: true })   // other events on this URL are acknowledged
}
```

Web Crypto verifies the HMAC over the signed timestamp and raw body before
anything is parsed or written. This is the lifecycle webhook's own HMAC;
`sw.jobs.verifyInvocation` is for job, queue and cron deliveries and does
not apply here.

Fired events: `auth.user.created`, `auth.user.updated`, `auth.user.deleted`.
The same URL also receives `refresh_token_reuse` and `payment.completed`;
acknowledge any type you don't handle.
- `created` fires on password signup, Google-created, and magic-link-created
  users. Body: `{ type, user: { id, email, display_name, project_id, created_at } }`.
- `updated` fires when a user edits their profile (display_name / metadata).
- `deleted` fires on account deletion.
A failed delivery is retried up to four attempts in all, about 10 seconds, 1 minute and 5 minutes apart; every attempt of one event carries the same `X-Somewhere-Event-Id` header, so dedupe on it.

## Verify signatures and imported passwords

Use `sw.crypto` inside a function when an integration needs its own signature
check or password-hash comparison. Normal app sign-in uses `sw.auth`; it already
handles passwords and sessions.

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `await sw.crypto.hmacSha256Hex(message, secret)` | HMAC-SHA256 of the UTF-8 message, returned as lowercase hex. Keep the secret in `sw.env`. |
| `sw.crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b)` | A boolean string comparison that checks every character when the lengths match; different lengths return false. |
| `await sw.crypto.bcrypt.verify(password, hash)` | A boolean password/hash match from the platform's bcrypt verifier. Request failures throw. |

For incoming webhooks, verify the sender's exact signing format against the raw
request body before acting on it. See `webhooks` for the platform event format;
auth lifecycle webhooks use the separate format above.

## Member contacts

Use `sw.auth.server.listUsers` in a deployed function to resolve member IDs
into your app's contact details. Authorize the caller first: this is explicit
server access to the app's users, so ordinary group membership alone does not
grant access to emails. For example, this route lets a group's owner or admin
read one page of member contacts:

```ts
// api/groups/[id]/contacts.ts
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req);
  const groupId = sw.params.id;
  const group = await sw.groups.get(req, groupId);
  if (group.error) return Response.json({ error: group.error.code }, { status: group.error.status });
  if (group.data.role !== 'owner' && group.data.role !== 'admin') {
    return new Response('Only a group owner or admin may read contacts.', { status: 403 });
  }
  const cursor = new URL(req.url).searchParams.get('cursor') ?? undefined;
  const page = await sw.groups.members(req, groupId, { cursor });
  if (page.error) return Response.json({ error: page.error.code }, { status: page.error.status });
  const contacts = await sw.auth.server.listUsers({ ids: page.data.items.map(member => member.user_id) });
  return Response.json({ users: contacts.users, next_cursor: page.data.next_cursor });
}
```

Continue with the returned cursor for the next roster page. Role, roster and
contact reads are separate; recheck permission for each request. For a custom
organiser role, make that permission explicit in your handler. Sending a message
also needs your app's permission and recipient-consent rules.

`listUsers({ ids })` accepts up to 200 distinct user
IDs. `listUsers({ emails })` looks users up by exact address, up to
200 at a time: addresses are matched without regard to
case or surrounding spaces, never by partial match, and an address with no
account is simply absent from `users`. Check the caller before telling anyone
whether an address has an account. To find one known address, call
`listUsers({ emails: [email] })`: a single exact lookup. Don't page with
`{ limit, cursor }` and filter for the address. Paging is for work that needs
the whole directory, such as an admin user list or an export. Without IDs or emails,
`listUsers({ limit, cursor })` pages through the app's users:
default 50, maximum 200 per
page. Use one mode at a time. Each user has `id`, `email`,
`display_name`, `email_verified` and `created_at`; the result has
`users` and `next_cursor`. The contact records carry no app roles. Declare
`appRole()` or an endpoint role guard for staff authorization. If you need
an app-managed list of staff for assignment, track it with your app's
role-assignment workflow. Suspended, deleted and agent accounts are
excluded. Missing IDs are omitted. Unverified addresses carry
`email_verified: false`; filter them when the action requires verification.
A failed directory read throws `AUTH_DIRECTORY_UNAVAILABLE` rather than
returning an empty list. Look up live users from a deployed production
function or an ordinary verified cron, job or queue handler. A current
deployed preview looks up only its own users. Sign up in the preview or
use `somewhere preview user-add` before testing there. Row-bound jobs,
development and `run_code` refuse directory lookups.

## Listing users in scheduled work

Use `sw.auth.server.listUsers({ limit, cursor })` in an ordinary verified cron,
job or queue handler when the work needs every app user. Verify the invocation
before directory access. Process `users`, then pass `next_cursor` as `cursor`
until it is null; an empty page is not the termination signal. This is the
same directory contract and exclusions as `member-contacts` above. A separate
`known_users` table is unnecessary for discovering signed-up users; store only
app-specific preferences in your own tables. Check consent and address
verification before any email side effect.

## Joining users from your app data — the `auth_users` table

For the current user's identity, use `sw.auth.requireUser(req)`. For other
users' contact details, use the authorized server helper above. Keep app-specific
profile fields in declared tables with your app's access rules.

The `auth_users` mirror can be absent or stale and is outside managed
declarations. Raw SQL in a split project cannot read it. Use structured queries
for app data and verified identity for authorization.

To stop firing webhooks for the project:

```text
auth_webhook_delete({ project_id: "my-app" })
```

## Logout

Sign-out is already wired. `SignedInLayout` passes the `useSignOut()` hook from `src/auth/hooks.ts` to the button in `AppShell`. To sign out from somewhere else in your UI, use the same hook:

```tsx
// src/pages/SignOutButton.tsx
import { useSignOut } from '../auth/hooks';

export function SignOutButton() {
  const signOut = useSignOut();
  return (
    <>
      <button type="button" className="button button--quiet" onClick={() => void signOut.signOut()} disabled={signOut.pending}>
        {signOut.pending ? 'Signing out…' : 'Sign out'}
      </button>
      {signOut.error ? <p className="error" role="alert">{signOut.error}</p> : null}
    </>
  );
}
```

The app clears private pages as soon as sign-out starts. If the server can't confirm the sign-out, the sign-in page says so and offers to try again.

Update `@somewhere-cloud/sdk` and your lockfile to 0.14.1 or later,
then deploy your app to use the current sign-out handler and runtime.
If account revocation fails, the account cookies stay and sign-out remains
unconfirmed. A temporary failure can be retried; `SESSION_NOT_FOUND` or
`LOGOUT_REFRESH_REQUIRED` needs a new sign-in. If only visitor sign-out
fails, the account cookies clear and the HTTP response carries
`VISITOR_SIGN_OUT_UNCONFIRMED`. The SDK client reports an unconfirmed
sign-out; use the starter's status and recovery UI.

```ts
// api/sign-out.ts — cookie sessions (browser default): revoke + clear the cookies
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Use POST.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } });
  const result = await sw.auth.logoutWithCookie(req);   // { ok: true }
  return Response.json(result);
}
```

```ts
// api/token-sign-out.ts — token mode: pass the session_token and/or refresh_token
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Use POST.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } });
  const input: unknown = await req.json().catch(() => null);
  const { session_token } = (input ?? {}) as { session_token?: unknown };
  if (typeof session_token !== 'string') return Response.json({ error: 'session_token is required.' }, { status: 400 });
  const result = await sw.auth.logout({ session_token });   // { logged_out: true }
  return Response.json(result);
}
```

Revokes that session and its refresh tokens. An access token bound to the
revoked session is refused on its next verification. Other sessions stay
signed in; use the session-management tools to end them too.

## Visitors (before sign-in)

Lots of apps let a visitor do something useful before signing up (fill a
cart, send a message, save a draft). Declare it on the table instead of
tracking it by hand:

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { id, owner, schema, table, text } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  cart: table({ id: id(), sku: text() }, {
    scope: owner({ visitors: true }),
    client: { read: true, create: ['sku'], delete: true, identity: 'visitor' },
  }),
});
```

The platform gives each visitor a signed session cookie that lasts 30 days.
Rows the visitor creates belong to that session. When the visitor signs in,
the platform moves those rows to the account in one step, and that visitor
session can never hand rows over again, so a later account can never take an earlier
account's rows. A retry or a second tab is a no-op; logging out issues a fresh
visitor session. If visitor rows conflict with rows the account already has,
sign-in still completes and the account's existing data is unaffected; the visitor data stays stored under the visitor session the sign-in replaced and is not merged automatically — the browser cannot reach it again. No helper and no
manual migration step is needed for the declared browser
flow. Server code can still read the visitor with `sw.auth.anonSession(req)`
(it resolves the signed visitor session); the old `sw.auth.migrateAnon`
refuses with `MIGRATE_ANON_REMOVED` (400) because the hand-over is automatic on sign-in. Full contract: the
`declared-data` topic.

## Social OAuth

**Somewhere manages the Google OAuth client for your app.** Call
`await sw.auth.oauthStart('google', { redirect_uri })` with a return URL on
your project's subdomain or a verified custom domain attached to your
project. If the return URL is rejected, check the project subdomain or
attach and verify the custom domain.

Google sign-in only identifies the person: it asks Google for their name and
email, nothing else. To add events to a signed-in user's Google Calendar, use
`sw.connect.googleCalendar` (`docs({ topic: 'google-calendar' })`). It runs on
the platform's Google client too, so the same rule holds: do not create Google
credentials or write your own Google OAuth flow.

GitHub and Discord use the same project-scoped flow:

- `oauthStart('github', { redirect_uri })` / `githubExchange({ code })` /
  `githubCallbackWithCookie(req, redirectTo)`. Identity-only scopes:
  `read:user user:email`.
- `oauthStart('discord', { redirect_uri })` / `discordExchange({ code })` /
  `discordCallbackWithCookie(req, redirectTo)`. Identity-only scopes:
  `identify email`.

All three providers return to the customer app with the same one-time
`?code=` shape and exchange into the same project-scoped session. When a
provider's verified email is the first verification of an unverified
account's address, earlier sign-in methods are cleared (`docs({ topic: 'sw.auth', section: 'keeping-your-password' })`).

**Sign-in is bound to the browser that starts it.** `oauthStart` sets an
HttpOnly cookie for this attempt on your app's response and puts only its
challenge in the URL; the code is redeemed only by your server handling a
request from that same browser. A browser may hold 8 open attempts
(`OAUTH_START_LIMIT` after that). The old `googleUrl` / `githubUrl` /
`discordUrl` refuse with `OAUTH_START_REQUIRES_BINDING`, and a start without
the challenge is refused with `OAUTH_BINDING_REQUIRED`.

```ts
// api/auth-google.ts — start sign-in and send the user's browser to Google
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  // The callback below answers /api/auth-callback on this app's own host.
  const url = await sw.auth.oauthStart('google', { redirect_uri: new URL('/api/auth-callback', req.url).toString() });
  return Response.redirect(url, 302);
}
```

After the user approves, the platform handles the Google code
exchange and then bounces them back to your `redirect_uri` with a
short-lived authorization code and its public attempt id in the query string:

  https://your-app.somewhere.site/api/auth-callback?code=...&attempt=...

The JWT is never put in the URL. To get the JWT, your callback
function exchanges the code while handling that browser's request (the
runtime presents the cookie of the attempt that `attempt` names):

  const { token, user } = await sw.auth.googleExchange({ code, attempt });

Codes are single-use and expire after 60 seconds. A server that is not a
`sw` function keeps its own verifier in an HttpOnly cookie, sends only
`challenge` (base64url SHA-256 of the verifier) on the start URL, and posts
`{ code, attempt, verifier }` to the exchange, where `attempt` is the callback's
`?attempt=` (the first 16 characters of that challenge).

Typical callback function — one line with the cookie helper:

```ts
// api/auth-callback.ts
export default async function(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  // Reads ?code, exchanges it, sets the httpOnly session cookies,
  // and 302s home. Tokens never touch client JS.
  return sw.auth.googleCallbackWithCookie(req, '/');
}
```

Call `googleExchange` directly only when you manage tokens yourself
(native apps / non-browser clients) — it returns the same
`{ user, token, refresh_token, session_token }` shape as `login`.

REST uses `GET /v1/auth/{google|github|discord}` for the URL and
`POST /v1/auth/{provider}/exchange` for the code. MCP currently exposes
`auth_google_url`; deployed functions use the `sw.auth` helpers above.

## Common pattern: protected endpoint inside a deployed function

```ts
// api/posts.ts — uses the posts table from the db/schema.ts above
export default async function(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(req);
  if (!user) return Response.json({ error: 'Unauthorized' }, { status: 401 });

  // posts is owner() in db/schema.ts: rows are already scoped to this user.
  const posts = await sw.db.from('posts', { order: [['created_at', 'desc']] });
  return Response.json(posts.data);
}
```

That's it. No cookie parsing, no header slicing, no try/catch on
expired tokens — all of that lives inside `fromRequest`. If you find
yourself writing `req.headers.get('cookie')` inside a function, you
re-implemented something that already exists.

## Auth emails

Your app's password reset, email verification, sign-in link, invitation and
welcome emails are sent automatically from `noreply@somewhere.cloud` unless
the project has a verified sender domain. Every project gets working auth
without email setup.

On the platform address, auth emails always use the platform's built-in
templates, with your project's name in plain text (at most 40 characters,
without link prefixes such as `https://` or `www.`). Set the subject and HTML
for your app's auth emails with the email-templates API. Custom templates take
effect once the project has a verified sending domain. Those emails then come from `noreply@<your domain>`. You can save app
auth templates before that. The templates API's `custom_templates_apply`
field reports whether app auth email can use them.

Somewhere's own lifecycle emails, such as the welcome email for a new
Somewhere account, use saved lifecycle template overrides without requiring
a verified project sending domain.

Auth emails reach any address, with a limit on the platform address: each
project can send at most 30 auth emails per clock hour and 200 per UTC day to
people who have not verified their address with the project (sign-in links,
invitations, sign-up welcome and verification emails, password resets). Email to
the project owner and to users who have verified their address is not counted;
signing up alone does not verify an address. The same 30 per hour and 200 per
day also apply per account: all the projects one account owns share them, counted
the same way, so a second project is not a second allowance. Because the account
budget is shared, unverified sign-ups on one of your apps (anyone can type any
address into a sign-up form) count against all of them: once it is used up,
sign-in links, invitations and verification emails to new, unverified addresses
are refused on every project of the account until the window resets. The owner
and users who have verified their address are not counted, so existing users'
email sign-in codes keep arriving. A project that sends from its own verified
domain is outside the shared budget.
Past the limit the request is refused with `EMAIL_FIRST_CONTACT_LIMIT` (HTTP
429), and its message names the limit that was reached and whether it is the
project's or the account's. Requests that send in the background keep their
usual answer: sign-up still succeeds without its verification email (a later
code request answers 429), and a password reset still answers 200. The limit applies on every plan and
does not apply once the project sends from its own verified domain.

A project owned by a guest account (connected without signing up, not yet
claimed) can send 10 auth emails per UTC day to people other than its owner who
have not verified their address, on any sender, and 10 per day across all of the
guest account's projects together. Past that the request is refused with `EMAIL_GUEST_PROJECT_LIMIT` (HTTP
429). The owner claims the account by verifying their email, which lifts the
limit. Test inbox addresses are not counted.

Your app's own mail through sw.email.send
uses the same zero-setup sender but reaches only this project's users and its
owner; to bring in someone new, use `sw.auth.invite` (Invitations above).
Add a verified sender domain to email anyone else, to use your own From
address, or for marketing mail.

Email
pages.body:
Send transactional email from a function with `sw.email.send`. There's no
sender account or domain to set up first. Without a `from`, mail goes out
from your app's own address, `<your-app-subdomain>@somewhere.site`, labeled
with your project's name. Replies to that address land in your project
mailbox (`sw.mail.project.list()`). Sign-in emails
(verification, magic links, password reset) are sent for you. Every project
also gets a test inbox, so an agent can sign up, send and read the actual
message without a real mailbox.

The app's own address reaches your project's owner and the app users who
have verified their email address and signed in at least once. The platform
adds an unsubscribe line and one-click unsubscribe headers to every such
email; a user who unsubscribes is refused afterwards
(`RECIPIENT_UNSUBSCRIBED`). To email anyone else, verify your own sender
domain and pass `from`.

A guest account (connected without signing up) cannot send email, and neither
can the apps it deploys: `sw.email.send` and notification email answer `CLAIM_ACCOUNT_REQUIRED` (403) until the owner claims the
account by verifying their email.

Save first, await durable job admission, then respond. Queued is not sent; the signed handler records the email outcome. `sw.waitUntil` is not a runtime API.

If sending email is the action itself, await `sw.email.send` and show its
confirmed result. This is different from a notification after a saved change.

## Send from an authorized action

This function emails the signed-in user a copy of something they wrote. The
recipient is the user's own address, used only once they have verified it,
never one from the request body. A signed-in session shows who is asking; a
password sign-up can name any address, so the function checks
`user.email_verified` first (`sw.auth` → `email-verification`).

```ts
// api/email-me.ts
export default async function emailMe(
  request: Request,
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
): Promise<Response> {
  if (request.method !== 'POST') {
    return new Response('Use POST.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } });
  }

  const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(request);
  if (!user) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Sign in to email yourself.' }, { status: 401 });
  }
  if (user.email_verified !== true) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Verify your email address first.' }, { status: 403 });
  }

  const input: unknown = await request.json().catch(() => null);
  const fields = typeof input === 'object' && input !== null ? input : {};
  const title = 'title' in fields ? fields.title : undefined;
  const body = 'body' in fields ? fields.body : undefined;
  const requestId = 'request_id' in fields ? fields.request_id : undefined;
  if (typeof title !== 'string' || !title.trim() || title.length > 120
      || typeof body !== 'string' || body.length > 10000
      || typeof requestId !== 'string' || !/^[\w-]{8,64}$/.test(requestId)) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Send a title, a body and a request_id.' }, { status: 400 });
  }

  const allowance = await sw.rateLimit.check(`email-me:${user.id}`, 10, 3600);
  if (!allowance.allowed) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'You have sent a lot of email. Try again later.' }, { status: 429 });
  }

  try {
    const sent = await sw.email.send({
      to: user.email,
      subject: `Your note: ${title.trim()}`,
      text: body,
      // A retried request reuses request_id, so it gets the stored message instead of a second send.
      idempotency_key: `email-me:${user.id}:${requestId}`,
    });
    return Response.json({ id: sent.id, status: sent.status });
  } catch (error) {
    const code = error instanceof Error && 'code' in error ? String(error.code) : 'EMAIL_FAILED';
    const status = error instanceof Error && 'status' in error ? Number(error.status) : 0;
    // 422 and 429 mean the platform refused this request. Anything else may have reached the provider.
    if (status === 422 || status === 429) {
      return Response.json({ error: 'The email request was refused.', code }, { status });
    }
    return Response.json(
      { error: 'Could not confirm the email. Check its status before trying again.', code },
      { status: 502 },
    );
  }
}
```

The page sends a fresh `request_id` for each click, for example
`crypto.randomUUID()`, and reuses it when it retries that same click.

## Test it with the test inbox

Deploy, then sign in to your app with a sign-in link sent to an address at
your project's test domain: `ana@<your-subdomain>.test.somewhere.site`
(`sw.auth` → `magic-links`). Run the command below and open the link it
prints; that verifies the address. A password sign-up alone does not, and the
function above answers it with 403. Send yourself a note, then read what
arrived:

```bash
# Replace my-app with your app's subdomain.
somewhere email test-inbox ana@my-app.test.somewhere.site
```

The command prints each captured message, including its subject, text and any
sign-in link. Sending to a test address returns `status: 'captured'`. The
message is stored in the test inbox, never delivered, and doesn't count
toward your email allowance. Sign-up verification and magic-link emails to a
test address land in the same inbox, so a whole sign-in journey can be
checked this way.

## Read the result

`sw.email.send` waits for the email provider's answer. On a real address,
`status: 'sent'` means the provider accepted the message. Delivery is a later
event. `sw.email.status(id)` returns the message and its events (`delivered`,
`bounced`, `opened` and so on). A refused request throws a 422 or 429 error with a
`code`, such as `MANAGED_SENDER_RECIPIENT_NOT_A_USER` (the built-in sender only
reaches your verified users and owner) or `EMAIL_SUPPRESSED` (the address bounced or
complained earlier).

**When the outcome is unknown.** A throw of `EMAIL_DELIVERY_UNKNOWN`, or a
result with `status: 'pending'`, means the platform couldn't confirm the
provider accepted the message. Look it up first, with `sw.email.status(id)`
when you have its id, or in `sw.email.history()`. Sending again with the same `idempotency_key` and the same
message never creates a second send. It returns the stored message with
`duplicate: true`. For a send whose acceptance was never confirmed, it reports
`delivery_unknown` instead of sending again. Reusing a key for a different
message is refused with `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT`. When the email follows
work that already succeeded, such as a saved order, record the email's outcome
on that record instead of failing the whole request.

## Your own sender domain

The built-in sender needs no setup on any plan, and reaches your project's
verified users and owner. To email anyone else, such as guest customers or
newsletter readers, to take replies at your own address, or to send more than
the built-in sender's daily limit, verify a domain you own once and send from it.

Add and verify the domain from a terminal or with the MCP `api` tool.
Set all four records returned by the first call at your DNS host. The three
CNAME records enable signing, and the TXT record at `_somewhere.<your domain>`
proves the project added the domain. Run the verification call until it
reports the domain as verified.

```bash
somewhere api POST /v1/email/sender-domains -d '{"project_id":"my-app","domain":"yourapp.com"}'
# add every entry of dns_records ({ type, name, value }) at your DNS host, then:
somewhere api POST "/v1/email/sender-domains/yourapp.com/verify?project_id=my-app"
```

Both calls return the domain with `verified` and its `dns_records`. Repeat
the verify call until `verified` is `true`; while a record is missing, the
verify response's `action_required` says which. A domain is verified only while
all four records are found, so each check needs the TXT record in place.
Adding the same domain again returns the existing entry. Removing a domain and
adding it again gives it a new TXT value; replace the old TXT record. A domain
bought through the platform, or one using its nameservers, is added and
verified automatically, TXT record included.

Verified domains are also re-checked about once a day. A domain verified
before the TXT record existed gets its record in `dns_records` on its next
check, or within a day; add it within 7 days to keep sending verified. Once a
domain's record is 7 days old, a daily check that can't find it pauses sending
from the domain (`verified` becomes `false`) until the record is back and the
verify call finds it. If the domain's three signing (CNAME) records are
removed, the daily check pauses sending the same way until they are added
again and the verify call finds them. A domain bought through the platform, or
one using its nameservers, needs nothing: its records are added for it. If the DNS check itself
can't complete, nothing changes; the verify call returns 503
`SENDER_DOMAIN_DNS_CHECK_UNAVAILABLE`.

A sending domain belongs to one project. Adding a domain that another project
has set up for sending returns 409 `SENDER_DOMAIN_IN_USE`; it can be added
after it is removed there.

Adding, checking and removing a sender domain need editor access. Adding one
needs a paid plan on the project owner's account; on Free the call returns 402
`UPGRADE_REQUIRED`.

Once verified:

- **Send with `from`** on that domain, such as
  `from: 'Acme <hello@yourapp.com>'`, to any recipient (example under
  `sw.email.send(message)` below). Suppression, allowance and rate rules
  still apply.
- **Leaving out `from` still uses the built-in sender**, with its
  recipient limit.
- **Sign-in emails switch on their own** to `noreply@` your
  earliest-added verified domain.
- **Marketing sends need your domain.** `category: 'marketing'` without
  `from` returns `CUSTOM_SENDER_REQUIRED`. See "Marketing email" below
  for what else it needs.
- **A `from` that isn't ready is refused.** A domain not added returns
  `SENDER_DOMAIN_NOT_FOUND`, and one still pending returns
  `SENDER_DOMAIN_NOT_VERIFIED` (400).
- **To list or remove domains,** use
  `GET /v1/email/sender-domains?project_id=…` or
  `DELETE /v1/email/sender-domains/<domain>?project_id=…`. Removing
  changes nothing at your DNS host.

To bring in someone who isn't a user yet, use `sw.auth.invite`
(`sw.auth` → `invitations`).

## Marketing email

Newsletters, announcements and offers go with `category: 'marketing'`.
Each marketing send needs four things:

- **`from` on your verified sender domain** (otherwise
  `CUSTOM_SENDER_REQUIRED`).
- **A `topic`**, one of the ids below (otherwise `EMAIL_TOPIC_REQUIRED`).
- **An `idempotency_key`** (otherwise `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED`).
- **Your postal address on the project**, set once as
  `marketing_postal_address`. Without it the send returns
  `MARKETING_POSTAL_ADDRESS_REQUIRED` and nothing is sent.

Set the address with `project_update`, or the API:

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/projects/<project_id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SOMEWHERE_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"marketing_postal_address": "1 Main St, Springfield, IL 62701, USA"}'
```

It is read back on the project. `null` clears it. Up to 300 characters;
line breaks become commas.

**The footer.** The platform adds a footer to every marketing email. App
code cannot remove or change it. It shows:

- your `marketing_postal_address`;
- an "Email preferences or unsubscribe" link to a page where the
  recipient picks topics or unsubscribes from all.

The message also gets one-click unsubscribe headers. After a recipient
turns a topic off, sends on that topic return `RECIPIENT_UNSUBSCRIBED`.

**Topics.** The recipient sees these labels on the preferences page:

| `topic` | Label |
|---|---|
| `project-updates` | Product updates |
| `milestones` | News |
| `announcements` | Announcements |
| `founder-notes` | Notes from the team |

```ts
// api/_lib/newsletter.ts — the address comes from your own subscriber records.
export function sendNewsletter(
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
  issue: { id: string; subject: string; html: string },
  subscriber: { id: string; email: string },
): Promise<SomewhereEmailSendResult> {
  return sw.email.send({
    to: subscriber.email,
    from: 'News <news@yourapp.com>', // a verified sender domain on this project
    subject: issue.subject,
    html: issue.html,
    category: 'marketing',
    topic: 'announcements',
    idempotency_key: `newsletter:${issue.id}:${subscriber.id}`,
  });
}
```

Transactional email (the default category) needs no postal address.

## sw.email.send(message)

```ts
// api/_lib/order-email.ts — call it from a handler that already checked who
// receives this; the address comes from your saved order, never the request.
export function sendOrderShipped(
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
  order: { id: string; email: string; trackingNumber: string },
): Promise<SomewhereEmailSendResult> {
  return sw.email.send({
    to: order.email,
    subject: 'Your order shipped',
    text: `Tracking: ${order.trackingNumber}`, // or html, or both
    idempotency_key: `order-shipped:${order.id}`,
  });
}
```

The send result's `message_id` is Somewhere's own identifier for the send.
To thread a reply, read the `Message-ID` header of the message your app
received and pass it as `in_reply_to`. Pass the earlier `Message-ID` values
in the thread as a `references` array, in order, ending with the parent.
Preserve the angle brackets in each value.

Test-inbox captures show their own `Message-ID` and any `In-Reply-To` and
`References` values in `headers`. To see them in the CLI, run
`somewhere email test-inbox <address> --json`.

With no `from`, the message goes from your app's own address,
`<your-app-subdomain>@somewhere.site`, with the project name as its sender
label. The response names the sender mode and address. It can only email the
project's owner and app users who have verified their email address with
this project and signed in at least once; a pending sign-in or an unverified
sign-up does not count. Other recipients return
`MANAGED_SENDER_RECIPIENT_NOT_A_USER`; verify your own sender domain for
outreach. The platform adds a one-line unsubscribe footer and one-click
unsubscribe headers; after a user unsubscribes, sends to them return
`RECIPIENT_UNSUBSCRIBED`. Sign-in emails are not affected. Replies to the
app's address are recorded in your project mailbox; read them with
`sw.mail.project.list()`. If the app draws many complaints or bounces, its
sending pauses (`EMAIL_PROJECT_PAUSED`) without affecting other apps.
Temporary (unclaimed) apps cannot send. Its `reply_to` must be the project's
owner or a verified user of the app, the people it may already email (for
example, a booking confirmation to a visitor that replies to the host); any
other address returns `REPLY_TO_NEEDS_OWN_DOMAIN`. Each
project can send at most 500 such emails per UTC day on every plan
(`EMAIL_SHARED_SENDER_DAILY_LIMIT`). Pass `from` to use your own verified
sender domain, where `reply_to` takes any address and this daily limit does not apply:

```ts
// api/_lib/order-email-own-domain.ts
export function sendOrderShippedFromYourDomain(
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
  order: { id: string; email: string; trackingNumber: string },
): Promise<SomewhereEmailSendResult> {
  return sw.email.send({
    to: order.email,
    from: 'notifications@yourapp.com', // a verified sender domain on this project
    reply_to: 'support@yourapp.com', // optional
    subject: 'Your order shipped',
    text: `Tracking: ${order.trackingNumber}`,
    idempotency_key: `order-shipped:${order.id}`,
  });
}
```

An explicit `from` must match a verified sender domain on this project.
Callers cannot explicitly name a platform domain. The managed default is for
transactional email; add a verified sender domain for your own branding and
marketing email. The plan's email allowance and send rate limit apply to both.
Limit: the Free tier has a daily + monthly send cap; paid tiers are metered
monthly. Read the current per-tier caps from /v1/pricing instead of copying
them into project policy or application code.

The platform sends your app's password reset, verification and welcome emails
automatically. See [Auth emails](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.auth#auth-emails)
for app auth templates and Somewhere's own lifecycle emails.
On the platform address each project, and each account across all of its
projects, can send at most 30 auth emails per hour and 200 per day to people
who have not verified their address (`EMAIL_FIRST_CONTACT_LIMIT`, see
`sw.auth` → auth emails); a project's own verified domain has no such limit.
The rules in "Sending reputation" below apply to them.

### Attachments

Pass up to 3 small files as `attachments: [{ filename, content_type?, content }]`,
with `content` in base64. They can total at most 256 KB. The filename
extension must be one of `ics`, `pdf`, `png`, `jpg`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `webp`,
`csv`, `txt` or `json`. `content_type` defaults from the extension; for `.ics`
it is `text/calendar; charset=UTF-8; method=REQUEST`, so a calendar invite
shows its accept button in Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail. A refused attachment
returns `VALIDATION_ERROR` naming the rule.

```ts
await sw.email.send({
  to: booking.email,
  subject: 'Your call is booked',
  text: 'The invite is attached.',
  attachments: [{ filename: 'invite.ics', content: btoa(icsText) }],
  idempotency_key: `booked:${booking.id}`,
});
```

## Result and errors

```ts
// api/_lib/order-email-result.ts — read the result's status; a refused send throws
export async function sendOrderShippedOnce(
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
  order: { id: string; email: string; trackingNumber: string },
): Promise<{ id: string; status: SomewhereEmailSendResult['status']; replay: boolean }> {
  const sent = await sw.email.send({
    to: order.email,
    subject: 'Your order shipped',
    text: `Tracking: ${order.trackingNumber}`,
    idempotency_key: `order-shipped:${order.id}`,
  });
  // → { id, tracking_id, message_id, status, duplicate?, sender?, test_inbox? }
  return { id: sent.id, status: sent.status, replay: sent.duplicate === true };
}
```

A new send returns one of three `status` values:
- `sent`: the provider accepted the message. The call waits for that.
  Accepted is not delivered.
- `pending`: that step was interrupted. Check `sw.email.status(id)`, or
  resend only with the same `idempotency_key`.
- `captured`: the recipient is this project's own test address, so the
  message was stored in the test inbox and not delivered (see "Test inbox"
  below). The result has `test_inbox: { address, delivered: false }` and no
  `tracking_id`.

Repeating an `idempotency_key` returns the stored result with
`duplicate: true` and the same `id`. Its `status` is that message's
current state: any of the three above, a later delivery state (`delivered`,
`opened`, `clicked`, `bounced`, `complained`), or `suppressed`,
`preference_blocked`, `delivery_unknown`, or `failed`. Check `status`,
not only that nothing threw. Do not gate follow-up work on
`status === 'sent'` alone: a captured test send and a replay of a delivered
message are both successful sends.

A message that is not sent THROWS an Error carrying `.code` and `.status`:
`MANAGED_SENDER_RECIPIENT_NOT_A_USER`, `EMAIL_SUPPRESSED`,
`RECIPIENT_UNDELIVERABLE_DOMAIN` (see "Sending reputation"),
`EMAIL_DAILY_LIMIT` / `EMAIL_MONTHLY_LIMIT` (422), `RATE_LIMITED` (429), or
`EMAIL_DELIVERY_UNKNOWN` (502 — acceptance unconfirmed; check
`sw.email.status(id)` or resend only with the same `idempotency_key`).
When the email is a side effect of work that already succeeded (a saved
row), catch the error and record it on that row instead of failing the
request — see https://somewhere.cloud/docs/recipe-signed-in-app.txt.

For the signed-in user's address, use
`const user = await sw.auth.requireUser(req)`, then `user.email`. To contact
other users, authorize the sending action in your function, then use
`sw.auth.server.listUsers({ ids })` for the permitted recipients' addresses.
For group contacts, check the caller's role and pass the IDs from
`sw.groups.members`; see `sw.auth` → **Member contacts** for a complete example.
Apply your app's recipient-consent rules and the sender requirements above.
For a fixed notification recipient such as the app owner, keep the configured
address in an env var.

## Sending to many recipients

Each send waits for its own result, so awaiting them one after another adds
up: five sends in a loop take about five times as long as one. Sends from
one handler can run at the same time. Start them together in groups of five
and give each its own `idempotency_key`, so a retried request never emails
anyone twice:

```ts
// api/_lib/send-round.ts — members come from your own records, never the request.
export interface Member { id: string; email: string }
export interface Round { id: string; subject: string; text: string }

/** Sends in groups of five; returns members whose send was refused or not confirmed. */
export async function sendRound(
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
  round: Round,
  members: readonly Member[],
): Promise<{ id: string; code: string; email_id?: string }[]> {
  const unsent: { id: string; code: string; email_id?: string }[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < members.length; i += 5) {
    await Promise.all(members.slice(i, i + 5).map(async (m) => {
      try {
        const sent = await sw.email.send({
          to: m.email,
          subject: round.subject,
          text: round.text,
          idempotency_key: `round-${round.id}-${m.id}`,
        });
        // pending: acceptance unconfirmed; check sw.email.status(sent.id) before any resend.
        if (sent.status === 'pending') unsent.push({ id: m.id, code: 'PENDING', email_id: sent.id });
      } catch (error) {
        const code = error instanceof Error && 'code' in error ? String(error.code) : 'EMAIL_FAILED';
        unsent.push({ id: m.id, code });
      }
    }));
  }
  return unsent;
}
```

Five at once finish in about the time of one. The send rate limit still
applies: about 60 sends a minute for the account that owns the project,
shared by all of its projects. Above that a send throws `RATE_LIMITED`
(429). Your plan's email allowance applies too. For larger lists, or when the
caller should not wait, run the fan-out in a job (`sw.jobs`), one job per batch of recipients.

## Test inbox

Addresses `<anything>@<project-subdomain>.test.somewhere.site` never reach a
real mailbox. Mail to this project's own test addresses is stored in its test
inbox instead. That covers both kinds of mail:
- the project's AUTH email (verification, magic link, password reset): sign
  up with a test address, then read the inbox;
- your own `sw.email.send` to that address. It returns `status: 'captured'`
  with `test_inbox: { address, delivered: false }` and no `tracking_id`.
  With the platform-managed sender, the address must belong to one of this
  project's users (for example, one who signed up with it, verified or not) or
  the owner. Otherwise the send is refused with
  `MANAGED_SENDER_RECIPIENT_NOT_A_USER`.

Read it with `somewhere email test-inbox <address>` (or
`sw.email.inbox(address)`) →
`{ address, messages: [{ id, to, subject, text, html, magic_link, verification_code, attachments, created_at }] }`,
where `attachments` is `[{ filename, content_type, content }]` (base64, empty when none).
`verification_code` is the code an auth message carries (the 6-digit email
verification or sign-in code), or `null`. A verified test user therefore
takes three calls and no HTML parsing: sign up with a test address, read
`messages[0].verification_code`, then verify with it
(`POST /api/auth/verify-email { code }` in the app's session). Verification
is the real flow; only the mailbox is a test one.
A captured send does not appear in `sw.email.history()` or the project's
sent-email list, and it does not count toward the email allowance. Repeating
its `idempotency_key` returns the same `id` with `duplicate: true` and
stores no second copy. Captures are kept for 7 days, up to 500 messages or
10 MiB per project; beyond that a send throws `TEST_INBOX_FULL` (422) with the
time the oldest capture expires.

A test address that belongs to ANOTHER project is refused:
`sw.email.send` throws `EMAIL_TEST_ADDRESS_NOT_OWNED` (422), and reading
its inbox fails with `VALIDATION_ERROR`. A send to any other domain is an
ordinary real send. `status: 'sent'` means the provider accepted the
message, not that it was delivered. To prove delivery, send to a real mailbox
you can read, or check the delivery events from `sw.email.status(id)`.

## Sending reputation

Every project shares the platform's sending reputation, so these rules apply
to all mail, including the auth emails the platform sends for you. Each
refusal is a typed event in the project's logs (`data.code`).

- Reserved domains are never sent to. An address at example.com, example.net,
  example.org or any subdomain of them, or ending in .example, .test,
  .invalid, .localhost or .local, cannot receive mail. An auth email
  (verification, magic link, password reset, welcome) to such an address is
  held in this project's test inbox under that exact address, so you can
  still read the code or link: `somewhere email test-inbox alice@example.com`.
  Your own `sw.email.send` to one throws `RECIPIENT_UNDELIVERABLE_DOMAIN`.
  Log event: `RECIPIENT_UNDELIVERABLE_DOMAIN` (`test_inbox: true` when held).
  Use a test inbox address for automated sign-ups.
- The platform does not send to app addresses. An address at an app's
  own host, such as `anyone@<subdomain>.somewhere.site` (any name under
  somewhere.site, or under any other app-host domain the platform owns), is
  not given a mailbox, so mail to it is refused before delivery and is not
  held in the test inbox. Its code or link is not delivered or stored in the
  test inbox. Requests that report the send answer `EMAIL_SUPPRESSED` (422):
  a magic link, an invitation, a requested verification code and an email
  sign-in code. Requests that send in the background keep their usual answer:
  a password reset still answers 200 for every address, and sign-up still
  succeeds while its welcome and verification emails are refused. Either way
  the refusal is in the project's logs. `sw.email.send` throws
  `RECIPIENT_UNDELIVERABLE_DOMAIN`. Log event:
  `RECIPIENT_UNDELIVERABLE_DOMAIN` with `reason: 'platform_app_host'`.
  The test inbox (`@<subdomain>.test.somewhere.site`) and the platform's own
  addresses at somewhere.site and somewhere.cloud are not affected. Any
  other domain is sent normally; the platform does not look up whether it
  accepts mail.
- Bounces and spam complaints stop further sends to that address. A permanent
  bounce pauses it for 30 days, a temporary one (such as a full mailbox) for
  24 hours, and a spam complaint permanently. The log event is
  `EMAIL_RECIPIENT_SUPPRESSED` with `reason` (`bounce`, `soft_bounce`,
  `complaint`) and `expires_at`. A send to a paused address is refused
  before delivery with `EMAIL_SUPPRESSED` (422 for auth email) and logged
  as `EMAIL_SUPPRESSED`.
- Password resets, magic links and verification emails do not consume your
  plan's email allowance and still send when ordinary email has used it up.
  Recipient suppression and sign-in abuse protections remain in force. Welcome
  mail and `sw.email.send` use the regular allowance shown by
  `limits.emails_per_day` and `limits.emails_per_month` in /v1/pricing.
  Messages captured in the test inbox use no email allowance.
- A project whose own mail bounces or is reported as spam too often is paused.
  Over a rolling 24 hours, once it has sent at least 50 messages, 5% permanent
  bounces or 0.1% spam reports (and at least 3 of either) pauses the project's
  sending: every send, auth email included, answers `EMAIL_PROJECT_PAUSED`
  (auth endpoints 503, `sw.email.send` 422) and nothing reaches a mailbox.
  Test inbox addresses keep working. The owner gets one email and the log event
  `EMAIL_PROJECT_PAUSED`; sending resumes on its own once the rate recovers
  (log event `EMAIL_PROJECT_RESUMED`). Check the state with
  `email_reputation({ project_id })`.
  - **Mail from the platform's shared address** also pauses on counts, whatever
    the volume: 2 spam reports or 5 permanent bounces of that mail in
    24 hours (`reason`: `complaint_count`,
    `bounce_count`). This pause stops only the project's mail from the shared
    address; mail from its own verified domain continues. It resumes on its own
    once the last 24 hours are back under both
    counts. A message's bounce or complaint is counted once.
  - **Scope:** one spam complaint alone does not pause a project; it stops mail to
    that one address. A rate pause or a manual pause covers real delivery from
    the project, including sign-in emails and mail from your own sender domain.
    Test inboxes remain available.
  - **The platform can pause a project by hand** (`reason`: `manual`). The owner
    gets the same email. A manual pause does not lift on its own; only the
    platform team resumes it.
  - **No resume button.** While delivery is paused, older events leave the
    rolling window. The platform rechecks paused projects and resumes sending
    when the reputation threshold clears. Reduce future complaints with an opt-out
    link in every mailing and by skipping `sw.email.bounces()`
    addresses.

## Delivery health (scrub bounces before sending)

The email provider posts bounce + complaint webhooks; the platform records
every event on the project automatically. Two MCP tools expose them:

- email_events_list({ project_id, limit?, offset? }) — recent sends
  with their latest event (sent | delivered | opened | clicked |
  bounced | complained | delivery_delayed). Build an audit view or
  spot a bounce spike after a blast.

- email_bounces_list({ project_id, days?, limit? }) — deduplicated
  recipients that bounced or complained inside the window
  (default 30 days, max 365). One row per address with last_status,
  last_at, occurrences.

From INSIDE a function, scrub before you send (no MCP round-trip):
- `sw.email.checkSuppression(address)` → `{ address, suppressed, status, last_at, occurrences }` — is this ONE recipient dead (bounced or complained)? Check it before `sw.email.send`.
- `sw.email.bounces({ days?, limit? })` → `{ bounces, window_days, limit }`.
  The `bounces` array contains the dead-address rows; the other fields report
  the effective query window and cap.

For a single message's full timeline use email_status({ id }).

## Delivery and engagement events

Every message sent through sw.email records delivery, open, and click events
when the recipient's inbox reports them. Recent-message lists include sent,
delivered, opened, and clicked counts; email_status returns the full timeline
for one tracking id. Opens are approximate because some inboxes block images.

**Before every send loop, scrub against email_bounces_list.**
Mailing a dead address repeatedly is the single fastest way to land
your verified domain in a spam folder. Inside a function, skip the addresses
in the returned list first. That list is bounded; every send also checks the
address's current suppression status:

```ts
// api/_lib/send-to-reachable.ts
import { sendRound, type Member, type Round } from './send-round';

/** Skips addresses in the returned recent bounce list, then sends. */
export async function sendToReachable(
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
  round: Round,
  members: readonly Member[],
): Promise<{ id: string; code: string; email_id?: string }[]> {
  const { bounces } = await sw.email.bounces({ days: 60, limit: 1000 });
  const bounced = new Set(bounces.map((row) => row.address.toLowerCase()));
  return sendRound(sw, round, members.filter((m) => !bounced.has(m.email.toLowerCase())));
}
```

pages.title: sw.mail — Mailboxes (inside deployed functions)
pages.body:
Read, search and send the mail your app receives. Every email in or out of a
mailbox is stored as one record with its conversation, status and attachments.

- `sw.mail.project` is the project's mailbox. Replies to your app's own
  address (`<your-app-subdomain>@somewhere.site`) and mail to addresses
  registered on the project land here.
- `sw.mail` is the signed-in app user's own mailbox. The platform picks it
  from the verified session, so no method takes a user id and one user can
  never read another's mail. Without a signed-in user it throws
  `AUTH_REQUIRED`.

`sw.mail.project` carries project authority, like `sw.db.server`: check the
caller before you return project mail or send from it.

