```ts
// api/support/inbox.ts: the support team's view of the project mailbox
export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'required',
  handler: async ({ user }, sw) => {
    if (user.role !== 'admin') return Response.json({ error: 'forbidden' }, { status: 403 });
    const { emails } = await sw.mail.project.list({ limit: 20 });
    return { emails };
  },
});
```

Every method below exists on both `sw.mail` and `sw.mail.project`. Failures
throw with the platform's error code; an email id from another mailbox reads
as not found.

## Read mail

- `list({ limit?, before?, conversation? })` returns
  `{ emails, mailbox }`, newest first, 50 by default (up to 200). Each email has `id`,
  `direction` (`'in'` or `'out'`), `from`, `to`, `subject`, `status`,
  `conversation`, `created_at` (epoch ms) and `attachments` (a count). Pass
  the oldest `created_at` as `before` for the next page, or a `conversation`
  to read one thread, oldest first. A mailbox that has never received mail answers
  `{ emails: [], mailbox: null }`.
- `get(id)` returns `{ email }` with the full record: `text`, `html`,
  `from_addr`, `to_addrs`, `cc_addrs`, `reply_to`, `message_id`, `status`,
  `attachments` (`{ n, name, type, size }`), `headers` (raw header lines,
  or `null` for older mail) and `checks` (`{ spf, dkim, dmarc }` as the
  receiving server recorded them, or `null`).
- `attachment(id, n)` returns a `Response` with the file and a download
  `Content-Disposition`. Return it to the browser as is. Check `res.ok`: a
  missing attachment answers 404 rather than throwing.

```ts
const { email } = await sw.mail.get(id);
if (email.attachments.length) return sw.mail.attachment(id, email.attachments[0].n);
```

## Search

`search(text, { limit? })` returns `{ results, searched }`: emails that
contain every word of `text`, newest first, 50 by default (up to 200). Each result has `id`, `subject`, `from_addr`,
`to_addrs`, `created_at`, `conversation`, `has_attachments`, `direction` and
`status`. `searched` names the mailbox that answered. Empty `text` is a
`VALIDATION_ERROR`.

## Send and reply

`send({ from, to, subject, text?, html?, reply_to_email_id?, idempotency_key?, once?, unless_replied? })`
returns `{ email_id, status, duplicate }`.

- `from` is an address registered in this mailbox, on a domain the project
  has verified for sending (`somewhere docs sw.email`).
- `to` is one address or a list of up to 10.
- `reply_to_email_id` replies to an email in this mailbox; the reply joins
  its conversation.
- `idempotency_key` makes a retry return the first result with
  `duplicate: true`.
- `once: '<step>'` sends this step to one recipient at most once;
  `unless_replied: true` sends nothing to someone this mailbox has received
  mail from and answers `status: 'skipped'`, `skipped: 'replied'`. A
  complete follow-up example: `somewhere docs recipe-email`.

```ts
const { email } = await sw.mail.project.get(id);
await sw.mail.project.send({
  from: 'support@example.com',
  to: email.from_addr,
  subject: 'Re: ' + email.subject,
  text: 'Thanks, we are on it.',
  reply_to_email_id: email.id,
});
```

For one-off notifications to your app's users, `sw.email.send` needs no
mailbox or address setup.

## Addresses

To receive at your own domain, turn on inbound mail for it
(`somewhere docs domains`), then register addresses on its `receiving_host`:

- `addresses.create(address)` returns `{ address, mailbox, sends_as }`.
  `sw.mail.project.addresses.create` adds it to the project mailbox;
  `sw.mail.addresses.create` gives the signed-in user their own address.
  An address is `name@host` without a `+` tag and must not already be
  registered (`ALREADY_EXISTS`).
- `addresses.list()` returns `{ addresses: [{ address, signs_as_user_id }] }`.
- `addresses.remove(address)` returns `{ removed }`.

pages.title: AI and search
Search — managed document search and named indexes
pages.body:
> Named-index writes also have a reported name-length failure: creation can
> succeed while upsert returns `UPSTREAM_ERROR`. Successful creation alone
> does not verify an index. The exact supported length is under investigation.

Managed search makes each user's own documents searchable by meaning. The
platform extracts the text, splits it into passages, indexes them, and keeps
them current. Rewriting a file replaces its passages, and deleting it removes
them.

## Managed file search — point it at a file (inside functions)

Declare per-user search once in `db/schema.ts`, next to your tables and file
collections:

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { owner, schema } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({}, { search: owner() });
```

Without this declaration, `sw.search.add` and string-form
`sw.search.query` are refused with `SEARCH_NOT_DECLARED` (409).

From a signed-in request:

```js
await sw.search.add('/documents/<file id>/report.pdf')
const { results } = await sw.search.query('How do I rotate the signing key?')
```

`add(path)` publishes one file owned by the signed-in user and returns `searchable: "shortly"`; a newly added document becomes searchable shortly after the add returns, which can take a few minutes on a new index. It refuses a file the user doesn't own. String `query`
searches only what that user added. Ownership comes from the session and is
never an argument. Each result carries `content`, `score` and a `source`
naming the file and the passage's location in it. Without a verified user,
`sw.search.add` and string-form `sw.search.query` throw `AUTH_REQUIRED`
(401). For server work without a signed-in user, use a named index and authorize
access in your function.

`sw.search.remove({ index, ids })` removes items from a named index. It does
not accept a file path and is not the inverse of managed `add(path)`. Deleting
a managed file removes its passages; do not delete a file merely to un-index it.

In a function, `sw.search.remove` takes any number of ids. More than 1000
are removed in sequential batches of 1000, and success returns
`{ index, removed, item_count, batches }`. The `removed` count is the number
of items deleted. An already-absent ID contributes zero. The first batch that
fails stops the rest. If any earlier batches completed, the error is
`SEARCH_REMOVE_PARTIAL`. Its `partial` gives the confirmed deletion count
(`removed`), the IDs confirmed absent after their batch (`removed_ids`),
the IDs in an unconfirmed batch (`unconfirmed_ids`), and the remaining IDs
(`not_removed_ids`). Check which
unconfirmed ids still exist before removing them again, and delete the record
or file the items describe only after the removal has succeeded.

Direct `POST /v1/search/remove` and the MCP `search_delete` accept at most
1000 ids per request; a longer list is refused with 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`
before anything is removed. A `SEARCH_REMOVE_UNCONFIRMED` answer means that
request's outcome is unknown. One `upsert` call accepts up to 100 items.

The object forms `sw.search.upsert({ index, items })` and
`sw.search.query({ index, query })` work on named indexes for content you
compose yourself. A named index is shared across the project: your function
decides which items each caller may see.

## File search — sw.fs.dev.search (developer run_code only)

Full-text search across the project's text files. Used by code agents
to grep code, search docs, find TODOs.

Available in developer run_code. File search, glob and diff are unavailable
in deployed functions, including the server file view. As a `run_code` input:

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-app",
  "code": "export default async function (sw) { return await sw.fs.dev.search({ path: '/src/', query: 'TODO', limit: 50 }) }"
}
```

The full contract is in `file-tools` → `search-glob-and-diff`. Per-project full-text index,
kept in sync automatically on every fs write/delete/move/replace.

## Semantic search — named indexes

Vector search for product features (FAQ search, semantic
recommendations, RAG retrieval). Embeddings are 768-dim
(cosine distance). Each project can hold many named indexes.

Manage indexes over MCP with `search_index_create`, `search_index_list`,
`search_upsert`, `search_query` and `search_delete`. Inside a deployed
function, use `sw.search` — the platform handles the connection and project
scope. See "From inside a function" below.

## search_index_create({ project_id, name })
Idempotent — returns the existing index if name already exists.
Returns { name, project_id, dimensions, distance_metric, created_at }.

## search_index_list({ project_id })
Lists every index on the project: [{ name, item_count, created_at }].

## search_delete({ project_id, index, ids? })
Delete from a search index. Pass ids (a JSON array of item id
strings) to remove specific items, up to 1000 per call (more is refused
before anything is removed); omit ids to drop the entire
index AND all items in it (irreversible).

## search_upsert({ project_id, index, items })
Insert or replace items. items is a JSON array of:
  { id, content, metadata? }

  search_upsert({
    project_id: "my-app",
    index: "faqs",
    items: [
      { id: "faq-1", content: "How do I reset my password?", metadata: { category: "account" } },
      { id: "faq-2", content: "Where can I see my billing history?", metadata: { category: "billing" } }
    ]
  })

content is embedded server-side — you never compute embeddings
yourself. metadata is returned alongside results but NOT searched.
Max 100 items per call.

## search_query({ project_id, index, query, limit? })
Returns top N matches by cosine similarity:
  { results: [{ id, score, content, metadata }] }

  search_query({
    project_id: "my-app",
    index: "faqs",
    query: "I forgot my login",
    limit: 5
  })

Score is 0–1. Higher is closer. Limit defaults to 10, max 100.

## From inside a function — sw.search.*

Same surface, same args, no API key. Use sw.search inside a deployed
function — the platform binding handles auth and project scope.

```ts
// api/_lib/faq-index.ts — server helpers over the project-wide 'faqs' index.
// A named index is shared across the project, so the calling handler has
// already decided who may change it and which results each caller may see.

// Index management
export async function setUpFaqIndex(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<string[]> {
  await sw.search.createIndex('faqs')
  const { indexes } = await sw.search.listIndexes()
  return indexes.map((index) => index.name)
}

export async function dropFaqIndex(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<void> {
  await sw.search.deleteIndex('faqs')
}

// Upsert
export async function saveFaq(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, id: string, content: string, category: string): Promise<number> {
  const r = await sw.search.upsert({
    index: 'faqs',
    items: [{ id, content, metadata: { category } }],
  })
  return r.upserted
}

// Query
export async function findFaqs(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, question: string): Promise<{ id: string; score: number; content: string }[]> {
  const { results } = await sw.search.query({ index: 'faqs', query: question, limit: 5 })
  return results.map(({ id, score, content }) => ({ id, score, content }))
}

// Remove specific items
export async function removeFaq(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, id: string): Promise<number> {
  const r = await sw.search.remove({ index: 'faqs', ids: [id] })
  return r.removed
}
```

For example, `saveFaq(sw, 'faq-1', 'How do I reset my password?', 'account')`
then `findFaqs(sw, 'I forgot my login')`. Pass a single string to
`removeFaq(sw, 'faq-1')`. The write helpers return the count for that
operation. Removing an already-absent FAQ returns zero. `item_count` is the
number of items in the index after the write.

## When to use which
- Searching files (code, markdown, configs in your project) from developer run_code → sw.fs.dev.search
- Semantic / "find similar meaning" over your app's content → sw.search.* (or search_index_* MCP)
- Searching log bodies or analytics → use sw.logs / sw.analytics.query

## What NOT to do
- Don't put PII in metadata if you don't have to — it's stored with
  the embeddings.
- Don't reindex a whole catalog on every write; batch upserts of 100.
- Don't expect exact-match — semantic search ranks by meaning, not
  keyword overlap.

pages.title: Somewhere agent loop — sw.agent
pages.body:
`sw.agent` runs bounded model-and-tool work in your deployed function.
Use `run` to wait inline; it stays in the current invocation and is not a
resumable background job. Use `start` for checkpointed durable work with
`status` and `cancel`. Durable callbacks re-enter the then-current deployed
function, so a run can cross a deploy; tools and hooks must be recreated there.

Set `maxSteps` and `maxSpendCents`; spend is checked between billed calls,
so one call can cross the cap. On the project's own provider key the platform
records no cost, so `maxSpendCents` never stops the run: bound it with
`maxSteps` and `maxTokens` (see `sw.ai` → provider credentials). `prepareStep`, `onStepFinish`, and `stopWhen`
control each step. Durable tool calls carry a stable `toolCallId` for your
side-effect deduplication; this does not make side effects exactly once.
Cancellation prevents later steps and cannot undo work already running.

Start with `recipe-ai-agent`; see `recipe-escalation` and `recipe-multi-chat`
for model escalation and conversation UI. History and compaction use the
`sw.ai` conversation options passed through each step.

```js
const result = await sw.agent.run({
  prompt: 'Summarize these notes: the delivery arrived, and the invoice is pending.',
  maxSteps: 4,
  maxSpendCents: 25,
})
console.log(result.text, result.completion_reason)
```

## Calling forms

```js
await sw.agent(options)          // durable compatibility form
await sw.agent.run(options)      // inline: wait for the terminal result
await sw.agent.start(options)    // durable: return after creating the run
await sw.agent.status(agentId)   // read durable status/result
await sw.agent.cancel(agentId)   // request durable cancellation
```

The direct call and `.start` both create durable work. They use the same step
engine but intentionally return different limit-field names:

```js
const direct = await sw.agent(options)
// { agent_id: string, status: string, max_turns: number }

const started = await sw.agent.start(options)
// { agent_id: string, status: string, max_steps: number }
```

Both durable forms require `options.model`. Use the returned `agent_id` with
`.status` and `.cancel`. `sw.agent.run` may omit a model and use the same
model default as `sw.ai.chat`.

## Inline execution: sw.agent.run(options)

`run` performs model calls and tool calls in the current function invocation,
then returns the terminal model response plus agent metrics:

```js
// Enumerable fields added by sw.agent:
result.iterations
result.tool_calls_made
result.total_input_tokens
result.total_output_tokens
result.completion_reason

// Present but deliberately non-enumerable:
result.steps
result.total_cost_cents
```

The rest of the terminal object is the final `sw.ai.chat` response, including
fields such as `text`, `content`, `provider`, `model`, `usage`, and
`stop_reason` when the model response supplies them. Because `steps` and
`total_cost_cents` are non-enumerable, object spread, `Object.keys`, and
`JSON.stringify` omit them even though direct property access works.

Completion reasons are `model_done`, `output_truncated`, `max_steps`,
`max_turns` when only that limit name was supplied, `stop_when`,
`cost_pending`, or the non-empty string returned by `stopWhen`.
`cost_pending` fires when a spend cap is configured and a delivered step's
cost is still pending: the loop returns that step and issues no further
model request against an unknown total. A pending step makes
`total_cost_cents` null — unknown, not zero — and without a spend cap the
loop may continue with a null aggregate. A partial tool call in truncated model
output is not executed. Reaching an agent step limit returns a terminal result;
it does not throw.

## Words as they arrive: onText

On Claude models, `sw.agent.run({ ..., onText: (text) => ... })` streams each
model call and hands every piece of the answer's text to `onText` as it
arrives. Use it to show the reply while it is still being written. The result
and the bill are the same as without it. A stream that stops early is billed
only after review, never estimated.

`onToolStart: (name) => ...` streams the same way and is called with a tool's
name as soon as the model starts writing that tool call, before its input has
arrived and before the tool runs. Use it to show each step as it begins. Either
hook turns streaming on; they can be used together or alone.

## Durable execution: sw.agent(options) and sw.agent.start(options)

A durable call stores the initial messages, creates background work, and returns
immediately. The platform invokes the same deployed function for each signed
step callback. Call the same durable form from that handler; the runtime detects
the callback envelope and advances exactly one step instead of creating another
run.

```ts
const config: SomewhereAgentDurableOptions = {
  model: 'claude-haiku-4-5',
  prompt: 'Reconcile yesterday’s orders.',
  tools: [
    {
      name: 'mark_reconciled',
      description: 'Mark one order reconciled.',
      input_schema: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: { id: { type: 'string' } },
        required: ['id'],
      },
      execute: async ({ id }, { agentId, turn, toolCallId }) => {
        // Use toolCallId as the idempotency identity for external side effects.
        return { id, agentId, turn, toolCallId }
      },
    },
  ],
}

const { agent_id, status, max_steps } = await sw.agent.start(config)
```

Tools, callbacks, and credentials are not serialized into the durable
checkpoint; the callback re-enters the deployed function and recreates them.
The tool context carries stable `agentId`, `turn`, and `toolCallId` values
for retry-safe deduplication. Inline runs set `agentId` to `null`; durable runs
use the durable id. A durable run can cross a deploy because callbacks execute
the then-current function code; checkpoint state records every observed
deployment version.

## Status and cancellation

`sw.agent.status(agentId)` reads the durable job and returns its complete job
status payload with a normalized `agent_id` field added:

```js
const state = await sw.agent.status(agent_id)
// { ...jobStatus, agent_id: jobStatus.job_id || agent_id }
```

The job payload carries the durable status, checkpoint/result or terminal error
when present, and the persisted agent state. See `docs({ topic: 'sw.jobs' })`
for the job status fields.

`sw.agent.cancel(agentId)` requests cancellation and returns the cancellation
job payload with the same normalized `agent_id` field:

```js
const cancelled = await sw.agent.cancel(agent_id)
// { ...cancelJobResult, agent_id: cancelJobResult.job_id || agent_id }
```

Cancellation prevents later steps. It cannot undo a tool side effect that
already completed or is already running. Both methods require a non-empty
string id; otherwise they throw `VALIDATION_ERROR` with status 400.

## Shared options

Every execution needs one input source: a non-empty `messages` array, a
`prompt` string, or an `input` string. Messages must be JSON-serializable and
are capped at 128 KiB of serialized text.

- `provider`, `model`, `system`, `systemPrompt`, `serviceTier`, and
  `maxTokens` select the model call. Camel-case `systemPrompt`,
  `serviceTier`, and `maxTokens` map to `system`, `service_tier`, and
  `max_tokens` unless the snake-case field is already present.
- `conversation_id` and other `sw.ai.chat` history options pass through to
  each model call. A conversation may span multiple inline or durable runs;
  `agent_id` identifies one durable run only.
- `maxSteps`, `maxIterations`, and `maxTurns` are accepted limit names.
  The first defined name in that order wins. The value must be an integer from
  1 through 20; the default is 8.
- `maxSpendCents`, when it is a positive number, is checked before each model
  call and again after each billed step: a run whose accumulated cost has
  already reached the cap makes no further call, and a completed call that
  takes the accumulated cost over the cap stops the run. Either throws
  `AI_SPEND_CAP_EXCEEDED` with status 402 and partial metrics on
  `error.metrics`. The cap bounds the run, not the price of any single call.

## Tools

`tools` accepts a keyed object or an array. Array entries have this shape:

```ts
const tool: SomewhereAgentTool = {
  name: 'look_up_order',
  description: 'Look up an order by ID.',
  inputSchema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: { id: { type: 'string' } },
    required: ['id'],
  },
  execute: async (input) => ({ id: input.id }),
};
```

Use `inputSchema` or `input_schema` to describe the input. An executor also
receives the tool context as its second argument.

Tool names must be unique and no longer than 64 characters. Missing schemas
default to an empty object schema. A thrown tool error becomes an
`is_error: true` tool result so the next model step can recover. A missing
tool result and a non-serializable result also become error results. Serialized
tool-result content is truncated after 24,000 characters.

## Step callbacks

- `prepareStep(context)` runs before the model call. `context.stepNumber` is
  0 for a run's first model call (it counts the steps already taken). It may return an object
  overriding `messages`, `provider`, `model`, `system`, `tools`,
  `toolChoice`, or `maxTokens` for that step; `null` and `undefined`
  mean no override.
- `onStepFinish({ step, steps, agentId })` runs after the step trace is recorded.
  `agentId` is the durable run's id (`null` for an inline run), so a durable
  callback can store per-step data against its run. `step.cost_cents` is this
  model call's cost (null while pending); a durable run's stored steps keep it.
- `stopWhen({ step, steps })` may return false, true, or a non-empty
  completion-reason string.
- `onStep(event)` is also supported. It receives
  `{ agentId, turn, maxTurns, output, toolCalls, done, stopReason }`; its
  JSON-serializable return value is stored as `step.on_step`.

Callback failures throw `AI_PREPARE_STEP_FAILED`, `AI_STEP_HOOK_FAILED`, or
`AI_STOP_CONDITION_FAILED` with status 422. Their `error.metrics` contains
the partial token/tool counts; `steps` and `total_cost_cents` on that metrics
object are non-enumerable.
## Known inconsistencies

- The direct `sw.agent(options)` form returns `max_turns`, while
  `sw.agent.start(options)` returns `max_steps`. Read the field that matches
  the form you called; they are not aliases in the returned object.
- `steps` and `total_cost_cents` exist on inline results and partial error
  metrics but are non-enumerable. Direct property access works; object spread,
  `Object.keys`, and `JSON.stringify` omit them.

These are the supported runtime shapes today, not documentation aliases.

pages.title: Jobs and schedules
pages.body:
Work that shouldn't hold up a request runs in the background with no worker
or queue server to operate. A background handler is an ordinary function in
`api/`. The platform calls it with a signed request, and one call,
`sw.jobs.verifyInvocation(request)`, tells a real delivery apart from anyone
else calling that URL.

## Choose the kind of work

| You need | Use | You get |
|---|---|---|
| Work with a status the user can check, such as an export or a report | `sw.jobs.create` | A durable job id, `sw.jobs.status`, retries |
| A side effect nobody reads back, such as logging an event | `sw.jobs.create`, without checking its status | Retries, an optional later start, a status if you ever need it |
| Work on a clock, such as hourly cleanup | A schedule (`somewhere cron create`) | The handler called on a cron expression |

Every kind can run its handler more than once. Make each handler safe to
repeat.

## Run a job and report its status

This job counts a user's notes and stores a summary row. It uses the `notes`
table from **Data**:

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { id, integer, owner, schema, table, text, timestamp } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  notes: table(
    { id: id(), title: text(), body: text({ default: '' }), created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }) },
    { scope: owner(), client: { read: ['id', 'title', 'body', 'created_at'], create: ['title', 'body'], update: ['title', 'body'], delete: true } },
  ),
  note_summaries: table(
    { id: id(), summary_id: text({ unique: true }), note_count: integer(), created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }) },
    { scope: owner(), client: { read: ['id', 'note_count', 'created_at'] } },
  ),
});
```

```ts
// api/summaries.ts — POST starts a summary job; GET ?id= reports it
export default async function summaries(
  request: Request,
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
): Promise<Response> {
  const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(request);
  if (!user) return Response.json({ error: 'Sign in.' }, { status: 401 });

  if (request.method === 'GET') {
    const id = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('id');
    if (!id) return Response.json({ error: 'Pass ?id=<job_id>.' }, { status: 400 });
    const job = await sw.jobs.status(id);
    return Response.json({ status: job.status });
  }
  if (request.method !== 'POST') {
    return new Response('Use GET or POST.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'GET, POST' } });
  }

  const input: unknown = await request.json().catch(() => null);
  const operationId =
    typeof input === 'object' && input !== null && 'operation_id' in input ? input.operation_id : undefined;
  if (typeof operationId !== 'string' || !/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,64}$/.test(operationId)) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Send an operation_id of 8–64 letters, digits, _ or -.' }, { status: 400 });
  }

  const allowance = await sw.rateLimit.check(`summaries:${user.id}`, 10, 3600);
  if (!allowance.allowed) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Try again later.' }, { status: 429 });
  }

  // The same user and operation_id always produce the same key and arguments,
  // so a retried request reaches the same job instead of creating another.
  const job = await sw.jobs.create({
    handler: '/api/jobs/summarize-notes',
    idempotency_key: `summary:${user.id}:${operationId}`,
    // user_id comes from the verified session, so the handler can trust it.
    payload: { summary_id: `${user.id}:${operationId}`, user_id: user.id },
  });
  return Response.json({ job_id: job.job_id }, { status: 202 });
}
```

```ts
// api/jobs/summarize-notes.ts — runs only when the platform delivers the job
export default async function summarizeNotes(
  request: Request,
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
): Promise<Response> {
  if (!(await sw.jobs.verifyInvocation(request))) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'forbidden' }, { status: 403 });
  }

  const payload: unknown = await request.json().catch(() => null);
  const fields = typeof payload === 'object' && payload !== null ? payload : {};
  const summaryId = 'summary_id' in fields ? fields.summary_id : undefined;
  const userId = 'user_id' in fields ? fields.user_id : undefined;
  if (typeof summaryId !== 'string' || !summaryId || typeof userId !== 'string' || !userId) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Invalid payload.' }, { status: 400 });
  }

  // Server authority, scoped by hand to the user your own code put in the payload.
  const { data: noteCount } = await sw.db.server.count('notes', { where: { user_id: userId } });
  // A repeated run inserts nothing: summary_id is unique.
  await sw.db.server.insert(
    'note_summaries',
    { summary_id: summaryId, note_count: noteCount, user_id: userId },
    { onConflict: 'ignore' },
  );
  return Response.json({ ok: true });
}
```

The page creates one `operation_id` per user action, for example with
`crypto.randomUUID()`, and reuses it if it retries that request. It posts
`{ operation_id }` to `/api/summaries`, receives `job_id`, and checks
`GET /api/summaries?id=<job_id>` until the status is `complete`, `failed`
or `cancelled`. `indeterminate` is not final on its own: the job may still be
recovering, so check again, and read its `recovery` before starting new work.
When it's `complete`, the summary row is in the user's `note_summaries`.

- **Verify before reading the payload.** `verifyInvocation` checks that the
  request is a platform-signed delivery for this project. Answer 403 when
  verification fails, including when the platform cannot confirm the
  signature. Validate the payload before using it.
- **Server authority, scoped by your code.** The handler writes with
  `sw.db.server` and names `user_id` itself. That's safe here because the job
  payload came from your own verified request, never from a browser.
- **Repeats are expected.** The platform retries a failed run, so the unique
  `summary_id` turns a repeat into a no-op. How many times a run can repeat:
  `sw.jobs` → `recovery-status-what-a-job-handle-can-tell-you`.
- **Status is per user.** `sw.jobs.status` serves a job only to the user who
  created it. In a signed-in handler, `sw.jobs.cancel(jobId)` cancels that
  user's job. An ordinary handler already running finishes; its side effects
  remain. Until that execution ends, the cancelled job keeps its concurrency
  slot and reports `completed_at: null`. A queued job releases its slot
  immediately.
- **One key per user action.** `user_id` comes only from the session, and
  the key is `summary:<user id>:<operation_id>`. If `sw.jobs.create` throws
  `JOB_ADMISSION_UNCONFIRMED`, send the same request again with the same
  `operation_id`. The same key and arguments reach the job that may already
  exist instead of creating a second one. Never retry with a new
  `operation_id` for the same action. A status of `indeterminate` carries
  `recovery` details. Read them before submitting new work.

## Job limits

- **Creation rate.** 600 `sw.jobs.create` calls a minute per account
  owner, counted across the account's projects. Above it the call throws
  `RATE_LIMITED` (429) with a retry delay.
- **Jobs at once.** At most 100 jobs queued, scheduled or running at once
  per account, on every plan. Above it the call throws
  `JOB_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` (429); create more as earlier ones finish.
  The two limits are separate: a job holds its slot from creation until it
  finishes, so how many jobs you can run per minute also depends on how long
  each one runs. Runs started by your cron schedules never use these slots;
  your plan's schedule limits pace them instead.
- **Start time.** `run_at` can be any future time.

Fanning out many small messages, one per item, does not fit these limits. Put
a batch of items in one job's payload and loop over them in the handler: one
job per batch, with each item's result recorded in your own table. Each run of
the handler is one function request under the usual time limits (`limits`),
so size a batch to finish well inside one run.

## In a preview

`sw.jobs.create`, `sw.jobs.status`, `sw.jobs.cancel` and
`sw.jobs.verifyInvocation` work in preview code. The job runs the preview's
own code against the preview's data, files, users and mail, and never touches
your live app. A preview sees only its own jobs; production and other
previews never see them. Smaller than production, and said in the answer:

- **One attempt, no retries.** Status shows `attempts_allowed: 1`.
- **At most 270 seconds.** A longer `timeout_seconds` is accepted and capped;
  the create answer says `preview_timeout_capped: true` with
  `preview_timeout_cap_seconds`, and the job's `timeout_seconds` is the
  effective one.
- **The handler is a path in this project**, such as `/api/report`; an
  address is refused with `PREVIEW_HANDLER_NOT_PREVIEW_CODE`. Redirects are
  not followed.
- **No result webhook** (`PREVIEW_WEBHOOK_UNSUPPORTED`), no row-bound jobs
  (`PREVIEW_ROW_JOB_UNSUPPORTED`) and no agent jobs
  (`PREVIEW_AGENT_UNSUPPORTED`).
- **At most 20 unfinished jobs per preview** (`PREVIEW_JOB_LIMIT`) and
  60 creates a minute; they never count against your production limits.
- **A job created by a signed-in preview user acts for that user** only for
  data, files and teams. It cannot use `sw.jobs` for that user (create, status
  or cancel answer `PREVIEW_NESTED_JOB_UNSUPPORTED`); the preview's own
  requests can. A run with no user (`preview run-job`, `cron run --preview`)
  can create further preview jobs.
- **When the preview closes, expires, is promoted or is saved again**, its
  unfinished jobs end with `PREVIEW_ENDED` within about a minute, delayed ones
  too; no new handler starts for the old version. A preview saved before jobs
  opened keeps `sw.jobs` refused until it is saved again.

`sw.cron` refuses in a preview (`PREVIEW_CRON_UNAVAILABLE`): a schedule is a
production setting. To test a job or scheduled handler from outside the app,
run it once in the preview with `somewhere preview run-job <handler-path>
[--payload <json>]`, or `somewhere cron run <name> --preview` for a
production schedule's handler and payload.

## Existing sw.queue code

Use `sw.jobs` for new background work. `sw.queue` is not recommended for new
code, but it keeps working unchanged for apps that already use it:
`sw.queue.push({ handler, payload, delay_seconds?, idempotency_key? })` is still
accepted, delivered with retries, and its terminal failures are listed at
`GET /v1/queue/dead-letters`. Its handler verifies with
`sw.queue.verifyInvocation(request)`, the same check as
`sw.jobs.verifyInvocation(request)`.

The two have different limits; jobs are not a higher-throughput replacement:

| | `sw.queue` (existing code) | `sw.jobs` (recommended) |
|---|---|---|
| Admission rate per account owner | 600 a minute | 600 a minute |
| Waiting or running at once | no limit | 100 on every plan (queued, scheduled or running) |
| Later start | up to 12 hours (`delay_seconds`) | any future `run_at` |
| Status, cancel, inspectable retries | none | yes |

When you move code from `sw.queue` to `sw.jobs`:
- `delay_seconds` becomes `run_at`, an ISO-8601 time with an explicit offset,
  such as `new Date(Date.now() + 2 * 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString()`.
- A burst that sent one message per item may exceed the job limits; put a
  batch of items in one job's payload, sized to finish in one run.
- Queue keys and job keys are separate: nothing dedupes a job against a queue
  message, and messages already sent are not moved or sent again. If both can
  run for the same work, keep the effect idempotent in your handler, for
  example a unique column for the work's own id.

## Run on a schedule

Deploy the handler first, then register the schedule:

```bash
somewhere cron create "0 * * * *" /api/jobs/cleanup --name cleanup
somewhere cron run cleanup --wait   # run it once now and wait for the result
```

A scheduled handler verifies with `sw.jobs.verifyInvocation` like any job. A
fire missed while the platform was unavailable isn't replayed, so design for
an occasional skipped run. Schedules work on every plan; the plan sets how
many a project can hold and how often each can run. The `cron_list` tool
returns your plan's `policy.min_interval_minutes` and `max_per_project`. A
tighter schedule is refused with `CRON_SCHEDULE_TOO_FREQUENT`, and one past the
count with `CRON_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`. Times are UTC unless you pass `--timezone`.

## Start once at a future time

Pass `run_at` to `sw.jobs.create` or the `job_create` tool: an ISO-8601
instant with a time zone, such as `2026-10-05T09:00:00Z`. This schedules a
single job at any future time. Omit it to start immediately: `sw.jobs.create`
answers once the job is saved (`queued`) and the job starts right after. In the
rare case that start is lost, the minute-by-minute dispatcher starts it, so it
can stay `queued` for up to about 75 seconds.
The job reports `scheduled` until its earliest start time; the minute-by-minute
dispatcher starts due work, so a busy batch can start later.

A waiting job reserves a slot in the account's job limit. List jobs with
`job_get({ project_id, status: 'scheduled' })` and cancel one to free its slot.
Keep the same idempotency key and arguments after a lost response: even after
the time has passed, that retry returns the original job. A new job with a past
time gets `RUN_AT_NOT_IN_FUTURE`. Changing the time requires a new logical job. A
scheduled job whose creator loses project access stops with
`JOB_CREATOR_ACCESS_REVOKED` before it starts. Cancelling before dispatch
prevents the handler from running; cancellation after a handler starts is best effort.

## More on jobs and schedules

| Need | Where |
|---|---|
| Idempotency keys, admission and replay rules | `sw.jobs` → `idempotency-key-safe-retries` |
| Retries, `indeterminate`, recovery codes | `sw.jobs` → `recovery-status-what-a-job-handle-can-tell-you` |
| Handler and signature details | `sw.jobs` → `job-handler-function` |
| Creation rate, jobs at once, batching | `sw.jobs` → `job-limits` |
| Cron format, time zones, plan limits, run now | `cron` → `schedule-format`, `minimum-interval`, `run-once-now` |
| A complete scheduled cleanup | `cron` → `recipe-hourly-cleanup-of-stale-rows` |
| Agent runs that continue in the background | `sw.agent` |
| A job that acts on one row for the user who started it | `sw.jobs` → `act-on-one-row-for-the-signed-in-user` |

## Retries and timeouts

Run work that shouldn't block a user request in a job.
`timeout_seconds` is how long the platform waits for your handler: 300 seconds
by default, up to 1800. A deadline of up to 270 seconds is waited for exactly.
A deadline from 271 to 300 seconds, which includes the default, is waited for
at most 270 seconds. A deadline above 300 seconds is waited for in full,
except in a preview, where a run is waited for at most 270 seconds.

When the deadline passes, the platform stops waiting and the job fails with
`JOB_TIMEOUT`. The job is not sent again. Your handler is not stopped: it may
still be running at that moment and may finish some of its work, so write it so
that a later run can pick up safely.

Once a job has ended (timed out, cancelled, failed or complete), the platform
refuses further `sw.*` calls from its handler with `JOB_ENDED`, so a handler
that outlives its job can no longer write through `sw.fs`, `sw.email`,
`sw.payments`, `sw.jobs`, or `sw.db` in a managed-mode database. This
narrows what a late handler can change. It does not stop the handler, and these
can still happen after the deadline:
- Calls started before the job's status changes. A timeout is recorded a
  moment after the deadline; until then calls still run.
- A call already accepted when the job ends. It completes.
- Outbound `fetch`, including requests to your own app's routes, which run as
  new, ordinary requests.
- Work started or scheduled before the job ended: jobs it created, schedules,
  queue messages, and calls already in progress.
- `sw.db` in a database that does not use managed mode. Its queries run
  directly and are not checked.
- Effects outside the platform, such as a call your handler made to another
  service. These cannot be refused or undone.
- Functions you last deployed before 17:18 UTC on October 18, 2026, until you
  deploy again with `somewhere deploy`.

An error your handler returns is retried, one attempt at a time and inside the
same deadline. When the connection fails after the request may have reached your
handler, the job fails with `JOB_DELIVERY_UNCONFIRMED` instead of being sent
again. The platform never sends a job again while an earlier delivery of it may
still be running, but a handler can still run more than once in sequence — see
Recovery status below.
Make handlers idempotent — they may run more than once.

## Create a job

`sw.jobs.create({ handler, payload, idempotency_key, timeout_seconds, run_at })`
starts the work; `api/summaries.ts` in **Run a job and report its status**
above is the complete example. The handler must be a deployed function path,
such as `/api/jobs/summarize-notes`. The platform POSTs the payload to your
function when the job runs. The call resolves to
`{ job_id, status, duplicate, recovery }`: `duplicate` is `true` when the same
idempotency key and arguments returned an existing job, and an
`indeterminate` status means read `recovery` before retrying.

## Idempotency key — safe retries

Pass an optional `idempotency_key` (1–200 characters, no surrounding
whitespace) in the body, or the `Idempotency-Key` header; if both are sent
they must match. Inside a deployed function, `sw.jobs.create` and
`sw.agent.run` generate one key per invocation when you do not supply one,
and the CLI and MCP forward one per call — so a lost response on a single
call is safe to retry with the same key. A separate invocation is new work
unless you reuse your explicit key.

- Same key + same effective arguments, within the same project and caller →
  the same job handle comes back; current authorization is always checked
  first, and a sequential replay does not consume a new concurrent job slot.
- Same key + different arguments → `409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`.
- Concurrent equal requests admit one job. Each request may still hit the
  per-request rate limiter before admission deduplicates; rate accounting is
  not part of admission.
- Unkeyed equal requests are independent jobs. A key lives as long as its
  job and receipt, not beyond project or job deletion.
- If admission cannot be confirmed you get `503 JOB_ADMISSION_UNCONFIRMED`:
  retry only with the same key. Concurrency caps return
  `429 JOB_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` (`job-limits`).

## Recovery status — what a job handle can tell you

A job handle is durable. Your handler may run more than once for one job and
must be idempotent; there is no exactly-once guarantee, and there is also no
promise that every admitted job is invoked (see the fenced crash below). A
response may carry `status: 'indeterminate'` with
`recovery` diagnostics instead of a final answer — read them, do not blindly
replay:

- `JOB_RESULT_UNCONFIRMED` — the provider reports complete but no product
  result was stored: unconfirmed, not success.
- `JOB_EXECUTION_STOPPED` — the run errored or was terminated without a
  product result; partial effects may exist.
- `JOB_STATUS_UNCONFIRMED` — the job was admitted (the id is real) but its
  status could not be read; poll it.
- A crash between the dispatch fence and invocation stays `unknown`; the
  platform does not create a second run on your behalf. Decide with your own
  records whether to submit new work.

The same rules apply to ingest jobs, which share this admission path.

## Job handler function
A job handler is an ordinary deployed function, so the database rules are the
same as for requests. Application tables are declared in db/schema.ts. sw.db.from reads them with caller-scoped access, and sw.db.server.from reads them once the caller is authorized for server access. The corresponding structured methods, such as sw.db.server.insert, change them. Raw query and batch go to the separate raw SQL database on current projects.

`api/jobs/summarize-notes.ts` in **Run a job and report its status** above
is the complete handler: it verifies with `sw.jobs.verifyInvocation` before
reading the body, answers 403 when that returns `false`, validates the
payload, scopes its server writes to the payload's user, and makes a repeated
run a no-op.

The platform signs each job delivery with X-Somewhere-Signature,
X-Somewhere-Invocation-Timestamp, and X-Somewhere-Body-SHA256.
Always verify before trusting the payload on public /api/jobs/*
handlers. This blocks a browser from calling the job handler directly
with forged payloads. `verifyInvocation` returns `false` whenever the
platform cannot confirm the signature, including when its database was
briefly unreachable; the REST check behind it answers that case
`503 INVOCATION_VERIFY_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`, because the one-time signature may
already be recorded (the same signed request can then be refused as a
replay). Answer 403 and do not run the work.

To test redelivery, enqueue through the app in a test project. For a test-only
payload, have the handler record a durable first-attempt marker and return
503 once, after a write you expect to be safe to repeat. The platform retries a
retryable response within the job deadline with a newly signed delivery.
Poll its status and check the final rows for duplicates. To test repeat-safe
writes without waiting for a platform retry, invoke two jobs with the same
business operation ID and different enqueue keys. Reusing the enqueue key
only returns the original job.

## Look up a job's status

`sw.jobs.status(jobId)` returns the job. Its `status` is `queued`,
`scheduled`, `running`, `complete`, `failed`, `cancelled` or
`indeterminate`, alongside `attempts`, `error`, `error_code`,
`started_at`, `completed_at`, `run_at` and `recovery`. Poll it from another
request: the browser calls your function, which calls `sw.jobs.status` for the
signed-in user, as the `GET` branch of `api/summaries.ts` above does. A job
is served only to the user who created it.

### Result size

A job keeps its handler's answer as its `result`, within two limits.

- The result and the record that carries it from your handler are measured
  together and must fit in 768 KiB (786,432 bytes). The measure is
  conservative: characters that need escaping (quotes, backslashes, control
  characters) count as their escaped form, and a result that contains any
  character outside Latin-1 counts two bytes for every character.
- The job as a whole — its `payload`, its attempt history, its `result` and
  its other fields — must fit in 1,999,000 bytes, measured when the result is
  saved. A job with a large `payload` therefore has less room for its result.

A JSON answer is kept exactly as sent; an answer that is not JSON is kept as
`{ "text": … }` with its first 100,000 characters.

A larger answer ends the job as `failed` with `JOB_RESULT_TOO_LARGE`. The
handler ran and answered, but the result was discarded and the job was not run
again. Anything the handler did before answering was not undone. Return a
smaller result, or write large output with `sw.fs` and return a reference to
it.

## Act on one row for the signed-in user

A job can read or change one row as the user who started it, with only the
operations its binding declares. Declare the binding in the schema options,
beside the table it acts on:

```ts
schema(
  {
    expenses: table(
      { id: id(), group_id: text(), amount_cents: integer(), status: text({ default: 'open' }) },
      { scope: group(), client: { read: true, create: ['group_id', 'amount_cents'] } },
    ),
  },
  { jobs: { settle_expense: { table: 'expenses', operations: ['read', 'update'], maxDurationSeconds: 900 } } },
);
```

Start it from the signed-in user's own request, naming the binding and the row:

```ts
// api/expenses/settle.ts — POST { id }: queue a settlement job for one expense
export default async function settleExpense(
  request: Request,
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
): Promise<Response> {
  if (request.method !== 'POST') {
    return new Response('Use POST.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } });
  }
  if (!(await sw.auth.fromRequest(request))) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Sign in first.' }, { status: 401 });
  }
  const body = (await request.json().catch(() => null)) as { id?: unknown } | null;
  if (typeof body?.id !== 'string' || body.id === '') {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Send the expense ID as a non-empty string.' }, { status: 400 });
  }

  const job = await sw.jobs.create({
    handler: '/api/jobs/settle-expense',
    row: { binding: 'settle_expense', id: body.id },
  });
  return Response.json({ job_id: job.job_id }, { status: 202 });
}
```

```ts
// api/jobs/settle-expense.ts — the job: reads and updates only its one row
export default async function settleExpenseJob(
  request: Request,
  sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext,
): Promise<Response> {
  if (!(await sw.jobs.verifyInvocation(request))) return new Response('Forbidden', { status: 403 });
  // Structured calls in a row-bound job reach only its row, as its user.
  const { data } = await sw.db.from('expenses', { limit: 1 });
  if (!data.length) return Response.json({ settled: false });
  await sw.db.update('expenses', { set: { status: 'settled' }, where: { status: 'open' } });
  return Response.json({ settled: true });
}
```

- **The row id is typed by its key.** `id()` keys take a string;
  `id({ uuid: false })` keys take a whole number. `'42'` never names row `42`.
- If the row is missing or the caller cannot use it for the declared job operations,
  job creation returns `403 FORBIDDEN`. Check the row ID and the caller's access.
- **The user's access still applies.** Each read and write runs with that user's
  current access to the row, inside the binding's operations. If they lose
  access, the job sees and changes nothing.
- **User authority for one row.** The job's structured `sw.db` calls on the
  bound table run as that user and reach only that row, with the binding's
  operations: no new rows, counts, aggregates, related rows or key changes. The
  grant gives that user no authority over other rows or other tables, and no
  file access: plain `sw.fs` is refused in the job, while `sw.fs.server`
  stays your project authority that needs your own check. A row-bound job
  can't use `sw.db.server` or a table's `publicRead` access; an ordinary
  job started by a user can still call `sw.db.server` explicitly.
- **Bounded in time.** The grant starts at the job's start (`run_at` when set)
  and ends `maxDurationSeconds` later; retries keep the same deadline. A
  cancelled or finished job keeps no access.
- **Created by the user, on the deployed app.** Only a signed-in user's own
  request starts one, never another job; a preview or local run can't.

pages.title: Cron — Scheduled Tasks
pages.body:
A schedule calls one of your deployed functions on a cron expression, such as
every hour or every day at 09:00 in a time zone you choose. The handler is an
ordinary function in `api/`, signed by the platform, so there's no scheduler
or worker for you to run. After creating a schedule, test it now with
`somewhere cron run <id or name> --wait`; do not wait for its scheduled time.

Schedules run on every plan. The plan sets the schedule count and minimum
interval; `cron_list({ project_id })` returns both in `policy` as
`min_interval_minutes` and `max_per_project`. A schedule that exceeds
them gets `CRON_SCHEDULE_TOO_FREQUENT` or `CRON_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`.

## Recipe — hourly cleanup of stale rows

Delete unpaid submissions older than a day, every hour. It takes two parts: a
deployed, signed handler and a registered schedule.

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { id, owner, schema, table, text, timestamp } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  submissions: table(
    { id: id(), status: text(), created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }) },
    { scope: owner() },
  ),
});
```

```ts
// api/jobs/cleanup.ts — deployed with the app; runs only when the scheduler calls it
export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'none', // The platform invocation signature authorizes this route.
  handler: async ({ request: req }, sw) => {
    if (!(await sw.jobs.verifyInvocation(req))) return new Response('forbidden', { status: 403 });
    const cutoff = new Date(Date.now() - 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();
    const r = await sw.db.server.remove('submissions', { where: { status: 'unpaid', created_at: { lt: cutoff } } });
    return { removed: r.changes };
  },
});
```

```bash
somewhere deploy                                   # the handler must be live first
somewhere cron create "0 * * * *" /api/jobs/cleanup --project <project> --name cleanup
somewhere cron run cleanup --project <project> --wait   # run once now and wait for the result (id or name)
```

- **Verify first.** `sw.jobs.verifyInvocation(req)` is true only for a call
  the platform signed for this project. Anyone else calling the URL gets 403
  before the handler touches data.
- **Make it safe to repeat.** A run can be delivered more than once. A delete
  by condition, like this one, gives the same result the second time.

## Create a schedule
cron_create({
  project_id: "my-app",
  schedule: "0 9 * * *",                    // 5-field cron expression
  timezone: "America/Los_Angeles",          // optional; defaults to UTC
  handler: "/api/jobs/daily-digest",
  payload: { segment: "daily" }             // optional
})

Schedules use UTC unless you pass an IANA `timezone`. With a time zone, the
schedule follows the local wall clock across daylight-saving changes: 09:00
in Los Angeles fires at 16:00Z in September (PDT) and 17:00Z in December
(PST). The CLI takes the same option as `--timezone`.

## Run once now

Use `cron_run({ cron_id })` (CLI: `somewhere cron run <id or name> --wait`)
to test the deployed handler immediately. It uses the same path as a
scheduled fire, leaves the schedule unchanged, and records the run with
`trigger: "manual"`. Read the run history with `job_get({ cron_id })`.

## Scheduled tasks and previews

Nothing runs on a schedule in a preview. To test a scheduled task there, run
it once on demand:

- `somewhere cron run <name> --preview` runs that production task's handler
  path and payload once in the folder's open preview (MCP: `cron_run` with
  `preview_session_id` and `preview_id`). The production schedule is only
  read: its last run, next run and failure streak never change.
- `somewhere preview run-job <handler-path> [--payload <json>]` runs any
  handler path once in the preview, as one signed job delivery: a schedule is
  only a handler path plus a payload.

Either way the run is a preview job: the preview's code, data, files, users
and mail, one attempt, at most 270 seconds, no user (as a scheduled run
has none). Preview code cannot create or change a schedule: `sw.cron` refuses
there with `PREVIEW_CRON_UNAVAILABLE`. Automatic preview schedules were
removed: their routes answer 410 `PREVIEW_SCHEDULES_REMOVED`.

## Observe a scheduled fire

To check automatic delivery, read `somewhere cron runs <id or name> --json`
(CLI `--limit` is 1–100, default 20). It shows the schedule and recent jobs.
Record the next scheduled occurrence, then read the history again after that
slot. Match a job with `trigger: "scheduled"` and `cron_scheduled_at` equal
to that occurrence. Read its `status`, `started_at`, `completed_at` and
result to distinguish dispatch from a completed handler. The same history is
available through `job_get({ cron_id, limit: 20 })`.

A manual run exercises the signed job path immediately; it does not establish
that the timer delivered an occurrence. Its `trigger` remains `"manual"`
and `cron_scheduled_at` is null. Keep the two checks separate in your test
results: handler exercised now, automatic scheduled delivery observed later.

The scheduler checks due schedules once a minute. Dispatch and job execution
can start later than the nominal slot, including delays of a few minutes;
there is no exact-second start guarantee. An overdue label says the schedule
has not advanced yet. Check the matching run history before concluding that
the handler ran or failed. Recent history is bounded, so a missing row in that
page alone does not establish that an older occurrence never ran.

## Handler
A handler is a deployed function, written and deployed like any other
(`functions`), so deploy it before you create the schedule. The platform
POSTs the schedule's `payload` when it fires.

Verify each call with `sw.jobs.verifyInvocation(req)`, the same check job
and queue handlers use. The platform signs every invocation; a header or a
shared secret of your own is not a substitute. A run may repeat, so make the
handler idempotent.

## Schedule format
  minute  hour  day-of-month  month  day-of-week
  0       9     *             *      *           → every day at 09:00 in the selected timezone
  */15    *     *             *      *           → every 15 minutes
  0       0     1             *      *           → first of every month

The finest granularity is one minute: a 5-field expression has no seconds
field. For updates faster than that, push as data arrives (`live-data`).

## When a schedule is the wrong tool

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| Work in response to a user action | The request itself, or `sw.jobs.create` from it (`recipe-background-jobs`) |
| One piece of work at a later time, such as a reminder in two hours | `sw.jobs.create({ handler, payload, run_at })`; `run_at` can be any future time |
| Each user picks their own time | One schedule every few minutes that reads due rows from your table; schedules per project are capped by plan |
| A retry after a failure | Nothing extra: a failed job run is retried |
| A page that shows changes as they happen | A live view (`live`), not a polling schedule |

## Minimum interval

Your plan sets the smallest gap allowed between two fires, and how many
schedules one project may hold. Read both from `cron_list({ project_id })` →
`policy.min_interval_minutes` and `policy.max_per_project`; `null` means the
plan sets no limit.

- A schedule tighter than `min_interval_minutes` is refused when you create or
  edit it, with `CRON_SCHEDULE_TOO_FREQUENT` naming both intervals. The check
  measures the schedule's real cadence, so a tight gap inside a
  sparse-looking expression is caught too.
- One more schedule than `max_per_project` is refused with
  `CRON_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` (429).
- The interval is checked when a schedule is created or its timing is edited.
  Editing the handler, payload or name, or resuming a paused schedule, leaves
  the cadence as it is.

## Missed fires
A fire time that passes while the platform is unavailable is not replayed.
Design schedules to tolerate an occasional skipped run: the cleanup above
catches up on the next hour.

pages.title: Payments
Deploy and domains
pages.body:
You deploy raw source. The platform compiles your React and TypeScript, bundles
the npm packages in `package.json`, applies `db/schema.ts`, runs its deploy
checks, and serves the new release at your project's address. There's no
build step and no `dist` folder. Every deploy is a numbered version you can
inspect. Every plan rolls back to the previous working version. Restoring a
chosen retained version is on paid plans; history listing and retention are
described separately below.

The CLI shows an app-role grant command after deployment when a manually assigned app-wide role has no holder. Sign in to the deployed app before granting the role. `project_deploy` and `somewhere deploy --json` return the same facts in `unassigned_app_roles`: the `role`, the `command`, and the `sign_in_url` when the app declares it. Roles held by verified email domain or assigned by the server have their own assignment rules. See `somewhere docs adopt` for owner setup and schedule verification.

## Deploy and check the result

Ask before destructive or paid actions unless the user already authorized them.

For an existing app, start with `somewhere pull <app>` in a fresh folder,
then edit the downloaded source. In a connector, read from `project_export`
first and update selected files with `project_patch`.

```bash
somewhere deploy         # publishes and prints the live URL
```

When the project has a `tsconfig.json` and its dependencies are installed,
`somewhere deploy` checks types locally and stops before uploading if it finds
errors. If dependencies are missing, deploy skips the local typecheck and
the platform compiles the source. `somewhere deploy-check` compiles without
publishing.

Run `somewhere claim` and open its link to keep a temporary app.

Over MCP, `project_deploy` and `project_patch` run the same pipeline
(below).

To deploy a folder over HTTP, send its tar.gz as the multipart `source`
field to `POST /v1/deploy`. See [the curl example](https://somewhere.cloud/auth.md).

**A redeploy over HTTP names the live release it was prepared from.** Send
`base_release_id`: the `release_id` from the last deploy response, or the
live version's id from a project read. A project with no source yet takes
`base_release_id: null`. Without it the deploy is refused with
`BASE_REQUIRED` and nothing changes; if live moved since, it is refused with
`STALE_RELEASE_BASE`. This stops one deploy from silently overwriting another
writer's. `force: true` is the deliberate overwrite.

A clone with `.somewhere.json` keeps its link to the original project. Use
`somewhere deploy --new` to publish a separate copy and update the clone's
link.

`somewhere deploy` from the project folder is a full deploy:

- **Static files are replaced.** A file that isn't in the folder is removed
  from the live site.
- **Functions are replaced too.** A function file that isn't in the folder is
  deleted. `--scope functions` deploys only functions and keeps the ones you
  left out, unless you add `--replace-functions`. `--scope static` leaves
  functions untouched.
- **MCP and JSON deploys keep omitted functions by default.** `project_deploy`
  replaces static files but keeps a function you didn't send, and names it in
  a warning. Pass `replace_functions: true` to drop it. For a single-file
  change, use `project_patch` instead of resending everything.
- **A tar.gz upload replaces files and functions.** Send the complete source
  folder.
- **Promoting a preview keeps production functions by default.**
  `somewhere promote <preview_session_id> <preview_id> --yes` leaves live a
  production function the preview lacks and names it; `--prune` removes it
  (`dev-environments`). A plain `somewhere deploy` removes it. The output
  of both names each function it removed or kept.
- **`db/schema.ts` is applied before the new version goes live.** If a deploy
  is refused after that step, the schema changes it made stay in the database
  while the previous version keeps serving. Before deploying again, read the
  live schema with `somewhere call db_describe '{"project_id":"<project>"}'`
  and make the next deploy match it.

To publish and run a saved journey in one command, use
`somewhere deploy --verify flows/journey.json`. Keep the flow file out of
the deployed source with `.somewhereignore` when it contains test credentials.

The deploy response carries the build log: the detected entry, bundle sizes
and warnings. A refusal names the file and the reason; no new version goes
live. Schema changes already applied stay in place (see below).

**When you can't tell whether a deploy finished**, for example because the
command was interrupted, look before deploying again. `somewhere call project_deploys '{"project_id":"<project>"}'` lists
recent versions, and `deploy_status` names the live release. Deploy again
only once you've confirmed your version isn't there and nothing is still in
progress.

**To undo a bad deploy**, run `somewhere rollback --yes` on any plan. It
restores the previous working version, including its functions (see
`rollback` below).

**After a deploy**, `somewhere errors` lists recent runtime and API errors,
and `somewhere logs` shows your functions' log lines (how long they are kept:
`sw.logs` → `retention`).

## Version notes

Give a production version an optional `message` when deploying, patching or
promoting. `project_deploy` and `project_patch` accept it; the CLI uses
`somewhere deploy -m "Change the heading"` and `somewhere promote <preview_session_id> <preview_id> --yes -m "Ready to share"`.
The HTTP deploy, patch and promote calls take the same field. Promotion remains
on full MCP, CLI and HTTP.

Notes are plain text, at most 200 Unicode characters after control and
direction-changing characters are removed. Line breaks become spaces.
Overlong or non-text input is refused. Empty notes are omitted.
The note stays on the release record; `project_deploys` shows it as `message`
with `message_kind: "user_supplied_note"`. Displays keep the note as text.
An unchanged deploy or a replay keeps the original version's note.
Change a note with `somewhere deploys note 3 "Keep this version"`,
`project_patch({ project_id, note_version: 3, message: "Keep this version" })`,
or `PATCH /v1/deploy/note` with `{ project_id, version: 3, message }`.
Changing a note requires editor access and takes effect in history without a deploy.

## Rollback

`somewhere rollback --yes` (MCP `project_rollback`) makes the previous working
version live again on every plan, and visitors see it immediately. That is
the version that was live just before the current one; a deploy that failed
never went live, so it never counts. Rolling back again returns to the version
the rollback replaced. `somewhere deploys` and `project_deploys` show each
version, time, note and restore call when available. Use
`somewhere restore 3 --yes`, `project_rollback({ project_id, version: 3 })`,
or `POST /v1/promote/restore` with `{ project_id, version: 3 }` to make
version 3 live again. Free projects can restore any retained deploy from the last 24 hours by number or roll back to the previous working version. Paid plans can restore any retained version.

To get one file from version 2, run `somewhere file index.html --version 2 > restored-index.html`
or call `project_file_read({ project_id, path: "index.html", version: 2 })`.
HTTP uses `GET /v1/deploy/file?project_id=...&path=index.html&version=2`.
This reads stored production source. Deploy the file to make your edit live.
Kept versions can still contain secrets removed from later source.

Retention has three distinct parts:
- **Source history policy:** Free keeps the latest 10 snapshots and every snapshot from the last 24 hours.
  Paid plans keep the latest 50 plus daily representatives for
  90 days. Release source follows a separate
  policy. To confirm that a version's source is still available, read a file
  from that version.
- **Release history rows:** `project_deploys` returns up to 150 successful releases
  plus 20 failed attempts, interleaved by time. That is a listing cap, not a source
  retention window or all retained history. `somewhere status` reports current
  project, deployment and workspace status; use `somewhere deploys`
  for history. Platform changes are attributed to Somewhere.
- **Compiled builds:** the latest six function builds plus the active and previous
  activation are kept. Free also keeps builds from the last 24 hours. A restore
  leaves the deploy time unchanged. `rollback_available` describes build availability, not source
  availability or a guarantee of schema-safe restoration.

Rolling back and restoring check that the earlier version's schema is safe for
the current database and refuse with the schema plan when it is not.
By default this changes code without restoring data. Restoring by number
leaves the database schema and data unchanged. Tables and columns a later
version added stay, with their data, and the earlier version ignores them.
The response says so in `database_notice` and its message. For a rollback
to the previous version, `project_rollback` with `with_schema: true` also
applies the earlier schema through deployment checks and can affect data.

## Before you change a project you didn't just deploy

Read the live state first. `project_get` gives the current version.
`somewhere pull` (MCP `project_export`) fetches the deployed source.

**When a deploy is refused because live is newer than the folder**
(`STALE_RELEASE_BASE`), the message names the live version, what put it
there (the CLI, an agent through the connector, the dashboard, GitHub, a
rollback or restore, or this folder's own `somewhere rollback --yes`/`restore`), and
the files that differ. Run `somewhere pull`, then deploy again. In a linked
folder, plain `pull` is the safe update: files you have not edited move to
live, your local edits and local-only files (AGENTS.md, notes, tests) stay,
and it stops without writing anything if a file changed both in the folder
and live. `pull --force` replaces your edits with live; it never deletes a
file a deploy would not upload.
`project_deploys` lists recent versions, so you can see whether someone else
is shipping. Recent runtime failures are in `somewhere errors`.

## Connect a domain

For dashboard steps, see [Custom Domains](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/domains.txt).

A domain you already own is connected by claiming it. Delegate its
nameservers once, then attach it to any project. Claiming moves the domain's
DNS to the platform. The new zone doesn't import your existing records, and
it adds mail (MX) records only if you turn on receiving mail. If the domain
already receives email or serves other records, use the DNS-record path
below instead, which keeps your nameservers and records where they are. These are MCP tools; from
the CLI, call them with `somewhere call <tool> '<json>'`:

1. `domain_claim({ domain: "example.com" })` returns two nameservers.
2. The owner sets those nameservers at their registrar.
3. `domain_check_ns({ id })` reports `claim_status: "active"` once
   delegation has propagated. The platform also checks on its own.
4. `domain_attach({ id, project_id, host: "apex" })` serves the project
   there. `host` can also be `"www"` or a subdomain label.

The claim belongs to the owner's account, not to one project. Moving the
domain to another project is `domain_detach` then `domain_attach`, with no
new verification.

Connecting a domain never changes who owns it: it stays registered to the
owner at their registrar. On the DNS-record path,
`domain_add` gives a CNAME and a verification TXT record for a single
hostname, and `domain_verify` checks them. A bare domain (example.com itself)
works only by claiming it, or by connecting www and forwarding the bare name
to www at the DNS company.

**Buying a domain is the owner's payment.** `domain_buy` returns a price and
a checkout link. The owner opens the link and pays, and registration begins
only after payment settles. An agent can't complete the purchase. A bought
domain is registered in the buyer's name.

## More on deploy and domains

| Need | Where |
|---|---|
| Full and partial deploys, function preservation, build log | `deploy` → `projectdeploy-replaces-files-preserves-omitted-functions-by-default` |
| Single-file patches | `deploy` → `projectpatch-incremental` |
| Dependencies and lockfiles | `deploy` → `dependencies-and-lockfiles` |
| Checks before deploying | `deploy` → `check-before-you-deploy-no-deploy-required`; `verify-before-deploy` |
| What runs after a deploy (screenshots, reviews) | `deploy` → `after-every-deploy-the-platform-automatically`; `deploy-intelligence` |
| Rollback and versions | `deploy` → `rollback`; `inspect` |
| Previews before production | `dev-environments` |
| Domain claim, DNS-record path, recovery | `domains` → `recommended-claim-by-delegating-nameservers`, `dns-record-setup`, `stuck-domain-recovery` |
| Buying a domain, ownership | `domains` → `buy-a-domain-through-checkout`; `domain-ownership` |

## Previews and deploy size limits

Deploys go straight to production. On every plan, an app with
real users can instead deploy to an isolated preview and promote it when
ready → docs({ topic: 'dev-environments' }). The size limits for one deploy
are in the table at the end of this topic: `deploy-size-limits`.


## Deployed SEO metadata

See `recipe-seo` → `deployed-seo-metadata` for the check's fields,
release identity and inspection limits.

## Optional analytics consent

The platform adds no analytics beacon or third-party analytics loader to your
pages. Aggregate pageviews are collected on the server. When optional consent
mode is off, existing platform pageview and event collection continues.

Set `analytics_consent: { mode: "required", policy_version: "v1" }` through
`project_update` or `PATCH /v1/projects/:id`; `project_get` shows the
policy. Versions use 1–64 letters, numbers, dots, underscores or hyphens.
The "Require analytics consent" mode adds a neutral same-origin UI with equal Accept/Reject controls
and a change/revoke control. It blocks the two platform collectors until a
matching acceptance; a version change requires a new choice. A restrictive
app CSP may block the UI; without matching acceptance collection stays
blocked. CSP is never loosened.

`GET /__sw/analytics-consent` returns `{ policy, state }` on the actual
project host: enabled, pending, declined or unavailable.
Same-origin `POST` with JSON `{ action: "accept" | "deny" | "revoke",
policy_version: "v1" }` requires the exact Origin. Responses are no-store.
Choice is remembered for 90 days in a Secure, HttpOnly, host-only cookie;
no visitor identifier or event history is added. Revoke stores denial and
blocks future requests; it does not cancel every in-flight event. There is no
pre-consent queue, replay or backfill.

Required-mode background and developer/MCP calls without an original browser
choice return `recorded: false` with consent_pending, consent_declined or
consent_unavailable. Runtime uses the original request; body/options and
non-runtime headers cannot replace that choice. Ingestion checks current
policy again. Existing function bundles need a new deploy to gain runtime
preflight and request-choice forwarding; older bundles may still send a
request, which ingestion blocks in required mode. After that upgrade, policy
changes do not need another deploy. Auth, security logs and bandwidth
accounting continue.
Coverage is platform pageviews and `sw.analytics.track`; arbitrary app or
third-party trackers need separate adapters. No whole-site or legal
compliance claim is made.

## Dependencies and lockfiles

Declare dependencies in `package.json`; the platform installs and bundles
them on deploy. You never run `npm install` and never upload `node_modules`.

- **With a lockfile** — `package-lock.json` (lockfile version 2 or 3) or
  `npm-shrinkwrap.json`, which wins when both are present — the deploy uses
  exactly the versions and integrity hashes the lock selects for the selected
  packages: every declared runtime dependency (only platform-provided compile
  tooling is excepted; runtime dependencies are not tree-shaken before lock
  selection), plus dev dependencies your source actually imports and declared
  `@types` packages, and their required transitive closure. Supported lock
  entries are exact packages from
  the public npm registry with integrity. A lock the platform cannot honour
  is refused with `DEPENDENCY_LOCK_INVALID` and there is no unlocked
  fallback: aliases, linked, workspace, file or git packages, custom
  registries, version-1 or malformed locks, and locks whose selected graph is
  incomplete or inconsistent all refuse.
- **Without a lockfile** — ranges in `package.json` resolve at deploy. This
  is supported, but it is not verified reproducible: two deploys of the same
  source can pick different versions. Ship a lock when that matters.
- **What a lock does not promise** — unused dev and tooling entries are not
  installed, and the platform's own build tooling is pinned separately.
  Pre-installed common packages are reused only when they match your lock's
  full dependency graph and integrity; otherwise the deploy installs fresh.
  When the current compiler compiles your source, the release records the
  package versions and dependency relationships selected or bundled for that
  compilation and binds that record to the release; a release never
  re-resolves. A static release, or a release served from an accepted
  earlier build, may carry no new compilation record. Without a supported
  lockfile the record is observational — versions, manifest hashes and
  relationships as resolved, with any dependency target it could not resolve
  left explicitly unresolved — and it does not claim a lock-verified
  dependency graph. It covers what that compilation selected or bundled, not
  packages your code loads dynamically at runtime, not the platform's own
  tooling, and it is not an assertion that every installed file byte was
  independently verified or that every dependency runs correctly.

## Developer-file protection + .somewhereignore

Deploys never accidentally publish local/dev/control files. The platform
strips these from the static payload on EVERY deploy path (CLI, MCP
`project_deploy`, REST, GitHub import) and lists each exclusion in the
deploy warnings: root `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`,
`AGENT.md`, `.env` / `.env.*` / `.envrc` / `.npmrc`,
`.git*` metadata, `.somewhere.json`, `.mcp.json`, ignore files
themselves, editor/system dirs (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.vscode/`,
`.idea/`, `.wrangler/`), `node_modules/`, and `.DS_Store` /
`Thumbs.db` anywhere. `package.json`, tsconfigs, and vite configs still
ship — the platform compiles from them.

To publish a root design file, run `somewhere deploy --include DESIGN.md`.
Use `.somewhereignore` or `.gitignore` to exclude files from CLI deploys. Both
use gitignore syntax.

## Reliability guarantees on every deploy

- **After-deploy check.** Right after every live deploy, the platform loads
  your home page in a browser, signed out and as a test user, on a computer
  and a phone, and probes the app's data access. A page that comes up blank,
  or throws while loading, is warned about, not rolled back: the deploy stays
  live. `project_deploy_log({ project_id })` (REST
  `GET /v1/deploy/log?project_id=…`) returns the result under `access_check`
  once the check finishes. When the version live before it worked, the
  sentence starts with the warning and the way back, and
  `access_check.go_back` carries it: `previous_version`, `cli`
  (`somewhere restore <version> --project <project_id> --yes`), `mcp`
  (`project_rollback({ project_id, version })`) and `http`
  (`POST /v1/promote/restore { project_id, version }`). The project overview
  (`GET /v1/projects/<id>/overview`) shows the same as `needs_a_look`. A
  deploy that fixes the cause also replaces it. The check's own requests and
  the deploy screenshot are never counted as the app's visits, requests or
  errors. Server code that fails to start is refused before anything goes
  live.
- **Version history + rollback.** Every deploy writes a versioned
  snapshot. On every plan, `project_rollback` returns to the previous working version.
  Free can restore a retained deploy from the last 24 hours by number. Paid plans can restore any retained version.
  The platform evaluates managed-schema rollback safety before activation and
  refuses restoration when the prior schema is unsafe; inspect the returned schema plan.
  A version that can never return as it is refuses with `409` and nothing
  changes: one built with the project's older configuration format
  (`HOT_CONFIG_LEGACY_RELEASE`) or across an access-rule change; a new deploy
  of that version's source puts it back.
- **Continuous code review.** Deterministic security checks run during
  compilation on every tier. Every plan can request a review. Paid plans get a longer report.
  Eligible paid plans also review when a preview is promoted.
  Run `security_review` to get a report for the deployed code.

Full reference: <https://somewhere.cloud/docs/llms.txt>.

---

**Ship raw source. The platform compiles JSX/TSX/TS automatically — for
both the frontend AND the backend.** `/v1/deploy` compiles
your sources at deploy time:

- Frontend: `.jsx` / `.tsx` / `.css` are bundled into hashed chunks
  under `/_compiled/`, and `index.html` is rewritten to point at them.
- Functions: each `api/*.ts` (or `.tsx`, `.js`) is compiled to JS the
  runtime can execute — no client-side `tsc`, no `esbuild api/chat.ts`,
  no pre-bundled `.mjs`. You ship the same files you write.

Do not run `npm run build`, `vite build`, `esbuild`, `tsc`, or
similar first. `/v1/deploy` still accepts pre-bundled output but returns a
warning (the deploy is not blocked), and bundled files lose cross-function
