imports and source round-trips. This includes pre-bundled `api/*.mjs`
functions, not just `dist/` static output. To accept the trade-off and drop the
warning: `somewhere deploy --prebuilt`, the project setting, or `allow_bundled: true`.

### Put large binary assets in file storage

Deploy trees are for code. Large binary assets such as images, fonts,
and video belong in file storage: upload them with `fs_upload` and
`public: true`, then call `fs_public_url` and reference the returned
URL from your app. `fs_write` is for text and small inline content, not
real binary files. Assets in the deploy tree are re-processed on every
release, so a big asset folder makes every deploy slower and can fail
the deploy outright.

```text
fs_upload({
  project_id: "my-app", path: "/assets/badge.png",
  file: attachedFile, public: true
})
fs_public_url({ project_id: "my-app", path: "/assets/badge.png" })
// Put the returned public_url in <img src="…"> or CSS.
```

Why the functions side matters: pre-bundling your functions yourself
defeats the read-source-back features (export, find/replace, the visual
editor) and often fails at runtime. Ship the `.ts` source and the
platform compiles it — cross-imports resolve correctly.

Escape hatch (specialized prebuilt pipeline, native binary, etc):
  - CLI, one-off: `somewhere deploy --prebuilt`.
  - REST/MCP equivalent: pass `{ allow_bundled: true }` in the deploy
    body.

Two ways to ship code (the MCP tools — CLI maps onto the same pipeline):

project_deploy — replaces static files (omitted files deleted), preserves omitted functions unless replace_functions:true; use for the initial deploy or a major rebuild
project_patch  — incremental, use for small edits, single-file changes, adding one endpoint

**Deploys go live immediately by default.** A normal `project_deploy`
or `project_patch` writes the live serving slot in one step — the
result is instantly at `https://{subdomain}.somewhere.site` and on any
verified custom domain. No extra step to publish.

## Start from a template

Templates are ready-made apps the platform stores and deploys. List them
(no key needed):

  GET /v1/templates
  // → { templates: [{ name, title, description, edit }] }

Deploy one in one call, signed in or on a temporary account:

  POST /v1/deploy { "template": "links", "name": "My links" }
  // → the usual deploy answer with project_id and url
  //   (and claim_url on a temporary account)

The call creates the project if the name is new and publishes the
template. Repeating it is safe: when that app is already published it
answers `already_existed: true` with the same `project_id` and `url`, and
changes nothing. A template's `words` are the few pieces of text written in
its `index.html` (for `links`, the name and the line under it); `edit` names
the file that holds everything else (for `links`, `src/links.json`: the
photo, the theme and the links). Change either with `project_patch` or a
normal deploy. `GET /v1/templates/{name}` returns the template's files, and
`POST /v1/templates/{name}/fill { "words": { "name": "..." } }` returns them
with those words written into the markup as text.

## Temporary deploys

[Deploy with two HTTP calls](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/start.txt) to publish a first app without an account.
After the human claims it, [check what the HTTP key can do](https://somewhere.cloud/auth.md#after-claim).

In the Somewhere MCP connector, you can call `project_deploy` without an
account. Send a `name` and a `files` map. Give the person the returned live
URL, claim link, and expiry. Keep the `session_id` private. Reuse it with the
returned `project_id` in `project_logs`, `errors`, and further deploys.
Connect a Somewhere account to use the rest of the tools.

`somewhere deploy --temporary` is the CLI path. Give the human the live URL, claim link and expiry returned by the deploy. Opening the claim link and signing in keeps the app. Redeploying keeps the same URL and expiry.

Deploy to the public live URL and verify it there. `project_rollback`
returns a temporary project to its previous working version. Temporary projects
can also restore a retained deploy from the last 24 hours by number. To go back
further, redeploy a saved copy of that source with `somewhere deploy`.

## project_deploy — replaces files; preserves omitted functions by default

project_deploy fully replaces static files — a file you omit is DELETED —
but a function you omit is KEPT LIVE (merge-preserved), NOT deleted, and the
deploy WARNS you, naming each preserved function. To actually drop a function
pass replace_functions: true (then omitted functions ARE deleted) or use
project_patch with delete_files. There is no partial / incremental file
update through this tool — use project_patch for that.

If you deploy this:
  { files: { "index.html": "..." } }
...then deploy this next:
  { files: { "about.html": "..." } }
...index.html is GONE. Only about.html exists.

To update one file through project_deploy you must include EVERY file
you want live in the same call. For small edits, reach for project_patch
instead.

**Partial deploys (`scope`).** Pass `scope: 'functions'` to deploy ONLY
your functions and leave the static frontend untouched — so a backend-only
deploy can't wipe the frontend — or `scope: 'static'` for the inverse.
The default touches both (static files replaced, omitted functions preserved unless replace_functions:true).

**Successful production publications with a predecessor carry `previous`:**
`{ version, rollback_available, note?, message }`, naming the version live immediately
before that activation. Its one-line message is "Version N is kept;
project_rollback returns to it." for connector/MCP, or names `somewhere rollback --yes`
for CLI callers (HTTP callers get `POST /v1/promote/rollback`). If the build is
no longer restorable it says "Version N is no longer restorable; deploy its source
again to bring it back." When that version has a note, the line ends with `Note "…".`
First deploys, preview-only writes and unchanged no-op
deploys have no new activation predecessor. The CLI prints the message; JSON keeps
the field. The hint describes that activation; a later publish or automatic rollback
can change the target, and rollback still checks schema safety.

`project_deploy_log({ project_id, version?, release_id? })` returns the
build log for a past deploy without re-running it — and also carries
`last_failed_build` (the most recent build that failed to compile),
`last_rejected` (the most recent deploy rejected before compile, e.g.
bundled-output detection), and `recent_failures` (up to 5 safe rows with
`failure_id`, `classification`, `message`, `remediation`, and version/time).
Resolve one exact reference with
`somewhere api GET /v1/deploy/failure/<failure_id>`; it requires project
access and never returns the private diagnostic or stack. A project whose first deploy
ever failed has no successful build to show — the call returns
`version: null` with an empty `build_log` and whatever failure context
exists, which IS the answer to "why did my deploy fail."

**The reference check finishes after live.** A deploy response can carry
`reference_check: { status: 'pending', requested_at }`: an advisory
TypeScript pass (undefined names, type mismatches) that runs after the release
is live and never changes or blocks it. Read its result from that version's
deploy log; in a linked folder `somewhere call` defaults to that project:

```bash
somewhere call project_deploy_log '{"version":<version>}' | jq '.data.reference_check'
```

`status` becomes `checked` with a `findings` count (the findings join
the log's `warnings`), or `unavailable` when the pass could not run or
never finished (`reason: 'not_finished'`); `unavailable` is never a clean
result.

## project_patch — incremental

Use `files` to write one or more whole files in a single patch, or
`edits` for ordered find/replace across files. Unchanged files are preserved. Static-file
changes go live in ~1 second; function changes in 2–4 seconds.
Read `project_export` first and pass the returned `active_release_id`
as `base_release_id` on each patch, including dry runs. An optional
`base_version` adds a version check; it does not replace the release anchor.

**Find / replace (~200 bytes on the wire — preferred for small edits):**

  project_patch({
    project_id: "my-app",
    base_release_id: "<active_release_id from project_export>",
    path: "index.html",
    find: "<h1>Pricing</h1>",
    replace: "<h1>Plans & pricing</h1>"
  })

Replaces every occurrence of `find` with `replace`. If `find` doesn't
match anywhere in the file, you get a 400 `FIND_NOT_FOUND` with a
snippet of what the file currently says. A sufficiently similar region
also appears in `data.closest_match`; unrelated text may have no match.
Re-read the source and correct the substring with that export’s release
anchor. This is the token-optimal path for visual-editor
iteration (Claude Design, Cursor).

**Ordered edits (many small changes, one patch):**

  project_patch({
    project_id: "my-app",
    base_release_id: "<active_release_id from project_export>",
    edits: [
      { path: "src/App.tsx", find: "const TITLE = 'Old'", replace: "const TITLE = 'New'", expect: 1 },
      { path: "src/App.tsx", find: "<Footer />", replace: "<Footer year={2026} />" },
      { path: "styles.css", find: "color: red", replace: "color: teal" }
    ]
  })

`edits` replaces top-level `path`/`find`/`replace`. The edits apply in
order to the source of `base_release_id` (a later edit to the same file
sees the earlier ones) and publish as one patch. If any edit does not
match, nothing is published: `FIND_NOT_FOUND` with zero-based
`data.edit_index`. `expect: n` requires exactly n non-overlapping
matches, else `FIND_COUNT_MISMATCH` with `data.expected` and
`data.actual`. At most 200 edits per call. A path is edited, written
whole (`files`), or deleted (`delete_files`) in one patch, never two of
these. Unified diffs are not a patch format: ordered exact replacements
plus whole-file writes cover the same changes without a second parser.
From a shell, `somewhere call project_patch --file args.json` reads the
arguments from a file, and `somewhere deploy` publishes a local tree.

**Full content (rewriting the file):**

  project_patch({
    project_id: "my-app",
    base_release_id: "<active_release_id from project_export>",
    path: "api/hello.ts",
    content: "export default async (req, sw) => Response.json({ v: 2 })"
  })

Paths are auto-routed: anything under `api/` or `_lib/` (or a root
`[id].ts`-style parametric route) is function source; everything else
is a static file. Every file under `api/` is a route except helpers: a
file or folder whose name starts with `_` (`api/_lib.ts`, `api/_lib/db.ts`)
is import-only and never becomes a route.

**Binary assets** (images, fonts) — `content` and `find`/`replace`
operate on text. Use the binary write surface (`update_binary_files`)
for raw bytes; trying to ship them through this tool's text fields
corrupts them via UTF-8.

**Delete:** `delete_files` is an array of paths. Works for both
static files and functions; missing paths are silently ignored.

**Conflict check.** Send the observed `active_release_id` as `base_release_id`
when deploying or patching released code. A stale base returns 409
`STALE_RELEASE_BASE`. The numeric `expected_version` field belongs to the
deploy counter for projects without releases. A patch to a released project
that also supplies `base_release_id` ignores `expected_version` and returns a
`source_base_note` on success, including on dry runs.

Everything you don't name stays untouched.

What is NOT affected by a deploy:
  - Env vars (list them with `somewhere env list`)
  - Database contents (managed by db_query, db_migrate)
  - Uploaded files written via fs_write / sw.fs (separate storage)

## Automatic sitemap and robots files

See `recipe-seo` → `automatic-sitemap-and-robots-files` for generated
files, app-supplied overrides and client-router paths.

## Example

project_deploy({
  project_id: "my-app",
  files: {
    "index.html": "<html>...</html>",
    "styles.css": "body { color: red }"
  },
  functions: {
    "api/hello.ts": "export default sw.endpoint({ auth: 'none', handler: async () => ({ ok: true }) });"
  },
  binary_files: {
    "images/logo.png": "iVBORw0KGgo..."
  }
})

files = static assets (stored source is unchanged; served HTML can receive the
temporary expiry and claim notice or a development/review overlay)
functions = server-side code with sw access, routed by file path
binary_files = images/fonts/PDFs as base64, decoded on the server

## After every deploy, the platform automatically:

1. **Screenshots the live site** — desktop + mobile, captured per
   version. The dashboard uses these as previews.
   → `project_screenshots({ project_id })` or
   `GET /v1/deploy/screenshots`.
2. **Generates a Mermaid architecture diagram** — rendered inline on
   the project Overview.
   → `GET /v1/deploy/architecture`.
3. **Writes a plain-English description of what your app does** —
   shown under the project name on the dashboard.
   → `GET /v1/deploy/description`.

Screenshots, architecture, and description run after the deploy
response returns. The LLM security review runs on demand — call
`security_review({ project_id })` or `POST /v1/security/review` after a
deploy. Every plan can request a review. Paid plans get a longer report.
Eligible paid plans also review when a preview is promoted. It returns
structured findings against 9 risk categories (auth bypass, raw SQL, unsafe
payment metadata, env leaks, privilege escalation, RCE, email spoofing,
conversation hijack, CSRF).
Separately, a quick regex scanner
also runs during compile and surfaces obvious footguns as advisory
`warnings` in the deploy response — cheap synchronous gate, every
tier. Full reference: `docs({ topic: 'deploy-intelligence' })`.

## Check BEFORE you deploy (no deploy required)

The default check gives a fast green/red without shipping, so you fix everything
before deploying once instead of deploy → error → fix → redeploy:

- **`project_check({ project_id, files?, functions? })`** — run this after
  editing source and before every deploy. It typechecks / compiles / lints
  the changed files with the SAME compile gate a
  real deploy runs (syntax, undefined symbols / dropped imports,
  JSX-in-.js, Vite-only `import.meta.glob`) and returns
  `{ ok, errors: [{ file, line, column, message, kind }], error_count,
  reference_checked, syntax_checked, notes }` — writing nothing, no
  version change. A green here means the deploy's compile step passes too.
  (`POST /v1/deploy/check`.) The response also carries `lint`: the same
  warning-only source checks as `somewhere lint` (`somewhere deploy-check
  --json` prints it).

## Deploy size limits

These size checks apply to every deploy on every plan and run before compilation.

| Ceiling | Value | Refusal | Instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| Decoded source, functions and assets together | 20 MiB | 413 `DEPLOY_TOO_LARGE`, naming the largest files | Put images, video and fonts in file storage and reference their public URLs |
| Files in one deploy | 1,500 | 400 `BUILD_ERROR` (too many files) | Move generated or media files to file storage |
| Text source (code, styles, markup) | 5 MiB | 400 `BUILD_ERROR` (source bytes) | Keep data files out of the source; load them from file storage |
| JSON request body of any deploy (CLI, MCP, API) | 40 MiB (default) | 413 `DEPLOY_TOO_LARGE` | Upload images, video and fonts to file storage first and reference their URLs |

## Image and font caching

Import images and fonts from source, or reference them with CSS `url()`, to
ship them at content-hashed `/_compiled/` addresses. PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF,
SVG, ICO, WOFF, WOFF2, TTF and OTF assets use the same
`public, max-age=31536000, immutable` policy as compiled scripts and styles.
Changing an asset changes its address; HTML references to emitted assets are
rewritten too.

Fixed-name media from `public/` or `static/` has a bounded policy:
`public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=60`, with an ETag. A changed file
can remain cached for at most two minutes. This policy requires source-folder
provenance from a new deployment; older deployments retain revalidation. It
does not apply to HTML, API responses or authenticated views. Deploy and
deploy-check name static-folder images or fonts of at least 32 KiB and suggest
importing them from source for a permanent address.

Project public configuration is inlined before module execution on ordinary
HTML document requests. The external no-store script remains a fallback; it
is not a shared cache across projects.

`deploy-check` includes imported binary images and fonts in the same source tree
as a real deploy. It compiles them and reports static-media cache notices without
publishing a new app version.

## Privacy facts

Source deploy output includes release privacy facts, also readable with `project_privacy_facts`
and `somewhere privacy`. They list declared owner tables, file collection names and outside
domains found in source. Requests built while the app runs are not covered. Warnings do not
block deploy. No collection or outside-domain signals means a short section with no warnings.
A privacy-page name is only a guess from file and route names. Sign-in configuration and
executed service usage are not included; unavailable signals are reported as unavailable.

pages.title: Custom Domains
pages.body:
## Connect your own domain in the dashboard

Open your app in the [dashboard](https://somewhere.cloud/app). In **Address**, choose **Set up** next to **Your own domain**. On **Use your own domain**, enter your domain and choose **Continue**. Add any DNS records the page shows at your DNS provider. The page checks when the domain opens your app.

A project serves a custom domain through one of three setup paths:

  Claimed domain — a domain the owner already has, on a paid plan. The
                   owner points its nameservers at the platform once; it
                   can then be attached to and moved between projects, and
                   it can receive email for the project.

  DNS-record setup — one project, one hostname, on every plan. The owner
                     adds two DNS records and keeps their nameservers.

  Bought domain — registered through checkout. It is set up as a claim
                  (its DNS is hosted here) after payment, with no further step.

## Recommended: claim by delegating nameservers

One claim covers the apex (`example.com`), `www` and any subdomain.
Once active, the domain can be attached to a different project without
verifying ownership again.

  // 1. Claim — returns the nameserver pair to set at the registrar.
  domain_claim({ domain: "example.com" })
  // → { id, claim_status: "pending_ns",
  //     nameservers: ["<ns1>", "<ns2>"],  // the pair for this domain
  //     instructions: [...] }

  // 2. The owner replaces the nameservers at their registrar.

  // 3. The platform checks pending claims every hour; check now with:
  domain_check_ns({ id })
  // → { claim_status: "active" } once the new nameservers are visible.

  // 4. Attach to a project. host = "apex" (default), "www", or a
  //    single subdomain label like "app".
  domain_attach({ id, project_id: "my-app", host: "apex" })

  // To move the domain to a different project later — no re-verify:
  domain_detach({ id })
  domain_attach({ id, project_id: "other-app", host: "apex" })

  // To list every domain the account has claimed (attached or not):
  domain_owned({})

`domain_attach` on a domain that is attached to another app changes nothing
and answers `409 DOMAIN_ATTACHED_ELSEWHERE`, naming that app: detach it there
first. Attaching again to the same app (for example to change `host`) is
accepted.

## Where the domain tools are

- **Full MCP (`/mcp`).** A bare `tools/list` shows the core set, which for
  domains is `domain_buy`, `domain_check` and `domain_list`. Every other domain
  tool (`domain_add`, `domain_verify`, `domain_remove`, `domain_claim`,
  `domain_check_ns`, `domain_attach`, `domain_detach`, `domain_owned`,
  `domain_enable_email`, `domain_publish`) works when called and is listed by
  `catalog({ load: "domains" })`, or for the whole session with
  `?groups=domains` on the MCP URL (or the `Mcp-Tool-Groups: domains` header).
- **The claude.ai connector (`/mcp/connector`).** It has `domain_add`,
  `domain_verify` and `domain_check`. The claim path goes through `api_write`
  and `api_read` with the same REST calls the tools make:

      api_write({ calls: [{ method: "POST", path: "/v1/domains/claim", body: { domain: "example.com" } }] })
      api_write({ calls: [{ method: "POST", path: "/v1/domains/<id>/check-ns", body: {} }] })
      api_write({ calls: [{ method: "POST", path: "/v1/domains/<id>/attach", body: { project_id: "<project id>", host: "apex" } }] })
      api_write({ calls: [{ method: "POST", path: "/v1/domains/<id>/detach", body: {} }] })
      api_write({ calls: [{ method: "PATCH", path: "/v1/domains/app.example.com/reassign", body: { project_id: "<project id>" } }] })
      api_write({ calls: [{ method: "DELETE", path: "/v1/domains/example.com" }] })
      api_read({ calls: [{ method: "GET", path: "/v1/domains/owned" }] })
      api_read({ calls: [{ method: "GET", path: "/v1/domains?project_id=<project id>" }] })

  Buying is not available through `api_write`: the owner buys on the
  purchase page (see below).
- **The ChatGPT app.** It has no domain operations; the owner connects a
  domain on the app's domain page in the dashboard.
- **The `somewhere` CLI.** It has no separate `domain` command; every
  domain tool runs through `somewhere call`, for example
  `somewhere call domain_claim '{"domain":"example.com"}'` or
  `somewhere call domain_attach '{"id":"<id>","project_id":"<project id>","host":"apex"}'`.

## What the domain owner does

- **Plan.** Claiming needs a paid plan; on Free, `domain_claim` returns
  `402 UPGRADE_REQUIRED`. The DNS-record path below works on every plan.
- **Their one step.** At their registrar (where the domain is registered),
  they replace the existing nameservers with the two in `nameservers`.
  Take the pair from the `domain_claim` response, or from `domain_owned`
  later, never from memory or an example.
- **A domain set up here before.** If the domain's nameservers still point
  at an earlier setup on the platform, `domain_claim` returns
  `409 NAMESERVERS_STILL_DELEGATED`: change them at the registrar to anything
  else, then claim again. The claim then starts fresh, and the domain goes
  live only after the registrar is pointed at the pair the new claim returns.
  This also applies to an owner re-claiming a domain they removed
  themselves: the nameservers have to move away and back.
- **Timing.** The change usually takes effect within minutes and can take up
  to 24 hours.
- **When it is live.** No email or notice is sent when a claim becomes
  active. `domain_check_ns` reports `claim_status: "active"`, and the
  domain serves the project as soon as it is attached.
- **Existing records.** Claiming moves the domain's DNS to the platform and
  does not copy existing records, so mail and any other records the domain
  serves stop when the nameservers move. A domain that already sends or
  receives email, or serves other records, stays on the DNS-record path.

## Claim lifetime + cleanup

A claim belongs to the owner's account, not to a project, so
`project_delete` does not remove it: deleting the app detaches the claim at
once, and it stays in `domain_owned`, ready to attach to another app. To
remove a claim from `domain_owned`, pending or active:

  domain_remove({ domain: "example.com" })

`domain_detach({ id })` frees the project binding and keeps the claim for
later.

## Sending mail on a claimed domain (automatic)

Attaching a claimed domain to an app also sets up sending as that domain for
the app, with no further call. A few minutes after the attach the platform:

- registers the domain with the mail provider that sends for the app;
- writes three DKIM records into the domain's zone (CNAME
  `<token>._domainkey.<domain>` → `<token>.dkim.amazonses.com`, comment
  "somewhere sender-domain auto-setup") and one TXT record at
  `_somewhere.<domain>` that proves the setup is the app's;
- adds the domain to the app's sending domains and marks it verified once the
  provider confirms the records.

It writes no MX or SPF record, so receiving mail stays as it was. A bought
domain gets the same setup, as a claim does. The setup belongs to the
app it was made for:

- `domain_detach` removes that app's setup first, then detaches the domain;
  the next app the domain is attached to gets its own. If the setup cannot be
  removed right now, nothing is detached and the call answers
  `503 SENDER_DOMAIN_REMOVE_FAILED`; the same call retries.
- `domain_remove` on an attached domain (bought ones included) removes that
  app's setup first, then the domain.
- The records stay in the zone in every case. Once the setup is removed they
  verify nothing, and a new setup writes new ones.

## Receiving mail on a claimed domain (opt-in)

`domain_claim` adds no MX records, and claiming does not copy the domain's
existing records. A domain that already receives email through Gmail,
Workspace or its own server stops receiving it when its nameservers move;
keep such a domain on the DNS-record path. Receiving mail is a separate step:

  domain_enable_email({ id })
  // → { receiving_host }. With no mail provider on the domain, mail is
  //   received on the domain itself. With one (Gmail/Workspace, Microsoft
  //   365, a forwarding catch-all, any other MX or SPF), its records are left
  //   unchanged and app mail is received on reply.<domain> instead.
  // Addresses on receiving_host are registered through the mail API (/v1/mail).

## Ownership

A domain bought through somewhere.cloud is registered in the buyer's name
from the moment of purchase. It can leave on the registry's transfer rules:

- to another registrar from 60 days after registration (the ICANN transfer
  rule for generic endings such as .com; country endings such as .uk follow
  their own registry's rules);
- to the buyer's own Name.com account from 5 days after registration.

Either move starts with an email to support@somewhere.cloud from the
account's email address, naming the domain. Full details:
https://somewhere.cloud/docs/domain-ownership

## Stuck domain recovery

A claimed, active domain that resolves to nothing is repaired with
`domain_publish({ id })`: `troubleshooting` →
`a-claimed-domain-is-active-but-does-not-resolve`.

## DNS-record setup

Use this path when the nameservers stay where they are, for example a
company domain whose DNS another team runs.

  domain_add({ project_id: "my-app", domain: "app.yourcompany.com" })
  // → { cname_target, registrable_domain, dns_record_host,
  //     verification_txt_name, verification_txt_value, instructions }

  domain_verify({ project_id: "my-app", domain: "app.yourcompany.com" })
  // → { verified, cname_ok, txt_ok, next_step, ... }

The owner adds the CNAME (to `cname_target`) and the TXT record
(`verification_txt_name` = `verification_txt_value`) at their DNS host,
with the values from the `domain_add` response. `dns_records` lists both
records, each with `host` (the name relative to the registrable domain, which
most DNS hosts expect because they add the domain themselves) and
`full_name` (for a host that wants the whole name):

  // domain_add({ project_id, domain: "app.example.com" }).dns_records
  [{ type: "CNAME", host: "app", full_name: "app.example.com", value: "proxy.somewhere.tech", purpose: "routing" },
   { type: "TXT", host: "_somewhere-verify.app",
     full_name: "_somewhere-verify.app.example.com", value: "smt-verify-…", purpose: "ownership" }]

**A bare domain** (`example.com` itself, not `app.example.com`) whose DNS is
at another company cannot be connected with DNS records. It works here in one
of two ways:

- **Claim it:** `domain_claim({ domain: "example.com" })` (paid plan) moves
  its nameservers here; the bare domain, `www` and mail then serve (see
  above).
- **Connect www instead:** `domain_add` with `www.example.com` (the CNAME and
  TXT records above), then forward `example.com` to `www.example.com` at the
  DNS company.

`domain_add` for a bare domain answers `400 BARE_DOMAIN_NEEDS_CLAIM_OR_WWW`
with those two ways and no records. A bare domain connected here before keeps
working. `domain_verify` marks every record with `in_place`.

`registrable_domain` is
the name the owner manages at their registrar (`example.co.uk` for
`shop.example.co.uk`, from the public suffix list) and `dns_record_host` is
the record name to enter there (`@` for the registrable domain itself,
otherwise `shop`). Every domain answer (`domain_add`, `domain_verify`,
`domain_check`, the project's domain list and status) carries both fields,
so no caller splits labels itself. `domain_verify` checks
both; until then `next_step` names exactly what is missing: which record
(CNAME or TXT) is absent or points elsewhere, with its name and the value it
needs, and then where the domain's DNS is managed when that is a known
provider (`third_party_dns_provider`). `next_step` is a plain sentence that
can be shown to the owner as it is. `cname_ok` and `txt_ok` say the same per
record.

When the subdomain's registrable domain is a domain the same account has
already claimed here, `parent_zone_in_account` is `{ id, domain }` (on
`domain_verify` and on each row of the domain list). That subdomain needs no
DNS records: `domain_attach({ id, project_id, host: "app" })` on the claim
serves it.

Adding a domain again to the same project answers `already_exists: true` with
its real `verified` state. A domain that cannot be added answers
`409 DOMAIN_TAKEN` with `data.reason`:

- `own_app`: it is on another of your apps. The message names the app and
  the move: `PATCH /v1/domains/<domain>/reassign` with `{ project_id }`, or for
  a claim, detach then attach.
- `own_claim`: it is a domain you claimed and it is not on any app. Attach it
  (`data.domain_id`), with no records.
- `deleted_app`: an app of yours that was deleted still holds it, until that
  deletion completes.
- `other_account`: another account holds it.

## Moving a domain to another app

`PATCH /v1/domains/<domain>/reassign` with `{ "project_id": "<project id>" }`
moves a DNS-record or bought domain to another app you can edit, with no new
DNS records or verification. The app's sending setup for the domain moves with
it, and it is refused (`409 SENDER_DOMAIN_CONFLICT`) when both apps send as
the domain. A claimed domain moves with `domain_detach`, then `domain_attach`.

Once verified, a DNS-record domain serves production within a couple of
minutes. A verified custom domain and the project's
`*.somewhere.site` subdomain serve the same immutable release named by
`active_release_id`.

## Buy a domain through checkout

The account owner pays for the domain in checkout, and it renews yearly.
Check availability, then request the purchase preview:

  domain_check({ domain: "acmedash.com" })
  // → { available: true, price: "<amount>/year", price_cents }

Domains cost the registrar's yearly price with no markup, so each name has
its own price: quote it from `domain_check` or the search (both carry the
same registrar quote), never from a fixed list. `GET /v1/pricing` states this
rule under `domains`.

A first year can be a registrar promotion priced below later years. Search
answers carry `renewal_price_cents`, the registrar's price for each later
year; each renewal charges the registrar's renewal price at that time, also
with no markup.

Purchase connects the domain to the app with no DNS steps. A bought domain
is a claimed domain: its DNS is hosted here, its nameservers are set at
registration, and it serves the bare name and www over HTTPS. A new name
usually serves within 30 minutes of payment, once the registry publishes it;
`domain_list` shows it as pending until then. Receiving email is off until
`domain_enable_email`, as for any claim.

  domain_buy({ project_id: "my-app", domain: "acmedash.com" })
  // → { ok: false, error: "PURCHASE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED",
  //     domain: "acmedash.com", price: "<amount>/year",
  //     dashboard_checkout_url: "https://somewhere.cloud/app/<project id>/buy/acmedash.com" }

The owner opens `dashboard_checkout_url` (the app's purchase page), signs in
if needed, and pays in checkout. No confirmation token is involved;
there is no agent-side purchase step. Registration and DNS/HTTPS setup begin
only after payment settles. The first paid domain on a Free account also
unlocks 30 days of Builder.

## Domain search

`GET /v1/domains/search?q=<word or name>` (or `domain_check({ domain: "acmedash", search: true })`)
checks priced endings for the word. Internationalized endings are not offered
as search suggestions.
A whole name (`acmedash.com`) is checked exactly, returned as `exact` and
listed first; its first label is searched for the alternatives.

  domain_check({ domain: "acmedash", search: true, max_price: 40 })
  // → { keyword: "acmedash", exact: null,
  //     results: [{ domain: "acmedash.foundation", available: true, premium: false,
  //                 price: "<amount>/year", price_cents, renewal_price_cents,
  //                 price_status: "quoted", tld, category }, ...],
  //     more_available, endings_total, endings_checked, partial,
  //     unanswered_count, unanswered }

- Every available name carries its first-year price (`price`, `price_cents`)
  and its renewal price when the registrar gives one (`renewal_price_cents`).
  These are the same quotes `domain_check` returns for one name, which is what
  checkout charges.
- `premium: true` marks a premium name, priced above its ending's standard price.
- `price_status: "unknown"` means the name is available but its price did not
  come back; check it with `domain_check({ domain })`.
- `max_price` (dollars) keeps only names at or under that price. `sort` is
  `price` (default: cheapest available first, after an exact match) or `name`.
  Without `max_price`, taken names follow the available ones.
- At most 60 names come back; `more_available` counts the available names
  left out, and `next_cursor` gives the next 60: pass it back as `cursor`
  (`domain_check({ domain, search: true, cursor })`). The cheapest endings are
  checked first. `endings_total` counts the priced endings within the search
  and `endings_checked` counts how many of those returned an answer.
- While checks are running, `partial` is true. Repeat the search after a few
  seconds for the finished result. After checks finish, `partial` is false and
  paging is available. `unanswered_count` and `unanswered` give the count and
  full names whose availability is still unknown. The list can include an exact
  name checked separately from the priced endings.
- Limits: 10 searches or checks per minute and
  100 per day per user; a repeated search returns cached
  results for 5 minutes.

## Listing + removal

  domain_list({ project_id: "my-app" })          // custom domains
  domain_remove({ domain: "app.yourcompany.com" }) // remove or release a claim

Deleting an app yourself (`project_delete`) frees its custom domains and
email sending setup at once, not at the end of the 30-day retention:

- A DNS-record domain is removed the way `domain_remove` removes it: the
  app's sending setup for that domain first, then its address.
- A claimed or bought domain is detached. It stays in your account,
  unattached and reusable; its DNS zone and a purchase's renewal are
  unchanged. The sending setup the platform made for it on the app is removed.
- Every sending domain the app held is released for another app.

Restoring a deleted app through support within the 30 days does not bring
back its domain connections or sending setup.

An app deleted because its subscription was cancelled is different: its
domains and sending setup stay connected to it until it is erased, 30 days
after its deletion began, so restoring it keeps them.

A domain the delete could not release stays with the deleted app, which
serves nothing. The answer is `503 DELETE_INCOMPLETE` with
`data.domains_pending` (each `{ domain, reason }`) and what was freed
(`domains_removed`, `domains_detached`, `sending_domains_removed`).
Repeating the delete releases the rest; if it is never repeated, the domain
is released when the app is erased.

pages.title: Test, observe and troubleshoot
pages.body:
`somewhere verify` drives your live app in a real browser at desktop and phone size. It reports each step, console errors and failed requests, and keeps screenshots. Logs, runtime errors and analytics come from the same project, so after a check you can read what happened without wiring any tooling. ## Check one real journey, including a refusal Test what a user actually does, plus one thing they must not be able to do. This flow opens the starter already signed in as a managed test user of the project, then confirms that a signed-out visitor is refused. It uses the `/api/account` function from **Auth**. Save it as `flows/journey.json`: ```json { "actors": { "ana": { "auth": { "user_id": "" } }, "visitor": {} }, "journey": [ { "as": "ana", "path": "/", "actions": [ { "expect": { "selector": ".topbar", "visible": true } }, { "eval": "fetch('/api/account').then((r) => r.status)" } ], "expect_requests": [{ "path": "/api/account", "status": 200 }] }, { "as": "visitor", "path": "/", "actions": [ { "eval": "fetch('/api/account').then((r) => r.status)" } ], "expect_requests": [{ "path": "/api/account", "status": 401 }] } ] } ``` ```bash echo "flows/" >> .somewhereignore # keep test credentials off the live site somewhere verify --flow flows/journey.json ``` The final line is JSON with `outcome` and `counts`. Exit 0 means the flow passed, 1 means a named check failed, and 2 means verification or cleanup could not finish. For unconfirmed cleanup, the report names the browsers or test users that may remain. `expect_requests` lists the answers the flow intends. Here, 401 for the signed-out visitor counts as a pass. A declared request must be seen with that status (its `path` matches by substring), or the step fails. A refused request you did not declare still fails the run's network check. Declare a refusal only when the flow is meant to be refused; an unexpected 4xx or 5xx is an app failure to fix, not to declare. Running more than one actor needs a claimed account and a credential allowed to keep named browser sessions. Project-scoped CLI logins refuse this multi-actor journey; a fresh one-user flow can use its approved project scope. `auth: { user_id }` takes the id of a managed test user of this project; other ids answer `AUTH_INVALID_CREDS`, so sign real accounts in through your UI. In a several-user flow, declare the actor as `{ "test_user": true }` instead and `verify` creates the test user for you (CLI 0.37.46 or later; see *Several users in one run*). Otherwise create test users (1–5 per call, up to 25 live per project, each expiring after 24 hours) with `somewhere api POST /v1/auth/test-users -d '{"project_id":"","count":2}'` and use each `identities[].user.id`. They are created verified, with no password, so they skip the signup/login UI and email verification. To test those genuine flows, sign up through your UI as `@.test.somewhere.site` (see *When signup or login is the behavior under test*); that mail lands in the test inbox, never externally. Run the flow against your deployed app. While you develop, `somewhere dev` serves the frontend from your machine and sends its `/api` requests to the deployed project, so data you save locally is written to production. To check that one user cannot see another's data, run two signed-in actors: `somewhere docs browser --section several-users-in-one-run` (MCP: `docs({ topic: 'browser', section: 'several-users-in-one-run' })`). ## Read what happened Browser actions use `[{"fill":"#email","value":"a@b.co"}]`; `--flow` wraps them as `{"actions":[{"fill":"#email","value":"a@b.co"}]}`. For a large journey, create a private directory outside the app root with `mkdir -p ../verify-reports`, then run `somewhere verify --flow flow.json --out ../verify-reports/journey.json`. This writes the full report (including evaluation values and screenshot links) to a new owner-only file and prints only a bounded summary. Add `--json` for a machine-readable summary. Without `--out`, `--json` retains the complete report on stdout. Keep full report files private. ```bash somewhere logs --tail 20 # recent log lines somewhere logs --level error --since 1h # only errors from the last hour somewhere logs --function /api/account # one route somewhere errors # recent runtime failures with stack and path ``` In a function, write your own entries with `sw.logs.info`, `warn` or `error`. They show in the same stream. Read the failure first, then change code. `somewhere deploy-check --run /api/hello` exercises a public handler without publishing. The CLI check sends a signed-out request, so an account handler that requires sign-in returns `401 AUTH_REQUIRED`. To check that handler while signed in, use `somewhere browser --path /api/account --auth-user ` against the deployed app with a managed test user. Read an error response's `hint` field when present. `troubleshooting` maps common codes to fixes. ## Count what users do Track a product event from a function, after the action it describes: ```ts // api/events.ts — records an allowed product event for the signed-in user const ALLOWED_EVENTS = new Set(['onboarding_completed', 'note_shared']); export default async function events( request: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, ): Promise { if (request.method !== 'POST') { return new Response('Use POST.', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } }); } const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(request); if (!user) return Response.json({ error: 'Sign in.' }, { status: 401 }); const input: unknown = await request.json().catch(() => null); const event = typeof input === 'object' && input !== null && 'event' in input ? input.event : undefined; if (typeof event !== 'string' || !ALLOWED_EVENTS.has(event)) { return Response.json({ error: 'Unknown event.' }, { status: 400 }); } const result = await sw.analytics.track(event, { properties: { source: 'app' } }); // When consent blocks recording, the result carries the reason. const reason = 'reason' in result ? result.reason : undefined; return Response.json(result.recorded ? { recorded: true } : { recorded: false, reason }); } ``` `analytics_query({ project_id, event, group_by: 'day' })` returns counts. Page views are counted on the server without a tracking script. Keep personal data out of `properties`. **Consent.** By default, collection runs without a consent prompt. Setting `analytics_consent: { mode: "required", policy_version: "v1" }` with `project_update` adds a same-origin Accept/Reject banner, and the platform collects page views and `sw.analytics.track` events only after the visitor accepts that exact policy version. Changing `policy_version` asks every visitor again. Without a matching acceptance, `track` returns `recorded: false` with the reason (`consent_pending`, `consent_declined` or `consent_unavailable`), and the example returns both. The platform enforces the policy as soon as you set it. Functions forward the visitor's choice and skip blocked events once the app is deployed on the current runtime; an ordinary deploy does that (`deploy` → `optional-analytics-consent`). Consent mode covers the platform's own collection; your privacy policy should describe what your app tracks. ## More on testing and observing | Need | Where | |---|---| | Flow actions, sessions, several users, limits | `browser` → `drive-a-flow-add-actions`, `several-users-in-one-run`, `limits` | | Checks before publishing | `verify-before-deploy` | | Scheduled health checks | `smoke` | | Writing and reading logs; log retention | `sw.logs` → `write-logs`, `reading-logs`, `retention` | | Reading error logs, codes and hints | `troubleshooting` → `how-to-read-your-error-logs`, `all-api-errors-include-a-hint-field` | | Analytics tracking and queries | `analytics` | | Consent mode details | `deploy` → `optional-analytics-consent` | | Local development | `local-dev` | ## The browser tool and its routes `browser` opens your DEPLOYED app in a real headless browser so you can SEE it, INSPECT it, and DRIVE it — one tool for the whole loop of "what does my app look like, is it healthy, and does it actually work?" The MCP `browser` tool selects the appropriate REST route. For direct HTTP, use `POST /v1/browser/test` for page inspection and actions, and `POST /v1/render/screenshot` for raw `html` (or `/v1/render/pdf` for PDF). The page-test route does not render HTML snippets. Every report includes `timing` in milliseconds: `admission_wait_ms`, `browser_acquire_ms` (with `browser_reused`), `page_setup_ms`, `start_navigation_ms`, `actions_ms` and `total_ms`, plus `auth_ms` when `auth: { user_id }` signed a user in. Multi-viewport flows belong to `somewhere verify --flow` or MCP `site_verify`; a page-test request uses one `viewport`, not `viewports`. For the complete verification loop, run `somewhere verify --url --flow flow.json` or MCP `site_verify`. The exact flow object is `{ "actions": [{ "fill": "#name", "value": "Potluck" }, { "click": "#save" }, { "expect": { "selector": "#status", "text": "Saved" } }], "expect_requests": [{ "path": "/api/private", "status": 401 }], "visible_only": true, "viewports": ["desktop", "mobile"] }`; omit it for a page load, health report, and both screenshots. Every viewport gets a fresh browser that closes inside the call, including when a step fails. The viewport runs happen concurrently. If your flow writes data, prefer the sequential several-user journey below with existing controlled test users; two viewport runs signed in as the same person share that person’s data. - **Eyes** — a screenshot of the page. - **Ears** — console errors, page errors, and failed network requests (a backend 500 shows here even when the page looks fine). - **Hands** — click / fill / assert your way through a real flow. `run_code` proves a function's backend; `browser` proves the rendered UI. The report includes action results, page errors, failed requests, and screenshots. Read `data.passed` in the REST response, not just HTTP status or the outer `ok` field: a completed check can report a failing app or a requested capture that could not be produced. Read the step and screenshot errors for the cause. The principle: **act by selector, verify by signals, screenshot small + last.** You wrote the DOM, so target elements directly — don't guess at pixel coordinates like a computer-use agent staring at a stranger's screen. ## Just look (omit steps) Omit `steps` and you get a small screenshot, the console/network signals, AND the data-testid map + an interactive-element outline (tag, id, testid, text, selector) — the handles you can act on, instead of reverse-engineering selectors from scraped HTML. Every entry also carries `visible` (false for hidden/display:none/visibility:hidden/aria-hidden, or a zero-size box) and, when true, `disabled` — so a control that a signed-out visitor cannot actually operate reads that way in the outline itself, no follow-up probing required: browser({ project_id: 'my-saas' }) // → { console_errors, page_errors, failed_requests, // screenshots: [{ label: 'page', fs_path: '/_browser_tests/.../00-page.jpg' }], // dom_outline: [{ tag:'button', testid:'submit', text:'Log in', selector:'[data-testid="submit"]', visible: true }, // { tag:'button', testid:'delete-user', text:'Delete', selector:'[data-testid="delete-user"]', visible: false }, ...], // testid_map: { submit: '[data-testid="submit"]', ... }, final_url, passed } For a quick screenshot of your app, this IS the call — a url or project_id with no steps. An explicit `include` list selects the report sections instead of the default DOM map; include `"dom"` to retain it. ## Capture any page, or render raw HTML You can look at any public page and you can photograph it. What you cannot do is operate it: actions, `eval` and signed-in sessions run only against the origins of an authorized project of yours. Navigation off those origins during such a run is REFUSED before the request is made — the run stops and reports the refusal as evidence, rather than quietly continuing with fewer powers. This bounds who the browser may act AS, not what your app may talk to. Your project's own pages keep making their ordinary outbound requests — API calls, assets, third-party scripts — exactly as they do for any visitor. Use `browser` to capture a public page or render raw HTML: // Any public third-party page — pass a url with NO project_id: browser({ url: 'https://example.com' }) // Render a raw HTML snippet straight to an image (e.g. an OG card): browser({ html: '

Hello

', width: 1200, height: 630 }) // → { content_type: 'image/png', size_bytes, base64 } // …or save the snippet straight to the project file store: browser({ html: '
…
', project_id: 'my-app', storage: '/og/card.png' }) // → { storage_path: '/og/card.png', size_bytes } The MCP tool routes `html` to the renderer; direct HTTP callers use `POST /v1/render/screenshot` with the same HTML fields, not the page-test route. `html` mode skips navigation/steps/DOM-map — it just returns the picture. `width` / `height` / `wait_for` tune it. With `project_id`, the `url` must belong to that project. To look at another public site, omit `project_id` — and that run is inspection and capture only. ## Drive a flow (add actions) Driving a page is a project capability. Supply `project_id`, and every action — including `eval` — runs against that project's own origins. The platform enforces this wherever this action shape is accepted: an action that would navigate outside those origins is refused before it is attempted, and the run reports that refusal instead of proceeding. `actions` is the one shared action shape used by the MCP tool, a CLI `--actions` JSON file, and `verify --flow`'s `actions` field. Each item has exactly one action key; selector-taking actions put the selector directly under that key: ```json [ { "fill": "#email", "value": "a@b.co" }, { "select": "#plan", "value": "pro" }, { "click": "button[type=submit]" }, { "wait": ".dashboard" }, { "expect": { "selector": ".welcome", "text": "Hi", "visible": true, "count": 1 } }, { "eval": "document.title" } ] ``` `wait` is a CSS selector (waited for up to 15 s) or non-negative milliseconds. A fixed wait longer than 45000 ms is refused with an error naming the step, never shortened: split a longer pause into several waits (each counts toward `budget_ms`) or wait for a condition. A condition wait's own `timeout` is at most 45000 ms. `expect` requires `selector` plus at least one of `text`, `value`, `visible`, or `count`. Actions stop on the first failure by default; in the `browser` tool, `continue_on_failure: true` runs the remaining actions too (`verify --flow` does not accept it). `text` succeeds when any visible match contains the requested case-sensitive DOM text and its rendered text matches ignoring case. Hidden text alone does not pass. `value` and `visible` check the first element matching the selector; `count` checks all matches of the selector, even when `text` is also given, so `count: 0` together with `text` can never pass. `visible: false` passes only when a matching element exists and is hidden; if nothing matches, it fails. To assert that an element is absent, use `count: 0` alone, with a selector narrow enough to match only that element. `verify` waits up to 15 s for each `expect`. Target a unique element when asserting a particular record. Expanded `steps` remain accepted for existing callers, but new flows use `actions`. A screenshot action needs a label, for example `{ "screenshot": "after-save" }`. `{ "goto": "/path" }` navigates within the app (a path starting with `/`; absolute, scheme-relative and relative values are refused). Add `"frame": "name | url-substring | child-index | css-selector"` to an action to run it inside an iframe; its wait, expect, eval and screenshot then observe that frame (CLI 0.37.58 or later forwards it). `{ "upload": "#file", "fs_path": "/uploads/big.mp4", "type": "video/mp4" }` puts a file already stored in the project's files into a file input (optional `name` and `type`; up to 50 MB per call, streamed into the page), while `"file"` carries inline base64 or a data URL up to 10 MB; send exactly one. Native dialogs (`alert`, `confirm`, `prompt`, `beforeunload`) never stall a run: each one is dismissed by default and listed in the report's `dialogs` with its type, its message (credentials redacted), the answer sent, and `handled`: `accepted` or `dismissed` once the browser confirmed it, `unconfirmed` if the call ended first, `failed` if it was refused. To accept one, put `{ "dialog": "accept" }` right before the action that opens it; add `"text"` to answer a prompt. `{ "dialog": "dismiss" }` states the default explicitly. An answer applies once, in the same call, to the next dialog opened by a page this run may act on; a dialog from any other frame is dismissed and the answer stays queued. One that no dialog used is listed in `dialog_actions_unused`. A dismissed `beforeunload` keeps the page, so the navigation that triggered it fails. An HTML `` element is ordinary page content: click it as usual. ## Logged-in flows browser({ project_id: 'my-saas', auth: { user_id: 'usr_123' }, actions: [...] }) Mints a 1-hour session for that app user (audited) and injects it before navigation, so authed pages work. Requires a project, and the seeded credentials are scoped to that project's origins — they are not handed to any other origin the page loads from, and a navigation that would leave those origins is refused rather than followed. There is no way to seed a session for a site you do not own. ## Reading the result `{ console_errors, page_errors, failed_requests, steps:[{step, ok, error?, duration_ms}], screenshots:[{label, fs_path}], final_url, passed }` `passed` requires successful steps and request expectations, no page errors, and no unexpected failed requests. It can be false even when every step succeeded. Console messages are additional diagnostic evidence; inspect them too. A failing run attempts to return `rendered_text` and a screenshot labelled `failure`; unavailable evidence is reported without hiding the original failure. Explicit `capture: false` or `screenshot: false` skips the automatic failure screenshot. With `continue_on_failure`, final evidence shows the state after the remaining actions, not necessarily the first failure. ## Screenshots — small by default Screenshots are tuned for cheap vision tokens: ~800px wide JPEG at quality 70. Need pixel precision? Override per run: browser({ project_id: 'my-saas', screenshot: { width: 1280, format: 'png' } }) Fields: width (default 800, never upscaled past the viewport), format ('jpeg' default | 'png'), quality (1–100, jpeg only, default 70). The override applies to the no-steps page shot and every screenshot step. On an actions run, `capture` or `screenshot` also requests a final capture. With a project, each capture is saved to the project's files: the result gives its `fs_path` and, beside it, a signed `url` to open. On a page shot with no steps, `inline: true` also returns the image as `inline_base64`. Without a project, the capture comes back as `inline_base64`; `store: true` returns a temporary `scratch_url` instead. ## Keep one browser across calls (session_id) Checking a whole flow? Prefer ONE `somewhere verify --flow` call (above): it runs every step, opens a fresh browser per viewport and closes it inside the call, so it never holds a session. To keep a page open between calls instead, name a session: MCP `browser({ project_id, url, session_id: "checkout", actions })` or CLI `--session checkout`. The same name in the same project continues on the same page. Another project can use that name for its own separate browser. A call without `session_id` is one-shot and needs no cleanup. Named sessions share the account's limit of 10 live sessions, the same on every plan (`browser_sessions` in `GET /v1/pricing`); an account runs at most 10 browser runs at once. Close your project's session when you are done: `browser({ project_id: "my-app", session_id: "checkout", close: true })`, or `somewhere browser --project my-app --close checkout`. A bare `browser({ session_id: "checkout" })` closes only a session without a project. If other projects hold the remaining slots, the limit error says when to retry; it does not tell you to close their sessions. A named session keeps its cookies and page after a failed step; a page crash, a page that leaves your app, or a call that ends in an error or an unknown outcome closes it. It ends after 5 minutes idle or 10 minutes in total. A call under that name within 24 hours of its launch reports `session_note`: a fresh, signed-out browser was started. With the CLI, `--url` only sets where a new session starts; move a live session with `--path` or a `goto` action. ## Several users in one run A flow file with `actors` and `journey` checks what several signed-in people see, each in their own browser: `somewhere verify --project --flow flow.json`. This one runs on the starter from `somewhere init --name my-app --features private-data` with two `test_user` actors, which `verify` creates for this run. Alice saves a note, an empty Bob account sees none of Alice's notes, and Alice checks her list on a phone. The seeded session skips signup/login UI; it does not test passwords, verification email. Test those genuine journeys separately when relevant, rather than creating a new email/account for every data check. ```json { "actors": { "alice": { "test_user": true }, "bob": { "test_user": true } }, "journey": [ { "as": "alice", "path": "/", "actions": [ { "wait": "#note-title" }, { "fill": "#note-title", "value": "Alice's note" }, { "click": "form:has(#note-title) button[type=submit]" }, { "expect": { "selector": ".note__title", "text": "Alice's note" } } ] }, { "as": "bob", "path": "/", "actions": [ { "expect": { "selector": ".empty__title", "text": "No notes yet." } } ] }, { "as": "alice", "path": "/", "viewport": "mobile", "actions": [ { "expect": { "selector": ".note__title", "text": "Alice's note" } } ] } ] } ``` - `actors`: 1–3 names; each is its own browser. `{}` starts signed out; `{ "auth": { "user_id": "…" } }` signs in as a managed test user of the project. Seeds go only to that actor, only on its first segment. - `{ "test_user": true }` (CLI 0.37.46 or later; not combined with `auth` or other seeds): before the first segment `verify` creates one verified test user per such actor with a single `POST /v1/auth/test-users` call, and starts no browser if that fails. Each actor signs in once, in its own browser. When the run ends, `verify` asks the platform to delete those users; `--keep-test-users` keeps them (test users expire 24 hours after creation). The report's `test_users` lists each actor's `user_id` and `email` and a cleanup `status` of `deleted`, `kept` or `unconfirmed`. - `--keep-actors` (CLI 0.37.66 or later): after a fully passed run, `verify` keeps each actor's signed-in browser and test user, keyed to this project folder, flow file and cast. The next run of the same flow file reconnects to them and re-signs in, so it skips test-user creation, browser startup and cleanup. - Each run still navigates every actor to its first segment's path and runs the same checks. Cookies, storage and app data the actors created carry over, so checks must not assume an empty account. A pass on a kept browser is a warm recheck, not fresh first-load evidence. - Any failed, stopped or unconfirmed run cleans up exactly as without the flag. One run per kept flow at a time. - `--close-actors` closes the kept browsers and deletes the kept test users for this project in this folder. Kept browsers close after 5 minutes without use, and at the latest 10 minutes after they started; the next run then starts fresh and says so on stderr. - A run that cannot reconnect (new or renamed flow file, or a changed cast) says so on stderr. - `--resume-page` (with `--keep-actors`; CLI 0.37.69 or later): an explicit stateful warm continuation, like reusing a Playwright page. - An actor whose first segment starts at exactly the page path the last passed run left it on keeps that page (no reload). - A different actor, flow, project or start path, a start path with a query, or a kept browser that has ended loads normally. - The kept page may run code from before the latest deploy. The report lists `keep_actors.resumed_pages`, and a resumed run is not evidence for the latest release: verify a deploy without `--resume-page`. - `journey`: 1–12 segments, run in order, each `{ as, path?, actions?, expect_requests?, viewport?, visible_only? }`. A later segment for the same actor continues in that actor's browser; its `path` becomes a leading `{ "goto": "/path" }` (counted in its 30 actions). - `{ "parallel": [segment, segment] }` (CLI 0.37.46 or later) runs 2–3 segments by different actors at the same time, for example one waits for a message while another sends it. Each keeps its own browser; groups cannot be nested, a group starts together or not at all, and its segments count toward the 12-segment limit. - `viewport` belongs to that segment (`desktop` by default, `mobile`, or `{ label, width, height }`): the journey runs once, not once per viewport, because it changes app data. The report's `layout` line flags contrast, horizontal overflow and tap targets. - A request a user should be refused passes only when declared in that segment's `expect_requests` (e.g. `{ "path": "/api/admin", "status": 403 }`; a refused generated-client update or delete is `/__sw/data` 404) and seen. The first failing segment stops the run; the verdict names the segment, actor, step and viewport, and later segments are reported not run. - Limits: 3 actors, 12 segments, 30 actions per segment, 120 in total, up to 180 s per segment, 10 minutes per journey. Each segment is one browser run against your plan's browser limits. Hosted apps only. - Browser time is reserved before a run: its `budget_ms` plus 45 s of startup headroom, and for a segment that keeps its actor's browser, up to 300 s that browser may idle afterwards (525 s for a verify segment). A run is charged its own time. A kept browser's idle time is charged until the next segment reuses it, the run closes it, or the browser service reports it closed; one nothing confirms stays charged at the full 300 s. Unused reserved time is returned when the run ends. A refusal is `BROWSER_DAILY_LIMIT` (429) with `data: { reason, used, limit, requested, unconfirmed }`, where `reason` is `duration_exhausted` and `unconfirmed` is the part of `used` only held for runs or kept browsers whose end is not yet confirmed; `BROWSER_SESSION_LIMIT` means too many runs at once. - Needs a claimed account and permission to keep named browser sessions. A temporary account is refused `CLAIM_ACCOUNT_REQUIRED`; a project-scoped CLI login is refused `SESSION_SCOPE_FORBIDDEN` for these persistent sessions. Fresh one-user flows can run within the CLI login's approved project scope. - When the run ends or is interrupted, cleanup attempts to close every actor's browser within a 20-second budget. A close that cannot be confirmed (for example a segment still running when the budget ran out) is listed as `unconfirmed` in `cleanup`, and the platform closes idle browsers within 5 minutes. An actor idle longer than that between its segments has lost its browser: the run fails at that segment rather than continuing signed out. - The journey writes through the app like its users do; nothing is cleared. Full schema: `somewhere verify --schema`. MCP `site_verify` takes only the one-user form; chain `browser({ session_id })` calls instead. ### When signup or login is the behavior under test Use signed-out actors (`{}`) and drive the real app forms. Authenticate each actor once, then use later segments for that actor to check the next state; its browser keeps the session. Replace these selectors and paths with your app's actual UI. Use controlled test addresses and the test inbox if the app requires email verification: a flow cannot read the inbox, so run `somewhere email test-inbox
` between flows and use the code or link in the next flow. A seeded `auth: { user_id }` actor above proves signed-in app behavior, not signup or login. ```json { "actors": { "alice": {}, "bob": {} }, "journey": [ { "as": "alice", "path": "/signup", "actions": [ { "fill": "#email", "value": "alice@.test.somewhere.site" }, { "fill": "#password", "value": "" }, { "click": "#sign-up" }, { "expect": { "selector": "#signed-in", "visible": true } } ] }, { "as": "bob", "path": "/signin", "actions": [ { "fill": "#email", "value": "bob@.test.somewhere.site" }, { "fill": "#password", "value": "" }, { "click": "#sign-in" }, { "expect": { "selector": "#signed-in", "visible": true } } ] }, { "as": "alice", "path": "/board", "actions": [ { "fill": "#item-title", "value": "Shared plan" }, { "click": "#create-item" }, { "expect": { "selector": "#item-title-display", "text": "Shared plan" } } ] }, { "as": "bob", "path": "/board", "actions": [ { "expect": { "selector": "#item-title-display", "text": "Shared plan" } } ] } ] } ``` Wait for the visible result of each click with `expect`, rather than adding fixed delays. Keep test credentials in a local ignored flow file, never in deployed app source. The example checks one possible shared-board app; it does not grant Bob access or create an account for him. Each segment makes one browser-test request, including segments that resume an actor; grouping consecutive steps for the same actor into one segment uses fewer daily runs without skipping those steps or their outcome checks. ## Local Playwright and agent-browser (CLI 0.37.63+) Pick by the job, not by a default: - `somewhere verify`: no local browser. It creates its own managed test users for the run (`test_user` actors, above) and reports every step's console and network checks. - Playwright on your machine: repeatable test files, native gestures, several tabs, network control. - agent-browser: exploring the app interactively from an agent. Both local tools sign in from the same prepared test users. In the linked project folder: ```bash somewhere test-users prepare alice bob ``` This creates preverified test users and writes `.somewhere/test/.state.json` (a standard Playwright storageState) and `manifest.json`. The folder is private and gitignored, holds each actor's app session and never your developer key. Only the app's production origin is supported. ```ts const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: '.somewhere/test/alice.state.json' }); // … the test … await context.storageState({ path: '.somewhere/test/alice.state.json' }); ``` ```bash # Set PROJECT to your app's subdomain. agent-browser --state .somewhere/test/alice.state.json open "https://${PROJECT}.somewhere.site" agent-browser state save .somewhere/test/alice.state.json ``` Save the state back after every run, as above. The app refreshes the short access token, and its first refresh rotates the session, so a file that was not saved back stops signing in. Import with `--state` at launch; with agent-browser 0.39.1, `state load` before a browser exists fails. The state from `prepare` starts with a session that ends an hour later. A refresh during a run renews it, and the saved-back state carries the renewed cookies, so a state you keep saving back goes on working past that hour. Do not rely on expiry to end it: run `cleanup` when you are done. A prepared actor is not evidence that signup or email verification works. To test those, use a fresh address and read only mail sent after its checkpoint: ```bash somewhere test-users address --json # { address, checkpoint } # sign up in the app with that address, then: somewhere test-users inbox
--since --wait 10000 --json ``` `inbox` returns the newest message after the checkpoint with its `verification_code`; it never returns older mail and never resends (`TEST_INBOX_NO_NEW_MESSAGE`). The magic link is printed only with `--json --include-link`, or written privately with `--link-out`. ```bash somewhere test-users cleanup ``` Cleanup deletes the test users this folder prepared, with their sessions, and the local state files, then writes `.somewhere/test/cleanup-receipt.json`. A copy of a state file signs nobody in once its short access token (up to a minute) has expired. App rows, files and stored test mail those users created are kept; a user who signed up through your app is not a prepared test user and is not removed. For full isolation, use a disposable project and delete it. ## Limits - At most 30 actions and a default 60-second action budget. - Account run, duration, and concurrency limits apply. A refusal supplies the limit and retry information; it is not a failed app assertion. - Project-backed runs require access to that project. Screenshots stored in project files also use its file allowance and write limits. - Temporary accounts may test their own project and cannot retain a browser session. - Signed-in accounts may inspect and screenshot other public websites; temporary accounts stay within their own project, as above. On either, actions, `eval` and seeded sessions are available only against an authorized project's own origins.

pages.title: sw.endpoint — declarative endpoint wrapper
pages.body:
`sw.endpoint` wraps a server function with auth, body validation, rate
limiting, error formatting, and CORS so you only write business logic. It is the
ordinary way to write a JSON endpoint. Set `auth` on every endpoint:
`'required'` unless it is public on purpose, then `'none'`. `body` and
`rateLimit` apply only when declared.

The starter's AGENTS.md has the ordinary endpoint shapes; read further for
validation, rate limits and other options. Endpoint files are routes:
api/items.ts → /api/items, api/items/[id].ts → params.id, and
api/items/[id]/sub.ts → /api/items/:id/sub; underscore-prefixed files are helpers.
GET/DELETE are named exports; POST with a JSON body uses the default export.
handler receives { user, params, body, request } and a second sw runtime argument;
auth: 'required' supplies user.id and user.email (string); declare body fields first.

With a rate limit configured, each endpoint path gets its own counter per
signed-in user, or per client IP when no user is resolved. A dynamic route
counts each concrete request path separately: `/api/notes/1` and
`/api/notes/2` have separate counters.

```ts
// db/schema.ts — owner() stamps each note with the signed-in user
import { schema, table, id, text, owner } from 'somewhere/db'
export default schema({
  notes: table({ id: id(), title: text(), note: text({ nullable: true }) }, { scope: owner() }),
})
```

```ts
// api/notes.ts
export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'required',
  body: { title: 'string', note: 'string?' },
  rateLimit: '30/minute',
  cors: 'same-origin',
  handler: async ({ body, user }, sw) => {
    const made = await sw.db.insert('notes', { title: body.title, note: body.note ?? null });
    return { ok: true, note: made.data[0], by: user.id };
  }
});
```

Sign-in itself is not an endpoint you write: the SDK's packaged handler serves
`/api/auth/*` (`docs({ topic: 'auth-client' })`).

## What the platform handles before your handler runs

- **auth** — exactly three modes (there is no `'public'`; a public endpoint for anonymous visitors is `'none'`):
  - `'required'` — calls `sw.auth.requireUser(request)` and returns
    401 `AUTH_REQUIRED` if the request isn't signed in. Use this for
    every signed-in endpoint.
  - `'optional'` — `user` when the caller is signed in, otherwise `null`.
  - `'none'` — public; no sign-in check. Write it for an endpoint that is
    public on purpose.

  A config written without `auth` is refused at deploy, patch and
  `deploy-check` with 400 `ENDPOINT_AUTH_OMITTED`, naming the file and
  line. The check reads the object literal in `sw.endpoint({ ... })`; a
  config passed as a variable or built elsewhere is not read, and if it
  has no `auth` it still runs as `'none'`. Endpoints already deployed
  keep serving as before.

  Any other value (`'user'`, a typo, `true`) is refused at deploy and
  by `deploy-check` with 400 `ENDPOINT_AUTH_MODE_INVALID`, naming the
  file, line, and value. It is never treated as public.
- **roles** — app roles (declared in `appRoles` in db/schema.ts), any of
  which admits the caller: `roles: ['staff']`. Roles imply a signed-in
  caller, so `auth` is `'required'` or left out. The caller's roles are read
  fresh on every request (grants, and roles held by verified email domain),
  before the body is read or your handler runs: signed out is 401
  `AUTH_REQUIRED`, signed in without a listed role is 403
  `APP_ROLE_REQUIRED`, and a read that fails is 503 `APP_ROLES_UNAVAILABLE`
  (never treated as "holds no role"). The handler's `user.appRoles` lists the
  caller's roles for that request. An empty list, a malformed value, or
  `auth: 'optional'`/`'none'` with roles, written as literals in
  `sw.endpoint({ ... })`, is refused at deploy with 400
  `ENDPOINT_ROLES_INVALID`; so is a role the app does not declare, when the
  deploy carries db/schema.ts. A roles list computed in code, and an
  undeclared role in a deploy without db/schema.ts, are refused at request
  time instead: the endpoint answers 500 `ENDPOINT_ROLES_INVALID` and the
  handler never runs. An endpoint that is an
  MCP tool (`mcp`) cannot declare roles yet. A revoked role refuses the next
  request; a request already admitted finishes.
- **body** — parses JSON, validates against the schema, returns 400
  `VALIDATION_ERROR` with a list of field-level messages if anything's
  off. Schema types: `'string'`, `'email'`, `'number'`, `'boolean'`,
  `'array'`, `'object'`. Suffix `'?'` to make a field optional
  (`'string?'`). Nest objects by nesting the schema.
  Without `body`, the wrapper does not read the request: `body` is
  `null` and the request stays unread for your handler. A handler that reads
  `body` with no `body` declared would drop what the caller sent, so it is
  refused at deploy, patch and `deploy-check` with 400
  `ENDPOINT_BODY_UNDECLARED`, naming the file and line. Declare the fields,
  or read the raw request (`await request.json()`, `request.text()`) for a
  webhook or form post. The check has the same limits as the `auth` check.
- **rateLimit** — use a string such as `'30/minute'`, `'60/hour'` or `'1000/day'` in `sw.endpoint`. The endpoint option takes the string directly.
  With `auth: 'required'` or `'optional'`, the counter uses the resolved
  user ID, falling back to client IP when there is no user. With
  `auth: 'none'`, it always uses client IP. Each endpoint path has its own counter.
  Returns 429 `RATE_LIMITED` + `Retry-After` header.
  An invalid limit returns 500 `ENDPOINT_RATE_LIMIT_INVALID` before your handler
  runs. Fix the value or remove it for an unlimited endpoint. Existing apps
  adopt this validation on their next source deploy.
- **cors** — `'same-origin'` (default; no CORS headers), `'*'` (allow
  any), or an allow-list array (`['app.example.com']` — subdomain
  matches accepted). Preflight `OPTIONS` is auto-answered with 204.
  `'*'` sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, so it is for a
  public endpoint called without credentials. It does not bypass the
  platform's origin check: a browser request from an unapproved origin that
  carries a cookie or `Authorization` is refused with 403
  `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED` before your handler runs (docs({ topic: 'cors' })).

## What your handler receives

`async ({ body, user, headers, params, request }, sw) => …`

- `body` — the validated, parsed JSON, or `null` when no schema is
  declared.
- `user` — the authed user, or `null` for `auth: 'optional'`/`'none'`. With
  `roles`, `user.appRoles` is the caller's own app-role names.
  Any endpoint can read them with
  `await sw.auth.requireUser(request, { appRoles: true })`, for a page that
  shows staff controls (a hint; every action is still checked).
- `headers` — the request `Headers` object.
- `params` — route params (from `api/[id].ts`-style paths).
- `request` — the original `Request` if you need it.
- `sw` — the per-request platform context, same as a plain handler's
  second arg.

Return a plain object → wrapped in `Response.json`. Return a
`Response` → passed through unchanged. Return `null`/`undefined` → 204.

With a `body` schema declared, the handler always receives a validated
body. GET and HEAD cannot carry one, so after the auth check they are
answered with 405 `METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED` and an
`Allow: POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS` header, and your handler does
not run. POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE must send valid JSON: a missing or
malformed body is 400 `INVALID_JSON`.

To serve GET from the same path, export it separately. The platform calls
the export named after the request method before the default export:

```ts
// api/inbox.ts
export const GET = sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'required',
  handler: async (_input, sw) => ({ notes: (await sw.db.from('notes', { limit: 20 })).data }),
});

export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'required',
  body: { title: 'string' },
  handler: async ({ body }, sw) => (await sw.db.insert('notes', { title: body.title })).data[0],
});
```


## Errors

Throw anywhere in your handler and the wrapper formats it. A thrown error
with a 4xx `.status` keeps that status and its `.code` (capital letters,
digits and underscores), but not its message: the wrapper cannot tell your
text from an internal error's. Platform errors marked safe for callers, such as
`AUTH_REQUIRED`, keep their message. Everything else is a 500
`HANDLER_ERROR`. Errors that are not shown to the caller are written to your
function logs. To answer with
your own message, return it, for example
`return Response.json({ error: 'INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS', message: 'Not enough credit.' }, { status: 402 })`.

An endpoint whose `auth` is set at runtime to anything other than
`'required'`, `'optional'`, or `'none'` answers every request with
500 `ENDPOINT_AUTH_MODE_INVALID` and never runs your handler.

## MCP tools for Claude

Endpoints can also be tools that Claude, or any MCP client, calls as the
person signed in to your app (a preview feature). The full steps, examples and
current limits are in one place: `somewhere docs app-mcp`.

## When NOT to use it

Write a plain `async (req, sw) => …` handler when you want to parse the
request, check sign-in and build error responses yourself: read the body from
`req`, call `sw.auth.requireUser(req)`, and return your own `Response`.

Related topics: `sw.auth`, `sw.rateLimit`.

pages.title: sw.fetch — outbound HTTP fetch from a function
sw.rateLimit — Rate limiting
pages.body:
Throttle abusive callers without standing up Redis or a token-bucket
library. One method, fixed-window counter, per-second granularity.

For one route, set `rateLimit: '30/minute'` on `sw.endpoint`.
With `auth: 'required'` or `'optional'`, signed-in callers are limited
by their verified user ID. Other callers are limited by IP. Each request path has its own counter
(each distinct URL on a dynamic route). The wrapper
answers 429 with `Retry-After` when the limit is reached; see `sw.endpoint`.

## sw.rateLimit.check(key, max, windowSeconds)
