Returns `{ allowed, remaining, reset, limit, window_seconds }`.
On `allowed: false`, return 429 to the caller. `reset` is the epoch
seconds when the current window rolls over.

A check stops waiting after five seconds. If it cannot confirm the answer,
it throws instead of allowing the action. The counter may already have
advanced; the failed check is not automatically retried.

## Optional per-IP action throttle

Built-in password sign-in already has automatic attempt limits and progressive
lockout (`somewhere docs sw.auth --section automatic-password-sign-in-protection`).
This example adds a separate limit to an app-specific action; it is not a
required login setup step. Choose a limit that fits that action's normal use.

```js
export default async function (req, sw) {
  const ip = req.headers.get('cf-connecting-ip') || 'unknown'
  const rl = await sw.rateLimit.check(`my-action:${ip}`, 5, 60)
  if (!rl.allowed) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: 'too_many_attempts', retry_at: rl.reset },
      { status: 429 }
    )
  }
  // …validate and perform the app-specific action
}
```

## Per-user API throttle

```js
const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(req)
if (!user) return Response.json({ error: 'sign in' }, { status: 401 })
const rl = await sw.rateLimit.check(`api:${user.id}`, 100, 60)
if (!rl.allowed) return Response.json({ error: 'rate_limited' }, { status: 429 })
```

## Per-endpoint global cap

```js
const rl = await sw.rateLimit.check('signup', 1000, 3600)  // 1k signups/hour
if (!rl.allowed) return Response.json({ error: 'paused' }, { status: 429 })
```

## Notes

- Keys are scoped per project automatically — `login:1.2.3.4` in your
  app does not collide with the same key in someone else's app.
- `max` is a positive integer up to 1,000,000.
- `windowSeconds` is between 1 and 86,400 (24h).
- Concurrent requests can exceed the requested count before all serving
  instances record them. Use this counter for request throttling rather
  than exact accounting.

pages.title: sw.notifications — unified notify primitive
pages.body:
One call → fan-out across push, in-app bell, and (when an address is
provided) email, with one result per channel: `{ bell?, push?, email? }`.

`sw.notifications` is the in-app inbox: it stores each notification for its
recipient with read state, and the bell helpers read only the signed-in
user's own rows. `sw.push` is browser delivery only: it stores nothing for the
user to list later. Use `sw.notifications` when users need a list and unread
count; use `sw.push` directly to target devices or your own browser.

## sw.notifications.send(userId, { title, body?, url?, email?, channels? })

```ts
// api/_lib/line-alert.ts — call after your code has decided this user gets the alert
export function alertNorthernDelay(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, userId: string): Promise<SomewhereNotificationsSendResult> {
  return sw.notifications.send(userId, {
    title: 'Northern line: minor delays',
    body: 'Reported 14:02 GMT. Estimated 10–15 min impact southbound.',
    url: '/lines/northern',
    channels: ['bell', 'push'],   // optional; default ['bell', 'push']
  })
}
```

Returns { bell?, push?, email? } with per-channel result. Each entry
is { ok: true, ... } or { ok: false, error: '...', code? } so the
caller can branch without a try/catch per channel. A missing `userId` raises
`VALIDATION_ERROR`. The recipient can be any user of the app: authorize
the caller before letting them send notifications to another user.

Channels:
- bell — stores the notification in the recipient's in-app inbox. Render
  it with sw.notifications.list() / unreadCount(). The recipient must be a
  user of this app; otherwise the bell result is
  `{ ok: false, code: 'APP_USER_NOT_FOUND' }` and nothing is stored. Each
  user keeps their newest 1,000 notifications, and notifications older than
  90 days are removed. Projects created before managed data instead keep
  these rows, without those two limits, in a _notifications table in the
  project's own database, hidden from db_describe / db_browse like every
  _-prefixed table.
- push — proxies to sw.push.send against every active subscription
  for that userId. Silent no-op if the user hasn't subscribed.
- email — only fires when opts.email is set explicitly. We don't
  auto-look up the address (your user-table shape is yours). Pair
  with sw.auth.fromRequest(req, { enrichFrom: 'members' }) to pull
  the email + send in two lines. It uses the platform-managed transactional
  sender with the project name as its label, so a new project needs no sender
  setup; opts.email must be the address of that userId (or the project's
  owner). Pass opts.from only when using a verified sender domain of your own.
  The project plan's email allowance and send rate limit still apply.

## Bell helpers

The bell helpers act for the signed-in user of the request: they take no
user id, and with no signed-in user they throw `AUTH_REQUIRED` (401).
`markRead` changes only that user's own notification.

```typescript
// api/notifications.ts
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  const { notifications } = await sw.notifications.list();
  const unreadCount = await sw.notifications.unreadCount();
  return Response.json({ notifications, unreadCount });
}
```

Mark one notification with `await sw.notifications.markRead(notificationId)`,
or all of your notifications with `await sw.notifications.markAllRead()`.
Call these from a function handling the signed-in user's request.

## What this is NOT (yet)

- No platform-level dedup, rate-limit, or per-user channel prefs.
  Roll those in your handler if you need them — this is the
  primitive.
- No retries — push / email failures surface immediately. Re-call
  after fixing the cause.

pages.title: sw.push — Web Push notifications
pages.body:
Send a notification to a user's browser, even when your app's tab is closed.
Each signed-in user turns notifications on in their own browser, the device
is registered to that user, and your function sends with
`sw.push.send({ user_id })`. The platform holds the signing keys, encrypts each
message, removes devices the browser has revoked, and keeps 7 days of
per-device send history.

In the page, `enablePush()` from `somewhere:push` turns notifications on for
the signed-in user. In a function, `sw.push.send({ user_id, payload: { title,
url } })` notifies them, and `sw.push.deliveries({ user_id })` shows what each
of their devices got.

## Turn on notifications in the page

The platform serves the browser helper and its service worker from your
app's own origin, so you write neither. `somewhere:push` is typed and builds
to the same-origin `/__sw/push/client.js`:

```ts
// browser — call from a click; browsers only prompt after a user gesture
import { enablePush, disablePush, pushStatus, listenToPush } from 'somewhere:push'

await enablePush()            // asks permission, subscribes, registers this browser for the signed-in user
await disablePush()           // removes this browser's device and unsubscribes it
await pushStatus()            // { supported, permission, subscribed, endpoint }
const stop = listenToPush(({ type, payload }) => {})  // 'push' or 'click' while a tab is open
```

The browser belongs to the user signed in on that page: the helper sends the
page's cookies, which is how platform sign-in (`sw.auth`, the SDK's
`createSomewhereAuth`) keeps the session. It sends no user id, and the
platform refuses one. `enablePush()` without a signed-in user fails with
`AUTH_REQUIRED`. Your app's functions serve the helper, so the project needs
at least one file under `api/`. The service worker lives at
`/__sw/push/sw.js` with scope `/__sw/push/`, so it runs alongside any service
worker your app already has. Each user keeps up to 10 browsers; adding another removes the one registered longest ago.

On iPhone and iPad, web push works after the user adds the app to the Home
Screen; until then `enablePush()` fails with `PUSH_UNSUPPORTED`.

## Send from a function

```ts
// api/notify.ts — notify the signed-in user
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response(null, { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } })
  const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(req)
  if (!user) return Response.json({ error: 'Sign in first.' }, { status: 401 })
  const result = await sw.push.send({
    user_id: user.id,
    payload: { title: 'Notifications are ready', body: 'Your browser is connected.', url: '/inbox' },
  })
  return Response.json(result)   // { sent, failed, gone, captured, recipients, history_recorded, devices }
}
```

`payload` is a string or a JSON value. The service worker reads these fields:

| Field | Effect |
|---|---|
| `title`, `body`, `icon`, `badge`, `image`, `tag`, `renotify`, `requireInteraction`, `silent` | Passed to `showNotification` |
| `url` | Opened or focused on click. Same-origin paths only; anything else opens `/` |
| `badge_count` | Sets the app icon badge where the browser supports it (0 clears it) |
| `data` | Kept on the notification and delivered to `listenToPush` |

A string payload becomes the title.

## Who receives a send

ONE object argument with exactly one target:

| Target | Reaches |
|---|---|
| `user_id` | Every device that signed-in user registered |
| `subscription_id` or `endpoint` | One device |
| `audience: 'developer'` | Devices you registered with developer credentials |
| `audience: 'all'` | Every device in the project |

A missing, `null` or empty target is refused with `VALIDATION_ERROR`, so an
unset id never becomes a broadcast. A send that would reach more than 500
devices is refused whole with `RECIPIENT_CAP_EXCEEDED`, and a project sends at
most 10 times a minute (`RATE_LIMITED`). `ttl` sets how
long the push service holds an undelivered message (seconds, default 86400).
A payload over 3000 bytes is refused with `PUSH_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`; push an
id or URL and fetch the rest. A device the browser has revoked answers `gone` and is
removed.

Sending and reading history are server operations: a function or a developer
key. A browser session can register and remove only its own devices.

## Register from a function instead

When your page already posts to your own function, register there:

```ts
// api/push-device.ts — POST the PushSubscription's toJSON()
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response(null, { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } })
  const subscription = await req.json()
  return Response.json(await sw.push.subscribe(subscription, { label: 'Phone' }))
}
```

`sw.push.subscribe(subscription, { label? })` and
`sw.push.unsubscribe(endpoint)` act for the signed-in user of the request and
fail with `AUTH_REQUIRED` without one. `sw.push.vapidPublicKey()` returns the
`applicationServerKey` for `PushManager.subscribe()`.

One browser subscription is one device. Re-registering the same endpoint
with the same keys moves it to whoever is signed in, so a shared browser
follows its current user; the same endpoint with different keys is refused
with `PUSH_SUBSCRIPTION_CONFLICT` unless it comes from the device's own user.
Endpoints must come from a browser push service (Chrome, Edge, Firefox,
Safari); any other URL is refused with `VALIDATION_ERROR`.

## Why didn't it arrive? Send history

```ts
const { deliveries } = await sw.push.deliveries({ user_id: 'usr_123', limit: 20 })
// [{ device_label: 'Chrome on Android', outcome: 'sent', http_status: 201, title, url, created_at, ... }]
const { subscriptions } = await sw.push.subscriptions({ user_id: 'usr_123' })
```

`outcome` is `sent` (the push service accepted it), `failed` (with
`http_status` and a reason), `gone` (the browser revoked the device; it was
removed) or `captured` (a test inbox device). Reads return the last 7
days and never contain keys or full endpoints. If a send could not record its
history, its result says `history_recorded: false`; the notifications were
still sent, so don't resend. The same reads are
`GET /v1/push/deliveries` and `GET /v1/push/subscriptions` with a developer
key, and the `push_deliveries` tool.

## Push test inbox

A test device captures sends instead of delivering them, so a hosted or
headless browser can prove a notification reached a user:

```ts
await enablePush({ test: true })   // no permission prompt, no service worker
```

or `sw.push.subscribe({ test: true })` in a function. A test device is an
explicit opt-in: each signed-in user can turn on one for themselves. Sends to
that user then record a `captured` delivery that includes the full payload,
which the developer can read with `sw.push.deliveries({ user_id })` for 7
days. `disablePush({ test: true })` removes it.

## Developer devices

`push_subscribe` and `POST /v1/push/subscribe` with a developer key register
your own browser for operator alerts. These devices carry no user id, so
`send({ user_id })` never reaches them; send to them with
`audience: 'developer'`.

A device listed with `owner: 'legacy'` has no verified owner.
No send reaches it, and a send that names it returns
`PUSH_DEVICE_REREGISTER_REQUIRED` (409). It becomes a normal device when its
browser registers again: the user turns notifications on with `enablePush()`,
or you call `push_subscribe` with the same subscription.

pages.title: Live updates — rooms and live lists
Rooms — shared state, presence and messages on one row
pages.body:
## Quick start

A room is a live place attached to one database row. Everyone who may read
the row may join it. The room holds one shared state object, the list of who
is here, and quick throwaway messages, all on one connection. The room owns
the state: every change goes to the room, which orders it, applies it and
tells everyone. When the room is empty, the row is the truth.

Declare `rooms` on a table that has a single `id()` key:

```ts
// in db/schema.ts: a shared board
import { schema, table, id, text, json, shared } from 'somewhere/db'

export default schema({
  boards: table(
    { id: id(), title: text({ default: '' }), state: json({ nullable: true }) },
    {
      scope: shared(),
      client: { read: ['id', 'title'], create: ['title'] },
      rooms: { save: 'state' },
    },
  ),
})
```

Join from the browser with the module the platform serves on your app's own
origin. In TypeScript or a bundled page, import the same module as
`'somewhere:rooms'`, which carries its types (`joinRoom`, `watchLive`):

```js
// browser
import { joinRoom } from '/__sw/rooms/client.js'

const room = await joinRoom('boards', boardId)
render(room.state)

const stopState = room.on('state', (state) => render(state))
room.on('people', (people) => showAvatars(people))
room.on('message', (data, from) => moveCursor(from, data.cursor))

await room.set({ title: 'Launch plan' })  // shows at once; the room confirms it
room.send({ cursor: [3, 4] })              // to everyone else; not stored
room.me.set({ name: 'Ana' })               // shown beside this tab in room.people
```

`room.set` needs the person to be allowed to update the row. `on()` returns
a function that unsubscribes. Call `room.leave()` when the page stops showing
the room.

A room is one row. To keep a list of rows fresh on screen, declare a live
list with `sw.rooms.live` and follow it with `watchLive` from the same
module (see "Live lists" below). Rooms work on the live app only; previews
and drafts refuse them with `ROOMS_DRAFT_UNAVAILABLE`.

More sections: `rooms` → `declare-a-room`, `the-browser-room`,
`a-referee-decides-every-change`, `server-code`,
`who-can-join-and-what-they-see`, `example-a-two-player-game`, `live-lists`,
`limits`, `recovery`.

## Declare a room

Set `rooms: { save: 'state', referee: '/api/game-room' }` in the table options
in `db/schema.ts`. Both properties are optional.

- `save` names a `json` column on the same row. The room writes the state
  there at most every 10 seconds while it changes, and again when everyone
  leaves. The next join starts from that column (or `{}` when it is empty).
  After a row exists, ordinary writes to that column are refused with
  `ROOM_COLUMN_RESERVED`: only the room writes it.
- Without `save`, state is temporary. It is gone about 60 seconds after the
  last person leaves.
- `referee` is the path of one of your app's own functions. It decides every
  change. Without it, people change state with `room.set`.

There is no room directory. A room is one row, so listing rooms is listing
rows. When you redeploy with a changed `rooms` declaration, open rooms save
and close, and browsers rejoin on their own.

## The browser room

```js
import { joinRoom } from '/__sw/rooms/client.js'

const room = await joinRoom('games', gameId)
room.state      // the current shared state, a plain object
room.version    // a number; +1 for each accepted change
room.people     // [{ id, user, me, info }]
```

In `room.people`, `id` is the connection id, `user` is the signed-in user id
or visitor id (`null` for someone with no session), `me` is `true` for this tab, and `info` is what that
connection set with `room.me.set(info)` (at most 1 KB). One person with two
tabs appears twice, with the same `user`.

Events:

```js
room.on('state', (state, change) => {})   // after every accepted change, and after each (re)join;
                                          // change.by is the connection id that made it, or 'server'
room.on('people', (people) => {})
room.on('message', (data, from) => {})
room.on('timer_failed', () => {})         // the referee's timer failed 3 times
room.on('status', (status) => {})         // 'open' | 'reconnecting' | 'closed'
```

Changing state:

- `await room.set(patch)` is for rooms **without** a referee. It merges the
  top-level keys of `patch` into the state; `null` deletes a key. It is
  applied at once in this tab, and the room's answer confirms or corrects it.
- `await room.act(action)` is for rooms **with** a referee. It is not applied
  locally. It resolves with the new state once the referee accepts. A
  refusal rejects with `err.code` `REFEREE_REJECTED` and `err.reason`, the
  plain reason your referee gave.
- `room.send(data)` sends a throwaway message to everyone else. It is not
  stored and never changes the state.

The connection reconnects with backoff by itself. On every rejoin the room
sends the full state and people list; missed messages are not replayed. The
module renews the person's access every 4 minutes.

If the connection drops while an `act` is unanswered, the act rejects with
`ROOM_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`, and `err.state` holds the fresh state. The action may
or may not have been applied. It is never sent again for you: look at
`err.state` and decide.

## A referee decides every change

A referee is an ordinary function at the declared path. It reads one event
and answers with one decision:

```ts
// the function at the declared referee path: a counter that only goes up
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  const ev = await sw.rooms.event(req)
  // ev: { type: 'join' | 'leave' | 'action' | 'timer', state, version, action?,
  //       who, row: { table, id } }
  if (ev.type !== 'action') return Response.json({})
  const count = typeof ev.state.count === 'number' ? ev.state.count : 0
  return Response.json({ state: { count: count + 1 } })
}
```

`who` says who caused the event:

| `who` | Caller |
|---|---|
| `{ user: '<user id>' }` | a signed-in user |
| `{ visitor: 'v_…' }` | an anonymous visitor; a stable id for that visitor in this app, not their session |
| `{ anonymous: true }` | someone with no session (a public-read row) |
| `'server'` | `sw.rooms.server.*` |

The `user` field in `room.people` is the same string as `who.user` or
`who.visitor` (`null` when anonymous), so the referee and the browser can
match seats.

`sw.rooms.event(req)` is the only way to read the event. It throws
`ROOM_EVENT_INVALID` unless the room really sent this event just now, so
nobody can call the path directly and forge a decision.

The decision is a JSON object; every field is optional:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state` | the whole new state |
| `reject` | a plain reason; the change is refused and the person sees it as `err.reason` |
| `timer` | seconds from now, 1 second to 7 days; `null` clears it; leave it out to keep the current timer |
| `send` | up to 10 messages, delivered to everyone like `room.send` |

How events arrive:

- Events are handled strictly one at a time per room. Two moves never race.
- `join` comes on a person's first connection; `leave` on their last. A
  rejected `join` does not stop the person joining: they are simply not
  seated as far as your state is concerned.
- `action` carries what `room.act` or `sw.rooms.act` sent.
- `timer` fires when the room's one timer runs out. A pending timer keeps
  the room and its state alive with nobody present: it fires and the
  referee runs even when everyone has gone.
- If the referee throws, answers with a non-2xx status or a bad shape, or
  takes longer than 3 seconds, the change is refused with
  `REFEREE_UNAVAILABLE` and the state is unchanged. A failed timer event is
  retried 3 times; then everyone gets `timer_failed`.

A referee must only decide. It must not send email, take payments or write
elsewhere, and it must not call back into its own room: when a call times
out, its effects are not undone. Do outside work from your own functions
after the state changes.

## Server code

Inside a function that is handling a browser request, `sw.rooms` acts as the
person who made the request, with that person's permissions:

If the room uses a referee, pass an action that the referee accepts. For
the game below, the player whose turn it is can play an empty cell.

```ts
await sw.rooms.act('games', gameId, { cell: 0 })
```

For a room without a referee, set state directly. The caller needs permission
to update the row.

```ts
await sw.rooms.set('boards', boardId, { title: 'Final' })
```

Send a message or read the room state with either configuration.

```ts
await sw.rooms.send('boards', boardId, { toast: 'Saved' })
const { state, version, people } = await sw.rooms.get('boards', boardId)
```

Jobs and schedules have no browser caller, so plain `sw.rooms.*` there is
refused with `ROOM_NO_CALLER`. Use `sw.rooms.server.act`, `.set`, `.send`
and `.get` instead. They act as the platform (`who: 'server'`) on any row of
a table that declares rooms. That is explicit platform authority: never pass
a browser's input to `sw.rooms.server.*` without checking it yourself.

For agents, the `rooms_get` tool (`project_id`, `table`, `id`) returns the
state, the version and who is here.

## Who can join and what they see

- Joining needs permission to read the row, by the row's own read rule, for
  a signed-in user or an anonymous visitor session. A row the person may not
  read is refused with `ROOM_NOT_ALLOWED`.
- `room.set` needs permission to update the row. `room.act` needs only to
  have joined; the referee decides.
- **Everyone who can join sees the whole state, the people list and every
  message.** A room must not hold anything some participants may not see.
  Keep secrets in the database behind your functions.
- Removing someone's access takes effect within 5 minutes.
- A room's stored state is erased within 10 minutes of its row or project
  being deleted.

## Example: a two-player game

Tic-tac-toe with seats, move checks and a 30-second turn clock. A player who
lets the clock run out loses.

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { schema, table, id, text, json, shared } from 'somewhere/db'

export default schema({
  games: table(
    { id: id(), title: text({ default: '' }), state: json({ nullable: true }) },
    {
      scope: shared(),
      client: { read: ['id', 'title'], create: ['title'] },
      rooms: { save: 'state', referee: '/api/game-room' },
    },
  ),
})
```

```ts
// api/game-room.ts — the referee
type Mark = 'x' | 'o'
type Game = { board: (Mark | null)[]; x: string | null; o: string | null; turn: Mark; winner: Mark | 'draw' | null }

const LINES = [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8], [0, 3, 6], [1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8], [0, 4, 8], [2, 4, 6]]
const TURN_SECONDS = 30
const NEW_GAME: Game = { board: Array(9).fill(null), x: null, o: null, turn: 'x', winner: null }

export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  const ev = await sw.rooms.event(req)
  const s = (Array.isArray(ev.state.board) ? ev.state : NEW_GAME) as Game
  const me = ev.who === 'server' ? null
    : 'user' in ev.who ? ev.who.user
    : 'visitor' in ev.who ? ev.who.visitor
    : null

  if (ev.type === 'join') {
    if (!me || s.x === me || s.o === me || s.winner) return Response.json({})
    if (!s.x) return Response.json({ state: { ...s, x: me } })
    if (!s.o) return Response.json({ state: { ...s, o: me }, timer: TURN_SECONDS })
    return Response.json({})                       // everyone else watches
  }

  if (ev.type === 'timer') {
    if (s.winner || !s.o) return Response.json({ timer: null })
    const winner: Mark = s.turn === 'x' ? 'o' : 'x'
    return Response.json({ state: { ...s, winner }, timer: null, send: [{ note: 'Time ran out.' }] })
  }

  if (ev.type === 'action') {
    const cell = (ev.action as { cell?: unknown } | undefined)?.cell
    if (s.winner) return Response.json({ reject: 'The game is over.' })
    if (!s.o) return Response.json({ reject: 'Wait for a second player.' })
    if (!me || s[s.turn] !== me) return Response.json({ reject: 'It is not your turn.' })
    if (typeof cell !== 'number' || !Number.isInteger(cell) || cell < 0 || cell > 8 || s.board[cell]) {
      return Response.json({ reject: 'Pick an empty square.' })
    }
    const board = s.board.slice()
    board[cell] = s.turn
    const won = LINES.some((line) => line.every((i) => board[i] === s.turn))
    const winner = won ? s.turn : board.every(Boolean) ? 'draw' : null
    const turn: Mark = s.turn === 'x' ? 'o' : 'x'
    return Response.json({ state: { ...s, board, turn, winner }, timer: winner ? null : TURN_SECONDS })
  }

  return Response.json({})                         // leave: the seat stays
}
```

Create a game row from the page with the generated client,
`data.games.create({ title: 'Tic-tac-toe' })` (`docs({ topic: 'declared-data' })`),
and open the game page with `?game=<id>`:

```js
// browser — game page
import { joinRoom } from '/__sw/rooms/client.js'

const gameId = new URL(location.href).searchParams.get('game')
const room = await joinRoom('games', gameId)
const status = document.querySelector('#status')
const squares = document.querySelectorAll('[data-cell]')

function draw(state) {
  squares.forEach((square) => {
    square.textContent = state.board?.[Number(square.dataset.cell)] ?? ''
  })
  const mine = room.people.find((person) => person.me)?.user
  const seat = mine && mine === state.x ? 'You are x. ' : mine && mine === state.o ? 'You are o. ' : ''
  status.textContent = seat + (state.winner ? 'Result: ' + state.winner
    : state.o ? state.turn + ' to move' : 'Waiting for a second player')
}
draw(room.state)
room.on('state', draw)
room.on('message', (msg) => { if (msg.note) status.textContent = msg.note })
room.on('timer_failed', () => { status.textContent = 'The turn clock stopped. Reload to continue.' })

squares.forEach((square) => {
  square.addEventListener('click', async () => {
    try {
      await room.act({ cell: Number(square.dataset.cell) })
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.code === 'REFEREE_REJECTED') status.textContent = err.reason
      else if (err.code === 'ROOM_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN') draw(err.state)
      else throw err
    }
  })
})
```

The first two signed-in people to join are seated;
everyone else watches. Everyone can leave and come back: the board is saved
in the row.

## Live lists

A live list keeps a list of rows fresh in every open tab: new rows, edited
rows, rows entering or leaving the filter, a changed order, and rows a person
gains or loses access to. The rows always come from your own function, so
every access rule applies to each refresh. The connection carries only
"refresh now" notices; no row, SQL, table name, filter or owner travels on it.

Declare the list in a function with `sw.rooms.live(name, read)`. This one
reads an `owner()` notes table (its schema is in `docs({ topic: 'live' })`),
so each person sees only their own notes:

```ts
// api/open-notes.ts — the declaration and the read stay server-side
export default async function (_req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) {
  return Response.json(await sw.rooms.live('notes.open', sw.db.from('notes', {
    where: { done: false },
    columns: ['id', 'title', 'done', 'created_at'],
    order: [['created_at', 'desc'], ['id', 'asc']],
    limit: 20,
  })))
}
```

Follow it in the browser with `watchLive(load, render, onError?)`:

```js
// browser: load re-calls your function, never the database
import { watchLive } from '/__sw/rooms/client.js'

const list = document.querySelector('#open-notes')
if (!list) throw new Error('Add a list element with id open-notes to the page.')

const stop = watchLive(
  async () => {
    const response = await fetch('/api/open-notes', { credentials: 'include' })
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Could not load your notes (' + response.status + ').')
    return response.json()
  },
  (rows) => list.replaceChildren(...rows.map((note) => {
    const item = document.createElement('li')
    item.textContent = note.title
    return item
  })),
  (err, { retrying }) => showBanner(retrying ? 'Reconnecting…' : 'Live updates paused: ' + err.message),
)
// Call stop() when the page stops showing the list.
```

`render(rows, result)` gets the function result's `data` array and the whole
parsed response. `onError(err, { attempt, retrying })` is optional; without
it, problems are written to the console with `console.error`.

What the declaration accepts:

- One direct `sw.db.from(...)` call on a declared table. Values may be
  dynamic; the shape (table, columns, filter columns, order, limit) must be
  written out, because deploy pins it to the release.
- `limit` is a positive integer literal and `order` is required, ending with
  the table's key column(s). `offset` and `asServer` are not allowed.
  Explicit `columns` must include the key and order columns.
- Tables with `owner()` (including `owner({ visitors: true })`), `shared()`,
  `member()` and `group()` rules, app-role rules, and parent chains ending in
  a group or an app role. A `member()` or `group()` list names one group by
  equality, for example `where: { team_id: teamId }`. `serverOnly()` tables
  are refused. Deploy refuses any other shape and says why.
- The name is unique within one release.

The function's result keeps `data`, `count` and the rest, and adds `live`:

  {
    data: [{ id: 1, title: 'Ship', done: 0, created_at: '2026-09-25T06:14:07.694Z' }],
    live: { state: 'ready', name: 'notes.open', release_id: '…', fingerprint: '…',
            subscribe_url: 'wss://your-app.somewhere.site/__sw/live/subscribe?…', expires_at: 1780000000000 },
  }

`subscribe_url` holds a signed one-minute ticket bound to the person whose
session ran the read. Do not log it. In a preview, `live.state` is
`'unavailable'`: the rows still load, nothing follows them.

How it stays fresh:

- Structured inserts and removals notify live lists that depend on the
  written table. Updates notify lists that depend on the written columns.
  This applies to `sw.db`, `sw.db.server`, and the generated browser client.
- A `shared()` list notifies all subscribers. An `owner()` list notifies
  subscribers for the owners identified before and after the write, including
  writes by another user or server code. When the write can identify only
  the signed-in writer, it can notify that writer's list. Other owners'
  lists catch up on refresh.
- A group list notifies the groups identified by the write. A role list
  notifies its role channel. When a membership change removes access, the
  affected connections close before the write returns.
- With a separate managed database, `sw.db.tx` and `sw.db.server.tx` use each
  step's write evidence to notify the same lists. On an older project that
  keeps declared tables and raw SQL tables in one database, transactions
  lack row-owner and group information. They can notify shared lists and
  the acting user's owner lists. Other owners and groups catch up on refresh.
- The connection is opened with a refresh, so a change made between the
  first load and the connection is shown.
- If the connection drops, `watchLive` reconnects through a fresh `load`,
  which checks the person's access again. It also refreshes when the tab
  becomes visible, when the network comes back, and every 60 seconds as a
  safety net for a lost notice. Normal updates never wait for it.
- A failed `load` or `render` is reported and retried after 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8
  and 15 seconds, then reported as stopped until the next reconnect, focus or
  safety refresh.
- A new deploy or a rollback closes the connection; `watchLive` reloads and
  follows the new release.
- Each live-list connection lasts up to 5 minutes, then `watchLive` reconnects
  through a fresh `load`. Each open live list counts toward the account's
  people connected at once (see Limits); when that is full, `watchLive` reports
  `ROOM_ACCOUNT_FULL` and stops until the tab becomes visible again or the
  network comes back.
  If admission is temporarily unavailable it reports
  `ROOM_ADMISSION_UNAVAILABLE` and retries with a growing delay.

A write's result can carry `live_delivery`:

- `{ delivery: 'queued' }` or `{ delivery: 'invalidated' }`: notices are
  queued for delivery or have already been sent. Queued notices go out just
  after the write returns and are retried up to three times.
- `{ delivery: 'resync_required', reason }`: the platform could not confirm
  every notice (for example, a write whose rows did not name all their
  owners). Open lists catch up on their next refresh, and the failure is in
  your app's logs.

Neither value means the write failed. Never retry a committed write because
of `live_delivery`.

Raw SQL writes through `sw.db.query`, `sw.db.batch`, or their `sw.db.server`
versions do not notify live lists. The
platform logs a `[SW_LIVE]` warning when one writes a live list's table; use
the structured write instead.

`sw.db.live` was the earlier name of this declaration. A deploy that still
calls it is refused with the rename to make.

## Usage

Rooms are measured in connected people-hours: the time each signed-in person
or visitor is connected to a room. Several tabs of the same person in one room
count once; the same person in two rooms counts in each. The project owner sees
`rooms.people_hours` (with a daily breakdown) in `GET /v1/usage`. The figure is
approximate: a room reports when it is already active, so a quiet room's
latest minutes can appear only after its next ticket renewal or when people leave.

## Limits

Refusals are typed and name the limit.

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| People in one room | 100 connections (`ROOM_FULL`) |
| People connected at once, across every room and live list in the account | Free: 200 (`ROOM_ACCOUNT_FULL`). Each signed-in app user or visitor counts once across all tabs and rooms of one project; the same identity in a different project counts separately. A connection with no identity, such as a shared live list, counts once per connection. Paid plans do not currently enforce an account-wide limit; that is not a promise of unlimited connections |
| State | 256 KB |
| One message | 4 KB |
| Presence info (`room.me.set`) | 1 KB |
| Inbound per connection | Sized for about 60 frames per second (frames beyond 75 in one second are refused) and 64 KB per second in total; of those, at most 20 `set`/`act` per second. Ticket renewals have their own budget, so heavy messaging never blocks them |
| Accepted changes per room | 10 per second |
| Referee events waiting per room | 50 (`ROOM_BUSY`) |
| Messages in one decision's `send` | 10 |
| Referee answer time | 3 seconds |
| Timer | 1 second to 7 days, one per room |

A limit other than the people count is refused with `ROOM_LIMIT`, which says
which limit.

## Recovery

| Code | Meaning and what to do |
|---|---|
| `ROOM_NOT_ALLOWED` | The person may not read this row (or may not update it, for `set`). Check the table's access rules and the signed-in user. |
| `ROOM_FULL` | 100 connections are already in the room. |
| `ROOM_ACCOUNT_FULL` | The account already has as many people connected at once as its plan allows, across all its rooms and live lists. Nobody is disconnected to make space. The client stops retrying; offer a deliberate retry later. |
| `ROOM_ADMISSION_UNAVAILABLE` | The connection could not be admitted right now. Nothing changed; try again shortly. |
| `ROOM_LIMIT` | A size or rate limit was hit; the message names it. Send less or less often. |
| `ROOM_BUSY` | 50 referee events are already waiting. Try again shortly. |
| `ROOM_HAS_REFEREE` | `set` was used on a room with a referee. Use `act`. |
| `ROOM_NO_REFEREE` | `act` was used on a room without a referee. Use `set`, or declare `referee`. |
| `REFEREE_REJECTED` | Your referee refused; show `err.reason`. |
| `REFEREE_UNAVAILABLE` | The referee threw, answered badly or took over 3 seconds. Nothing changed. Read the function's logs. |
| `ROOM_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` | The connection dropped before an `act` was answered. Use `err.state` to decide whether to act again. |
| `ROOM_EVENT_INVALID` | `sw.rooms.event` got a request the room did not send. Only the room may call the referee. |
| `ROOM_NO_CALLER` | Plain `sw.rooms.*` ran with no browser caller. Use `sw.rooms.server.*`. |
| `ROOM_COLUMN_RESERVED` | A write tried to change the `save` column. Only the room writes it. |
| `ROOMS_DRAFT_UNAVAILABLE` | Rooms do not run in previews or drafts. Test on the live app. |

### Referee decisions and visitor sessions

A decision with a `reject` key is a rejection, including `reject: ''`. Its `state`
is ignored, but its `timer` and `send` still apply. This lets a refused action
correct a clock or send an explanation without changing state.

Anonymous participants must have a platform visitor session. The ticket door
resolves that session; it refuses entry when visitor identity is unavailable.
There are no sessionless room tickets. Referee failure alerts are aggregated
per project for one hour, across action, membership and timer failures.

pages.title: Project groups
pages.body:
A group is a developer-owned collection of projects that share members and a
design theme — organize related apps and widen access in one grant instead of
adding collaborators to each project separately.

## The model

- One group per project. Adding a project already in another group returns
  409 GROUP_CONFLICT — remove it from the old group first.
- Effective access = union of project owner, direct collaborator, and group
  member. When the same user appears at more than one level, the most
  permissive role wins.
- Groups do not transfer ownership or affect billing. Work always bills the
  project's owner.

## Roles

Both owners and editors can manage group membership, change
the shared theme and delete the group. Adding a project also requires editor
access to that project. The group’s creator remains its owner and cannot be
removed through the member-removal route.

## Effective role on member projects

A group member's role grants access to ALL of the group's projects —
effective role on a project = MAX(direct collaborator role, group role).
Every group member is at least an editor: read + write, including deploy,
promote, restore, and database writes. Project OWNERSHIP never comes from a
group — billing and delete stay with the project owner regardless of
group membership.

## Membership invites

Sending new group invitations is unavailable. The API answers
410 GONE and stores or sends nothing. Existing members keep their access,
and invitations already sent can still be listed, revoked and accepted.

  group_invite_list({ group_id }) → { invites: [{ email, role,
    invited_at, expires_at }] }  — pending invites only.

  group_invite_accept({ group_id, token })
    → { accepted: true, group_id }
    The caller must be signed in as the invited email with a verified
    email. Errors: EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED, INVITE_INVALID, INVITE_USED,
    INVITE_EXPIRED, INVITE_WRONG_ACCOUNT, GROUP_NOT_FOUND.

  group_invite_revoke({ group_id, email }) → { revoked: true }
    Revokes a PENDING invite only — an accepted invite is membership,
    not an invite. 404 NOT_FOUND if there's no pending invite for that
    email.

## Removing an accepted member

Use the REST route below, or the MCP `api` tool with the same DELETE call
and `confirm: true` after approving the removal.

  DELETE /v1/groups/:id/members/:user_id → { removed: true, group_id,
    user_id }
    Any group member can remove another member. The group’s creator
    cannot be removed through this route.
    404 NOT_FOUND if that user isn't an accepted member.

## Create and organize

  group_create({ name, description? })
    → { id, owner_id, name, description, created_at, updated_at,
        role: 'owner', project_count: 0 }

  group_add_project({ group_id, project_id }) → 409 GROUP_CONFLICT if taken

  group_get({ group_id })
    → { ...group, projects: [{id,name,subdomain,status}],
        members: [{user_id,role}], design_tokens: {} }

For group_add_project, project_id accepts a project UUID, slug or subdomain.
You must belong to the group and have editor access to the project.

group_remove_project({ group_id, project_id }) requires the project UUID from
project_list or project_get. A group member or a project editor can detach it;
the project stays live. group_list() returns all groups you own or belong to,
with your role and each group’s project_count.

Example flow:
  1. group_create({ name: "Acme Suite" }) — save the returned id
  2. project_list() — find the UUID for each project to add
  3. group_add_project({ group_id, project_id })
  4. group_get({ group_id }) — verify the roster and token shape

## The shared theme

A group carries design_tokens (a flat JSON object, 64 KB max). For example,
`{ "--brand": "#0a7" }` defines a CSS custom property on every member
project's served HTML. Use it in your CSS with `color: var(--brand)`.
The theme is inserted before the project's own styles, so a later project
value can override the group default. Pages using the Tailwind v4 browser
runtime also receive the tokens in `@theme`.

  GET /v1/groups/:id/tokens → { tokens, updated_at }
  PUT /v1/groups/:id/tokens  body: { tokens: { ... } }  (owner or editor)

## Deleting a group

Any group member can call group_delete({ group_id }). It removes the group,
its membership and shared theme, and detaches its projects. The projects stay
live. A caller without membership receives 403 FORBIDDEN.
REST: DELETE /v1/groups/:id
