sw.image — Image transformations
pages.body: Available inside any deployed function via the sw argument provided to the handler. sw.image.resize builds a transformation URL — it doesn't fetch the image, it returns a URL that triggers transformation at the edge when the browser (or your code) fetches it. Stick the URL in for free, no extra hop. ## sw.image.resize(source, options) Returns a string URL. source: '/uploads/foo.png' — relative path on this project's domain 'https://example.com/foo.png' — absolute URL (must be reachable from the project's zone) options (all optional): width number pixel width height number pixel height fit 'cover' | 'contain' | 'scale-down' | 'crop' | 'pad' format 'auto' | 'webp' | 'avif' | 'json' (default: format=auto) quality 1–100 JPEG/WebP/AVIF quality dpr number device-pixel ratio (1, 2, 3) gravity 'auto' | 'left' | 'right' | 'top' | 'bottom' | 'face' | '0.5x0.5' background '#ffffff' fill colour for pad/contain blur 1–250 sharpen 1–10 rotate 90 | 180 | 270 trim '20;30;20;30' edge trim (top;right;bottom;left) metadata 'keep' | 'copyright' | 'none' anim true | false (animated GIF/WebP support) Example: ```ts // api/photo.ts — a thumbnail and a larger WebP of /photo.jpg; nothing is fetched here export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext) { const thumb = sw.image.resize('/photo.jpg', { width: 200, height: 200, fit: 'cover' }) // → https://your-project.somewhere.site/cdn-cgi/image/width=200,height=200,fit=cover/photo.jpg const webp = sw.image.resize('/photo.jpg', { width: 800, format: 'webp', quality: 80 }) return new Response(``, { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' } }) } ``` ## Billing 5,000 unique transformations / month free per project; usage beyond that is at /v1/pricing. Repeated fetches of the same transformed URL are cached at the edge — only the first fetch counts. Cached for 1 year by default. ## Source restrictions The source URL must be on the project's subdomain (default) or on a verified custom domain attached to the project. Cross-origin external URLs are blocked by default and return 403 — if you need to transform images from a domain you don't own, file via the `feedback` tool. For files in sw.fs, point at the project URL with the path: sw.image.resize('/api/files/photo.jpg', { width: 400 }) where /api/files/photo.jpg is a function that does sw.fs.read. ## Errors The transformed URL returns 4xx if Image Transformations isn't enabled on the zone, or 415 if the source isn't an image. The helper itself only validates the inputs and builds the URL — it does not pre-flight.

pages.title: Calendar — atomic holds and reservations
pages.body:
`sw.calendar` is the built-in reservation primitive for booking apps. It
atomically holds one resource + time range, counts active holds and pending
payments before accepting a booking, and gives you a hold token that can be passed into
Checkout. Use it instead of a SELECT-then-INSERT booking table when a
double-booking would cost money or trust.

To put events in a user's own Google Calendar, use `sw.connect.googleCalendar`
instead (`docs({ topic: 'google-calendar' })`).

The normal booking path runs in a function:

1. `sw.calendar.availability({ resource, range })` returns the `busy` and
   `free` ranges to show the customer.
2. `sw.calendar.hold({ resource, range, ttl_seconds })` holds the range they
   pick. An overlapping active hold, pending payment or booking on an exclusive
   resource gets `409 CALENDAR_CONFLICT`, so show the next free range.
3. Pass the returned `hold_token` to `sw.payments.checkout` as
   `calendar_hold_token`. A completed payment confirms the reservation. The
   Checkout session expires with the hold, and an unpaid session releases it
   when it expires.

For appointments (a person's time, such as a 15-minute call), set the
resource's weekly `hours` once and offer `sw.calendar.slots(...)`: see
`appointments-hours-and-slots`.

`calendar` → `hold-checkout-confirm` shows that call with its timing rule,
`availability-and-booking-reads` the read shapes, and
`resource-policies-blocks-cancellations-and-rebooking` minimum stays, notice
and turnaround.

## Runtime methods

- `sw.calendar.hold(resource, range, ttl?)`
- `sw.calendar.hold({ resource, range, ttl?, ttl_seconds?, ttl_ms?, metadata? })`
- `sw.calendar.blackout(resource, range, options?)`
- `sw.calendar.removeBlackout(reservationId, options?)`
- `sw.calendar.cancel(reservationId, options?)`
- `sw.calendar.rebook(reservationId, newRange)`
- `sw.calendar.setPolicy(resource, policy)`
- `sw.calendar.getPolicy(resource)`
- `sw.calendar.availability(resource, range)`
- `sw.calendar.availability({ resource, range })`
- `sw.calendar.slots({ resource, range, duration_minutes, step_minutes? })`
- `sw.calendar.list(resource, { range?, statuses?, limit?, cursor? })`
- `sw.calendar.list({ resource, range?, statuses?, limit?, cursor? })`
- `sw.calendar.get(reservationId)`
- `sw.calendar.pending(token, { payment_reference? })`
- `sw.calendar.confirm(token, { payment_reference? })`
- `sw.calendar.release(token, { payment_reference?, release_reason? })`
- `sw.calendar.expire({ resource? })`

REST equivalents are `POST /v1/calendar/hold`, `/blackout`,
`/blackout/remove`, `/cancel`, `/rebook`, `/policy/set`,
`/policy/get`, `/availability`, `/slots`, `/list`, `/get`, `/pending`,
`/confirm`, `/release`, and `/expire`. The REST
body includes `project_id`; the runtime helper injects it for you.

## Resource policies, blocks, cancellations, and rebooking

`setPolicy` declares optional `min_stay_nights`, `max_stay_nights`,
`advance_notice_hours`, `bookable_from`, `max_days_ahead`, `turnaround_hours`,
`capacity`, and `hours` for one resource; pass `null` for a field to clear it. Holds and
rebooks enforce the policy with stable 409 codes: `CALENDAR_MIN_STAY`,
`CALENDAR_MAX_STAY`, `CALENDAR_ADVANCE_NOTICE`, `CALENDAR_TOO_FAR_AHEAD`,
`CALENDAR_BUFFER_CONFLICT`, and `CALENDAR_OUTSIDE_HOURS`.

Use `blackout` / `removeBlackout` for operator-owned unavailable ranges,
`cancel` for a confirmed reservation, and `rebook` to move a confirmed
reservation atomically. Each operation is project-scoped and returns the
updated reservation or the stable conflict/not-found code named in its error.

## Appointments: hours and slots

Set the person's weekly hours once, in their own IANA time zone, from your
setup or admin code. Days you leave out are closed. Windows are wall-clock
`HH:MM-HH:MM`, so daylight-saving changes follow the zone.

```js
await sw.calendar.setPolicy('host:dana', {
  advance_notice_hours: 12,
  max_days_ahead: 14,   // starts at most 14 days from now
  hours: {
    timezone: 'America/Los_Angeles',
    weekly: { mon: ['09:00-12:00', '13:00-17:00'], tue: ['09:00-17:00'] },
  },
});
```

`setPolicy` replaces the whole policy, so send `hours` with every change.
`hold` and `rebook` refuse a range that does not fit inside one window with
`409 CALENDAR_OUTSIDE_HOURS`. Use `blackout` for days off.

`slots` returns the starts a visitor can book: inside the hours, after
notice and `bookable_from`, within `max_days_ahead`, and clear of holds, bookings, blackouts and
turnaround. Show them in the visitor's own time zone; the times are absolute.

```js
const { slots } = await sw.calendar.slots({
  resource: 'host:dana',
  range: { start: Date.now(), end: Date.now() + 14 * 86400000 },
  duration_minutes: 15,
  step_minutes: 30,   // starts on the hour and half hour; defaults to duration_minutes
});
// -> { resource, range, duration_minutes, step_minutes, timezone: 'America/Los_Angeles',
//      slots: [{ start_ms, end_ms, start: '2026-12-01T17:00:00.000Z', end: '...' }] }
```

`range` spans at most 62 days, and at most 2000 slots are returned. `slots` is
a read: two visitors can see the same start. `hold` decides atomically, so
the second one gets `409 CALENDAR_CONFLICT`. For a booking without payment,
`hold` and then `confirm(hold.hold_token)` once you have what you need (for
example, after the visitor confirms their email). Send only the start times to
the browser. `availability` returns reservation ids. Visitor cancel and
reschedule links need their own random secret, stored server-side, because
`cancel` and `rebook` take the reservation id. A link that carries only the id
lets anyone who sees one cancel it.

To email the visitor from the platform address, they must be a user of your
app or your project needs a verified sending domain. Confirm the booking with
`sw.auth.signInWithOtp({ email, redirect_uri, purpose: 'confirm' })`: the
visitor gets a "Confirm your request" email, and once they press it they are a
verified user you can email (`sw.auth` → `magic-links-passwordless-sign-in`). Attach the invite as a `.ics` file with
`sw.email.send({ attachments })` (`sw.email` → `attachments`).

## Class seats

For a class, call `sw.calendar.setPolicy(resource, { capacity: 12 })` once
from your authorized setup or admin code. One hold reserves one seat.
Reservations share seats only when their start and end match exactly;
a different overlapping range still conflicts. Turnaround separates classes,
not seats within the same class, and a blackout blocks the whole class.
A full class returns `409 CALENDAR_FULL`.

Leave `capacity` out or set it to `null` for an exclusive resource.
`setPolicy` replaces the policy, so include capacity when changing another
field. Lowering it below an existing class's active reservations returns
`CALENDAR_CAPACITY_BELOW_BOOKINGS` and leaves the policy and bookings intact.

Availability also returns `capacity` and `slots`: each existing class has
`start_ms`, `end_ms`, `capacity`, `reserved`, and `remaining`.
Your app supplies the class schedule; a class with no reservations yet is absent.
A partly filled class stays in `busy`, with its seat count in `slots`.
Seat counts describe the current bookings; `hold` also checks notice,
blackouts and turnaround before reserving. Cancel, release and expiry free a
seat. Rebooking into a full class leaves the original booking intact.

After a timeout or lost hold response, read the reservation state before
trying again: a second hold reserves another seat. There is no party-size
or waitlist parameter; store a waitlist in your app and offer a freed seat
through the same hold-and-checkout flow. A payment after hold expiry confirms
only if a seat is still free; otherwise the existing paid-but-slot-lost
result lets your app handle the refund or alternative booking.

## Hold input

```js
const hold = await sw.calendar.hold({
  resource: 'room:queen-204',
  range: {
    start: '2026-08-01T15:00:00-07:00',
    end:   '2026-08-03T11:00:00-07:00',
    timezone: 'America/Los_Angeles',
  },
  ttl_seconds: 40 * 60,
  metadata: { party_size: 2 },
});
```

`range.start` and `range.end` accept epoch milliseconds or ISO timestamps
with an explicit `Z` / offset. `hold` and `blackout` require
`range.timezone`, a valid IANA timezone; a missing one is a type error and a
400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`. `availability` and `list` ranges take only
`start` and `end`, and `rebook` keeps the reservation's timezone when
its new range omits one. Ranges are half-open: `[start, end)`. Adjacent reservations are
allowed; overlapping reservations conflict. The conflict set is active
`hold`, `pending_payment`, and `confirmed`; expired/released rows do not
block new holds. Default TTL is 35 minutes, minimum is 1 second, maximum is
24 hours.

## Hold response

```json
{
  "token": "calh_...",
  "hold_token": "calh_...",
  "expires_at": 1785625200000,
  "reservation": {
    "id": "cal_...",
    "project_id": "...",
    "resource": "room:queen-204",
    "start_ms": 1785612000000,
    "end_ms": 1785765600000,
    "timezone": "America/Los_Angeles",
    "status": "hold",
    "hold_token_prefix": "calh_...",
    "metadata": {
      "party_size": 2
    },
    "payment_reference": null,
    "expires_at": 1785625200000,
    "confirmed_at": null,
    "released_at": null,
    "release_reason": null,
    "created_at": 1785622800000,
    "updated_at": 1785622800000
  }
}
```

Store the token server-side or return it to the browser only long enough to
start checkout. Later operations require the token and the same project.

## Availability and booking reads

Use the calendar read side to render availability; you do not need a shadow
table of holds. Availability returns active `hold` / `pending_payment` /
`confirmed` conflicts clipped to the requested range, plus the maximal free
ranges between them. Expired holds are ignored even before an explicit
`expire()` sweep.

```js
const availability = await sw.calendar.availability({
  resource: 'room:queen-204',
  range: {
    start: '2026-08-01T00:00:00-07:00',
    end: '2026-08-08T00:00:00-07:00',
  },
});
// -> { resource, range: { start_ms, end_ms },
//      busy: [{ reservation_id, kind: 'hold'|'booking', status,
//               start_ms, end_ms, expires_at }],
//      free: [{ start_ms, end_ms }] }

const page = await sw.calendar.list('room:queen-204', {
  range: { start: Date.now(), end: Date.now() + 30 * 86400000 },
  limit: 100,
});
// -> { reservations: [...], next_cursor: string|null }
// Pass next_cursor back as cursor. By default list returns active holds and
// confirmed bookings. Pass statuses: ['released', 'expired'] for audit rows.

const { reservation } = await sw.calendar.get(page.reservations[0].id);
```

`range.start` / `range.end` use the same epoch-millisecond or explicit-
offset ISO format as holds. `list` requires a resource, accepts an optional
overlap range, defaults to 100 rows, and caps `limit` at 500. `get` is
project-scoped and returns `CALENDAR_RESERVATION_NOT_FOUND` for a missing or
cross-project id.

## Hold → checkout → confirm

```js
const hold = await sw.calendar.hold({
  resource: body.resourceId,
  range: body.range,
  ttl_seconds: 45 * 60,
});

const checkout = await sw.payments.checkout({
  env: 'prod',
  mode: 'payment',
  calendar_hold_token: hold.hold_token,
  line_items: [{ amount: 2500, currency: 'usd', name: 'Reservation deposit' }],
  success_url: 'https://my-app.somewhere.site/booked',
  cancel_url: 'https://my-app.somewhere.site/book',
});
```

Checkout marks the hold `pending_payment`, sets the Stripe Checkout expiry to
the hold expiry, and records a payment reference. The hold must have at least
31 minutes remaining when checkout starts; otherwise the platform returns
`CALENDAR_HOLD_TTL_TOO_SHORT` and releases the hold. On
`checkout.session.completed`, the platform confirms the hold. On
`checkout.session.expired` it releases the hold, so a failed or abandoned
payment frees the slot when the session expires. A single checkout may
use `calendar_hold_token`, `quote_id`, or both. When both are supplied the
stored quote prices the Checkout session and the calendar hold reserves the
dates; both records are bound to the same session in one atomic database batch.
Completion confirms the hold before completing the quote booking, and a lost
slot leaves the quote unfulfilled for recovery instead of double-fulfilling.

Manual confirmation is also available:

```js
await sw.calendar.pending(hold.hold_token, { payment_reference: 'order_123' });
await sw.calendar.confirm(hold.hold_token, { payment_reference: 'order_123' });
await sw.calendar.release(hold.hold_token, { release_reason: 'customer_canceled' });
await sw.calendar.expire({ resource: 'room:queen-204' }); // optional resource filter
```

`confirm` is idempotent once confirmed with the same payment reference.
If a paid checkout arrives after the original hold expired and another hold
has taken the slot, the reservation is marked
`payment_received_slot_lost` and the webhook payload surfaces the problem
for refund/manual recovery.

pages.title: Google Calendar — add events to a user's own calendar
pages.body: A signed-in user of your app connects their Google Calendar and chooses one calendar they own. Your functions then add, update and delete the app's own events in that calendar, from a request or from a scheduled job when the user is away. The platform owns the Google client, keeps the user's grant, and calls Google for you. You do not create a Google Cloud project, request scopes, or store tokens, and no token or calendar id ever reaches your code. It covers only events your app created, in the one calendar the person chose. Your app cannot list, read or change their other events, see free/busy, invite attendees, or use other Google services. Writes answer the event's id and when Google recorded the change, never its contents. `sw.calendar` is something else: atomic booking holds inside your own app (`docs({ topic: 'calendar' })`). The calls are `sw.connect.googleCalendar.*`, in server functions: | Call | Result | |---|---| | `connect(request, { return_to })` | A redirect `Response`. Return it from your connect endpoint. | | `status({ user_id? })` | `{ connected: false }` or `{ connected: true, reconnect_needed, calendar: { name, time_zone }, connected_at }`. The person's main calendar is named "Primary calendar". | | `createEvent({ user_id?, event })` | `{ id, updated }` | | `updateEvent({ user_id?, event_id, event })` | `{ id, updated }`. Only the fields you pass change. | | `deleteEvent({ user_id?, event_id })` | `{ deleted }`, which is `false` when it was already gone | | `disconnect({ user_id? })` | `{ disconnected, google_permissions_url }`. This app loses access at once. | **Who a call is for.** In a request, every call acts for the signed-in caller, and `user_id` is left out. A signed-in caller naming another `user_id` is refused with `IDENTITY_CLAIM_NOT_ALLOWED`. `user_id` is accepted only inside a scheduled job (`docs({ topic: 'cron' })`) or a background job (`docs({ topic: 'sw.jobs' })`). The platform checks that the call comes from a running job of your app. Anywhere else, `user_id` is refused with `JOB_REQUIRED`, so a public endpoint can never act for someone a visitor names. ## Recipe: put a user's events in their Google Calendar and keep them updated from a scheduled job ### 1. Connect: one endpoint and one link ```ts // api/calendar/connect.ts — open it in the signed-in person's browser export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise { const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(req) if (!user) return Response.redirect(new URL('/signin', req.url).toString(), 302) return sw.connect.googleCalendar.connect(req, { return_to: '/settings' }) } ``` ```html Connect Google Calendar ``` The same endpoint starts and finishes the connection: 1. The person's browser opens it. 2. They approve access at Google. 3. They choose a calendar on the platform's page. 4. Their browser comes back to this endpoint. 5. It finishes for the same signed-in person, in the same browser, and sends them to `return_to` with `?google_calendar=`: | Value | Meaning | |---|---| | `connected` | Done. | | `cancelled` | They said no. | | `missing_permission` | They unticked a permission at Google, so nothing was connected. Ask them to connect again and allow all of them. | | `failed` | It did not complete. Examples: the link expired after 30 minutes, it was finished in another browser, or Google refused. Try again. | Use your app's own address or a custom domain attached to it. Localhost and preview addresses are refused. `return_to` is a path on the same site. ### 2. Show the state ```ts // api/calendar/status.ts export default sw.endpoint({ auth: 'required', handler: async (_input, sw) => sw.connect.googleCalendar.status(), }); ``` `reconnect_needed: true` means the person removed the app's access in their Google account, or Google ended it. Show the Connect link again. If a person connects again with the same Google account and the same calendar, your app can still update the events it added before. With another account or calendar, those earlier events can no longer be changed through the app. ### 3. Write events with ids you choose, so updates find them Give each event an `id` from your own record. It is 1 to 200 letters, digits or `.` `_` `:` `-`. A later run then updates the same event instead of adding a copy. Only events created through `createEvent` for this person can be updated or deleted. Any other id answers `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_EVENT_NOT_FOUND`. ```ts // api/_calendar.ts — shared helper (files starting with _ are import-only) type Game = { id: string; title: string; start: string; end: string; place: string } /** Create the event, or update it when it already exists. */ export async function putGame(sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext, userId: string, game: Game): Promise { const event_id = 'game-' + game.id const event = { title: game.title, start: game.start, end: game.end, location: game.place } try { await sw.connect.googleCalendar.updateEvent({ user_id: userId, event_id, event }) } catch (err) { if ((err as { code?: string }).code !== 'GOOGLE_CALENDAR_EVENT_NOT_FOUND') throw err await sw.connect.googleCalendar.createEvent({ user_id: userId, event: { id: event_id, ...event } }) } } ``` Times are ISO date-times with an offset (`2026-12-01T19:30:00-08:00`), or a local time plus `time_zone: 'America/Los_Angeles'`. An all-day event takes `all_day: true`, with `start` and `end` as `YYYY-MM-DD`; `end` is the day after the last day. Event fields are `id`, `title`, `description`, `location`, `start`, `end`, `all_day` and `time_zone`. If `createEvent` fails with `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_UNAVAILABLE`, call it again with the same `id`. You get the one event, never a copy. ### 4. Keep them updated from a scheduled job Create a schedule that calls this endpoint (`docs({ topic: 'cron' })`). Inside that run, `user_id` is accepted. The same code in an ordinary request answers `JOB_REQUIRED`. ```ts // api/jobs/calendar-sync.ts — called by a schedule import { putGame } from '../_calendar' export default sw.endpoint({ auth: 'none', // the platform's invocation signature authorizes it below handler: async ({ request }, sw) => { if (!(await sw.jobs.verifyInvocation(request))) return new Response('forbidden', { status: 403 }) const { data: people } = await sw.db.server.from('calendar_follows', { limit: 500 }) const { data: games } = await sw.db.server.from('games', { where: { changed: true }, limit: 100 }) let updated = 0, reconnect = 0 for (const person of people) { try { for (const g of games) { await putGame(sw, String(person.user_id), { id: String(g.id), title: String(g.title), start: String(g.start), end: String(g.end), place: String(g.place) }) updated++ } } catch (err) { const code = (err as { code?: string }).code if (code === 'GOOGLE_CALENDAR_RECONNECT_REQUIRED' || code === 'GOOGLE_CALENDAR_NOT_CONNECTED') { reconnect++; continue } throw err } } return { updated, reconnect } }, }); ``` `calendar_follows` is your own table of who wants calendar updates. Make it an `owner()` table, so `user_id` is the person. Anyone who has not connected, or must reconnect, is skipped and counted, and the page shows them the Connect link. ### 5. Disconnect ```ts // api/calendar/disconnect.ts export default sw.endpoint({ auth: 'required', handler: async (_input, sw) => sw.connect.googleCalendar.disconnect(), }); ``` On disconnect, this app loses access at once. Events already in the calendar stay, because they belong to the person. Access also ends in the same way when: - a user of your app is deleted; - the project is deleted; - the project is transferred to a new owner. People connect again after a transfer. Show the person this, with the link `disconnect()` returns: "When your last Somewhere connection to this Google account ends, we ask Google to withdraw Somewhere's access and then delete the token. You can also remove Somewhere in your Google Account at any time: myaccount.google.com/permissions." ## Errors Every error has `code`, `message` and `retry`. | `code` | Status | What to do | |---|---|---| | `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_NOT_CONNECTED` | 409 | The person has not connected. Show the Connect link. | | `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_RECONNECT_REQUIRED` | 409 | Access ended. They removed it at Google, Google ended it, or the chosen calendar is no longer theirs. They connect again. | | `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_EVENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | This app has no event with that id for this person, or it was deleted. Create it. | | `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_EVENT_EXISTS` | 409 | The app already created an event with that id. Update it, or use another id. | | `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_INVALID_EVENT` | 400 | The message names the field. | | `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | `retry: true` with `retry_after_ms`. Wait, then retry. | | `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_UNAVAILABLE` | 503 | `retry: true`. Google did not answer. | | `JOB_REQUIRED` | 403 | `user_id` outside a scheduled or background job. | | `IDENTITY_CLAIM_NOT_ALLOWED` | 400 | A signed-in caller named a different `user_id`. | | `AUTH_REQUIRED` | 401 | `connect` without a signed-in caller, or another call with neither a signed-in caller nor `user_id`. | | `APP_USER_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | `user_id` is not a user of this app. | | `VALIDATION_ERROR` | 400 | `connect` from localhost, a preview, or another site; or `return_to` is not a path. | | `DRAFT_SIDE_EFFECTS_BLOCKED` | 409 | Called from a draft preview. It works once the draft is promoted. | | `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_NOT_AVAILABLE` | 404 | Google Calendar is not available to this app. | ## Limits - One connected calendar per person per app, chosen by the person. To change it, they connect again. - Only calendars the person owns, not calendars shared with them. - 600 Google Calendar calls a minute per app. - 10 connect attempts per person every 10 minutes, and 300 per app every hour. - Calls are not charged. - Agents connected to your app cannot connect a calendar: the person does. - A temporary (unclaimed) app cannot use Google Calendar. Claim it first.

pages.title: sw.billing — plans & feature gating for YOUR app's users
Use your app from Claude (app MCP tools)
pages.body:
**Preview feature.** It works end to end today and its shape may still change.

A signed-in Somewhere app can serve its own MCP tools at
`https://<your-app-address>/mcp`. Anyone who uses your app can then add that
address as a custom connector in Claude, or in another AI client that connects
to remote servers with OAuth sign-in. Claude then works with the app as that
person, using the app's own sign-in. The app's MCP sign-in uses standard OAuth
with PKCE and open client registration, so any OAuth client can use it.

## Steps

Ask before destructive or paid actions unless the user already authorized them.

1. Start from an app with sign-in. Run
   `somewhere init --name my-app --features auth,private-data` to create one
   with a `notes` table each user owns.
2. Add one `api/*.ts` endpoint per tool, with an `mcp` declaration (below).
3. Keep `somewhere.auth.json` at the project root. The `somewhere init` starter
   ships it.
4. `somewhere deploy`.
5. In Claude: Customize, Connectors, Add custom connector. Paste
   `https://<your-app-address>/mcp`, then Connect. Leave the OAuth client on
   its default, or choose Register automatically. The project address works as
   is; a custom domain serves the same `/mcp` path.
6. Sign in with an account of the app, not your Somewhere login, and approve
   the page that lists the tools.
7. In a chat with the connector on, ask Claude to use a tool, for example "add
   a note called Hello, then list my notes". Open the app as the same account to
   see the result.

## Test tools with a prepared app user

From the linked project folder, run `somewhere test-users prepare owner` and
grant the printed user ID any app role the tested data requires. For a
headless check, seed one browser context with
`.somewhere/test/owner.state.json` and open the authorization URL from an
OAuth-capable MCP test client. Use the same context for consent and approval
so the transaction cookie and same-origin request headers are retained.
After the client's PKCE exchange, use it to list and call tools at the app's
`/mcp` URL, then run `somewhere test-users cleanup`. Keep the session file and
OAuth tokens private. The CLI has no command that takes a prepared actor and
calls the app's MCP tools directly.

## Declare tools

A signed-in app can be used from Claude, or any other MCP client, as the
person signed in to the app. Each tool is an ordinary endpoint with an `mcp`
declaration; its arguments arrive as the JSON body:

```ts
// api/listNotes.ts — tool list_notes
export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'required',
  mcp: {
    name: 'list_notes',
    description: 'List the signed-in user\'s notes.',
    inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: {}, additionalProperties: false },
    annotations: { readOnlyHint: true },
  },
  handler: async (_input, sw) => ({ notes: (await sw.db.from('notes', { limit: 100 })).data }),
});
```

```ts
// api/addNote.ts — tool add_note
export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'required',
  body: { title: 'string' },
  mcp: {
    name: 'add_note',
    description: 'Add a note for the signed-in user.',
    inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['title'], additionalProperties: false },
  },
  handler: async ({ body }, sw) => ({ note: (await sw.db.insert('notes', { title: body.title })).data[0] }),
});
```

A tool is the default export of a static `api/*.ts` route with
`auth: 'required'`: file and folder names are letters, digits and underscores
(`api/listNotes.ts`, not `api/list-notes.ts` or `api/[id].ts`). Everything in `mcp` is a plain literal:
a unique name (a letter, then up to 63 letters, digits or underscores), a
description, a draft-07 `type: 'object'` input schema, and optionally
`outputSchema` and the standard `annotations` hints. Return a JSON object.
At most 100 tools; arguments up to 64 KiB, results up to 1 MiB. A failed or
uncertain call is never retried. An invalid declaration fails the deploy.

**Sign-in.** `somewhere.auth.json` at the project root names the page where a
signed-out person signs in:

```json
{ "version": 1, "signInPath": "/" }
```

The file is public configuration, served like any other app file: never
put secrets in it. The platform sends them there with `sw_auth_return` set to
`/mcp/consent?signin=<id>`; after signing in, the app loads exactly that
path. The `somewhere init` starter ships the file and that step
(`src/auth/connection-return.ts`). Without the file, a signed-out person
cannot connect (`409 app_auth_return_adapter_required`).

## Who signs in and what a tool may do

**Who signs in.** The app's own user, with the account they use in the app,
never the developer's Somewhere login; the owner connects with an app account
too. They approve a page that lists the tools.

**What a tool may do.** A tool is your code, run as the signed-in user:
`user` is them, and `sw.db` reads and writes apply their declared access
(`owner()`, `member()`, roles); `sw.db.server` and server-only tables are
refused inside a tool call. Everything else the handler does is up to your
code, not that user's row access: explicit server files (`sw.fs.server`), raw
SQL, email and outbound requests can reach beyond what the user may see, so
check the user before using them. The consent page tells the person exactly
this.

**Re-consent.** Approval covers each tool's name, description, schemas and
route. Change any of them, or add a tool, and connected clients stop seeing
that tool until the person reconnects (in Claude: disconnect, connect again)
and approves. Changing only the handler's code keeps the approval. Access
lasts an hour and refreshes for up to 30 days, then the person reconnects.

**Revocation and deletion.** Each tool call is checked fresh when it starts:
the person's access, their account (signed out, banned), the app's MCP
setting and the live version. Revoking access, disabling MCP, banning or
signing the person out, or publishing a new version stops new calls at once;
a call already running can finish its work for at most 60 seconds after it
started. Deleting the person's account stops a running call at its next
platform call (`sw.db`, `sw.fs` and the other user-scoped calls).

**One call, 60 seconds.** A tool's user-scoped platform calls must happen
within 60 seconds of the call starting; after that they are refused with
`MCP_CALL_EXPIRED` and nothing changes. Within those 60 seconds a tool call's
platform authority is not single-use: if its delivery were captured and sent
again, the same tool would run again with the same arguments as the same
person, including after the original call completed. Make tools that change
data safe to repeat (an idempotency key from the arguments), as you already
do for client retries.

## Current limits

- At most 100 tools per app. Arguments up to 64 KiB, results up to 1 MiB. A
  failed or uncertain call is never retried.
- A tool's user-scoped platform calls must happen within 60 seconds of the
  call starting (`MCP_CALL_EXPIRED` after that).
- Tool routes are static `api/*.ts` files with `auth: 'required'`. Names use
  letters, digits and underscores only.
- Inside a tool, `sw.db.server` and server-only tables are refused.
- Changing a tool's name, description, schemas or route, or adding a tool,
  hides it from connected clients until the person reconnects. The client is not
  told.
- Access lasts an hour and refreshes for up to 30 days; then the person
  connects again.
- The server speaks MCP revisions 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 over
  Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`. The 2025 revisions use initialization; 2026-07-28
  uses per-request metadata without an initialization handshake. Existing app
  source does not need to change.
- Each caller address can register up to 30 clients and make up to 120 token
  requests per minute per app.
- The consent page shows the name the connecting app gives itself. It is not
  verified.

pages.title: Run a public repo as your own instance
pages.body:
## Run a public repo as your own instance

### 1. Clone and inspect

Run `git clone <public-repo-url> <new-instance-folder>` and `cd <new-instance-folder>`. Run `git remote get-url origin` and `git rev-parse HEAD` to record what you copied. Keep any inherited `.somewhere.json` in place for the new-instance deploy.

Read any setup notes. With or without notes, run `rg -n 'signInPath|createSomewhereAuth|somewhereAuth|appRoles:|verifyInvocation|mcp:' .`. Read `somewhere.auth.json` for the sign-in path when present. Otherwise trace auth UI and routes from the auth calls. Read `db/schema.ts` for app-wide roles, the invocation guard in each job handler for its caller, and each endpoint's `mcp` declaration for the tool name and input. Use `grep -R -n -E` with the same pattern if ripgrep is unavailable.

### 2. Check the CLI and account

Use CLI 0.38.115 or later. Run `somewhere --version` and `somewhere whoami`. If needed, run `npx -y @somewhere-cloud/cli@latest --version` and use that invocation for every command below. Run `somewhere login` if needed and check `somewhere whoami` again for the intended account.

### 3. Deploy a new instance

From the clone, run `somewhere deploy --new`. It publishes raw source and updates the link to a new project named for the folder. The current CLI keeps control of deploy when the installed repo pin is older. Use the new ID in `somewhere project view <new-id> --json` to verify ownership and confirm that it differs from the inherited ID.

### 4. Check the public page and inputs

Run `curl -fsS <printed-app-url>/` and confirm it serves the app. If a required input is missing, run `somewhere deploy --list-unpublished` to inspect omissions. For an app with a sign-in adapter, run `somewhere file somewhere.auth.json --version <deployed-version> --project <new-id>` and check its `signInPath`.

### 5. Give the owner access

Have the intended owner sign in to the app and confirm their identity. Use the deploy cue or run `somewhere auth roles grant <app-email-or-user-id> <declared-role> --project <new-id>`. Verify with `somewhere auth roles list --role <declared-role> --project <new-id>` and have the owner exercise a private action.

On a disposable project, run `somewhere test-users prepare owner --json` from its linked folder and use the actor's email or ID for the grant. To check the owner page, run `somewhere browser --project <new-id> --path <owner-path> --auth-user <app-user-id>` with the ID from the manifest. Run `somewhere test-users cleanup` after the proof.

### 6. Register and test schedules

Run `somewhere cron list --project <new-id>`. The `sw.jobs.verifyInvocation` guard accepts jobs as well as cron. Trace its callers to tell which handlers need a recurring schedule. Read the handler for the route and payload, and use the setup notes or confirm the cadence with the owner when source gives none.

For each missing schedule run `somewhere cron create '<cron>' <route> --name <name> --project <new-id>` with `--payload '<json>'` and `--timezone <IANA-zone>` as needed. Add `--disabled` on a fixture. Run `somewhere cron run <name> --project <new-id> --wait` and verify the effect. For captured mail, run `somewhere email test-inbox <test-address>`. Use an address allowed by the handler. For a recurring schedule, check the enabled status and next run in `somewhere cron list --project <new-id>`.

### 7. Connect app tools and record the result

If the app declares tools, run `somewhere docs app-mcp`. Connect `<printed-app-url>/mcp` in a client that supports remote MCP with OAuth. Start signed out, check that the app redirects to its sign-in page, then sign in as the app owner and approve. List the tools, perform a reversible private action and check its effect in the app. For a headless app sign-in, keep one cookie jar across consent and sign-in, use a browser user agent and send the app's origin on same-origin form POSTs.

Record the live URL, owner access, private action, tool and schedule results, and the public upstream URL and commit.

pages.body:
Give each page a title, a description and a link preview, let the platform serve `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml`, then check what the live release actually ships. If the project has no `robots.txt` or `sitemap.xml` of its own, the platform serves both: robots allows every crawler and points at the sitemap, and the sitemap lists every deployed HTML page. ## 1. Title, description and link preview Search results and link previews read the HTML the server sends. Put the tags in `index.html`, which serves every route of a single-page app: ```html Notes — write it down, find it later
``` Put the preview image at `public/og.png` and reference it by its full URL: link-preview services don't resolve relative image paths. A 1200×630 image fits the large preview card. ## 2. A different preview for a shareable page Link-preview services read the HTML without running your JavaScript, so every route of a single-page app shares the tags in `index.html`. For a page that people share on its own, such as `/pricing`, ship an HTML file at `pricing/index.html` with its own head and the same app script: ```html Pricing — Notes
``` The deploy compiles every HTML page's app script, so `/pricing` runs the same app and your router renders the pricing route. The generated sitemap lists `/pricing` too. For routes that only exist inside the client router, set the tab title as the route renders: ```tsx // src/pages/PricingPage.tsx import { useEffect } from 'react'; export function PricingPage() { useEffect(() => { document.title = 'Pricing — Notes'; }, []); return

Pricing

; } ``` ## 3. Sitemap and robots The generated sitemap lists each deployed HTML page with its upload date. Routes that exist only inside the client router aren't deployed pages, so it can't list them: give them their own HTML file (step 2) or ship your own `public/sitemap.xml`. Shipping `public/robots.txt` or `public/sitemap.xml` replaces only that generated file. Your rules are served as written, including `noindex` or `Disallow` rules. ### Change notification (IndexNow) After a release is live, the platform tells the IndexNow search engines (Bing and the others that share IndexNow submissions) which public pages are new or changed since the previous live release. Nothing needs to be configured. - **Which pages:** deployed HTML pages, by the same rule as the generated sitemap. A page counts when its file is new or its bytes changed; at most 1,000 URLs are sent per release. When the previous release can't be read, every public page is sent. - **Which hosts:** one submission per serving host, meaning the project's `.somewhere.site` address and each attached custom domain. The dev slot's address is never sent. - **Ownership key:** each serving host answers `/.txt` with the project's IndexNow key, which the engines fetch to confirm the host. The key is derived from the project and grants no access to it. A file you deploy at that path is served instead. - **Nothing is sent** for temporary (unclaimed) or test projects, for draft, frozen, archived or deleting projects, for a release that a newer release or a rollback has already replaced, when `robots.txt` disallows every crawler (`User-agent: *` with `Disallow: /`), or when no public page changed. - **Errors never block a deploy.** An engine that is slow or refuses the submission changes nothing about the release; the attempt is logged. A submission asks the engines to recrawl those URLs. It is not indexing: whether and when a page appears in results is up to each engine. Google does not use IndexNow; Google Search Console handles sitemap submission for Google. ## 4. Check the live release After a deploy, read what the active release ships: ```text project_seo_check({ project_id: "my-app" }) ``` It inspects the deployed `index.html`, `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` of the active release, without fetching the site. Each item has a `status`: - `automatic`: the release uses the platform fallback configuration. - `app-supplied`: the release contains your file. - `needs-attention`: something to fix, such as a missing title or description, with a `suggestion`. - `unknown`: the check couldn't inspect this item. Open the public URLs to check the served pages and files. Verify ownership and submit the sitemap in Search Console. ## 5. Server-rendered pages and redirects For database-backed articles, return HTML from a root `[...path].ts` handler. The `functions` topic's server-rendered pages recipe shows a public article route alongside a React editor. Return each article's title, description, canonical URL and body in that HTML; link previews do not run browser JavaScript. A page handler can also return `Response.redirect(url, 301)`. A client-only React route still renders in the browser. Use the static HTML approach above for fixed pages, or the HTML handler for dynamic content. Generated sitemap and IndexNow discovery cover deployed HTML files; they do not enumerate database-backed article URLs. Supply a sitemap containing those public URLs and check its served response alongside the articles. ## Deployed SEO metadata `project_seo_check({ project_id })` and `GET /v1/projects/:id/seo` return the same authenticated, read-only inspection. The response identifies `release_id`, `version`, `source_manifest_hash` and `compiled_artifact_digest` for the exact active release. It inspects only `index.html`, `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml`; missing, changed or unverifiable release evidence is unavailable, not a pass. Each item carries `status` (`automatic`, `app-supplied`, `needs-attention`, `unknown`), `provenance`, bounded `values`, a `value_count`, `values_truncated`, a `note` and optional advisory `suggestion`. At most five values of 512 characters are returned per item; duplicate detection retains the full count. Automatic means a platform fallback is configured because an app-supplied file is absent; read the public URL to confirm a request serves it. App-supplied robots rules and metadata, including intentional noindex or Disallow rules, are preserved. No source is edited. Inspecting a file larger than 256 KiB returns unknown. Title, description, canonical and Open Graph values come from the deployed homepage HTML. Static body text there reflects the file only: check the rendered page for what is visible; crawlability stays unverified. `coverage.public_response` is `unobserved`: no HTTP fetch, function execution, authentication check, JavaScript rendering or crawl occurs. Client routes, indexing and ranking remain unknown. Generated sitemaps include static HTML paths only, not routes hidden behind a client router. Search Console verification and submission are separate from this inspection. ## Automatic sitemap and robots files If a project does not ship its own `sitemap.xml` or `robots.txt`, the platform serves both automatically. The sitemap lists deployed HTML pages and uses their upload times for ``; robots points crawlers at that sitemap. Shipping either file overrides only that generated fallback. Routes that exist only inside a client-side router are not separate deployed HTML pages, so the generated sitemap cannot discover them. Ship crawlable HTML for those routes or provide your own `sitemap.xml`. ## Going further | Need | Where | |---|---| | A custom domain for the canonical URL | [Custom Domains](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/domains.txt) | | How the check reports each field | `recipe-seo` → `deployed-seo-metadata` | | The generated sitemap and robots files | `recipe-seo` → `automatic-sitemap-and-robots-files` | | Visitor counts and top pages | `analytics` → `page-views` |

pages.body:
A Vite + React app deploys as it is. The platform compiles raw source on
every deploy, so it needs no build step and no layout change. What you move by hand is whatever ran on another backend: server
routes become functions in `api/`, and Supabase data, users and files move
with the steps below.

## From a GitHub repository

```bash
somewhere git connect owner/name --project <project> --branch main
```

This connects the repository to the project, opens GitHub once if the GitHub
App is not yet installed, deploys the branch's current commit, waits for it
and prints the live URL. Every later push to that branch deploys the same
way. Inside a folder already linked with `somewhere init`, `--project` is not
needed. For a monorepo, add `--root <app folder>`. The MCP tools for the same
flow (`github_app_install`, `github_installations`, `github_connect`) are in
`github`.

## From a folder on disk

Ask before destructive or paid actions unless the user already authorized them.

```bash
cd my-app
somewhere init --name my-app # link this folder to a new project and keep its source
somewhere deploy-check  # compiles exactly what deploy would publish, publishes nothing
somewhere deploy
```

`somewhere init` adds `.somewhere.json` to link the folder.
To update an app already live on Somewhere, start with `somewhere pull <app>`
in a fresh folder, then apply your changes to that source. The CLI never uploads `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`, `dist`
or `.next`. Deploy from the project root; the platform builds `src/`, so
`dist/` is not needed.

## From a zip

Unzip it, then deploy the folder as above. The zip itself is not a deploy
input.

## What has to change in the code

| You have | Do this |
|---|---|
| Vite + React (any folder layout under a root `index.html`) | Nothing. Deploy it. |
| Plain HTML, CSS and JS | Nothing. A root `index.html` is enough; `package.json` is optional. |
| Create React App (`public/index.html`) | Move `index.html` to the root, remove `%PUBLIC_URL%` from it, rename `src/index.js` to `src/index.jsx` (a page script compiles only as `.jsx` or `.tsx`; a `.js` one is served as-is), and add `<script type="module" src="/src/index.jsx"></script>`. Other `.js` files with JSX compile as they are. |
| Express, Fastify or Koa routes | Rewrite each route as a function file in `api/` that returns a `Response` (below). A server file is not run. |
| Next.js | Pages become a Vite React app with a router; API routes become functions in `api/`. Server-side rendering does not run here. |
| Environment variables | `somewhere env set NAME value` (`--stdin` for a secret); functions read `sw.env.NAME`. A `VITE_` value the page reads needs `--public` (`sw.env`). |

A function is one file per route. `api/users/[id].ts` serves
`/api/users/:id`:

```ts
// api/users/[id].ts — what an Express `app.get('/api/users/:id', …)` becomes
export async function GET(request: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(request);
  if (!user) return Response.json({ error: 'Sign in.' }, { status: 401 });
  const id = new URL(request.url).pathname.split('/').pop();
  return Response.json({ id, viewer: user.id });
}
```

Export `GET`, `POST` and the other methods by name, or one default function
that handles every method; a method with no handler answers 405. Database,
auth, files, email and AI are `sw.*` calls inside the function, not HTTP
clients you configure. Contract: `functions`.

## From Supabase, or a Lovable app on Supabase

A Lovable export is a Vite + React app on Supabase, so the frontend deploys
unchanged and the backend moves in four steps (`migration-supabase` has each
in full):

1. Declare your tables and who may read and write them in `db/schema.ts`,
   then replace `supabase.from(...)` calls with the generated `somewhere:data`
   client (`declared-data`).
2. Switch sign-in to the starter's cookie session (`recipe-login`). Remove the
   Supabase keys from browser code.
3. Users create their accounts again with the same email address (importing
   users with their passwords is not available). New accounts get new
   IDs; remap ownership columns by email before loading rows.
4. Copy files with their visibility (`declared-files`), and move each table's
   rows. To keep the data in PostgreSQL instead, attach it (`postgres`).

Edge Functions become functions in `api/` as in the table above.

## From another builder's code export

Put pages and components under `src/` with a root `index.html` and a router,
and move each server endpoint into `api/` as a named `GET` or `POST` export
that returns a `Response`. A Floot export maps file by file:
`endpoints/<route>/<name>_GET.ts` becomes the `GET` export of
`api/<route>/<name>.ts`, and its `.schema.ts` input check moves into that
function.

## Check it

```bash
somewhere typecheck && somewhere deploy-check && somewhere deploy
somewhere verify --project <project> --flow flow.json
```

`deploy-check` reports compile and function errors before anything is
published. After the deploy, sign in with two accounts and a signed-out
visitor and confirm each sees only what it should (`verify-before-deploy`).

pages.title: Recipe — AI agent with tool calls
Recipe — Booking / calendar app
Recipe — Fixed-price catalog checkout
Recipe — Multi-chat (Claude.ai-style conversation list)
Recipe — Cheap model escalates to smart model when stuck
pages.body:
Run your chatbot on a cheap fast model (Haiku, GPT-4o-mini) for the
90% of turns that are easy — navigation, simple lookups, short
answers. When a turn is actually hard (a real bug, architecture
advice, a code review), the cheap model hands the hard question, restated with the code, errors
and constraints it needs, to a smarter model in one call. The application receives the final
answer from the same agent run.

## The pattern

Add one tool — `ask_expert` — to a `sw.agent.run` call. The cheap model
calls it with the question restated in full; the tool sends that to the
smart model in one `sw.ai.chat` call and returns the answer as the tool
result. The cheap model relays it. The run's conversation is stored for the
signed-in user automatically, so the next request continues it with the same
`conversation_id`.

## Code

`SomewhereRuntimeContext` is supplied by the current generated runtime types.

```ts
// api/chat.ts — POST { message, conversation_id? } → { reply, conversation_id }
export default async (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> => {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Method not allowed', { status: 405 })
  const user = await sw.auth.requireUser(req)
  // Every message is a paid model call, so throttle each verified user before
  // the run starts. Sample policy: 20 messages per hour.
  const turns = await sw.rateLimit.check(`chat:${user.id}`, 20, 3600)
  if (!turns.allowed) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'rate_limited', retry_at: turns.reset }, { status: 429 })
  }
  let body: unknown
  try { body = await req.json() } catch { return new Response('Invalid JSON', { status: 400 }) }
  if (!body || typeof body !== 'object' || Array.isArray(body)
      || !('message' in body) || typeof body.message !== 'string' || !body.message.trim()) {
    return new Response('message required', { status: 400 })
  }
  const message = body.message
  const conversation_id = 'conversation_id' in body && typeof body.conversation_id === 'string' && body.conversation_id
    ? body.conversation_id
    : crypto.randomUUID()

  const askExpert = {
    name: 'ask_expert',
    description: 'Ask a more capable model. Use for real debugging help (stack traces, "why does this fail"), architecture advice, code review and genuine unknowns. Do NOT use for simple lookups, navigation or status questions.',
    input_schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: {
        question: { type: 'string', description: 'The question restated in full, with the code, errors and constraints the expert needs.' },
      },
      required: ['question'],
    },
    execute: async (input: { [key: string]: unknown }) => {
      // Throttle escalations per user before calling the smart model. The
      // count is approximate under concurrency, not a spend guarantee.
      const quota = await sw.rateLimit.check(`escalate:${user.id}`, 3, 86400)
      if (!quota.allowed) return 'Expert limit reached for this 24-hour window.'
      const question = typeof input.question === 'string' && input.question.trim() ? input.question : message
      const expert = await sw.ai.chat({
        provider: 'anthropic',
        model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
        system: 'You are an expert assistant. Be precise and thorough.',
        messages: [{ role: 'user', content: question }],
      })
      return expert.text
    },
  }

  const r = await sw.agent.run({
    provider: 'anthropic',
    model: 'claude-haiku-4-5',
    conversation_id,
    system: 'You are a helpful assistant. When a user asks for real debugging help, architecture advice or a code review, call ask_expert with the full question. Otherwise answer directly.',
    messages: [{ role: 'user', content: message }],
    tools: [askExpert],
  })
  return Response.json({ reply: r.text, conversation_id })
}
```

Two per-user limits run before paid calls: 20 messages an hour for the
cheap model, then 3 escalations a day for the smart one. Over the first, the
request answers 429 with `retry_at`. Both are sample values. `sw.rateLimit`
is a request throttle: concurrent requests can pass slightly more than the
limit, so it is not exact spend accounting. To bound what one run may spend,
set `maxSpendCents` on `sw.agent.run` (`docs({ topic: 'sw.agent' })`).

## When the cheap model should escalate

Four typical escalation signals:

- **Debugging** — user pastes a stack trace, error, or asks "why
  doesn't X work?". The cheap model is usually wrong on these; the
  smart model spots the missing `await` / wrong destructure / off-by-
  one.
- **Architecture / design advice** — "how should I structure my
  database for…", "where should this logic live…". The cheap model
  picks one option confidently; the smart model weighs trade-offs.
- **Code review** — user pastes 30+ lines of code asking for feedback.
- **Genuine unknown** — the user is asking about a domain the cheap
  model hasn't been taught (your product, a niche library).

Typical non-escalation signals:
- Navigation ("where do I find X?").
- Project status ("am I healthy?", "what's my usage?").
- Simple how-to questions answered in your existing system prompt.

## Cost math

See /v1/pricing for current per-model rates. Cheap and smart models
typically differ by an order of magnitude or more on per-turn cost.

If 10% of turns escalate, your blended cost is roughly 6× the
cheap-model-only rate — but your bot now gets the hard questions right.
Cheap-everywhere costs less per turn and gets half the hard answers wrong.

## Tier gating

Don't expose the same cap to every user. Pick the limits passed to
`sw.rateLimit.check` from the plan you store for the user. These are
approximate throttles, not billing limits. A reasonable starting shape for
escalations:

- **Free** — 3 escalations / day.
- **Paid** — 20 / day.
- **Top tier** — unlimited.

When the cap is hit, the tool result reports that the daily expert quota was
reached. The application retains authority over how that state is presented.

Related topics: `sw.ai`, `recipe-ai-agent`, `recipe-multi-chat`.

pages.title: Live data — one poller, fan out to every client
Architecture Patterns — How to wire common app shapes
Migrating a Supabase app
pages.body:
Somewhere is not a drop-in Supabase replacement. Migrate the app's data and
access contract; changing an import does not migrate queries, permissions,
authentication, files, or live-update behavior.

If you would rather keep your data in PostgreSQL than port it to the managed
database, you can: attach your own database and query it with the provider's
driver (`docs({ topic: 'postgres' })`). That decision is only about the
data layer — auth, files, functions and live updates are still the separate
moves described below, and an attached database gets none of the declared
permissions this page is about.

## Declare the data contract

Declare tables, fields, access scopes, relations, and browser operation grants
in `db/schema.ts`. The platform generates the typed `somewhere:data` client
for permitted browser operations. Use `sw.db` inside functions for business
logic. A foreign key describes a relationship; it does not grant access.

An existing `from().select()` call is not the new browser data API. Rewrite
ordinary browser reads and writes against the generated operations. See
docs({ topic: 'declared-data' }) and docs({ topic: 'sw.db' }) for exact syntax,
supported relations, and the rules for adopting existing tables.

## Keep authentication and files explicit

Use same-origin cookie sessions for browser authentication. The optional
`@somewhere-cloud/sdk` auth and function helpers do not make an existing
Supabase app source-compatible. Never put a developer key in browser code.
See docs({ topic: 'auth-client' }) for setup and docs({ topic: 'sw.auth' })
for session behavior.

Copy files with their intended visibility; private files need authenticated
access or signed URLs. Review old public URLs rather than assuming they keep
working. See docs({ topic: 'sw.fs' }).

## Users

Importing users with their existing passwords is not available
(`POST /v1/auth/import` answers 501 `AUTH_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE`). Today each
user creates their account again with the same email address: password
sign-up, a sign-in link, or Google, GitHub or Discord sign-in. New accounts get
new user IDs, so map each old ID to the new one by email and rewrite every
ownership column and foreign key that pointed at it. Sessions do not carry
over.

## Move data before switching traffic

Keep a verified export before modifying the source app. Map old user IDs,
row ownership, and foreign keys explicitly. Test the imported app with two
users and a signed-out visitor, including denied access and writes, before
switching traffic. A column named `user_id` does not declare its policy.
See docs({ topic: 'portability' }) for export and import capabilities.

Supabase channels are not the browser live-data contract. Use the supported
named live-view path described in docs({ topic: 'live' }); its scope
limits apply. Do not assume every declared table supports subscriptions.

pages.title: Setup — Use the CLI, or connect MCP without a shell
pages.body:
Install the CLI and sign in through your browser, or connect MCP from chat. ## Connecting from a terminal For an agent with a terminal, the Somewhere CLI is the better way to deploy: `somewhere deploy` reads files from disk without putting their contents in conversation tool arguments. The default auth/styled starter avoids about 28,734 tokens of inline deploy arguments (114,934 UTF-8 JSON bytes, estimated at four bytes per token). Sign in with `somewhere login`: browser sign-in gives a full CLI session that renews itself. Beyond the connector's named tool list, the CLI covers project lifecycle and collaborators, database import and export, file history, jobs and cron, search indexes, push notifications, payment administration and PostgreSQL migration. Many of these operations are also reachable through the connector's `api_read`, `api_write` and `run_code` tools. `auth_cli_pair` links a CLI inside a sandbox or container with no browser; it keeps the connector's limits: AI image, audio and video generation and financial asset transfers are unavailable, domain purchases happen in the dashboard, and generic API access cannot reach credential, OAuth, CLI, code-runner, admin, internal or system endpoints. ## 1. Install the CLI Ask before destructive or paid actions unless the user already authorized them. ```bash npm i -g @somewhere-cloud/cli ``` The package is `@somewhere-cloud/cli`. The binary is `somewhere`. Requires Node.js 22.19.0 or newer. The CLI works on macOS, Linux, and Windows (via WSL or PowerShell). ## 2. Log in (browser-based, no key paste) ```bash somewhere auth login ``` The command prints an eight-character code and a sign-in link, opens a browser if the machine has one, and waits. A human approves that code in their own browser; the session then lands in `~/.somewhere/config.json`. Same flow as `gh auth login`. The code is good for ten minutes. To keep a separate CLI login, set `SOMEWHERE_CONFIG_DIR` to a directory: the CLI keeps its login, temporary-project session, device id and caches there instead of `~/.somewhere`, and `HOME` is unchanged. An empty directory starts signed out, so a test or a second identity never touches your own login. `somewhere mcp` passes the same value to the MCP server it registers; files other tools keep in your home directory (such as `~/.claude.json`) stay there. **What the CLI sends about this machine.** Device-code sign-in (`somewhere auth login`) and the first signed-out deploy of a project, which registers its claim link, send a device label, `CLI · · <8 characters of a random device id>`, and the machine's host name, CLI version, Node.js version, operating system and release, and CPU architecture. The platform stores these with the CLI session, together with the request's IP address and approximate city, region and country. Browser sign-in sends only the device label, which names the key it creates. The device id is random, created on first use and kept in `device.json` in the config directory. Open [Connected agents](https://somewhere.cloud/app/agents) to find the CLI by its device label and disconnect it. Nothing has to open a browser on the machine running the command, so this is also the login path on a hosted VM (ChatGPT Work, Claude Work), a remote container, or any SSH session — the terminal and the browser can be different devices. Signing an account in is the account owner's decision: confirm consent before starting the flow, show the code and the link exactly as printed, and leave the approval to the person in the browser. A code should only ever be approved if it matches the one on that person's own terminal. The session persists on that machine: every later command and shell reuses it. The access credential lasts 24 hours and the CLI renews it silently; the renewal right lasts 30 days and resets each time it is used, so a machine touched at least monthly stays signed in. A sign-out, or approving the same device name again, ends the old session. After this you can run `somewhere deploy`, `somewhere logs`, and the MCP bridge — all read the same config file. For a human setup flow, use `somewhere auth login` instead of putting a developer key in the config file. Developer keys serve CI and server-to-server calls. For a disposable shell already connected through MCP, use the pairing flow below. ## 3. Optionally connect MCP to Claude Code The Somewhere CLI includes the MCP bridge. Register it with Claude Code: ```bash somewhere mcp install claude-code # reload Claude Code ``` After reload, the Somewhere MCP tools are available in context. The bridge uses the CLI session, so you don't paste a key. This step is optional when the agent has a shell — the CLI needs no MCP setup: routine work uses first-class CLI commands, `somewhere call ''` covers the full tool catalog, and `somewhere run ``` `src/main.tsx` — React app (raw TSX, deployed as-is): ```tsx import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'; import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'; function App() { const [msg, setMsg] = useState('loading...'); useEffect(() => { fetch('/api/hello').then(r => r.json()).then(d => setMsg(d.message)); }, []); return

{msg}

; } createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(); ``` `api/hello.ts` — server function (raw TS, deployed as-is): ```ts export default sw.endpoint({ auth: 'none', handler: async () => ({ message: 'hello from a function' }), }); ``` Now deploy: ```bash somewhere deploy ``` The CLI uploads the source files. The platform's compiler bundles `src/main.tsx` into a hashed JS chunk under `/_compiled/`, rewrites `index.html` to load it, and compiles `api/hello.ts` into a function the runtime can execute. The public URL serves that live deploy. (For just-a-static-page, you can ship a single `index.html` with plain HTML — the JSX/TSX compiler only runs on files that need it.) ## Common follow-up commands ```bash somewhere logs # tail recent function logs somewhere deploy # redeploy current directory somewhere mcp # raw stdio MCP bridge (for hosts you wire by hand) somewhere auth status # show current login ``` For everything else (custom domains, project rename, env vars, billing), run `somewhere call --list` and invoke the matching platform tool, or use the dashboard at https://somewhere.cloud. Without a shell, use the matching MCP tool. ## Ephemeral environments (Claude Code Web, sandboxes, containers) This is for a machine whose home directory does NOT survive (Claude Code Web, a fresh CI container, a sandboxed runner). A hosted VM with a lasting home directory does not need it — use `somewhere auth login` above, which stays signed in across sessions. Where the home directory is discarded, the browser-based `somewhere auth login` won't survive the session — but the MCP connection already has an authenticated session. Pair the CLI to that session: ```text 1. npm i -g @somewhere-cloud/cli 2. Call MCP tool auth_cli_pair # returns { key, expires_at } 3. Put the returned key in the command environment as SOMEWHERE_TOKEN. 4. somewhere auth set # reads SOMEWHERE_TOKEN 5. somewhere whoami # confirm identity 6. somewhere deploy ``` `auth_cli_pair` mints a short-lived `smt_` key (kind='cli_pair', 24h TTL) scoped to the same user as the MCP session. `somewhere auth set` stores this pairing key in the CLI config, using the identity already verified by MCP. The key auto-expires; revoke early with `DELETE /v1/keys/` if you need to. Pure-MCP path (Claude.ai connector, no shell at all): skip the CLI entirely and use the platform tools directly. With a shell, `somewhere call` invokes those same tools without requiring an MCP client, while first-class commands handle the routine workflows.

pages.title: @somewhere-cloud/cli — full command reference
pages.body:
When a shell is available, the CLI is the primary platform surface. It has
first-class commands for routine operator work,
`somewhere call <tool> '<json>'` for every platform tool, and
`somewhere run <script>` to execute code against your live project without
deploying. Nothing else needs installing: no MCP setup is required to use the
CLI, and on a persistent machine you install and log in once. MCP is for
connected clients without a shell (Claude.ai, ChatGPT and other MCP hosts).
Start with the working loop below. The CLI and its local MCP bridge share
one login; a Claude.ai or ChatGPT connection uses its own OAuth session.

## The working loop

For an existing Somewhere app, start with `somewhere pull <app>` in a fresh
folder. Then edit and run the working loop. `somewhere help <command>` prints
every flag.

| Step | Command | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Deploy | `somewhere deploy` | Publishes raw source and prints the live URL. |
| Verify | `somewhere verify [--flow flow.json]` | Runs the live app at desktop and phone sizes: named steps, console/network health, both screenshots. |
| Inspect | `somewhere browser [target]` | One page: screenshot, snapshot, DOM, network, or an evaluated expression. |
| Diagnose | `somewhere logs --tail 10`, `somewhere errors` | Recent function output, then failures split into refused and exception. `errors` also works on a temporary project. |
| Email | `somewhere email test-inbox <address>` | Mail sent to `<name>@<subdomain>.test.somewhere.site` — sign-in email and your own sends — with the magic link. |

MCP clients use the same platform tools. Through the Claude directory
connector, `run_code` cannot generate AI media or move money. The Advisor is
optional on both surfaces.

Ask before destructive or paid actions unless the user already authorized them.

No account yet? Deploy the current directory immediately:

```bash
npx -y @somewhere-cloud/cli@latest deploy
```

The anonymous command returns a live URL and claim link; login is optional until
you decide to keep the project.

```bash
npm i -g @somewhere-cloud/cli
somewhere signup          # no account yet — opens the sign-up page (from 0.30.1)
somewhere login           # opens a browser; session lands in ~/.somewhere/config.json
```

`somewhere login` prints a short device code and opens a page where you
approve this machine by name. If you are not signed in yet, that page signs you
in first. It has no way to create an account, so `somewhere signup` is the
front door for a stranger: it prints the sign-up URL as plain text before it
opens anything, so a headless agent can relay a link it can read, then tells you
to run `somewhere login`.

The same session powers the CLI, the MCP bridge, and `somewhere deploy`.
The CLI signs in only two ways: a person approves it in the browser (the
device code `somewhere login` prints), or it uses a saved `smt_` key
(`somewhere auth set`). An agent without a person at hand needs that key.
Do not pass an API key for a human setup flow; the `smt_` key is for CI/CD.

`somewhere deploy` ships raw source (`src/`, `index.html`, `public/`,
`package.json`, `api/`) unless you explicitly opt into `--prebuilt`. The
normal path has no local build step. → docs({ topic: 'deploy' }).

## Global commands and flags

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere --version` | `-V`, `--version` | Print the CLI version. |
| `somewhere --help` | `-h`, `--help` | Print top-level help. |
| `somewhere help [command]` | none | Print help for one command. |

## Auth

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere signup` | none | Create an account — prints the sign-up URL and opens it. (from 0.30.1) |
| `somewhere login` | `--signup`, `--browser-callback` | Authenticate with the device-code browser flow. `--signup` opens account creation instead; `--browser-callback` signs in with Google in the browser and receives the key on a localhost port. (from 0.30.1) |
| `somewhere logout` | none | Revoke and remove stored credentials. |
| `somewhere whoami` | `--json` | Show current user info; `--json` prints the raw account response. |
| `somewhere auth` | none | Credential command group. |
| `somewhere auth login` | none | Authenticate with the browser flow. |
| `somewhere auth set` | none | Save an `smt_` token from standard input, `SOMEWHERE_TOKEN`, or the hidden prompt. Positional tokens are refused. |
| `somewhere auth status` | none | Show current login state, device ID, and key name. |
| `somewhere auth print-token` | none | Print the current `smt_` token to stdout for shell scripts. |
| `somewhere auth roles grant <user> <role>` | `--project <ref>`, `--json` | Give an app user an app role declared in `db/schema.ts` `appRoles`; `<user>` is the address they signed up with or their app user id. |
| `somewhere auth roles revoke <user> <role>` | `--project <ref>`, `--json` | Take an app role away, whoever granted it. |
| `somewhere auth roles list` | `--project <ref>`, `--user <user>`, `--role <role>`, `--json` | Who holds which app role, with the roles the live schema declares. |

## Projects

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere init` | `--name <name>`, `--link`, `--project <ref>`, `--bare`, `--template <name>`, `--features <ids>`, `--ui <mode>`, `--catalog`, `--dry-run`, `--json` | Initialize a project in the current directory. An empty directory gets the recommended React + TypeScript starter with sign-in (`--template minimal`: without; `--ui headless`: plain views, no CSS); `--bare` links without starter files. `--catalog --json` lists the modules `--features` accepts (no login, project or files); `--dry-run` prints the file plan. `--name` skips the prompt; `--link` links a folder that already contains source, or scaffolds an unpublished project in an empty folder. Init installs the pinned dependencies when it writes a starter. |
| `somewhere project` | none | Project command group. |
| `somewhere project create <name>` | `--subdomain <subdomain>`, `--json` | Create a new project. |
| `somewhere project list` | `--json` | List all projects. |
| `somewhere project view [name-or-id]` | `--json` | View project details. |
| `somewhere project delete <name-or-id>` | `--json` | Tombstone a project, take its hosts offline, and start the 30-day recovery period. |
| `somewhere project allowed-origins list` / `set` | `--project`, `--clear`, `--json` | Show or replace the project's exact cross-origin allowlist. |
| `somewhere call project_allowed_origins_set '<json>'` | `--json` | Replace the project's cross-origin allowlist, which is for THIRD-PARTY origins only (owner or platform admin only). Pass `"allowed_origins": []` to clear it. → docs({ topic: 'cors' }). |
| `somewhere status [project]` | `--json` | Show current project, active release, and hosted workspace status. For version history use `somewhere deploys`. `--json` prints `project`, `deployment`, `workspace` and, when the plan doesn't include previews, `deployment_entitlement` with its code. When previews are unavailable, status still reports production and exits successfully. |
| `somewhere open [project]` | `--dashboard` | Open the project URL in your browser; `--dashboard` opens the dashboard. |

## Advisor

Ask how to build or diagnose a problem in plain language. The Advisor uses your question, the facts sent with it and public docs; it reads nothing itself. Signed in, in a folder linked to an app, the CLI reads that app's overview (pages, routes and their sign-in rule, tables, scheduled jobs) and last deploy with your sign-in and sends them with the question, and says so in one line. It keeps your last three questions and answers in that folder's `.somewhere/` for 30 minutes and sends them with a follow-up; `--new` starts over and `--no-context` sends only the question. It never sends file contents, rows, env values, users or your previous commands. Generic questions work without login.

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere advisor "<question>"` | `--json`, `--no-context`, `--new` | Ask the platform advisor. `--json` wraps the question and answer; `--no-context` sends only the question (no app, earlier questions or file); `--new` forgets this folder's earlier questions. No previous-command context is attached. |
| `somewhere advisor --resume <request-id>` | `--json` | Continue waiting for the same saved durable request. |
| `somewhere advisor --status <request-id>` | `--json` | Inspect a saved durable request once. |
| `somewhere advisor --cancel <request-id>` | `--json` | Request cancellation of the same saved durable request. Cancellation can race completion. |

### Saved requests

The saved-request commands require CLI 0.37.3 or later and a request ID
returned by the platform. If the answer has no saved request ID, use the
ordinary question command.

For a durable request, the CLI saves its handle and prints the reconnect command before waiting. Closing the terminal or pressing Ctrl-C stops waiting; it does not cancel the request. Reconnect using the same CLI configuration and owning account. Anonymous receipts are private capabilities; do not share them. After a disconnect, resume the saved request to avoid starting a second answer.

Durable requests have no fixed answer deadline, but provider failures, unavailable response records and bounded documentation rounds can leave an answer incomplete. Read its stated limits and verify the proposed behavior in your app. A connection timeout does not by itself mean the model stopped. Explicit `--async` requests do not retain file excerpts.

## Platform tools and operator workflows

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere catalog` | `--json` | Browse the live platform tool catalog. |
| `somewhere call <tool> '<json>'` | `--all-projects`, `--json` | Invoke any platform tool by name (the MCP implementation). Run `somewhere call --list --json` to enumerate names and input schemas. In a linked directory, a tool that takes `project_id` runs against the linked project unless the JSON names one, and says so on stderr; `--all-projects` omits this project default; the tool's own scope still applies. |
| `somewhere tasks list` | filters, `--json` | List tasks. Use `somewhere tasks get/create/update` to read and maintain the task system without an editor. |
| `somewhere feedback list` | `--project <ref>`, `--json` | Read feedback from the app’s users in the project owner inbox; `somewhere feedback submit <message>` adds to it. For a platform bug, use `somewhere call support_ticket` (see `feedback`). |
| `somewhere grep <pattern>` | `--project <ref>`, `--glob <glob>`, `--json` | Regex-search deployed source and print stable `file:line` matches. |
| `somewhere usage [project]` | `--period <period>`, `--json` | Show account or project usage through `usage_summary`. |

## Deploy and pull

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere deploy [dir]` | `-m, --message <text>`, `--project <ref>`, `--scope <scope>`, `--dry-run`, `--include <paths>`, `--replace-functions`, `--prebuilt`, `--temporary`, `--new`, `--force`, `--yes`, `--json` | Deploy a directory to the linked or specified project. `-m` supplies an optional version note (at most 200 characters). `--include` publishes a root file the deploy would otherwise hold back. `--scope functions` deploys backend only; `--scope static` deploys site files only. `--dry-run` prints the diff without deploying. `--replace-functions` removes deployed functions missing locally. `--prebuilt` opts into bundled output. `--temporary` creates a temporary workspace without an account. `--new` publishes to a new project and updates the folder’s link. `--force --yes` overwrites remote changes without prompting. |
| `somewhere pull [project]` | `--out <dir>`, `--force`, `--json` | Download the live deployed source files and scaffold local typecheck files when absent. `--out` defaults to the current directory.
