In a linked folder it is the safe update when live is newer: unedited files move to live, local edits and local-only files stay, and it stops if a file changed both here and live. `--force` replaces local edits with live; it never deletes files a deploy would not upload. |
| `somewhere typecheck [dir]` | `--json`, `--deploy`, `--watch`, `--hook <host>` | Run `tsc --noEmit` over the project. `--deploy`: the deploy's narrower reference check, no `tsconfig.json` needed. `--watch` re-checks on save; never deploys. `--hook` is what `somewhere hooks install` runs. It regenerates `__somewhere_data.d.ts` and `__somewhere_files.d.ts` from `db/schema.ts`; CLI 0.37.47+ starters `.gitignore` them. |
| `somewhere lint [dir]` | `--json`, `--generic` | Check source offline (no login, network or file changes) for secrets, `db/schema.ts` declarations, directory index routes, request input choosing a server write's owner, and `sw.email.send` awaited in a loop. Warnings only; authorization and type correctness are not assessed. `--generic` adds the project's installed Oxlint. Exit 0 with warnings; 2 if source was skipped or `--generic` failed or found no Oxlint. |
| `somewhere hooks install [dir]` | `--host <host>`, `--json` | Add an after-edit `typecheck --deploy` check to this project's own agent settings (`.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json` or `.cursor/hooks.json`; never user-wide), merged with existing hooks. Hosts: `claude-code` (default), `codex`, `cursor`. Edits made through shell commands are not checked; run `somewhere typecheck --deploy --watch` for those. |
| `somewhere rollback [project]` | `-y, --yes`, `--json` | Select the previous retained production release. By default this changes code without restoring data. |
| `somewhere restore <version>` | `--project <ref>`, `-y, --yes`, `--json` | Make an earlier version live again by number (MCP `project_restore_version`). Free can restore retained deploys from the last 24 hours. Paid plans can restore any retained version. Restoring by number leaves the database schema and data unchanged. Nothing is re-uploaded; `somewhere pull` then brings the folder to it. |
| `somewhere deploys` | `--project <ref>`, `--json` | List versions, times, notes and available restore commands. |
| `somewhere deploys note <version> <message>` | `--project <ref>`, `--json` | Set or correct the note on an existing version. |
| `somewhere file <path> --version <number>` | `--project <ref>` | Print one source file from a retained production version. Redirect stdout to save it. |
| `somewhere deploy-check [dir]` | `--project <ref>`, `--run <path>`, `-X, --method <method>`, `-d, --body <json>`, `-q, --query <querystring>`, `--json` | Upload source for a server-side dry compile without deploying. `--run` instead runs one handler with development bindings, on every plan. |

## Project file storage

For the full file-tool surface, use `somewhere call fs_<verb> '<json>'`.
`somewhere call --list --json` lists each tool's required arguments.

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere fs put <local> <remote>` | `--project <slug>`, `--content-type <type>`, `--json` | Stream a local file into project storage. |
| `somewhere fs get <remote> <local>` | `--project <slug>`, `--json` | Stream a stored file to disk. |
| `somewhere fs ls <remote>` | `--project <slug>`, `--json` | List a directory in project storage. |
| `somewhere fs rm <remote>` | `--project <slug>`, `--json` | Remove a file or directory from project storage. |

## Database

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere db` | none | Database command group. |
| `somewhere db query <sql>` | `--project <id>`, `--json` | Run SQL against the project database. |
| `somewhere db dump` | `--project <id>`, `-o, --output <file>`, `--json` | Export the full database as SQL. |
| `somewhere db tables` | `--project <id>`, `--json` | List tables in the project database. |

## Environment, logs, and errors

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere env` | none | Environment variable command group. |
| `somewhere env list` | `--project <id>`, `--json` | List names, scope, visibility, labels and references. Values are not returned. |
| `somewhere env pull` | `--project <id>`, `--out <file>`, `--force`, `--json` | Write a local env template for the local-dev loop. Values are not included. |
| `somewhere env set <key> [value]` | `--project <id>`, `--stdin`, `--public` / `--private`, `--scope all|dev|prod`, `--provider <label>`, `--purpose <description>`, `--json` | Save or rotate a value. Use `--stdin` to keep a secret out of process arguments. New values are server-only. |
| `somewhere env delete <key>` | `--project <id>`, `--json` | Delete an environment variable. |
| `somewhere logs [project]` | `--level <level>`, `--source <source>`, `--function <route>`, `--endpoint <path>`, `--since <duration>`, `--tail <n>`, `--follow`, `--trace <id>`, `--json` | Show recent logs. `--tail` defaults to 20; `--follow` keeps polling; `--trace` shows one failed request's lines and stack. |
| `somewhere errors [project]` | `--limit <n>`, `--exceptions`, `--json` | Show recent failures with a `kind` column: **refused** for a 4xx your own handler returned on purpose, **exception** for an uncaught throw or a 5xx. The summary counts exceptions, deliberate refusals and platform diagnostics separately. `--exceptions` hides deliberate refusals; platform diagnostic failures stay visible. `--limit` defaults to 20 and caps at 100. |

## Local execution and inspection

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere dev` | `--project <id>`, `--port <port>`, `--open` | Frontend hot reload on localhost with the project's own Vite (installed in the project); API requests are proxied to your deployed project, so backend code runs only after deploy or preview. `--port` defaults to 8787. Install the frontend's Vite dependencies first (`npm install`). |
| `somewhere preview` | `--project <id>`, `--once` | `--once` syncs, prints the preview link and the promote command, and exits instead of watching. Each preview link works once; `somewhere preview link` mints another for the open preview. Every save goes to a private hosted URL; production keeps serving what was last promoted. Every plan for signed-in accounts; Free allows three open previews. The session starts with an isolated copy of managed data. Projects with a separate raw SQL database rehearse raw SQL migrations on a test project. |
| `somewhere run <script>` | `--project <id>`, `--timeout <ms>`, `--include-env`, `--arg <name=value>`, `--json` | Run a one-off ES module script once against the live project bindings. `--timeout` defaults to 10000 and caps at 30000. Output limits: the result is capped at 256 KB (cut to a preview with a notice); logs keep at most 100 entries; each log message is cut at 64 KB with a `[truncated: …]` marker at its end; all logs together stop at 4 MB, followed by one final `[logs truncated: …]` entry; `logs_truncated: true` is set when entries were dropped by either limit; the error message and stack are each cut at 64 KB; a returned `session` over 64 KB is not stored and the call answers `SESSION_TOO_LARGE`. |
| `somewhere browser [target]` | `--project <ref>`, `--url <url>`, `--path <path>`, `--wait <selector>`, `--eval <js>`, `--screenshot`, `--snapshot`, `--viewport <size>`, `--store`, `--include <sections>`, `--extract`, `--session <id>`, `--close <session>`, `--auth-user <email|user_id>`, `--json` | Inspect and drive a web page. Without `--project`, works against any public URL; with `--project`, verifies a deployed app. `--viewport` accepts `desktop` or `mobile`; `--include` accepts `network`, `dom`, and/or `markdown`; `--session` keeps one live page, with its sign-in, across calls until closed, idle 5 minutes or 10 minutes old (an ended one restarts signed out). `--close <session>` closes it in the selected or linked project (or `--project <ref>`). `--auth-user <email|user_id>` starts signed in as a managed test user (`somewhere docs browser`). `--path`, `--wait` and `--eval` combine with action flags: the path first, then the actions, then the wait and eval. |
| `somewhere verify [target]` | `--project <ref>`, `--url <url>`, `--path <path>`, `--flow <file.json>`, `--json`, `--out <file>`, `--schema`, `--keep-test-users`, `--keep-actors`, `--close-actors`, `--resume-page` | Run one action flow across desktop and phone viewports and return named steps, page/console/network health, and both screenshots. Omit the flow for a default page-health check. `--path /settings` opens that path on the linked or selected app; use it without `--url`. A flow with `actors` and `journey` runs several users, each in their own browser (`docs({ topic: 'browser' })`); `--keep-test-users` keeps the test users made for `test_user` actors; `--keep-actors` keeps signed-in actors between runs, `--close-actors` closes them, `--resume-page` continues kept pages (warm, not fresh-release evidence). `--schema` prints both flow forms. `--out` writes the full report to a new private file and prints a bounded summary (JSON with `--json`). |
| `somewhere api <method> <path>` | `-d, --data <json>`, `--raw` | Make a raw API call with auth attached. `--raw` prints non-JSON responses as-is. |

If `somewhere run` or the `run_code` tool returns `CODE_RUN_NOT_STARTED`
(HTTP 502 from the runner), credential preparation failed before the script
started. Nothing ran; a later identical request can succeed.

A script that reaches its own time limit can return HTTP 200 with a `TIMEOUT`
error and its logs. If the platform has not received the complete result within
that limit plus 500 ms from invocation, it returns HTTP 408 `CODE_TIMEOUT`
without the script's logs. This does not confirm execution stopped or undo
completed effects. Retrying runs the script again and can repeat those effects.
Setup before invocation and saving returned session data can add time to the
whole request.

One-off runs allow 30 starts per minute per project and 60 per minute across
an owning account's projects. A refusal returns HTTP 429 `RATE_LIMITED` with
`Retry-After` and `retry_after_ms`; no run credential is created. If the limit
cannot be checked within two seconds, the response is HTTP 503
`RATE_LIMIT_UNAVAILABLE` and nothing runs.

Pass per-run values with `somewhere run script.mjs --arg label=trial --arg limit=10`.
The script receives them as `export default async (sw, args) => { ... }`:
`args.limit` is the string `"10"`. The object is read-only and defaults to
`{}`. These inputs stay separate from project env and saved sessions.
Use project secrets with `--include-env` for credentials; command-line arguments
can appear in shell history and process listings.

## Docs and MCP

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere docs [topic]` | `--list`, `--full`, `--section <id>`, `--json` | With no topic, prints the topic index; `somewhere docs search <term>` lists matching sections with the command that opens each, and `somewhere docs --full` prints the whole manual. When the installed CLI is a minor release or more behind the one the docs describe, `somewhere docs` says so. The bundle topics are `start`, `docs`, `guides`, `security`, `migration` and `llms`; any single capability topic from the index — `somewhere docs cli`, `somewhere docs sw.db` — prints that page. |
| `somewhere mcp` | none | Run the Somewhere MCP server over stdio. |
| `somewhere mcp install <host>` | none | Configure an MCP host to use Somewhere. Supported hosts are `codex`, `claude-code`, and `cursor`. |
| `somewhere mcp doctor` | none | Check MCP setup: login, token validity, server reachability, and host configs. |

## Keeping the CLI current

A project records the CLI version it was built with: `somewhere init` writes it as the `@somewhere-cloud/cli` devDependency in `package.json`, and a linked folder without one gets `cli_version` in `.somewhere.json` at its first deploy. A different CLI run in that project prints one line naming both versions and hands the command to the pinned version when it is installed in `node_modules`; `somewhere upgrade` moves the project to the CLI you are running and prints the changelog entries in between.

| Command | Flags | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `somewhere upgrade` | `--json` | Move this project's recorded CLI version to the running CLI and print the CHANGELOG.md entries between the two. Run `npx -y @somewhere-cloud/cli@latest upgrade` for the newest release, then `npm install` when the pin is in `package.json`. Agent skills are not changed; `somewhere skills update` refreshes them. |
| `somewhere update` | `--check` | Update the CLI to the latest published version through npm. `--check` only reports whether an update is available. A refused update exits non-zero and prints `npm i -g @somewhere-cloud/cli@latest`. CLI 0.37.0 and older cannot update themselves (they refuse every current release as having no signed provenance); install the latest with that npm command. |

## deploy — what gets published, and what is held back

A project root usually holds more than the app. Coding agents keep notes,
TODOs, transcripts and scratch logs next to the code, and publishing one of
those to a live URL is a privacy incident, not a cosmetic mistake.

So the root is filtered by publish surface, not by "everything that is not a
dotfile" (from 0.30.1). A root file is published when it is a known app-surface
name or extension, when something in the published source references it by
name, or when you opted it in. Everything else is held back — and named, never
dropped silently:

```
Not published: 3 local files (notes, tests, tooling) stay on your machine. See them: somewhere deploy --list-unpublished
```

Run `somewhere deploy --list-unpublished` to see the specific files and
why each stays local.

Unreferenced operational files also stay local: root folders `scripts`, `fixtures`,
`e2e`, `tooling`, `tools`, `design-v2`, `build`, `out`,
`storybook-static`, `artifacts` and `reports`; `__fixtures__`,
`test-fixtures`, `test-results`, `playwright-report` and `coverage` at any
depth; and `.log`/`.jsonl` files. Files named by app imports, HTML/CSS references
or URL paths are retained, including their transitive imports and assets under
`public`. Dynamic paths that cannot be discovered need an explicit include.
Other app folders, including `src`, `public`, `api`, assets and invented
folder names, keep their normal behavior. Existing test-file, dotfile and
sensitive-file rules still apply; an include cannot publish a secret.

To publish one on purpose:

```bash
somewhere deploy --include NOTES.md          # once; comma-separate or repeat for several
```

or make it permanent with a `!` line in `.somewhereignore`:

```
!NOTES.md
```

`.somewhereignore` is read alongside `.gitignore`: plain patterns exclude
files from the deploy, and a leading `!` publishes one the filter would
otherwise hold back.

## deploy-check — the server-side compile oracle

`deploy-check` uploads source to the exact compiler used by deploy, but writes
nothing and makes nothing live. It catches server-only bundling and import
resolution failures that a local typecheck cannot see. For the full local
compiler diagnostic when a summary only shows the first line, run
`npx tsc --noEmit --pretty false` from the app root. For a reusable column
projection, define the array with `as const` so its elements keep their
literal column-name types.

```bash
somewhere deploy-check
somewhere deploy-check --run /api/hello -X POST -d '{"name":"Ada"}'
somewhere deploy-check --json
```

Use `--run` to invoke one handler from your function source with the
method, body and query string you supply, without deploying. Static and client
files are skipped. It works on every plan, requires editor access and never
uses your live database.

| Project | Handler access |
| --- | --- |
| Has a live release, or the plan does not include `somewhere preview` | No database or network. A `sw.db` call returns `409 DRAFT_DB_NOT_ISOLATED`; rate limits are not evaluated. |
| No live release and the plan includes preview | Uses the development database when available; writes persist, network calls are allowed and rate limits are evaluated. If only a live database exists, the check is refused with `409 DRAFT_DB_NOT_ISOLATED`. |

For the no-database case, a schema containing visitor tables stops the check before execution with `503 DRAFT_DB_NOT_ISOLATED`. Use a preview or the live route for those handlers.

Both cases use the values saved for development in project settings. Run database-dependent
checks on a preview or the live route when `--run` has no database.

On plans
without `somewhere preview`, each project gets 60 handler checks per hour
(`429 RATE_LIMITED` after that).

## browser — verify the live app, not just the deploy response

```bash
somewhere browser https://my-app.somewhere.site
somewhere browser --project my-app --path /login --wait '#email' --snapshot
somewhere browser https://example.com --include network,dom --json
```

It exits non-zero when a step fails, a request fails, or page JavaScript throws.
Use EYES mode (a public URL, no project) for any page; use `--project` for an
owned app and optional stored screenshots.

**Local and hosted are two halves of one command.** A `localhost` or
`127.0.0.1` target — the app `somewhere dev` is serving — is driven by the
browser already installed on your machine, because a browser running on the
platform can never reach an address only your machine serves (from 0.30.0). Each
local run gets an empty throwaway profile, so it never reads or writes your real
one, and if there is no browser at all the command says so and names the
environment variable that points at one. The flags only the hosted half can
honour — `--store`, `--session`, `--extract`, and any `--include`
section other than `dom` — are refused by name rather than silently dropped
from a report that would still look complete. Everything else, including
`--screenshot`, `--wait`, `--eval`, `--snapshot` and
`--viewport`, behaves the same on both halves; `--snapshot` requests the
interactive-element outline it prints. So the same command checks the app before
it is deployed and after.

## api — authenticated REST escape hatch

```bash
somewhere api GET /v1/projects
somewhere api POST /v1/db/query -d '{"project_id":"my-app","sql":"SELECT 1"}'
somewhere api POST /v1/db/dump -d '{"project_id":"my-app"}' --raw
```

The CLI attaches auth automatically. `-d` sends a JSON body. JSON parsing is
the default; use `--raw` only for a successful non-JSON response, such as the
SQL text `/v1/db/dump` returns. `/v1/db/dump` takes `POST` with the
project in the body; without `project_id` it answers 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`.

## update

```bash
somewhere update --check
somewhere update
```

The first command only compares the installed version with npm; the second
installs the current `@somewhere-cloud/cli` globally.

## Anonymous `deploy --json` contract

A temporary (signed-out) deploy keeps the server deploy result, the same
fields an authenticated deploy prints (for example `version`, `release_id`,
`warnings` and `stage_timing_ms`). It sets `url` to the live URL the CLI
displays and adds three claim fields: `claim_url`, `expires_at` and
`claim_connects_agent`. `next_step` appears only in human-readable output.

<!-- CLI_DEPLOY_JSON_SCHEMA_BEGIN -->
```json
{
  "url": "https://<subdomain>.somewhere.site",
  "version": 1,
  "release_id": "rel_…",
  "warnings": [],
  "stage_timing_ms": { "deploy_total": 4200 },
  "claim_url": "https://somewhere.cloud/claim/swtc_…",
  "expires_at": "<ISO-8601 timestamp>",
  "claim_connects_agent": true
}
```
<!-- CLI_DEPLOY_JSON_SCHEMA_END -->

The sample shows a few of the server's fields; every other field the deploy
API returns is kept as it is. `expires_at` is `null` when the session has no expiry
on record. `claim_connects_agent` is `true` only when the claim page can
connect this CLI without another sign-in.

For an authenticated deploy, `--json` prints the server deploy result without
adding the temporary-session claim metadata. Both modes include the `--verify`
outcome fields when verification runs: `deployment_outcome: "live"` and
`verification` (or `verification_error`), plus `next_steps` when verification
fails.

To talk to the platform from app code (browser / Node), use the client SDK
instead → docs({ topic: 'sdk' }). To serve the app on localhost while you build
it, and to typecheck before you ship — see docs({ topic: 'local-dev' }).

pages.title: @somewhere-cloud/sdk — optional adapter, one auth path
pages.body:
There is one auth map:

- **Browser app:** httpOnly cookie sessions. The browser holds no access token,
  refresh token, or developer key. Declared data and file collections use the
  generated `somewhere:data` and `somewhere:files` clients; sign-in and custom
  logic go through same-origin `api/*` functions that call `sw.auth`,
  `sw.db`, and `sw.fs`.
- **Non-browser client:** bearer token mode, because a script/CLI/native client
  has no browser cookie boundary.

This is the one JS/TS package. Its root client plus tree-shakeable
`@somewhere-cloud/sdk/auth`, `@somewhere-cloud/sdk/react`, and
`@somewhere-cloud/sdk/server` entry points adapt that contract without
defining a second transport.

```bash
npm i @somewhere-cloud/sdk
```

## createClient

```ts
import { createClient } from '@somewhere-cloud/sdk'

// Browser: same origin, no credential. auth.* and functions.invoke() ride httpOnly cookies.
// window is read only when browser code calls this.
export function createBrowserClient() {
  return createClient(window.location.origin, undefined, { fetch: window.fetch.bind(window) })
}

// Script, CLI or trusted server: use the app URL, project ID and your credential.
export function createScriptClient(projectUrl: string, projectId: string, credential: string) {
  return createClient(projectUrl, credential, { projectId })
}
```

- The first argument is your project URL, https://<project>.somewhere.site; in
  the browser that is the page's own origin. The SDK uses it for
  `functions.invoke`. For project resources such as files, pass the project ID
  explicitly as `{ projectId }` for `*.somewhere.site` and custom domains.
- The second argument is optional in a browser. In non-browser/header mode it
  is an app-user bearer token or a developer `smt_` key restricted to a
  deployed function or trusted server process. Do not invent a placeholder
  credential.
- `new Somewhere({ key, projectId })` remains the explicit compatibility
  constructor for existing bearer-based integrations.

## Database — declared client and server functions

For ordinary browser reads and writes, declare client grants in `db/schema.ts`
and import the generated `data` client from `somewhere:data`. See
`docs({ topic: 'declared-data' })` for its named, typed operations.
The SDK's generic database interface is not this generated client: direct
app-user SQL/database API access is refused (`BROWSER_DB_ACCESS_REMOVED`).
For custom logic, call an `api/` function that uses `sw.db`.

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { id, owner, schema, table, text, timestamp } from 'somewhere/db';

export default schema({
  notes: table(
    { id: id(), title: text(), created_at: timestamp({ default: 'now' }) },
    { scope: owner() },
  ),
});
```

```ts
// api/notes.ts — the signed-in caller's notes; owner() scopes the read to them.
export default async function notes(req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  const user = await sw.auth.fromRequest(req);
  if (!user) return Response.json({ error: 'Sign in first.' }, { status: 401 });
  const { data } = await sw.db.from('notes', { order: [['created_at', 'desc']], limit: 50 });
  return Response.json({ notes: data });
}
```

The browser calls that function on its own origin; the session cookie identifies the caller:

```ts
// src/notes.ts
import { createClient } from '@somewhere-cloud/sdk';

type Note = { id: string; title: string; created_at: string };

export async function listMyNotes(): Promise<Note[]> {
  const client = createClient(window.location.origin, undefined, { fetch: window.fetch.bind(window) });
  const { data, error } = await client.functions.invoke<{ notes: Note[] }>('notes', { method: 'GET' });
  if (error) throw error;
  if (!data) throw new Error('notes returned no body');
  return data.notes;
}
```

On managed projects, ordinary `sw.db.query` / `sw.db.batch` calls are
refused with `MANAGED_RAW_SQL_REQUIRES_SERVER_AUTHORITY`. Use the structured
calls for declared access. When a read truly requires raw SQL, authorize the
caller first and use `sw.db.server.query` or `sw.db.server.batch`; those
calls run exactly as written and do not apply declared row permissions. Raw
writes remain refused in managed mode. SQL-mode projects retain ordinary raw
SQL behavior.

### Structured queries — the platform composes and scopes

For platform-proven per-user scoping, use the structured builder. You describe
the query; the platform renders the SQL (identifiers validated, every value
bound) and scopes it automatically to the request's signed-in user. It never
parses a string it did not write. The operations (`from`, `count`, `insert`,
`update`, `remove`) are documented in
`sw.db` → `per-user-scoping-the-structured-builder-not-raw-sql` and
`builder-verbs-and-where-shapes`. In brief:

`where`: `{ col: value }` (=), `{ col: { gt|gte|lt|lte|ne|like: v } }`,
`{ col: { in: [...] } }` (empty array matches nothing), `{ col: null }`
(IS NULL), `{ col: { not: null } }` (IS NOT NULL), a per-column array of
conditions ANDed (`{ created_at: [{ gte: a }, { lte: b }] }`). A shallow
`$or` group accepts 2-8 single-column leaf branches, for example
`{ $or: [{ status: 'draft' }, { status: 'published' }] }`; the whole group
remains inside the platform's owner/member scope. Nested OR, relation-filter OR,
and named-live OR are refused. Every structured table needs an
explicit declared intent (scoped / shared / server-only). Scoping is automatic
and mandatory: on a declared user-owned table every structured query is scoped
to the request's verified user. Each request checks the credential; a valid
check may be reused for up to 60 seconds, so a revoked app session or a ban is
refused within 60 seconds. Without a
signed-in user, the operation throws `AUTH_REQUIRED` before reading data.
A `shared()` table also needs a signed-in user (`AUTH_REQUIRED`, 401):
reads return every row and writes are attributed to that user.
`serverOnly()` tables and `sw.db.server.*` calls run unscoped, under the
authority of your function. The platform owns the ownership column and refuses to let
insert/update set or reassign it (`OWNER_COLUMN_NOT_ASSIGNABLE`). A table
with NO declared intent cannot be structured-queried at all — it fails the
deploy and throws `TABLE_INTENT_REQUIRED` (403) at runtime; declare it or,
for an intentional raw read, authorize the caller and use
`sw.db.server.query`. Cross-user raw reads and reads from undeclared tables
use that explicit server-authority path. A third scope argument
throws `SCOPE_ARGUMENT_REMOVED`. Responses match
`sw.db.query` (`{ data, error, count, last_row_id, changes }`; `count()`
returns exactly `{ data, error }`); mutations `RETURNING *`. The
`last_row_id` result field is always
null; read an inserted ID from its returned row in `data`.

The release records the DECLARED shape, never a reconstruction from
reading code: each deploy pins the project's table intents (scoped/shared,
owner column) and a schema snapshot captured from the live database
(`SCHEMA_CAPTURE_FAILED` if the snapshot cannot be taken). Explicit
`sw.db.server.query`/`batch` reads run as written and are never analyzed —
the deliberate server-authority escape hatch. `POST /v1/db/migrate` is the same
trust class: a production target takes a named restore point BEFORE any
statement runs (a recorded marker: restoring a database in place is not
available, so it is not an undo), then runs your SQL atomically, exactly as written. A preview
target runs against the disposable clone and takes no production restore
point. It does NOT analyze the SQL and cannot warn about or refuse what a
statement drops or breaks. If a production restore point cannot be taken,
nothing applies (`RESTORE_POINT_FAILED`, retryable). A managed
`db/schema.ts` instead runs through the schema planner on production deploy;
its table access intents are declared
by the file. `GET
/v1/db/access-map` (developer key) returns the release's data-access map
at per-table granularity: declared intents with ownership scope, the schema
snapshot, and a plain note that explicit server-authority SQL is not analyzed.

## Auth — sw.auth

Browser sign-in starts here: the backend route is one line and the page uses
`createSomewhereAuth` (`somewhere init` writes both).

```ts
// api/auth/[...path].ts
export { somewhereAuth as default } from '@somewhere-cloud/sdk/server'
```

```ts
// src/auth.ts — page code
import { createSomewhereAuth } from '@somewhere-cloud/sdk/auth'

export const auth = createSomewhereAuth()

// Call from your sign-up form; throws AuthError with the message on failure.
export async function signUp(email: string, password: string) {
  return auth.signUp({ email, password })   // or auth.signIn({ email, password })
}
export async function signOut() {
  await auth.signOut();
  if (auth.getState().signOutUnconfirmed) {
    throw new Error('Sign-out could not be confirmed. Please try again.');
  }
  // Only navigate or reload after confirmed logout.
}
```

The root client carries the same methods with `{ data, error }` results:

```js
await client.auth.signUp({ email, password })
await client.auth.signIn({ email, password })               // preferred name
await client.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password })
await client.auth.sendMagicLink({ email })
await client.auth.verifyMagicLink({ token })
const { data: oauth, error: oauthError } = await client.auth.signInWithOAuth({ provider: 'google' })
if (oauthError) throw oauthError
if (!oauth) throw new Error('Sign-in URL unavailable')
window.location.href = oauth.url
const { data: me, error: userError } = await client.auth.getUser()
if (userError) throw userError
const user = me?.user ?? null
client.auth.onAuthStateChange((event, session) => { /* SIGNED_IN / SIGNED_OUT / ... */ })
await client.auth.signOut()
```

In a browser these auth methods run in **cookie mode** by default
(0.14.1): the SDK posts to your app's own auth routes
(`/api/auth/*` — the one-line packaged route above, see
`docs({ topic: 'auth-client' })`) and the session is set as httpOnly cookies.
No tokens land in JS or localStorage; `error.message` carries the real cause
("Wrong email or password."). `getSession()` returns
`{ cookie_session: true, user }`.

Scope boundary: `functions.invoke()` also rides that cookie. Direct
`from()`, storage, and channel calls go to the platform API. Bearer-based
browser calls still work and warn before any future enforcement; cookie sign-in deliberately does not credential those surfaces.
Node/CLI keep header mode (tokens in SDK memory); pass
`{ authMode: 'header' }` only when the client is meant to hold tokens.

Name/result alignment for new code:

| Intent | Preferred method | Compatibility alias | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Password sign-in | `signIn` | `signInWithPassword` | `{ data: { user, session }, error }` |
| Send passwordless link | `sendMagicLink` | — | `{ data, error }` |
| Complete passwordless link | `verifyMagicLink` | — | `{ data: { user, session }, error }` |
| Complete password reset | `verifyPasswordReset` | `verifyOtp` (same call) | `{ data, error }` |

No compatibility alias is removed here. A future removal or result-shape break
requires a major version.

## Storage — client.storage.from(bucket)

For browser uploads and downloads, declare a file collection in
`db/schema.ts` and use the generated `somewhere:files` client
(`docs({ topic: 'declared-files' })`). `client.storage` is a compatibility
API over `/v1/fs`, which accepts only a developer key or a project runtime
key: an app-user session token is refused, and a developer key is refused
from a browser. Use it from server code only.

```js
await client.storage.from('avatars').upload('me.png', file)
client.storage.from('avatars').getPublicUrl('me.png')         // { data: { publicUrl } }
await client.storage.from('avatars').download('me.png')
await client.storage.from('avatars').remove(['me.png'])
```

To mint a signed download URL while the file exists, send
`POST /v1/fs/<project_id>/sign` with your developer key and the JSON body
`{ "path": "/avatars/me.png", "expires_in": 3600 }`.

## Live updates — not client.channel

The adapter has no realtime channel. Supabase-style `channel()`, broadcast and
presence are not available, and the channel transport refuses app-user and
visitor sessions. The live path a browser can use is a declared live view:
the function returns rows plus a subscription URL, and `watchLive` re-reads
through your function on every invalidation.

```js
import { watchLive } from '/__sw/rooms/client.js'

watchLive(
  () => fetch('/api/open-notes', { credentials: 'include' }).then(r => r.json()),
  (rows) => render(rows),
)
```

Declare the list server-side with `sw.rooms.live(name, sw.db.from(...))` →
docs({ topic: 'rooms' }), "Live lists".

## Functions — client.functions.invoke

```js
const { data, error } = await client.functions.invoke('checkout', { body: { plan: 'pro' } })
```

Other languages → docs({ topic: 'sdks' }). Porting an existing app → the
migration guide via docs({ topic: 'migration-supabase' }).

pages.title: Client SDK — JavaScript and TypeScript
pages.body:
Use the JavaScript/TypeScript SDK for browser sign-in, typed function calls
and developer automation. The default starter already includes its auth
client and server route. Extend those working files when building an app.

| Package | Install | Version |
|---|---|---|
| @somewhere-cloud/sdk | npm i @somewhere-cloud/sdk | 0.14.1 |

Choose the entry for the code you're writing:

- **Browser sign-in:** `@somewhere-cloud/sdk/auth` manages same-origin cookie
  sessions. → `auth-client`
- **App data and files:** declare access in `db/schema.ts`, then use
  `somewhere:data` and `somewhere:files` in pages. Functions receive `sw`.
  → `declared-data`, `declared-files`, `functions`
- **Calls to your functions:** use the generated typed function client.
  → `typed-functions`
- **Developer scripts:** use the SDK with a developer key kept on the server,
  or use `somewhere call <tool> '<json>'` from the CLI. → `sdk`, `cli`

See `sdk` for exports and result shapes, and `api-surface` for the HTTP
contract. Keep developer keys out of browser code.

pages.title: Local dev — `somewhere dev`
pages.body:
# somewhere dev — the frontend loop

`somewhere dev` serves your browser application on localhost with hot
reload while you shape the UI. If the frontend doesn't already have Vite,
install it with `npm install -D vite`. The backend you rely on is the deployed one:
`api/` functions, `sw.*` calls, the database and files are reached
through your project's live URL. Deploying is how you see the real app —
the platform compiles raw source on deploy — so for anything behind an API
call the loop is `somewhere deploy` then `somewhere verify`.

Data the local app saves goes to the project's own database and files, the
same ones your users' app reads, so local writes change production data.

  somewhere dev              # serve the frontend on http://localhost:8787
  somewhere deploy           # publish; the platform compiles
  somewhere verify           # prove the live app in a real browser

If port 8787 is in use, run `somewhere dev --port 8788` and open the URL it prints.

Do not run a build step before `somewhere dev` or `somewhere deploy`;
the platform compiles raw source. Local dev never needs a developer key or
a browser database client.

To try changes without touching production data, `somewhere preview` runs
the whole app hosted on a private URL against an isolated, populated copy of
your production database; nothing your users see changes until you promote
that preview. Which plans include it, and how to start one:
docs({ topic: 'dev-environments' }).

pages.title: Auth on the client — the correct session code
Typed functions — one contract, both sides
pages.body:
Opt in per function. Declare the contract next to the handler; the browser gets
a typed client generated from what you actually deployed, not from a router you
maintain separately.

## Server — `api/tasks/create.ts`

The table it writes, declared in `db/schema.ts`; `somewhere typecheck` types
its rows from this file:

```ts
// db/schema.ts
import { schema, table, id, text, owner } from 'somewhere/db'

export default schema({
  tasks: table({ id: id({ uuid: true }), text: text() }, { scope: owner() }),
})
```

```ts
// api/tasks/create.ts
export const typed = 'somewhere:v1' as const
export type Contract = {
  input: { text: string }
  output:
    | { ok: true; task: { id: string; text: string } }
    | { ok: false; error: 'TEXT_REQUIRED' | 'TEXT_TOO_LONG' }
}
const MAX_TEXT = 500

export default (async (req, sw) => {
  await sw.auth.requireUser(req)                    // signed out: 401 before any write
  const input: unknown = await req.json().catch(() => null)   // the contract is a type, not a check
  const raw = typeof input === 'object' && input !== null && 'text' in input ? input.text : undefined
  const text = typeof raw === 'string' ? raw.trim() : ''
  if (!text) return { ok: false, error: 'TEXT_REQUIRED' }
  if (text.length > MAX_TEXT) return { ok: false, error: 'TEXT_TOO_LONG' }
  const { data: [task] } = await sw.db.insert('tasks', { text })   // owner column set by the platform
  return { ok: true, task: { id: task.id, text: task.text } }
}) satisfies ServerFunction<Contract>
```

Three parts, all required: the `typed` sentinel, an exported `Contract` type
with `input` and `output`, and `satisfies ServerFunction<Contract>` on the
default export. A function without the sentinel is a normal function and keeps
working exactly as before — this is additive, never required.
`ServerFunction` is a global type from the platform's generated declarations,
like `SomewhereRuntimeContext`, so there is nothing to import.

The contract types the call; it does not check what arrives. Read the body as
`unknown` and validate it. A typed function returns its `output` type, so
report an expected refusal as a value in that type, as `{ ok: false, error }`
does here. Errors from platform calls, such as the 401 from
`sw.auth.requireUser`, reach the browser as a `FunctionError` with that
status.

## Browser — `src/main.tsx`

```ts
import { api } from 'somewhere:api'

try {
  const result = await api.tasks.create({ text: 'ship' })
  if (result.ok) console.log('created', result.task.id)
  else console.log('not created:', result.error)   // TEXT_REQUIRED or TEXT_TOO_LONG
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof Error && 'status' in err && err.status === 401) console.log('sign in first')
  else throw err
}
```

`somewhere:api` is a virtual module the platform generates at deploy. The file
path determines the client path and the route: `api/tasks/create.ts` becomes
`api.tasks.create(...)` calling `POST /api/tasks/create`.

## What the platform does with it

Each deploy writes a manifest — one entry per procedure with its file, client
path, route, input type and output type — plus a `contract_digest` over the
whole surface. Because the digest is versioned with the release, the platform
compares the contract you are shipping against the one currently live and warns
when a change would break existing callers. That check is only possible because
the platform holds both the previous and the incoming contract.

## Portability — what you take with you

The contract is plain data at `_internal/typed-functions.json` inside the
release, and your handlers are ordinary async functions with no framework
imports. Porting means keeping the handler bodies and replacing the generated
client with any HTTP client — the routes are the same paths you already see.
There is no adapter to reimplement and no runtime to replace.

Related: `functions`, `deploy`, `portability`, `sw.db`.

pages.title: GitHub push-to-deploy
pages.body:
Connect a repository to a project and every push to the tracked branch
deploys automatically — the same raw-source pipeline as `somewhere deploy`.
Live for every project; no tier gate.

## Preferred path: GitHub App

The dashboard's Import from GitHub flow and `somewhere git connect` use the
GitHub App. A human grants an account/repository on GitHub once; the platform
stores the installation identity, mints short-lived tokens when needed, and
receives signed App-level push events. No PAT paste and no manual repository
webhook are required.

CLI:

  somewhere git connect owner/name [--project my-app] [--branch main] [--root web]
  somewhere git status [--project my-app]
  somewhere git disconnect [--project my-app]

`git connect` opens GitHub only when consent is missing, resumes
automatically, deploys the selected branch's current HEAD immediately, waits
for that exact commit, and prints commit, status, logs, and live URL. All
three commands support `--json`, and `git disconnect` stops future pushes
from deploying while leaving the currently deployed site live.
Pass `--yes` to confirm the disconnect in a non-interactive shell.

MCP / REST App flow:

  github_app_install({ return_to? })
  → { install_url }                 // give this link to the human

  github_installations({})
  → { app_configured, installations: [{ installation_id, account_login }] }

  github_list_repos({ installation_id: 123 })
  → [{ name, private, default_branch, ... }]

  github_connect({
    project_id: "my-app",
    repo: "owner/name",
    installation_id: 123,
    branch: "main",
    deploy_head: true
  })
  → { repo, branch, via_app: true,
      initial_deploy: { status: "deploying", commit_sha, commit_message } }

Poll `github_status` for that exact commit until `last_status` is
`deployed` or `failed`. Dashboard import and the CLI perform this wait;
until that terminal status, a `connected` import is still pending.

## REST connect shape

  POST /v1/github/connect
  {
    "project_id": "my-app",
    "repo": "owner/name",
    "branch": "main",          // optional, default "main"
    "root_dir": "web",         // optional — deploy one subfolder (monorepos)
    "installation_id": 123,    // preferred — caller-owned App installation
    "deploy_head": true         // resolve + deploy branch HEAD immediately
  }
  → { repo, branch, root_dir, hook_installed, via_app, initial_deploy }

For compatibility, `github_token` still installs a per-repository webhook
and supports private repositories without an App installation. With neither
App installation nor token, public repositories can use the returned
`manual_setup` URL + secret. Both webhook forms verify the raw GitHub HMAC
before dispatching a deploy.

## Status + disconnect

  GET /v1/github/connection?project_id=…
  → { connected, repo, branch, root_dir, hook_installed, via_app,
      last_commit_sha, last_commit_message,
      last_status: "deploying" | "deployed" | "failed", last_error }

  DELETE /v1/github/connection?project_id=…   // current site stays live

## What deploys

A push to the tracked branch deploys the repo (or `root_dir` subfolder) as
raw source. Pushes to other branches are ignored. GitHub-driven versions record
deploy source `github` plus the GitHub commit SHA and first-line message.

- Vite/React SPAs deploy unchanged.
- Monorepos: set `root_dir` to the app folder.
- Env var changes reach new requests within 60 seconds, without a push.
  When saving a value answers `requires_deploy: true`, the project needs one
  production deploy from source first; a push is one.
- Next.js SSR is not supported; use a Vite SPA plus functions.
- GitHub's archive of the whole repository cannot exceed 100 MB. The limit
  applies before `root_dir` picks a folder, so for a larger repository deploy the
  folder with `somewhere deploy`. Files over 5 MB are skipped.

pages.title: Preview — `somewhere preview` (every plan)
pages.body:
Every project has ONE production environment. On every plan, signed-in users
can additionally create **previews**: immutable builds with their own database
clone and environment variables, reachable behind a login gate and promoted
to production only when you say so. Preview saves never change production —
only a production deploy, a promote, or a rollback does.

Where a change lands depends on the command:

- `somewhere deploy` publishes to production when the deploy finishes. This
  is the normal path.
- `somewhere dev` serves the frontend on your machine with hot reload against
  the deployed project. Its `sw.db` and `sw.fs` calls use the project's own
  database and files, so local writes are production writes.
- You can also run the CLI in an agent's hosted terminal. Sign in there with
  `somewhere auth login`. The same `dev`, `deploy`, and `preview` rules apply.
- `somewhere preview` saves each change as a new preview at a private URL,
  running against its own copy of the production database. Review what a
  preview can show (see the next section), then promote that exact preview
  with `POST /v1/promote`; if production moved since the preview was created,
  the promote conflicts instead of replacing it.
- A project that has never been published can open a preview too; no deploy
  is needed first. Promoting it publishes the project's first version.

## Signing in to a preview

A preview has its own sign-in. Your app's `sw.auth` sign-up, sign-in, session
check (`/api/auth/me` in the starter), refresh, sign-out, email verification and
password reset work in a preview, against the preview's own user list:

- **A preview starts with no users.** Sign up in the app, or add a test user
  with `somewhere preview user-add [email]` (it prints the password once).
  `somewhere preview users` lists the preview's users; `somewhere preview
  user-remove <id-or-email>` deletes a test user. Production accounts,
  passwords and sessions are never copied into a preview.
- **Copied rows that belong to a production user stay private.** The preview's
  data is a copy of production, but a new preview user is not that production
  user, so rows private to an existing user are not visible to them. Public rows
  and the preview users' own new rows are.
- **Sessions belong to one preview.** A preview session means nothing to the
  live app or to another preview of the same project, and a live-app session or
  token means nothing to a preview. Previews of one project share the
  `<subdomain>-dev` address, so opening another preview signs you out of the
  first one's app. Sign-up and sign-in in a preview return `token` and
  `refresh_token` but no `session_token`; `sw.auth.logout` there takes the
  `refresh_token` or the access token (a `session_token` alone answers
  `VALIDATION_ERROR`).
- **You stay signed in as on the live app.** A preview access token lasts 60
  seconds, as on the live app, and the session check (`/api/auth/me` in the
  starter) renews it from the preview's own refresh cookie and sets new
  cookies, so a reload keeps you signed in. Requesting, resending and entering
  an email verification code renew the same way, so a code entered minutes
  later still works. Renewal happens only for the session the access token
  belongs to; `X-No-Auto-Refresh: 1` opts out.
- **Sign-in mail is captured, never sent**, whatever the address: verification
  codes and reset links (the link opens the preview) are stored in the
  project's test inbox, labelled with the preview. Read them with
  `somewhere preview mail`. A preview link lets someone view and use the
  preview; it never lets them read its mail. A preview keeps up to 100
  captured messages, and all of a project's previews together up to 200
  (4 MiB), for seven days; closing a preview deletes its mail. A reset request
  for an address no preview account uses captures a short note saying so, so a
  reset answers the same whether or not the account exists. At a limit, the
  verification or reset request that would capture a message answers
  `TEST_INBOX_FULL` (HTTP 507) and changes nothing, so a code or link already
  captured keeps working.
- **Public reads work.** Rows and pages that are public in production
  (`client.publicRead`) are public to whoever holds the preview link.
- Ten wrong sign-ins for one address lock that address for 15 minutes
  (`RATE_LIMITED`, HTTP 429), whether or not a preview account uses it.
- **Server user lookups and roles work.** In a preview's server code,
  `sw.auth.server.listUsers` (by `ids`, by `emails`, or page by page) lists
  that preview's own users, with the same fields, order and cursor as on the
  live app, and `sw.auth.server.setRoles` grants and removes roles declared
  `assignedBy: 'server'` for that preview's users, in the preview's copy of
  the data, under the role rules of the code you saved. A grant made in a
  preview never counts on the live app or in another preview. Preview user ids
  start with `pvu_`; the platform assigns them (sign-up ignores an `id` it is
  sent, as on the live app, and `somewhere preview user-add` cannot choose
  one), so no preview user is ever a
  production user, and a role or team row copied from production names nobody
  in the preview. A preview whose users were created before preview ids began
  with `pvu_` keeps signing them in, but `listUsers` and `setRoles` there
  answer `PREVIEW_RECREATE_REQUIRED` (HTTP 409): "Create a new preview to use
  roles and teams; this preview's users use the older identity format."
- **Built-in teams work.** Every `sw.groups` call (create, list, get,
  invite, invitations, remove, leave, delete, roles) acts on the preview's own
  users and its copy of the data, under the role rules of the code you saved;
  the live app's teams, members, invitations and users are never read or
  changed, and a team made in a preview means nothing in another preview.
  Teams and members copied from production name production users, so they
  match nobody in the preview. An invitation is captured, never sent
  (`delivery: "captured"`): read it with `somewhere preview mail`; its link
  opens your `redirect_uri` on the preview with an `invite_id` and does not
  sign anyone in. The invitee signs up or signs in to the preview with the
  invited address and verifies it, and is admitted at once: at verification,
  at sign-in, or the next time they list their teams (on the live app
  admission can take a moment longer). An account in the preview that already
  verified the address is admitted when the invitation is made. Invitation
  limits count on the preview's own counters, never the live app's. A preview
  saved before teams worked in previews answers `PREVIEW_RESAVE_REQUIRED`
  (HTTP 409) for invitations until its next save (`somewhere preview` again);
  a preview whose users use the older identity format answers
  `PREVIEW_RECREATE_REQUIRED` for every `sw.groups` call.
- Every other account operation refuses in a preview with HTTP 409
  (`PREVIEW_AUTH_UNSUPPORTED`, or `PREVIEW_SUBJECT_UNSUPPORTED` for other
  signed-in features): "<operation> is not available in a preview. Use
  preview sign-up or preview user tools; nothing ran." That covers sign-in
  methods other than email and password (social sign-in, magic links, sign-in
  codes and second factors), profile and password changes, invites, provider
  tokens, exports and account administration.
- A preview saved before sign-in reached previews keeps refusing it until its
  next save (`somewhere preview` again).
- A project still on the older preview runtime has no sign-in in its previews
  yet. Every sign-in call there, and every request that presents a sign-in
  token, answers `PREVIEW_AUTH_UNAVAILABLE` (HTTP 409, "Sign-in is not
  available in previews of this project yet"); a preview never reads the live
  app's users. Signed-out requests work as before, and the live app is
  unaffected. A preview of such a project saved before 2026-11-15 does not run
  until it is saved again: it answers `PREVIEW_RESAVE_REQUIRED` (HTTP 409), and
  `somewhere preview` in its folder saves it, keeping its data and files.

### The preview credential

`somewhere preview` gets a credential for each preview it opens, kept
owner-only in `~/.somewhere/previews/`, outside your project folder. The
preview commands above use it and nothing else, never your own sign-in. It
works only on that preview's users, test users and captured mail; every other
command and endpoint refuses it (`PREVIEW_CREDENTIAL_NOT_ACCEPTED`), so it
cannot promote, close or deploy anything or change production settings. It
stops working on the next request after the preview is closed, promoted or
expires, after its links are revoked (`POST /v1/projects/:id/preview/revoke`),
or once the person who opened the preview can no longer edit the project.

## What a preview cannot do yet

A preview runs your new code against a copy of production data, but these
parts of an app do not work in a preview today. Check them in production
after you promote (`somewhere rollback --yes` undoes a promote).

- **Scheduled tasks.** Nothing runs on a schedule in a preview, and
  `sw.cron` refuses there with `PREVIEW_CRON_UNAVAILABLE`: a schedule is a
  production setting; run a scheduled handler once with
  `somewhere cron run <name> --preview` or `somewhere preview run-job`.
  Background jobs do work in a preview, with smaller limits (see `sw.jobs` →
  "In a preview").
- **AI calls and rooms.** `sw.ai` and rooms refuse in a preview.
- **Signed-in calls other than data, files and teams.** A preview user can
  read and write the app's data and files and use its teams. Signed-in inbox,
  push, notifications and payment calls answer `PREVIEW_SUBJECT_UNSUPPORTED`
  in a preview.
- **Tests.** `somewhere test --preview` (and `openTestApp({ preview: true })`)
  test the preview; `somewhere test-users` and `somewhere browser --auth-user`
  run against production only.
- **The raw SQL database.** Only the managed tables are copied; a raw SQL
  query against a preview answers `RAW_PREVIEW_DATABASE_NOT_READY`.
- **Reading logs from preview code.** `sw.logs.tail` in a preview answers
  `DRAFT_PLATFORM_CAPABILITY_DENIED`: a project's logs are not separated by
  preview. Read them with `somewhere logs`. A
  preview's own `console` output and `sw.logs` writes are still recorded.
- **Most platform tools and endpoints.** Only the preview commands, the
  database query/batch/migrate target, exact preview source reads, the
  preview cron run and the test-inbox filter take a preview. Every other tool
  or endpoint (`db_browse`, `somewhere db rows`, `run_code`, env, files, logs,
  users, imports, cron and job runs, …) acts on production only: a request
  that names a preview, draft, development slot, environment or release in
  any spelling or position (a field, a query parameter, a header) is refused
  with `PREVIEW_TARGET_NOT_SUPPORTED` before anything runs or is written.
  Nothing falls back to production. Your own data is never read as a request
  to target a preview: file contents, upload bytes, row values, function
  arguments and webhook payloads can contain fields named `env`, `release`,
  `preview` or `draft`. A production-only change sent from a preview's own
  address, or with the platform's preview headers (`X-Sw-Env-Slot` other than
  `prod`, `X-Sw-Draft-Id`, `X-Sw-Draft-Candidate`), is refused the same way. To see a preview's rows, call one of your
  app's own endpoints with `POST https://runner.somewhere.cloud/v1/deploy/preview/invoke` (below).

What does work: sign-in for the preview's own users and everything they do
with the app's data and files, public reads, your schema change applied to the
copied rows, `sw.db` and `sw.fs` on the copies, email to the project test inbox,
Stripe test-mode checkout, and writing logs (read them with `somewhere logs`).

A preview answers each request somewhat more slowly than production: in our
measurements a data read took about 365 ms against 110 ms, and creating a team
about 630 ms against 310 ms. On every call the platform re-checks that the
preview is still open and current and looks up the signed-in user in the
preview's own users, so a preview never acts for a closed preview or a
production account.

Next: `dev-environments` → `create-a-preview` to start one, `promote` and
`roll-back` to ship or undo, and `local-dev` for the local loop.

## When to use this — not by default

**Default to shipping to production.** `somewhere deploy` deploys straight to
production and is the right path for almost all work: iterating on a new
project, building something that has no users yet, fixing your own site.
Every deploy reaches production the moment it finishes — that immediacy is the point.

Reach for a preview only when you have a **concrete reason to
protect production**: real users on the site, a risky change you want to
preview against production-shaped data before promotion, or a migration you
want to rehearse. If you don't have users yet, don't add the preview → promote
loop — just deploy.

## Who has this

Available to signed-in accounts on **every plan**. Free allows three open
previews across projects. Anonymous accounts cannot create previews. The
builder spending allowance is separate. Production deploys are unaffected. On every plan, `somewhere dev` serves the frontend on
your machine against the deployed backend, and `somewhere deploy-check --run`
runs one handler before you deploy.

## The mental model

- **Production** — what visitors see. Served at your project URL. Changed
  only by a production deploy, a promote, or a rollback.
- **Preview** — an immutable build created from a complete snapshot of your
  source. Each save mints a NEW preview in the same preview session. Previews
  run against an isolated, populated copy of your production database, taken
  when the preview session is created (on a never-published project, an empty
  database and no files), and see the dev-scoped environment
  variables, so nothing a preview does can touch production data or read
  production-only secrets. A preview function cannot make outbound requests
  (`DRAFT_EGRESS_DENIED`).
  A preview function resolves the signed-in user of the preview's own copy
  read-only: no refresh, no session minting, and the public sign-in API is not
  available from a preview. If that identity lookup cannot be completed, or
  returns something that is not a valid identity, the request fails with
  `AUTH_VERIFY_UNAVAILABLE` (503) — it never falls back to a visitor.

## Email and payments in a preview

A preview keeps its own database and file copy, but it is not a separate app:
the services below behave as described, and everything else shared stays
unavailable in a preview: a preview function's call fails with
`DRAFT_SIDE_EFFECT_BLOCKED`, and a platform API request made from a draft
returns `DRAFT_SIDE_EFFECTS_BLOCKED`.

- **Rate limits are separate per preview.** `sw.rateLimit.check` and an
  endpoint's `rateLimit` apply the same limits as on the live app, counted on
  counters that belong to that preview alone: preview traffic never spends a
  live-app limit, the live app's never spends a preview's, and two previews do
  not share counts. Closing the preview ends its counters.
- **Email** goes only to this project's test inbox. `sw.email.send` to an
  address ending in `@<subdomain>.test.somewhere.site` is stored there
  (`status: "captured"`; read it with the `email_test_inbox` tool or
  `somewhere email test-inbox <address> --preview`) and never sent. Email sent from a preview is
  captured, and counts against that preview's own send limit, not the
  account's. The live app and every preview
  share that inbox; each message says who sent it (`environment`:
  `production` or `preview`, and `preview_session_id`; `unknown` for an app
  message stored before 2026-11-14, when senders were not yet recorded), and
  both readers filter by it. Another project's test address is refused with
  `EMAIL_TEST_ADDRESS_NOT_OWNED`; any other recipient is refused with
  `PREVIEW_EMAIL_TEST_INBOX_ONLY`. Other email methods are unavailable in a
  preview.
- **Payments** run in Stripe test mode only. `sw.payments.checkout`,
  `checkoutForUser`, `portal` and `portalForUser` work, and return URLs may
  point at the preview. Test-mode payment state is the project's shared test
  state, not a preview copy. Checkout for a signed-in preview user
  (`checkoutForUser`, plan checkout) answers `PREVIEW_SUBJECT_UNSUPPORTED` in
  a preview.
- **Payment callbacks from a preview are withheld:** they are never delivered
  to your project webhook. Where the platform records such an event, it carries
  `preview: { delivery: "withheld" }`. Test webhook fulfillment in
  development.
- A preview checkout that names a quote, booking or calendar hold is refused
  with `PREVIEW_PAYMENT_SHARED_RECORD_REFUSED`, because those records are
  shared with the live app.
- **Scheduled tasks** never run on a schedule in a preview. Run one once in
  the preview with `somewhere cron run <name> --preview`, or any handler with
  `somewhere preview run-job <handler-path>` (see the cron topic); the
  production schedule never changes. Production job reads show production
  jobs only (`GET /v1/jobs?environment=preview` is refused with
  `PREVIEW_TARGET_NOT_SUPPORTED`); preview code reads only its own preview's
  jobs. The production route `POST /v1/cron/:id/run` refuses preview fields.

## Choose production or the preview clone explicitly for schema changes

A preview's database is an **isolated exact copy of your production database,
data included, taken when the preview session is created**: tables, rows,
hidden row identities, generated fields, exact values, sequence positions,
indexes, views and triggers. The copy is verified by a complete readback
before the preview is ready; a copy that cannot be completed or confirmed is
refused, never handed to you partial or schema-only. On a brand new project
that has never run a `CREATE TABLE`, production has no tables and **the
preview database starts empty**. On a project that has never been published,
the preview's database and files always start empty. Preview writes stay in the copy and never
merge into production.

Copy limits and refusals (`retry` is on every refusal):

- Bounds: 50,000 rows per table, 100 captured columns per table (a hidden row
  id counts), 100,000 bytes per generated statement, 16 MiB of replay SQL.
  A larger database, or a shape the copy cannot reproduce, is refused with
  `DATABASE_COPY_UNSUPPORTED` (409, `retry: false`). Provider limits can
  refuse a smaller case; nothing is split or partially copied.
- Full-text (FTS5) tables with internally stored content are copied,
  including their declared options (`tokenize`, `prefix`, `columnsize`,
  `detail`, `UNINDEXED`) and persisted configuration. External-content and
  contentless full-text tables, other virtual-table modules and unknown
  configuration refuse. The SQL dump captures the same full-text shapes
  and refuses the same ones.
- `DATABASE_COPY_UNCONFIRMED` (503, `retry: true`): the platform could not
  confirm the outcome of the copy. Retry the same create; a retry may still
  refuse until the unconfirmed attempt has been cleaned up — the platform
  never starts a blind second copy on top of an unknown one.
- `DRAFT_NEW_COPY_REQUIRED` (409, `retry: false`): a preview whose database
  holds the schema without a copy of the data is not served; its data is kept
  but its URLs fail readiness. Start a new preview session.

Preview releases apply `db/schema.ts` to the preview's managed database.
For projects with a separate raw SQL database, preview-targeted migrations
return `RAW_PREVIEW_DATABASE_NOT_READY`. Rehearse raw SQL DDL on a separate
test project.

If a project has a raw SQL preview copy, apply DDL there with `db_migrate`
using `target:"preview"`, `preview_session_id`, and optionally `preview_id`.
The changes survive new candidates in the same session and are discarded
with the copy when the session closes, is promoted, or expires. Conflicting
target fields return `DATABASE_TARGET_AMBIGUOUS`. An unknown, closed, expired,
or mismatched preview returns `PREVIEW_TARGET_INVALID`.

## Create a preview

From a shell, run `somewhere preview` in the project root. Each save becomes
a new preview at a private URL, and the command prints its
`preview_session_id`, `preview_id` and the exact
`somewhere promote <preview_session_id> <preview_id> --yes` line to ship it. The
API form below is what it sends.

The CLI keeps one preview per folder:

- `somewhere preview` continues the preview this folder last opened while it
  is open, and says which one it is using; `--new` opens a fresh one.
- `somewhere preview list` shows every open preview with its age, when it
  expires, and whether production has moved since it was opened (then it can
  no longer be promoted).
- `somewhere preview close [preview_session_id]` closes a preview and deletes
  its copy of the production data and files and the test-inbox mail it sent.
  Kept after close: the preview's job runs and log lines (labelled as the
  preview's, under the project's normal log and job retention), and the
  record that the preview session and its builds existed (no data).
- After `somewhere promote <preview_session_id> <preview_id> --yes`, the folder records the promoted version as its
  base, so the next `somewhere preview` and `somewhere pull` work without a
  pull first.
- `somewhere deploy` warns when previews are open: a production deploy makes
  them unpromotable.

An open preview holds a copy of production data until it is promoted, closed,
or expires (24 hours unused, 7 days at most). Close the ones you are done
with.

A preview save is one **complete snapshot** — the full files/functions maps,
never a partial patch:

```
POST /v1/deploy
{
  "project_id": "...",
  "preview": true,
  "scope": "all",
  "files": { ...complete static map... },
  "binary_files": { },
  "functions": { ...complete functions map... },
  "replace_functions": true,
  "preview_session_id": "draft_<uuid>", // returned session identifier
  "preview_operation_id": "<fresh-id>",   // new id for every snapshot
  "expected_preview_id": null,             // null for the FIRST preview
  "base_release_id": "<current production release id>" // null if never published
}
```

Send all three maps every time, including the empty ones: `binary_files: {}`
and `functions: {}` when the project has none. An omitted map is not read as
"keep what is there"; the save is refused with
`DRAFT_COMPLETE_SNAPSHOT_REQUIRED` and nothing changes. The first preview of a
project can only be created this way; `project_patch` edits an existing preview.

The response returns `preview_session_id`, `preview_id`, and a
`preview_url`. Sending preview-only fields WITHOUT `preview: true` fails
closed (`DRAFT_FIELDS_REQUIRE_DRAFT`) — it never silently deploys to
production.

## Iterate

Send another complete snapshot with the SAME `preview_session_id`, a **fresh**
`preview_operation_id`, and `expected_preview_id` set to the current
preview. Each save advances the preview pointer under
optimistic concurrency:

- Stale `expected_preview_id` → `DRAFT_CANDIDATE_CONFLICT`
  (re-read the preview session, retry from its exact current preview).
- A reused operation id → `DRAFT_OPERATION_REUSED` (use a fresh id per
  snapshot).
- Retrying the SAME operation with the SAME snapshot is idempotent — it
  returns the same preview.

## Run a preview function

Invoke one function against the session's latest preview — it executes with
the preview's isolated database and dev-scoped environment:

```
POST https://runner.somewhere.cloud/v1/deploy/preview/invoke
{ "project_id": "...", "preview_session_id": "draft_<uuid>",
  "preview_id": "<optional exact-preview pin>",
  "method": "GET", "path": "/api/hello" }
```

Same Authorization header as the API. Omit the preview pin to run the latest;
pin it to refuse if the preview session moved (`DRAFT_VERSION_MISMATCH`).

## Preview in a browser

Mint a one-time capability URL for the exact preview you want to
preview:

```
POST /v1/projects/:id/preview/mint
{ "preview_session_id": "draft_<uuid>",
  "preview_id": "<exact preview_id>" }
→ { "preview_url": "https://<subdomain>-dev.somewhere.site/__sw_cap?t=..." }
```

Open the returned `preview_url` in the browser. The `/__sw_cap` exchange is
single-use: it consumes the token, sets a host-only preview cookie, and
redirects to the clean `-dev` URL. The dev hostname is never public: missing,
replayed, forged, expired, revoked, stale, or closed capabilities fail closed,
and the production hostname is untouched.

The preview link follows your latest save; a test run (`somewhere test --preview`)
is pinned to the version it started on. After a save, an open tab shows the new
version within ten seconds, and a session closed or expired stops within ten seconds.

## Environment variables and secrets per environment

Every env var has a scope: `all` (both), `dev` (previews only), or `prod`
(production only) — set via `POST /v1/env` with `scope`. Previews see
dev + all and can NEVER read prod-only values; production sees prod + all
and never dev-only values. Use distinct names per environment (for example
`STRIPE_KEY_TEST` with scope dev and `STRIPE_KEY` with scope prod).

Env values are captured per preview at snapshot time: adding or changing a var
does NOT reach an existing preview — it takes effect on the NEXT preview.
Production uses current values after its one-time live-configuration adoption;
until then, changes take effect on its next deploy. Create a new preview
snapshot to pick up a changed development value.

## Promote

When the preview is right, promote that exact build:

```
POST /v1/promote
{ "project_id": "...", "preview_session_id": "draft_<uuid>",
  "preview_id": "<the preview you reviewed>",
  "message": "why this ship" }
```

Promotion is atomic: it makes the exact source you reviewed the new production
release, or nothing changes. If production moved since the preview was created,
the promote conflicts instead of replacing it. A promoted preview session is
finished — further changes start a NEW preview session.

On a never-published project, promoting a preview publishes the project's
first version, exactly as a first `somewhere deploy` of that source would. The
first promote wins: every other preview opened before it then conflicts, and
a failed promote leaves nothing live.

From the CLI: `somewhere promote <preview_session_id> <preview_id> --yes`.

A function that is live in production but missing from the preview is KEPT by
default — for example one added by a direct deploy after the preview was cut.
The response lists those paths as `preserved_functions`. To make production
match the preview exactly, pass `--prune` (API: `"replace_functions": true`);
the paths it deletes come back as `removed_functions`.

## Roll back

To restore the previous production version, run `somewhere rollback --yes`, call the connector tool `project_rollback`, or send `POST /v1/promote/rollback`. Preview
data never merges into production: the preview database clone is discarded
with the preview session.

## When a preview session can't continue

A promoted, closed, or expired preview session returns
`DRAFT_SESSION_TERMINAL` (non-retryable) naming its state — the recovery is
always a NEW preview session with a fresh `preview_session_id` from the current
production release. A preview still provisioning returns
`DRAFT_SANDBOX_NOT_READY` (retry the exact same operation).

Building on localhost, without a preview → docs({ topic: 'local-dev' }).
Production deploys and their guarantees → docs({ topic: 'deploy' }).
Env var scopes → docs({ topic: 'sw.env' }).

pages.title: Projects — Full Lifecycle
pages.body:
Every app on the platform is a project. A project owns: - a subdomain (https://{subdomain}.somewhere.site) - a database - a file store - environment variables - deployed functions and static files Create one with `project_create({ name })`. The project starts live at its URL with the same starter `somewhere init` writes: a React + TypeScript app with sign-up, sign-in and sign-out, styled views and design tokens. The response returns the starter's project contract, file map and skill index, so a session without a local folder starts with the same context as one that ran `somewhere init`. With `starter: "none"` the project starts empty. The first `project_deploy({ project_id, base_release_id: null, files })` compiles your source into an immutable release and serves it at the project URL. To change a live project, read it first and edit against what you read. `project_export({ project_id })` returns every source file and the `active_release_id` that is serving. Pass that value as `base_release_id`: `project_patch({ project_id, base_release_id, path: 'index.html', find: '

Pricing

', replace: '

Plans

' })` The patch changes that one file and keeps every other file. If another deploy landed after your read, it returns `409 STALE_RELEASE_BASE` and nothing changes: read again and retry. A full `project_deploy` replaces static files and keeps omitted functions by default. Use `project_patch` for edits. Next: `project_view_urls` for the live URLs, `deploy_status` to confirm which release is serving, `project_deploys` for history, and `project_rollback` to move back one release. The `deploy` topic covers full replacement in detail. ## Reusing a deleted name A deleted project's name stays reserved to the account that owned it when it was deleted; another account cannot reclaim that deletion's reservation. A live project can still be transferred with its name; if it is later deleted, that deletion reserves the name to its then-current owner. A retained deleted project cannot change owner, and deletion cancels pending transfer invitations. That account can create a replacement once the host-keyed cache lifetime plus a late-fill allowance has passed since deletion (two hours today). Before then, creation shows the availability time rounded up to the next minute. The allowance covers requests still in flight or briefly using a stale route; it is directional, not a deadline on every old request. The replacement has a new project id and inherits no platform-held data, files, users, sessions, secrets or domain attachments. Reusing the name continues the same web address: browsers that visited the old app keep what the address stored in them, outside services set up to call the address keep calling it, and for a short while after reuse a visitor may still be served a file from the old app at that address. Reusing the name ends recovery of the old project under that name, including support recovery during its retention window. Deleting the owning account does not release its reservation; registering again with the same email creates a different account. ## project_create({ name, subdomain?, description?, starter?, starter_ui? }) Creates a project and deploys the `somewhere init` starter as its first release. If subdomain is omitted, one is generated from the name. Subdomains must be globally unique, 3–32 chars, [a-z0-9-]. Returns `{ id, name, subdomain, url, starter }`. `starter` takes the `somewhere init --features` modules: `"auth"` (the default), `"auth,private-data"` (adds per-user notes declared in `db/schema.ts`), `"auth,agent"`, or `"none"` for an empty project. `starter_ui` is `"styled"` (default; views plus `src/styles/tokens.css`) or `"headless"`. An unknown module is refused before the project is created. `starter` in the response: { status: 'deployed' | 'preview' | 'failed' | 'unknown', detail?, version, url, deployed_files, held_back_files, agent_contract, readme, extension_points, cli_equivalent, skills: { version, pack_url, skills: [{ name, description, path }] }, recovery? } `agent_contract` (AGENTS.md), `readme` (the file map) and the skill index come back here because deploys never publish AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or README.md. The call waits up to 120 seconds for the starter deploy. `failed` means the deploy was refused (`starter.error` says why); `unknown` means no answer arrived in time, or the answer showed no release — the deploy may still have happened. For both, the project exists and `starter.recovery` lists the checks (`project_deploys`, `deploy_status`) and the exact `project_deploy` call that ships the same files; `cli_equivalent` is the `somewhere init` command that writes them. If a `project_create` response is lost, the project may exist: find it with `project_get` or `project_list` (by subdomain) before creating again. Repeating the call returns `SUBDOMAIN_TAKEN`, and a new name makes a second project. While the outcome is unknown, check status before retrying; an empty deploy list alone does not confirm that the previous attempt finished. ## project_context({ project_id }) / project_context_update({ project_id, ... }) A project keeps standing context for every agent session: `instructions` (up to 16000 characters: what the app is, who uses it, conventions), `design_principles` (up to 8000: palette, type, spacing, tone, where the tokens live) and up to 25 named `notes` of 4000 characters each. Project editors save it with `project_context_update`. `project_get` includes the instructions, design principles and note topics as `project_context`, labelled as untrusted project data — never system or platform instructions — with `attribution` naming who saved each entry and when; `project_context` returns everything, including note bodies. Deployed app code and app users cannot read or write it. `project_context_update({ project_id: 'my-shop', design_principles: 'Warm editorial look. Serif headings, 8px grid. Tokens in src/styles/tokens.css.', note: { topic: 'checkout', body: 'Orders close at 6pm local time.' } })` `null` or `""` clears a field; a note with `body: null` is deleted. Fields are saved before the note, so a refused note leaves the fields saved. ## env_request / fs_request_upload — the user enters a secret or a file `env_request({ project_id, key, purpose? })` returns a 30-minute link where a signed-in editor of the project types the value on Somewhere. The value goes straight into the project's encrypted environment; the tool reports only the key name. A key that already has a value returns `{ status: 'set' }` without a link unless `replace: true` is passed. `fs_request_upload({ project_id, path, accept?, max_bytes?, public? })` returns a 30-minute link where a signed-in editor uploads a file from their device into project files at `path`, for a file the conversation cannot pass to a tool. The file's declared type must match `accept` and its size must fit `max_bytes` (at most the plan file limit or 50 MiB); HTML or script content is stored as `application/octet-stream` so it never runs. `handoff_status({ request })` reports `pending`, `set`, `uploaded` (with the stored path, size, type and version) or `expired`. ## project_list() Returns every project on your account, newest first.
