Each row: { id, name, subdomain, status, state, address, created_at, last_deployed_at, latest_screenshot_url, favicon_url } `state` is the platform's one answer to "is this app live": { code: "live" | "publishing" | "temporary" | "offline" | "paused" | "not_deployed", label, detail, expires_at } `label` and `detail` are plain sentences to show a person as they are. `publishing` means a first version is on its way: the address answers within seconds, and the state turns `live` once it does. `live` always means the address answers. `address` is `null` while the state is `publishing` or `not_deployed`. `temporary` means live on a temporary account; `expires_at` says when it goes unless it is kept (claimed). `offline` means nothing is published now (for example after `project_undeploy`); `paused` means the plan ended. `address` is the URL people open: the first verified custom domain, else the `*.somewhere.site` address. `project_get` returns the same two fields. The list fields are ready to render without per-project metadata calls. `latest_screenshot_url` and `favicon_url` are null until the project has the corresponding live-release asset. The screenshot URL is a temporary signed capability that an image element can render; the favicon URL is public. ## Account overview: GET /v1/account/overview One read for an account home, the same for every caller: { account: { id, email, name, plan, trial, temporary_expires_at, ai_tools }, apps: [{ id, name, state, address, is_owner, last_changed_at }], apps_truncated, needs_you: [{ kind, title, detail, due_at, project_id, action: { label, url? | method + path } }] } `apps` carry the same `state` and `address` as `project_list`, most recently deployed first. `needs_you` is decided and ordered by the platform: `keep_apps` (a temporary account's apps go at `due_at` unless the person saves an account; `action.url` is their link), `accept_transfer` (someone offered this person an app), `finish_domain` (a custom domain whose DNS is not in place; `action` is the verify call). Show `title`, `detail` and `action.label` as they are; `action.url` is a page for the person, `action.method` + `action.path` an API call. `last_visit_at` is when the person was last here (their own browser reading this overview at least 30 minutes earlier; `null` on a first visit), and each app then carries `since_last_visit: { changed, failed_changes }`: whether a new version went live since, and how many changes failed since. Keys, agents and the CLI read the same answer without moving the window. `ai_tools` is the list of AI tools the person said they use (from `claude`, `chatgpt`, `claude-code`, `codex`, `cursor`, `opencode`; `[]` when not chosen). The signed-in person sets it with `PATCH /v1/auth/platform-me { "ai_tools": ["claude", "cursor"] }`. Page views for every app in that list, in one call: `GET /v1/account/pageviews?days=7` (or `30`, `90`) → { days, apps: [{ project_id, views }] }, most viewed first. Counted as in the `analytics` topic (HTML page loads, no bots or previews). ## Project overview: GET /v1/projects/{id}/overview One read for a project home: { project: { id, name, state, address, is_owner }, abilities, live_version: { id, version, published_at } | null, last_change: { kind, at } | null, errors_24h: { total, top_codes: [{ code, count }] }, needs_you: [ ... same item shape as the account overview ... ] } `errors_24h` is the same count as `GET /v1/errors/stats` for the last day. `needs_you` here can also hold `fix_deploy`: the newest deploy failed after the live release (or before any), with its code and message in `detail` and `GET /v1/deploy/failure/{id}` as its `action`. A connected agent's key (from a connect code) may read `GET /v1/projects/{id}` and this overview for the projects in its connection, so it sees state, address and its own `abilities`; nothing else in the account. A temporary account's key may read `GET /v1/account/overview` for its own account. ## project_get({ project_id, include_overview? }) Single project record + tier + deploy state, `state`, `address`, and `abilities`: what this caller may do on this project, so no caller ranks roles itself: { deploy, publish, rollback, manage_domains, manage_secrets, manage_collaborators, delete: { allowed: true } | { allowed: false, reason, message } } Each is judged by the checks that the matching request meets (deploy, promote, rollback, domain add, env, collaborator invite, project delete) for this credential, and a refused one carries the code and message that request would answer with. `live_release: { id, version } | null` is the release serving the app now; pass its `id` as `base_release_id` to deploy over it. Plus `project_context` (instructions, design principles, note topics) when the project's editors have saved any. Reading a project includes `project_overview` when the active release has a source map. It summarizes the entry files, pages, API routes, tables and job handlers. Use `docs_query` for a route, symbol or file. Older maps indicate when declared tables and route auth are missing. A redeploy includes both. `project_overview_status` explains when the overview is unavailable. Pass `include_overview: false` to skip the source map read. The dashboard's project Monitoring view also shows Page views: 7/30-day totals, top paths, and referrer hosts. ## project_view_urls({ project_id }) Returns the project's URLs and current version. The bare subdomain and every attached custom domain serve the immutable release named by `active_release_id`. Browser verification uses that public live URL. ## project_deploy({ project_id, base_release_id, files, functions?, binary_files? }) Full replacement from authored source. The platform compiles the source into one immutable release and moves `active_release_id` to that exact release only after publication succeeds. Pass `base_release_id: null` on a project with no source. For a live project, use the `active_release_id` from the source export you edited. See the deploy topic for the exact semantics and when to choose project_patch instead. ## project_patch({ project_id, base_release_id, path, content? | find?+replace?, delete_files? }) Single-file edit, served live. Two modes — `content` rewrites the whole file; `find`+`replace` does a server-side substring substitute (~200 bytes on the wire, preferred for tweaks). Unchanged files are preserved. Pass the current release as `base_release_id`, including dry runs: `deploy_status` returns it as `active_release_id` (`retained_release_id` after an undeploy), and `project_export` returns the same id with the source when you also need to read the file. `delete_files` removes paths. See the deploy topic for the full shape. ## project_rollback({ project_id }) Move `active_release_id` to the previous retained release. This changes the serving pointer; it does not rebuild or mutate either release. ## project_deploys({ project_id }) Deploy history, up to 150 successful releases plus 20 failed attempts interleaved by time, each tagged with `status`: { deploys: [ { status: "success", version, promoted_at, is_live, deployed_by, commit_sha, ... }, { status: "rejected", version, reason, message, at, is_live: false }, ] } Each version shows the user-supplied note given when it was deployed or patched, if any. A successful entry's `rollback_available` describes build availability, not source availability or schema-safe activation. Each successful entry also carries `can_restore`: `{ allowed: true }` (with a `restore` action) or `{ allowed: false, reason, message }`, the code and words `project_restore_version` would answer with (`FORBIDDEN`, `RELEASE_IS_LIVE`, `ROLLBACK_UNAVAILABLE`, `RESTORE_LOCKED`). Restoring needs editor access. This history is the project's release resource: the response's `live_release` names the version serving the app now. A rejected entry's `version` is the version it would have become (may be `null`); it never went live. ## project_restore_version({ project_id, version }) Restore a specific past version as the live version. ## project_undeploy({ project_id }) Take the project off the public subdomain. Files and database stay. Reverse with project_deploy. While the project is undeployed, a deploy that names no `base_release_id` is accepted against the retained release. ## project_archive({ project_id }) / project_unarchive({ project_id }) Hide from the project list and revoke the subdomain. Data preserved. Use for old projects you don't want cluttering project_list but might revive later. ## project_rename({ project_id, name?, description? }) Changes the display name or description. The app keeps its address. ## Change the app address The owner of a claimed project can change its Somewhere address in **Settings → App address** or with `PATCH /v1/projects/{project_id}/hostname`. Send `{"subdomain":"my-clean-name"}` using a developer key and the project ID. The response includes the project's `id`, `subdomain`, and new `url`. Use that URL and keep the same project ID for future deploys. The old address redirects to the new one for 30 days, including the path and query. Update any integration that calls the old address before then. ## project_export({ project_id }) Pull every file in a project (static + functions) in one call — works from any MCP client. Pair with project_deploy to write back. (CLI: somewhere pull does the same to disk.) ## project_transfer({ project_id, to_email }) Invite an existing platform account with a verified email to take ownership. Ownership changes only when the recipient explicitly accepts the invitation. Before sending the invitation, tell the current owner: “When the transfer is accepted, your connected keys and database connection will be disconnected, and we recommend changing the database password with your provider because only that fully ends access through the old connection string. The app’s environment variables go with it, so remove or change any secret you put there before transferring.” If the live deployment contains the connection string, disconnect the database and deploy once before transferring. Older deployments stay in the project history. After transfer, versions that still carry the old database connection cannot be restored. Deploy their source as a new version if you need it. Includes the project's data, files, functions, and env vars. Payment callbacks remain tied to the original payment owner: pending payment callbacks tied to the previous owner stop when the project changes owner. The new owner cannot view their delivery history or retry them. ## project_delete({ project_id }) → project_delete_confirm({ project_id, code }) Two-step. The first call is a successful response, { ok: true, status: "needs_confirmation", confirmation_code }: issuing that code is the whole result of this step. (`code` carries the same value for callers already reading it.) Pass that code to project_delete_confirm within 10 minutes only after human authorization. Before confirmation, nothing changes. Confirmation immediately takes the project and its hostnames offline, blocks new project effects, and frees its custom domains and email sending setup at once (domains claimed or bought stay in the account, unattached). It retains its database, files, functions, and environment variables for 30 days, then permanently erases them. Recovery during the retention period requires support and does not bring back domain connections or sending setup. ## deploy_status({ project_id }) Returns deploy metadata including the active release, current version, last-deploy timestamp, and file counts on every plan. Use it to verify the intended immutable release is the serving authority. Preview details require hosted-preview read access; without it, `preview_comparison` is `unavailable` and comparison values are null. That means preview was not inspected, not that it is empty or synchronized with production. It reports release metadata only. It does not run or report access, permission or data checks. The checks a deploy ran appear in that deploy's own output, such as its `warnings` and `smoke` result. ## What NOT to do - Don't call project_deploy when you only want to change one file — use project_patch. project_deploy fully replaces static files (any file you omit is deleted), but functions you omit are merge-preserved, NOT deleted — and the deploy warns you, naming each preserved function. Pass replace_functions:true only when you actually intend to drop them. - Don't call project_delete in a script without surfacing the confirmation code to a human first. ## Outbound webhook subscriptions — the raw-body signature Subscribe a URL to one event with `PUT /v1/webhooks/` (developer key; body `{ project_id, url, enabled?, secret? }`); list with `GET /v1/webhooks?project_id=…`. Events the platform sends today: account lifecycle (`user_signup`, `user_login`, `user_updated`, `user_deleted`, `user_banned`, `user_unbanned`, `password_reset`, `password_changed`, `email_verified`, `google_linked`), sessions (`session_created`, `session_revoked`), email (`email_bounced`, `email_complained`), `deploy_complete`, `ingest_complete` and `ingest_failed`. Other names the registry accepts have no sender. Deliveries and redrives: `webhook_deliveries_list`, `webhook_delivery_redrive`. Wire format (from the sender): the JSON body is `{ id, event, project_id, timestamp, source, data }` — `timestamp` is an ISO string, `id` is the stable event ID, and `source` is `"live"` or `"test"`, `data` is the event payload. Headers: `X-Somewhere-Event`, `X-Somewhere-Project`, `X-Somewhere-Event-Id`, `X-Somewhere-Delivery-Id`, `X-Somewhere-Attempt` (and `X-Somewhere-Retry: 1` on retries). When the subscription has a secret, `X-Somewhere-Signature` is the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the RAW body bytes with that secret — no timestamp, no `t=`/`v1=` prefix. Verify the raw body, then use its `id` to deduplicate the event in your storage. The same event keeps this ID and the same signed bytes across retries and manual redrives. `X-Somewhere-Event-Id` mirrors the ID for troubleshooting; use the signed body value for deduplication. This differs from the project auth-webhook drain (`auth_webhook_set`), which signs `t={ms},v1={hex}` over `${ms}.${rawBody}` — verify each surface with its own scheme. Older stored deliveries keep their original signed body and may lack `id`. Use the developer webhook delivery history to reconcile those before processing. Neither an unsigned header nor a body hash distinguishes every older event. Retries and redrives retain the signature made when the event was created. After rotating a subscription secret, keep the previous verification key for retained deliveries you may retry or redrive. New events use the new secret. Setup: store the same secret you passed to `PUT /v1/webhooks/` with `somewhere env set WEBHOOK_SECRET ` and read it as `sw.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Verification only — what you do after is your app's contract: ```ts export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise { const raw = await req.text(); const expected = await sw.crypto.hmacSha256Hex(raw, sw.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET); const received = req.headers.get('X-Somewhere-Signature') ?? ''; if (!sw.crypto.timingSafeEqual(expected, received)) return new Response('bad signature', { status: 401 }); const { id, event, project_id, timestamp, source, data } = JSON.parse(raw); // Verified. For new events, id is inside the signed body. // Make your next action idempotent on that id in your own storage. return new Response('ok'); } ```

pages.title: Connect an agent, claim an app, disconnect
pages.body:
A person lets an agent work on their Somewhere account with a **connect code**,
keeps an app an agent made without an account by **claiming** it, and ends an
agent's access by **disconnecting** it. Issuing, claiming and disconnecting are
done by the signed-in person; the agent only redeems.

## The person's own sign-in

A person signs in to Somewhere in the browser: `POST /v1/auth/platform-signup`,
`/platform-login` or `/platform-magic-link`, then `GET /v1/auth/platform-me` and
`POST /v1/auth/platform-logout`. These set an HttpOnly cookie session for the
dashboard; they are for the person, not for agents. An agent works with a
connect code (below) or with `somewhere login` on the person's machine, which the
person approves. A step that only the person may take answers a key or an agent
with `403 PERSON_APPROVAL_REQUIRED`.

## Connect

1. The person issues a code while signed in: the dashboard's **Copy prompt for
   your agent**, or `POST /v1/auth/connect-codes` from their signed-in session.
   A code starts with `swcc_`, works once, and expires after 10 minutes.
2. The agent redeems it, with no other credential:

```bash
curl -s https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/auth/connect-codes/redeem \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"connect_code":"swcc_..."}'
# → { "data": { "key": "smt_...", "expires_at": ..., "projects_remaining": 3 } }
```

Somewhere's own apps (the Guide) skip the copy and paste: the person presses
Allow on a Somewhere page, which issues the same kind of code and returns it to
that app's fixed address. That page is not open to other apps. Inside the dashboard, the Guide signs in as the
person without any page at all: the dashboard hands it a one-time sign-in for the
person's own account (the same authority as their `somewhere login`, ended from
Devices and sessions). Only Somewhere's own listed apps can be handed a sign-in.

Keep the returned key on your server. Never put it, or the code, in a model
conversation or browser code.

### What the key may do

It may create a few projects (`projects_remaining`), deploy them by id
(`POST /v1/deploy { project_id, ... }`, including `template`), run their SQL,
read their logs, and read each of them (`GET /v1/projects/{id}` and its
`/overview`). It cannot see or touch the person's other apps, account, billing,
domains or secrets. Deploy and SQL pause on a project once its owner adds
private configuration to it. An unused key expires after 30 days.

Deploying files to a live project needs `base_release_id`: keep the
`release_id` your last deploy returned and pass it on the next one. If someone
else changed the app in between, the deploy is refused instead of overwriting
their work.

## Disconnect

The person lists their codes with `GET /v1/auth/connect-codes` (statuses
`available`, `connected`, `disconnected`, `revoked`, `expired`) and ends one with
`DELETE /v1/auth/connect-codes/{id}`: an unused code is revoked, and a used code
disconnects the agent it connected (`{ "disconnected": true }`). The dashboard
does the same. The agent's next call is refused with `401`; tell the person in
plain words that it is no longer connected.

## Claim an app made without an account

A deploy made without an account answers with a `claim_url`. Give that link to
the person: they open it signed in to their account and the app moves to it. The
agent can also ask the platform to email the link with the temporary deploy's
own key: `POST /v1/auth/claim { "email": "..." }` (`202 accepted`). Claiming
itself is always the person's step on the claim page.

Related topics: `projects`, `deploy`, `security-model`.

pages.title: Inspect — Read live state before writing
pages.body:
You open a session and the user says "fix the auth bug in adapted-co"
or "add a /pricing page to my-saas". The local workspace may be
stale, empty, or out-of-date — and another agent (or the user
themselves on another machine) may be editing the same project
right now. Inspecting before writing is the difference between a
clean patch and overwriting someone else's work.

## The default inspect-first order

  1. project_get { project_id }
     → Confirms the project exists. Returns subdomain, current code
       `version`, custom domain, owner. Save the version for deploy history and diffs.

  2. project_export { project_id }
     → Pulls the live deployed source (static + functions) in one
       call. The platform is the authoritative copy. (CLI equivalent:
       `somewhere pull <id>` writes it to ./<slug>/.)

  3. project_deploys { project_id }
     → Up to 150 successful releases plus 20 failed attempts, with timestamps. Look
       for: deploys in the last hour (someone is active), gaps
       between versions (interrupted shipping), unfamiliar deployers.

  4. deploy_status { project_id }
     → Confirms which immutable release is named by
       `active_release_id` and served on every project hostname.

For runtime symptoms, layer on:

  errors { project_id }
     → Last 50 runtime errors with stack and request path. Run this
       BEFORE assuming the bug is wherever the user pointed you.

  project_logs { project_id, function_path?, since? }
     → console.log output from deployed functions. Filter by
       function path or time window when investigating a specific
       endpoint.

  project_diff_versions { project_id, from, to }
     → Per-file delta between two preserved versions: added,
       removed, changed (with truncated text previews), plus
       function source. Use after a STALE_RELEASE_BASE refusal to see what
       the other agent shipped before merging and retrying.

  fs_versions { project_id, path }
     → History for a single user-uploaded file (anything written
       under /v1/fs/*). NOT for project code — see below.

## Two version namespaces, never confused

There are TWO independent histories. Picking the wrong one is a
common mistake.

  Code history:    project_deploys / project_restore_version
                   Covers files + functions shipped by
                   project_deploy or project_patch.

  Upload history:  fs_versions / fs_restore
                   Covers user-uploaded files under /v1/fs/* —
                   uploads, generated PDFs, cached blobs. Each
                   path has its own version chain.

`project_restore_version` rolls back code but leaves uploaded
data alone. `fs_restore` rewinds one uploaded file without
touching code. Pick the right tool for what is broken.

## Editing what you pulled

Keep the export's `active_release_id`. Send it as `base_release_id` when you
deploy or patch. A stale release ID returns `STALE_RELEASE_BASE`. On a project
with a production release, omit the numeric `expected_version` field.

```text
project_export({ project_id: "adapted-co" })
```

Here `version` is 47. After editing:

```text
project_patch({
  project_id: "adapted-co",
  base_release_id: "<active_release_id from project_export>",
  path: "api/auth.ts",
  content: "<the edited file>"
})
```

If another agent deployed between your export and your patch, the platform
refuses the stale release. Use the `base_version` and `active_version` fields
in the 409 response, when present, to inspect the intervening changes:

```text
project_diff_versions({ project_id: "adapted-co", from: 47, to: 48 })
```

Merge their changes, export again, and retry with that export's
`active_release_id` as `base_release_id`.

## Subscribe to deploys in real time

Every successful `project_deploy` / `project_patch` /
`project_restore_version` publishes a message on the
`system:project` system channel for that project. Subscribe with a
developer key to be notified the instant another agent ships. This is
developer tooling, not an in-function capability:

  events_subscribe_project({ project_id: "my-app" })
  // → { channel: "system:project", websocket_url, event_types: [...] }
  // open websocket_url; each frame is the envelope below

Event shape:

  {
    event: "deployed" | "patched" | "restored" | "rolled_back",
    data: {
      version: 49,
      by: "user_…",          // actor user_id
      message: null,         // optional deploy message
      has_functions: true,
      at: "2026-05-12T18:04:11.000Z",
    }
  }

A long-running editing agent should subscribe to this channel and
treat any `event: "deployed"` with a higher version than its
last observed version as "stop, re-clone or diff, then retry."

## Who deployed v13?

`project_deploys` now returns each row with a `deployed_by`
object containing the actor's `user_id` and `email`. NULL means
the row was written before actor tracking was added (the project
owner is the safe fallback in that case).

## When you can skip the inspect-first dance

  - You just created the project in this session.
  - The user says "I'm the only person editing this."
  - You are only reading (db_query, project_logs, errors).

Inspect before writing whenever:

  - The user mentions another machine, another agent, or a
    collaborator.
  - `project_deploys` shows multiple deploys today.
  - You see "I have local edits" or "I cloned this last week".
  - The last `project_deploy` response is more than ~10 minutes
    old in your conversation — assume someone else may have
    shipped since.

## Remaining limits (be honest with the user)

  - `project_deploy` is full-replacement for static files (every file
    in `files` replaces the live set). Functions are merge-preserved
    by default — pass `replace_functions:true` to delete omitted
    functions. `dry_run:true` previews the diff before anything writes.
  - Single-file optimistic concurrency for `fs_write` does not
    exist yet — `base_release_id` is a project-code check, not
    a per-file CAS for uploads under /v1/fs/*.

When either of those limits matters, surface it to the user
instead of pretending the platform has the feature.

Historical deployed-source file reads are unavailable. Source readers refuse unsupported
`version` or release selectors; `project_diff_versions` shows what changed.
The SEO check reads only the active release and refuses version selectors.
The docs HTTP readers keep their supported `version` (and docs-query filters)
and refuse unsupported selectors.
A history row alone does not guarantee retained source or a restorable build.

pages.title: Testing your app
pages.body:
Load when: testing the deployed app or an open preview from your own Node or Playwright script, or reading the platform smoke check.

## Write a test for your app

Install the test helper with `npm install -D @somewhere-cloud/cli`. In the
linked app folder, save your script in the `tests/` folder and run it with
Node. Import the installed package so each call runs in the same process.
The helper creates signed-in test users and sends their calls to the linked app. For an open preview, use
`openTestApp({ preview: true })`.

This example uses the app's own task and membership routes. A member can
read the task, the stranger gets 404, and the owner reads back the stored
title after the update.

```js
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { openTestApp } from '@somewhere-cloud/cli/testing';

const app = await openTestApp();
try {
  const [owner, member, stranger] = await app.users(3);
  const id = await app.create(owner, 'tasks', { title: 'Draft' });
  const task = '/api/tasks/' + encodeURIComponent(id);

  // Use the same membership route the app uses.
  const membership = task + '/members';
  const grant = await owner.session.post(membership, { user_id: member.id });
  assert.equal(grant.status, 204);
  app.onCleanup('task membership', async () => {
    const removed = await owner.session.request(membership, {
      method: 'DELETE',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ user_id: member.id }),
    });
    assert.equal(removed.status, 204);
  });

  const readAsMember = await member.session.request(task);
  assert.equal(readAsMember.status, 200);
  assert.equal((await readAsMember.json()).title, 'Draft');
  await stranger.session.expectRefused('GET ' + task, undefined, { allowed: member.session });

  const save = await owner.session.request(task, {
    method: 'PATCH',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Ready for review' }),
  });
  assert.equal(save.status, 204);
  const stored = await owner.session.data('tasks', { operation: 'get', id });
  assert.equal(stored.status, 200);
  assert.equal((await stored.json()).data.title, 'Ready for review');
  console.log('Member read, stranger hidden, and owner update verified.');
} finally {
  await app.cleanup();
}
```

- **Playwright.** Pass `storageState: await owner.session.storageState()` to
  `browser.newContext()`. Open the page and call `waitForApp(page, 'signed-in')`
  before interacting with it.
- **Private fields.** [Check for leaked fields](#privacy-checks-that-say-where-a-secret-leaked)
  with `app.plantMarker()` and `assertNoLeak()`.
- **Jobs.** `await app.runJob({ schedule: 'daily-digest' })` or
  `await app.runJob({ handler: '/api/jobs/import', payload: { batch: 1 } })`
  submits once and waits. Check `status`, `job_id`, `request_id` and
  `timed_out`. Keep an unknown admission for investigation.
- **Cleanup.** Put `await app.cleanup()` in `finally`. It removes the rows
  made with `app.create()` or `app.plantMarker()`, then the test users.
  Register cleanup for records your custom routes create with `app.onCleanup()`.

## After an edit

After a backend edit, run `somewhere deploy` from the linked app folder. Then
use the test helper to check the changed response on the live app.

This example checks that the public `/api/ping` route returns `ready` in its
`version` field. Save it as `tests/ping.js` and run `node tests/ping.js` from the linked app folder.

```js
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { openTestApp } from '@somewhere-cloud/cli/testing';

const app = await openTestApp();
const response = await app.anonymous.request('/api/ping');
assert.equal(response.status, 200);
assert.equal((await response.json()).version, 'ready');
```

Before handing over, confirm the full smoke check for the final deploy with
`somewhere test`.

## Saved checks, run by the platform after every deploy

Save a journey as `checks/<plain-name>.json` in the app's folder and deploy. After every
live deploy, Somewhere runs each saved check in its own browser (up to five; nothing to
install). The result is part of the deploy's one sentence (`access_check` on
`GET /v1/deploy/log`). `POST /v1/deploy/checks { "project_id": "…" }` runs the check now
on the live release. A failing check warns; it never stops a deploy.

Run `somewhere test` to read the latest smoke check. Add `--again` to start a fresh
run. The final line is JSON with `outcome` and `counts`. With `--json`, the
same fields are included in the one-line report.

| Exit | Outcome | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `passed` | Checks passed. Warnings leave the exit status unchanged. |
| 1 | `failed` | A named check failed. Its result gives the actor, what was sent, and what came back. |
| 2 | `could_not_check` | A check could not finish or cleanup could not be confirmed. The result names test data that may remain. |

An access probe that sees another test user's data runs once more as the
same actor. If the responses disagree, the result says “Inconsistent: tell
us” and gives the request IDs. The report summarizes what each response
showed and leaves out row contents and credentials. A crash warning
identifies a request with a platform-recorded function exception.
An app function or API route that returns 5xx without a matching error record
shows its HTTP status and any available request ID.

```json
{ "actions": [
    { "fill": "[data-testid=note-title]", "value": "Lunch with Ana 42" },
    { "click": "[data-testid=note-save]" },
    { "expect": { "selector": "[data-testid=note-item]", "text": "Lunch with Ana 42" } } ],
  "viewports": ["desktop", "mobile"],
  "signed_in": true }
```

- **Format:** the `actions` format `somewhere verify --flow` runs. `viewports` defaults to
  `["desktop"]`.
- **Who runs it:** `"signed_in": true` runs it as a test user the platform creates and
  removes. Without it, the check runs signed out.
- **Custom routes.** Saved checks run their steps as written. Use your app's
  own tests to check who can call an endpoint.
- **Writing it:** give each check one plain name and find controls by `data-testid`, so
  renaming a button does not break it.

## Run a schedule on your preview

From a folder with an open preview, run `somewhere cron run daily-digest --preview --wait`.
The handler uses the registered schedule's payload and can change preview data.
The CLI describes mail, payment and network behavior before starting, then
reports the job status, duration and IDs. An unknown admission is never retried.

Use `somewhere cron run daily-digest --preview --twice` to see repeat behavior.
It waits for the first run to finish, starts a second, and shows which declared
table row counts changed after each run. The observations
can include concurrent preview writes and do not establish retry safety.
Connector agents can use `cron_run` with both preview IDs and
`preview_test: "inspect"` for the notice. Show it and pass it as `notice` with
`preview_test: "run"` to submit once. Inspect with the returned `job_id` for status. Use `row_counts: true`
on inspections to read counts before admission and after a terminal job.

## Test with an ordinary Playwright script

Use `openTestApp()` with your own Playwright browser. Pass an actor's
`storageState()` to the browser context and call `waitForApp(page, 'signed-in')`
before checking the signed-in UI. To test the sign-up form itself, start with a
signed-out context and drive the form with Playwright.

`openAppTest()` from `@somewhere-cloud/cli/script` supports existing Node test scripts.

### Privacy checks that say where a secret leaked

Using the test users above, import `assertNoLeak` from
`@somewhere-cloud/cli/testing`. Choose a writable private text field and a
route that includes the test row in the member's task list.

```js
const marker = await app.plantMarker(owner, 'tasks', 'private_note', { title: 'Draft' });
const response = await member.session.request('/api/tasks');
assert.equal(response.status, 200);
await assertNoLeak(marker, [response]);
```

For a browser page, import `captureResponses` from the same package and set
`const seen = captureResponses(page)` before navigation. Pass `await seen.all()`
to `assertNoLeak()` after the responses you want to check have arrived. A failure
names the response without printing its body.

## Run Playwright Test specs with `somewhere test` (optional)

The Playwright Test fixtures in `@somewhere-cloud/cli/testing` support existing Playwright Test suites.

## Testing access rules

To send a data request as an actor, call `actor.session.data(table, request)`.
It supplies the app's origin and the release's data contract. Read the HTTP
status and JSON body from the returned `Response`. Scoped reads include
`access.filtered: true`, including when they return rows.

### Prove a refusal

Create a fixture the owner can read, then run these checks with an unrelated user.

```js
const id = await app.create(owner, 'notes', { title: 'Draft' });
await stranger.session.expectRefused('notes', { operation: 'get', id }, { allowed: owner.session });
await stranger.session.expectRefused('notes', { operation: 'delete', id }, { allowed: owner.session });
```

`allowed` is the positive control. An empty read requires the same read to
return data for that session. An update or delete returning 404 requires the
control session to see the same row before and after the attempt. For a custom
route, pass `'METHOD /path'` and its JSON body, or `undefined` for a GET. A 404
requires the same call to succeed for the control session. Choose a fixture
route where a successful control call has safe effects. Malformed requests and
stale contracts fail the assertion.

## Two users sharing through the app

Platform-made users are visible to this app's `sw.auth.server.listUsers` by
email or id. They are verified, so they can also join built-in groups; the
verified-email requirement still applies. Other projects cannot look them up.

The complete team app and its spec are `somewhere docs sw.groups --section team-example`:
the owner invites test users by email, each one's next groups read shows the
team, and the spec checks members, outsiders, removal and leaving.

Test-user cleanup removes identities, sessions and platform-owned role grants and group memberships; rows in your app’s own tables remain your app’s data and must be removed by your test when needed. A test user who is the only owner of a group is not deleted: an explicit cleanup answers `LAST_OWNER` naming the group, and the automatic 24-hour expiry leaves that user in place. Delete the group (or make another test user its owner) in your test's teardown.

pages.title: Verify before deploy
pages.body:
Pick the narrowest check that answers the question. These tools are
complementary; a green local typecheck is not a live browser health check.

| Question | Command | Runs where | Changes live state? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Are TypeScript types and imports coherent? | `somewhere typecheck` | Local `tsc --noEmit` | No |
| Will the real deploy compiler accept this source? | `somewhere deploy-check` | Platform compile pipeline | No |
| Does one handler answer correctly before I deploy? | `somewhere deploy-check --run /api/<path>` | Platform check runner, every plan (Free: 60 per project per hour) | No; never your live database |
| Does a seed/backfill/check script work against real bindings? | `somewhere run <script>` | One-off local module + real bindings | No deploy; may mutate project data |
| Is the deployed page healthy for a real browser? | `somewhere browser <url>` | Live browser | Read/drive only unless your steps submit actions |

Every deploy is followed by the after-deploy check, at no extra step: it
loads the homepage in a real browser and reports a blank page, or errors the
page throws while loading, as a warning (`access_check` in the deploy log).
A blank or throwing page is never rolled back for you; the release stays live.
When the previous version worked, `access_check.go_back` names it, and
`somewhere restore <version> --project <project_id> --yes`, or over MCP `project_rollback({ project_id, version })` puts it back.
`somewhere verify` adds what one page load cannot show: named flows (clicks, forms, expected requests), the phone
viewport, and screenshots on demand.

Recommended sequence for a new TypeScript app: `typecheck` → deploy →
`verify`/`browser`. Deploy runs the same compile, schema and secret checks as
`deploy-check`, then applies `db/schema.ts` before the new version goes live;
use `deploy-check` to diagnose a refusal or review a change without
publishing. Add `run` only for a one-off operation against the live project.
A tiny JavaScript app with no `package.json` can skip local typecheck.

`somewhere dev` serves only the frontend; it runs no backend code, so it
cannot test a handler. Use `deploy-check --run` for that. See the
deploy-check section of docs({ topic: 'cli' }).

## Unit tests

The platform does not run your tests; a deploy compiles and checks the app.
Run unit tests locally, with Vitest for example, on logic that is pure and
easy to get wrong: parsing, pricing, validation, date handling.

```bash
npm install -D vitest
npx vitest run
```

```ts
// src/lib/price.ts
export function totalCents(lines: { cents: number; qty: number }[], taxRate: number): number {
  const subtotal = lines.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.cents * line.qty, 0);
  return Math.round(subtotal * (1 + taxRate));
}
```

```ts
// src/lib/price.test.ts
import { expect, test } from 'vitest';
import { totalCents } from './price';

test('adds tax once', () => {
  expect(totalCents([{ cents: 1000, qty: 2 }], 0.1)).toBe(2200);
});
```

Add `*.test.ts` to `.somewhereignore` so test files are not uploaded; a
test file under `api/` would otherwise become a route. Unit tests check a
function's logic. `deploy-check --run` invokes one handler without
deploying; its database and network access depend on the project (see
`cli`). `somewhere verify` runs a journey in a real browser.

pages.title: Limits
pages.body:
These are the same on every plan. Plan quotas (storage, email, deploys per hour,
the per-file upload size, the monthly AI spend cap) are separate: `GET /v1/pricing` and
docs({ topic: 'pricing' }).

CPU time counts computation. Time spent waiting for a database or network
response does not use the CPU allowance. An ordinary HTTP function has no
fixed wall-clock deadline while its client stays connected.

| Ceiling | Value | Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Request body into a function | about 100 MB | Have the browser upload big files straight to file storage with `sw.fs.uploadUrl` |
| Memory shared by concurrent requests in one runtime instance | 128 MB | Stream or process in chunks; move heavy work to `sw.jobs` |
| CPU time per request | 300 s for newly deployed functions | Use `sw.jobs` for work that must finish independently of the browser |
| Wall-clock time per HTTP request | No fixed deadline while the client stays connected | Use `sw.jobs` when work must survive a disconnected client |
| One database record | about 4 MB | Store large values with files (`sw.fs`) and keep the path in the row |
| Environment values | about 5 KB (5,120 bytes) for all of a project's values together | Keep large configuration in files; a save above the limit is refused with 413 `ENV_VALUE_TOO_LARGE` (one value) or `ENV_VALUES_TOO_LARGE` (all values together), naming the key and the limit |
| One uploaded file | per plan (`max_upload_mb` in `GET /v1/pricing`) | Above about 25 MB, use `sw.fs.uploadUrl`; above 90 MB, upload it in parts through its `multipart_url` — docs({ topic: 'sw.fs' }) |
| One deploy | 20 MiB, 1,500 files, 5 MiB of text source | docs({ topic: 'deploy' }) states the deploy limits |

## What a runtime limit hit looks like

A stopped runtime can return HTTP 500 with `FUNCTION_RUNTIME_FAILED` in the
platform's JSON error envelope, `{ ok: false, error, message, request_id }`.
Check the matching project log for the cause: the response alone cannot
distinguish CPU exhaustion, memory exhaustion or a runtime outage. Retry a
write only after checking whether it committed. Your function's own 503
response passes through unchanged.

Redeploy an older function to adopt the current CPU allowance. Disconnecting
the client can end its request; use `sw.jobs` for durable work. Outbound fetch,
code evaluation and job attempts have their own deadlines, described in their
respective topics. These bound stalled connections and individual attempts.
A request body over the ceiling is refused with 413 before your function runs.

## Creating a project with a starter

`project_create` waits up to 120 seconds for the
starter deploy to answer. If the answer has not arrived, the project still
exists and deployment may still complete. Check `project_deploys` and
`deploy_status` with the returned project ID before deciding what to do next.
Do not create a second project to recover a missing deploy answer.

## Monthly AI spend cap

Each project's AI spending has a monthly cap from your plan
(`ai_spend_cap_cents` in `GET /v1/pricing`), counted per project per
calendar month (UTC). At 80% the owner gets one email, a warning in the
project's logs and on every deploy. At 100% every AI call from the project
is refused with 429 `AI_SPEND_CAP_REACHED` until the month turns; the rest
of the app keeps working. The owner can raise it, lower it or turn it off
for one project with `PATCH /v1/projects/{id}` `{ "ai_spend_cap_cents": … }`
(MCP `project_update`); the prepaid balance still bounds spend.
Details: docs({ topic: 'sw.ai' }).

## Usage levels and time left

Account reads say how close each meter is, so no caller picks its own
thresholds: `GET /v1/usage/summary` gives `level` (`ok`, `warning` from
80% of the limit, `critical` at 100%) and a plain `level_label` on
`account_database`, `account_files` and each project's `combined_storage`.
The account read (`somewhere whoami --json`, `GET /v1/auth/platform-me`) and
`GET /v1/account/overview` give `trial: { ends_at, days_left }` while a
trial runs (null otherwise), and
`temporary_expires_at` for a temporary account.

Related: `sw.jobs`, `sw.fs`, `deploy`, `sw.env`, `database-engine`.

pages.title: Deploy intelligence — what a deploy records, and where to read it
pages.body:
A successful live deploy, patch or promote queues two background jobs for the
release that just went live:

- **Project docs**, generated from that release's exact source. `project_get`
  includes an overview. Read the full document with `project_docs`.
- **Homepage screenshots**. Read them with `project_screenshots`.

The deploy response returns while these jobs run. If a job fails, the release
stays live; the reads below show which outputs are available. A **security review** of your deployed
functions runs when you call `security_review`. Your plan decides how deep it
goes and whether reviews also run automatically.

## Project docs

Start with `project_get({ project_id: "my-app" })` for entry files, pages, API
routes, tables and job handlers in the active release. Active schedules are
configured separately and listed by `cron_list`. Use `docs_query` for a specific
route, symbol or file. To read the full generated document, call `project_docs`:

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app" }
```

```json
{
  "version": 42,
  "version_source": "active_release",
  "release_id": "rel_…",
  "docs": { "status": "deterministic", "markdown": "…", "prose": null, "prose_label": null },
  "mermaid": "flowchart LR …",
  "routes": [], "symbols": [], "tables": [], "graph": {}, "coverage": {}, "files": [],
  "partial": false
}
```

The response above is trimmed. REST: `GET /v1/project-docs?project_id=my-app`,
plus `&version=41` for an earlier release.

- **What it describes.** The release that is live now, built from the source it
  was published from. Routes, tables, symbols and the dependency graph come from that source.
  Check `coverage` and `partial` for parts the analysis could not resolve. `mermaid` is a diagram of the same facts; the dashboard draws
  it on the project overview.
- **What to trust.** `docs.markdown` and the structured fields are generated
  from source without a model call.
- **Which version.** With no `version`, you get the active release's docs only.
  There is no fallback to another version.
- **No docs stored.** The call returns 404 `PROJECT_DOCS_NOT_FOUND`, and
  `status` and `no_sidecar_reason` say why. Read the source instead
  (`project_files_list`, `project_file_read`). The next successful live deploy
  queues docs again.
- **After a rollback.** Nothing new is queued. You read whatever docs are stored
  for the release now active.

For one route, file or symbol, `docs_query` answers from the same docs:
`docs_query({ project_id: "my-app", route: "POST /api/checkout" })`, or
`GET /v1/docs-query?project_id=my-app&route=POST%20/api/checkout`.

## Screenshots

Call `project_screenshots`:

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app" }
```

It returns one entry per stored image (`version`, `viewport`, `captured_at`,
`size_bytes`). Pass `"include_data": true` for the PNG as a data URL. REST:
`GET /v1/deploy/screenshots?project_id=my-app[&version=42]` includes `data_url`
and `signed_url` by default; add `include_data_url=false` to leave the image out.

The capture covers the homepage on your custom domain if one is attached,
otherwise your `*.somewhere.site` address. It shoots desktop
(1280 × 800) and mobile (375 × 667).
Previews are not captured. A failed capture never affects the deploy; that
version just has fewer images. A blank page is warned about by the
after-deploy check, never rolled back for you (`docs({ topic: 'deploy' })`).

## Security review

Call `security_review` after a deploy. `focus` is optional:

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app", "focus": "the new checkout handler" }
```

```json
{
  "status": "risks_found",
  "verdict_reasons": [],
  "findings": "## Findings\n### …",
  "finding_count": 1,
  "tier_unlocks_deep_review": false,
  "review_run_id": "…",
  "version": 42,
  "release_id": "rel_…",
  "files_shown": 6,
  "files_total": 6
}
```

The response above is trimmed; it also carries `model`, `release_seq`,
`source_authority` and `usage`. REST: `POST /v1/security/review` with the same
body. It needs editor access to the project.

**What it reads.** The live release's server functions: up to
40 files, and the first
8,000 characters of each. Frontend code and declared
data access are outside its scope. `focus` (up to
500 characters) points it at one area.

**Reading the result.** `findings` is a Markdown report rendered from a
validated result: findings, then platform best practices, then a risk summary.
Act on `status`:

- `risks_found` — fix each finding. Each one names its severity, file, region,
  impact and fix.
- `clear` — no risks found. A review returns `clear` only after reading every
  function in full.
- `indeterminate` — no conclusion either way. The review has already re-asked
  once before answering. Check `verdict_reasons` and compare `files_shown` with
  `files_total` before doing anything else:
  - `partial_input`, or `files_shown` below `files_total`: the code was cut to
    fit, so the review can report risks but can never return `clear`. Running it
    again on the same release reads the same cut-down input. To get a full read,
    split oversized function files, then deploy.
  - Any other reason: the reviewer's answer failed validation, and the platform
    has been alerted. Review again after your next deploy instead of repeating
    it now; each run is a fresh AI review.

Errors carry a `retry` field. Retry only when it says to.

**What it looks for:**

1. **Auth bypass** — a public route trusts a caller-supplied user id, session or
   role instead of `sw.auth.fromRequest(req)`.
2. **Raw SQL exposure** — request input concatenated into a query string.
3. **Unsafe payment metadata** — `sw.payments.checkout` with caller-controlled
   metadata or user id.
4. **Env leakage** — a handler returns `sw.env` values to the caller.
5. **Privilege escalation** — a public handler performs an admin-level action
   for any caller.
6. **Code execution** — `eval`, `new Function` or dynamic `import` of
   caller-controlled strings.
7. **Email spoofing** — `sw.email.send` with a `from` taken from the request.
8. **Conversation access** — `sw.ai` already ties a signed-in user's
   conversations to that user. The risk is code that reaches another user's
   history: `sw.ai.conversations.forUser(id)` or `sw.ai.scoped(id)` with an `id`
   taken from the request.
9. **CSRF** — a destructive POST with no origin or token check.

It also suggests **platform best practices**: an ownership filter missing from
raw SQL on a user-owned table, queries inside a loop, repeated endpoint
boilerplate, `fetch` calls from a function to the platform's own REST API, and
hand-written CORS headers. Best practices never change `status`. A review only
advises; it never blocks or changes a deploy.

**What your plan changes.** Every plan can request a review. Paid plans get a
longer report. Eligible paid plans also review when a preview is promoted.
When `tier_unlocks_deep_review` is `true`, the on-demand output limit is
2,048 tokens, versus 1,024 on Free. Both use the same
review model and `minimal` reasoning. Eligible promote reviews also use
`minimal` reasoning, with output limits of 2,048, 4,096 or 6,144 tokens for the
existing `pro`, `scale` and `enterprise` review depth settings respectively.
These settings limit report length; they do not certify the whole app.
Automatic runs appear in review history with `trigger: "deploy"`.
Historical scheduled runs remain in review history. There is no daily scheduled review.

```http
GET /v1/security/reviews?project_id=my-app[&limit=20][&cursor=…]
GET /v1/security/reviews/{review_run_id}?project_id=my-app
```

Each history entry carries `trigger`, `outcome`, `failure_reason`, `coverage`
(including `complete` and `limitations`) and `finding_count`. `limit` runs from
1 to 50.

## Where to read each output

| Output          | Queued or run                                          | MCP                          | REST                                                   |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Project docs    | After a successful live deploy, patch or promote       | `project_docs`, `docs_query` | `GET /v1/project-docs`, `GET /v1/docs-query`           |
| Screenshots     | After a successful live deploy, patch or promote       | `project_screenshots`        | `GET /v1/deploy/screenshots`                           |
| Security review | On demand; automatically on some plans                 | `security_review`            | `POST /v1/security/review`, `GET /v1/security/reviews` |

`GET /v1/deploy/architecture` returns the same diagram as `project_docs`, with
`superseded_by: "/v1/project-docs"`. For what an app does, read `project_docs`.

pages.title: Smoke tests — deploy and recurring checks
pages.body:
Smoke checks request your homepage, custom domains and the paths you
choose, then report which checks passed. Use them to catch a broken page,
an unexpected status or missing data after a deploy. Authenticated probes
use a fresh session for your designated test user. Check the HTTP status,
that fields are present in its JSON, and that its text contains or omits
what you expect.

Run `site_check({ project_id: "my-app" })`. If the result is still
`running`, read `site_check_status({ project_id: "my-app" })` for the
finished checks. Manual and deploy-triggered checks are available on every
plan. Recurring checks run on Builder and higher. Read the current interval
from your plan's `smoke_cadence_minutes` in `GET /v1/pricing` → `plans`.

Status per run: `pass` / `partial` / `fail`. A fail-after-pass
transition is detected and alerted automatically, debounced by
`alert_cooldown_seconds` (default 3600).

## MCP

  site_check_status({ project_id })
    → { latest: SmokeRun, history: SmokeRun[] }

  site_check({ project_id })
    → { run: SmokeRun }            // may return status: "running"; read status next

  smoke_config_get({ project_id })
  smoke_config_update({ project_id, enabled?, test_auth_flow?, alert_cooldown_seconds?, extra_checks?, test_user_email?, canary_enabled? })

`extra_checks` is an array of additional URL probes:
  [ { name: "users-list", path: "/api/users", expect_status: 200 }, ... ]

## Probe fields

Each probe accepts:

- `path` (required) — must start with `/`.
- `method` — default `GET`.
- `name` — label in run results (max 80 chars); auto-generated if omitted.
- `expect_status` — exact HTTP status. Without it, anything below 500
  passes — useful for "POST /api/login with no body should be 4xx, not
  500" and similar contract checks.
- `headers` — extra request headers (max 10 per probe).
- `body` — request body. An object is sent as JSON (Content-Type set
  for you); a string is sent raw. Max 8 KB.
- `auth: "test_user"` — the probe runs authenticated: the platform
  mints a fresh session for the project's designated test user at probe
  time. Set the test user first with
  `smoke_config_update({ project_id, test_user_email })` — it must be an existing
  app user of the project (create one via signup). No credentials are
  ever stored in the manifest. When `auth` is set, the Authorization
  header can't be overridden via `headers`.
- `expect_json_path` — dot-path (or array of them, max 10) that must
  resolve to a non-null value in the JSON response, e.g.
  `"data.reply"` or `"choices.0.message"`.
- `expect_contains` / `expect_not_contains` — substrings the response
  text must / must not contain (string or array, max 10 each).
- `expect_max_ms` — fail the probe if it takes longer than this, even
  on HTTP 200.

## 15-minute canary (opt-in)

  smoke_config_update({ project_id, canary_enabled: true })

Runs the full check set (homepage + custom domains + extra_checks +
`/_smoke_tests.json`) every 15 minutes, on top of the regular
plan cadence. Off by default. A fail-after-pass transition alerts the
project owner (debounced by `alert_cooldown_seconds`).

## Auto-detected: `/_smoke_tests.json`

Deploy a JSON file at `/_smoke_tests.json` in your project and the
cron picks up the entries automatically — same shape as
`extra_checks`, no config call needed. Up to 20 entries per project.
Useful when you want the smoke contract to ship with the code, not
sit in the dashboard. With the CLI, publish the root file explicitly:

  somewhere deploy --include _smoke_tests.json

Manifest contents:

```json
[
  { "name": "homepage",     "path": "/",                 "expect_status": 200 },
  { "name": "auth-page",    "path": "/login",            "expect_status": 200 },
  { "name": "api-list-no-auth", "path": "/api/users", "method": "GET", "expect_status": 401 }
]
```

If both `extra_checks` and `/_smoke_tests.json` are present, both
run — they're additive.

## Opt out

  smoke_config_update({ project_id: '...', enabled: false })

Disabling checks stops manual runs as well as automatic checks. While
disabled, `site_check` returns `400 NO_TARGETS`; set `enabled: true`
before running it again. For a private app,
configure authenticated probes or explicit expected status codes instead
of turning checks off.

pages.title: SQL compatibility — what Postgres code ports, and what doesn't
pages.body:
Use familiar SQL for joins, JSON and full-text search, and commit related
writes in atomic batches. The
platform translates the Postgres forms listed below into the project
database's dialect. For semantic search, use `sw.search` without a separate
vector database.

Translation differs between developer SQL tools and a SQL-mode function's
raw `sw.db.query` or `sw.db.server.query`. The sections below name each
surface and its supported forms. Expression, typing and ordering follow
the project database's dialect.

## Common SQL spellings

- `NOW()` becomes `datetime('now')`
- `TRUE` / `FALSE` become `1` / `0`
- `ILIKE` becomes `LIKE` (case-insensitive for ASCII)
- In migrations, `SERIAL` becomes `INTEGER`; declare
  `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` for generated IDs.
- `BOOLEAN` becomes `INTEGER`
- `$1, $2, …` placeholders become positional `?`
- `col->>'key'` and `col->'key'` become `json_extract(col, '$.key')`

`RETURNING` works natively on INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on write-capable
surfaces. In managed projects, `sw.db.server.query` accepts read queries
only; change declared rows through the structured operations. Run schema
changes through `db_migrate` for hand-managed tables or deploy
`db/schema.ts` for declared tables.

## Query semantics

- `SELECT 1 / 0` returns `NULL`; it does not throw a Postgres-style
  division-by-zero error. Guard the divisor explicitly when zero is invalid.
- Ascending `ORDER BY` places `NULL` first by default. Add `NULLS LAST`
  when that ordering is required.
- `LIKE` is case-insensitive for ASCII by default. Use explicit normalization
  when case behavior is part of the application contract.
- Integer operands use integer numeric affinity (`5 / 2` is `2`); use a real
  operand such as `2.0` when fractional division is required.

The database has a 30-second hard query ceiling. The runtime `sw.db.query`
surface does not expose a shorter true-cancellation contract. The external
`db_query timeout_ms` stops the caller waiting; database work already accepted
can continue.

## Additional translations in developer SQL tools

`db_query`, `db_batch`, `db_migrate` and managed
`sw.db.server.query` also translate the following forms, subject to
their read/write permissions. For `sw.db.query` or `sw.db.server.query`
inside a SQL-mode function, write the equivalent form on the right so the
query works through either the project binding or the SQL API:

- Date math: `created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'` → `created_at > datetime('now','-7 days')` (units: second, minute, hour, day, month, year)
- A standalone `SELECT generate_series(1, 10)` → `WITH RECURSIVE s(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM s WHERE n<10) SELECT n FROM s`
- `CREATE TYPE … AS ENUM('a','b')` → `col TEXT CHECK(col IN ('a','b'))` (auto-translated when the CREATE TYPE and the table using it are in the same migration)
- `array_agg(tag)` → `json_group_array(tag)`

JSONB containment `data @> '{"k":"v"}'` auto-translates to `json_extract(data,'$.k') = 'v'` for the **flat case** — one or more keys whose values are scalar strings or numbers (multiple keys are AND-ed together, matching containment). Nested objects, array values, and boolean/null values are NOT auto-translated — they would risk silently matching the wrong rows, so they fail loud; write the explicit `json_extract` conditions yourself for those.

## Forms to replace

The developer SQL tools reject these forms with a corrective error. Raw
queries through a function's project database binding return the database
error; queries routed through the SQL API receive the corrective error.

- `DISTINCT ON (user_id) … ORDER BY user_id, created_at DESC` → use
  `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)`
  and keep `rn = 1`.
- `tags TEXT[]` (any array type) → store as JSON text: `tags TEXT DEFAULT '[]'`, query with `WHERE tag IN (SELECT value FROM json_each(tags))`
- `BEGIN; … COMMIT;` in one query → use `sw.db.tx([...])` for declared tables (atomic, all-or-nothing); in a SQL-mode project `sw.db.batch([{ sql, params }, …])` is the raw equivalent
- `GEOMETRY`, `GEOGRAPHY`, `TSVECTOR`, `HSTORE`, `INET`, `BYTEA`, … → use full-text / `sw.search` / `sw.fs`; otherwise move the workload to Postgres

Arrays are the most common: store them as a JSON text column and unroll with `json_each()` for querying.

## Built-in alternatives

- Full-text search — native: `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE docs USING fts5(title, body)`, then `WHERE docs MATCH 'term'`. Or `sw.search` for embeddings + ranking.
- Vector / semantic search — `sw.search` (no separate vector database).
- Per-user row security — the structured builder
  `sw.db.from/insert/update/remove` on a declared `scoped` table, instead of
  CREATE POLICY.

## Not available on the managed database

PL/pgSQL (write logic in your server function), PostGIS, table
partitioning, and custom engine index types (GIN/GiST/BRIN — use an
app-managed index table + FTS5). For genuinely Postgres-only needs you can
attach your own PostgreSQL database and query it alongside `sw.db` —
`docs({ topic: 'postgres' })` — or export and move the workload out entirely.
Either way the platform does not provide a managed Postgres adapter or an
automatic migration service: an attached database is pass-through, and moving
existing data into it is yours to do.

Related: `database-engine`, `sw.db`, `postgres`, `portability`.

pages.title: PostgreSQL
pages.body:
Attach one PostgreSQL database that you own to a project, then query it from
your deployed functions as `sw.postgres`. The provider is Neon. You keep the
Neon account and Neon bills you directly. Attaching works on every plan.

The steps below use `jq` to build request bodies.

## Connect and attach

Create a Neon API key in your Neon account. The CLI reads it from
`SOMEWHERE_NEON_API_KEY`, stdin or a hidden prompt, never from an argument.

```bash
# Set NEON_PROJECT_ID to your existing Neon project's ID.
printf %s "$NEON_API_KEY" | somewhere postgres connect --project my-app --neon-project "$NEON_PROJECT_ID"
somewhere postgres attach "$NEON_PROJECT_ID" --project my-app
```

To start with a new database instead, run `somewhere postgres create --project
my-app` with an organization or account key. Neon bills you for it, and the
default region is `aws-us-east-2` unless you pass `--region`.

## Separate application credentials

```bash
somewhere api POST /v1/postgres/credentials/separate -d '{"project_id":"my-app"}'
```

After this, deployed functions connect as a restricted role that can read and
write table rows but cannot change the schema. Schema changes go through
migrations. Details are in **Restricted application role** below.

## Create a table

Keep migration SQL outside your app folder, so it is not deployed as a public
file. Save this as `../my-app-migrations/0001_tickets.sql`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tickets (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id text NOT NULL,
  title text NOT NULL,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX tickets_owner_status ON tickets (owner_id, status, created_at DESC);
```

Apply it:

```bash
jq -n --rawfile sql ../my-app-migrations/0001_tickets.sql \
  '{project_id: "my-app", target: "production", name: "0001_tickets", sql: $sql}' \
  | somewhere api POST /v1/postgres/migrations/apply --data-file -
```

The restricted role created above can read and write the new table.

## Query from a function

Derive the user from the verified session with `sw.auth.requireUser(req)`, and
pass every value to SQL as a parameter. Your `WHERE` clause decides which rows
the user can see.

```ts
// api/tickets.ts
export default async function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> {
  const user = await sw.auth.requireUser(req); // 401 when not signed in
  const status = new URL(req.url).searchParams.get('status') ?? 'open';

  const tickets = await sw.postgres.query(
    'SELECT id, title, status FROM tickets WHERE owner_id = $1 AND status = $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50',
    [user.id, status],
  );
  return Response.json({ tickets });
}
```

Deploy with `somewhere deploy`. A deployed release keeps the connection it was
built with, so deploy again after any connection change.

`sw.postgres` is the callable that `neon(connectionString)` returns from
`@neondatabase/serverless` 1.1.0, bound to your database.
Its shapes, results and errors are the driver's:

- A query resolves to an array of rows, and errors throw. There is no
  `{ data, error }` envelope.
- The tagged-template form sends each interpolated value as a parameter.
- `sw.postgres.transaction([...])` sends a list of statements in one round trip
  and applies them together. A failing statement makes the call throw and none
  of the list applies. Use it to batch independent reads, too.
- The list is fixed before the call. Express read-then-write logic in SQL, with
  a conditional `UPDATE`, a CTE or `RETURNING`.
- Each `query` call is its own request, so separate `BEGIN` and `ROLLBACK` calls
  undo nothing. Use `transaction([...])`.
- The third argument of `query(text, params, options)` is the driver's options.
  It does not filter rows; the `WHERE` clause does.
- `sw.postgres.unsafe(text)` splices text into a tagged template unparameterized. Use it
  only for SQL you wrote, never for a value.

---

## Restricted application role

`POST /v1/postgres/credentials/separate` requires project owner access. It
does the following:

- Creates a login role with `NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOREPLICATION
  NOBYPASSRLS NOINHERIT`.
- Grants it `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on tables in schema
  `public`, and usage of their sequences.
- Grants it the same on tables and sequences the attached role creates in
  `public` later.
- Logs in as the new role and confirms that it owns no objects and cannot run
  persistent DDL.

The attached role becomes the migration credential, which deployed functions
never receive. The attached role must be able to create roles. If existing
grants would give the new role more than the above, the call fails with
`POSTGRES_RUNTIME_ROLE_UNSAFE`. Review those existing grants in your database;
the platform leaves them unchanged.

Row-level security policies apply to the restricted role. The platform does
not write policies or tell the database which app user is calling, so the
authorization in your handler stays required.

Re-check both credentials with `POST /v1/postgres/credentials/verify`. If a
separation was interrupted, finish it with `POST /v1/postgres/credentials/recover`
and body `{"project_id":"my-app","action":"finalize"}`, or discard it with
`"action":"abandon"` after you have inspected and removed the role. No second
login role is created for the same setup.

## Migrations

Migrations need separated credentials. Each request applies one SQL file of up
to 1 MiB, as the migration role, over a direct
connection. Do not put `BEGIN`, `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` in the file.

- **Ledger:** applied migrations are recorded in
  `_somewhere_migrations.history` in your database. Read it with
  `somewhere api GET "/v1/postgres/migrations/status?project_id=my-app&target=production"`.
- **Re-applying:** re-applying an applied name with the same SQL returns its
  existing receipt. A failed migration is rolled back and can be applied again.
  Reusing a name with different SQL is refused with
  `POSTGRES_MIGRATION_CHANGED`.
- **Unknown outcome:** if the connection ends before the platform can confirm the outcome, the migration is marked
  `POSTGRES_MIGRATION_UNCERTAIN`. Its SQL may have committed, and later
  migrations are refused until you inspect the database.
- **Preview database:** use `"target": "preview"` to migrate the preview
  database instead.

## Preview databases

A preview release receives only the preview database's connection. It never
receives the production connection. If the project has no preview database,
or the preview database is not ready or no longer matches the attached
production credentials, `sw.postgres` in a preview throws
`POSTGRES_NOT_ATTACHED`. Draft runs receive no connection.

```bash
somewhere api POST /v1/postgres/preview -d '{"project_id":"my-app","action":"create"}'
```

`create` makes one child branch of your production branch in your Neon account,
which Neon bills to you.

- **What it holds:** a full copy of production data at creation, including any
  personal data production holds. Writes to the preview database do not reach
  production.
- **Binding:** deploy a preview after `create` to bind it.
- **`reset`:** replaces the preview's data with production's current data.
- **`delete`:** deletes exactly that branch.
- **Data loss:** both `reset` and `delete` discard everything written to the
  preview.

Creating one needs separated credentials and an attachment that records its
branch. Previews themselves depend on your plan: check `preview_allowed` under
`tiers[].limits` in `GET /v1/pricing`. Read the preview database's state with
`somewhere api GET "/v1/postgres/preview?project_id=my-app"`.

## Copy your project database into PostgreSQL

A project owner can copy the project database's tables into a new schema of
the attached Neon database. The copy needs separated credentials. The project
database keeps serving the app until you change your code to use
`sw.postgres`.

```bash
somewhere api POST /v1/postgres/copy/prepare -d '{"project_id":"my-app","schema":"app_copy"}' > copy-plan.json
jq '{project_id: "my-app", plan: .plan}' copy-plan.json | somewhere api POST /v1/postgres/copy --data-file -
somewhere api GET "/v1/postgres/copy/status?project_id=my-app&schema=app_copy"
```

- **Prepare and copy:** `prepare` writes nothing. It returns the plan, the
  tables and the refusals. `copy` runs exactly that plan, or refuses when the
  source or destination changed since.
- **Atomicity:** the copy runs in one transaction. A refusal, failure or
  timeout rolls it back. Only `POSTGRES_COPY_OUTCOME_UNCERTAIN` means it may
  have committed. In that case read the copy status. Retrying the same plan
  returns the saved receipt if it committed.
- **Fidelity:** values are copied exactly, with primary keys, unique rules,
  foreign keys and `NOT NULL`. Supported defaults are translated, and integer
  row-id keys become identity columns.
  - CHECK rules, triggers, views, non-binary collations, unsupported defaults,
    virtual search tables and references to tables that are not copied refuse
    the copy.
  - Non-unique partial and expression indexes are listed, not recreated.
  - Platform tables and app user accounts and sessions are excluded and
    listed.
  - Rows written after the snapshot are not copied.
  - Later writes follow PostgreSQL semantics; the response lists the
    differences under `fidelity`.
- **Access:** access rules are not copied. The new schema belongs to the
  migration role, and other roles cannot read it until you grant access; the
  receipt lists the administrative roles that still can. To query it from
  functions, grant the application role access or move the tables into
  `public`.
- **Limits:** one copy holds up to 64 tables,
  20,000 rows and 4 MiB of values,
  and must finish within 60 seconds.

## Where your functions run

Functions run near the visitor by default. To ask for them to run closer to
the database:

```bash
somewhere api PATCH /v1/projects/<project-id> -d '{"placement":"near-data"}'
```

Use the project's id here, not its slug. Change back with
`"placement":"near-user"`.

- **When it applies:** placement takes effect on the next deploy. If it cannot
  be applied, the deploy still succeeds, says so and retries on the next
  deploy. Static files stay at the edge. Placement is not a data-residency
  guarantee.
- **Automatic placement:** if you have never set a placement, attaching sets
  `near-data` for releases that carry a database connection.
- **Disconnect:** disconnecting undoes only a placement the attachment set.
- **Status:** `somewhere postgres status --json` reports
  `function_placement.preference` and its `provenance` (`default`, `explicit`
  or `neon-attachment`).

To choose, measure your own workload under each placement with the same data,
indexes, statements and authorization `WHERE`. Report first and repeated
requests separately, and report p50 and p95.

## Changing or removing the connection

- **Disconnect unlinks; it never deletes.** `somewhere postgres disconnect`
  leaves your Neon project and data as they are, including a database the
  platform created. It keeps the stored API key unless you pass `--forget-key`.
- **To cut off access, rotate the password in Neon.** Releases already deployed
  keep the credential they were built with. Attaching does not rotate it.
- **Functions receive only the connection string.** It arrives as a secret
  binding that is not in `sw.env`. Your function code and its dependencies run
  with that role's authority. The Neon API key is used only by the attachment
  management calls, and no management call returns either credential.
- **A function deleted from your source keeps serving** until you deploy with
  `--replace-functions`.
- **Access:** the management routes are under `/v1/postgres/` and take a
  developer credential. Changes need project owner access. Status, migration
  status, copy status and preview status need editor access.

## Creating a database: no automatic retries

Neon's create call has no idempotency key, so a retried create can make a
second billed database. Each request makes one create attempt and never
retries it, and parallel requests cannot both create.

- **`POSTGRES_CREATE_UNCERTAIN`:** the outcome was unreadable, so a database
  may exist. Check your Neon account. Then attach it with
  `somewhere postgres attach <neon-project-id>`, or disconnect to clear the
  state.
- **`POSTGRES_CREATE_IN_PROGRESS`:** an earlier create is unresolved. The error
  names the database, its start time and, when known, the Neon project id.
  Nothing expires this state. Wait if the create is still running. Otherwise
  attach the database if you find it, or disconnect once you have reconciled.
- **Disconnecting during an unresolved create** returns the Neon project id (or
  name and start time) once, with `unresolved_note`. The database stays in your
  Neon account, billing, until you attach or delete it.
- **`POSTGRES_CREATE_SUPERSEDED`:** the database was created, but the project
  changed during the create, so it was not attached. Its id is in the error.

## Errors

| Code | Meaning and fix |
|---|---|
| `POSTGRES_NOT_ATTACHED` | No database, or the release predates the attachment. Attach, then deploy again. |
| `POSTGRES_NOT_CONNECTED` | No API key stored. Run `somewhere postgres connect`. |
| `POSTGRES_KEY_SCOPE_UNKNOWN` | The key cannot list projects. Pass `--neon-project` for a project-scoped key. |
| `POSTGRES_PROVIDER_UNAUTHORIZED` | Neon refused the key. Store a valid key. |
| `POSTGRES_PROVIDER_UNREACHABLE` | Neon could not be reached. The key was not stored. |
| `POSTGRES_BRANCH_AMBIGUOUS`, `POSTGRES_DATABASE_AMBIGUOUS`, `POSTGRES_ROLE_AMBIGUOUS` | More than one candidate. Pass `--branch`, `--database` or `--role` to `attach`. |
| `POSTGRES_CONNECTION_URI_INCOMPLETE` | Neon returned no password for that role. Choose another role. The platform never resets a role password. |
| `POSTGRES_CREDENTIALS_NOT_SEPARATED` | Separate application credentials before migrations, preview databases or copy. |

Related: `sw.db`, `sw.auth`, `security-model`, `database-engine`,
`sql-compatibility`.

pages.title: CORS — which browser origins may call your project's functions
pages.body:
Read this when a browser call to your API returns
`403 {"ok":false,"error":"ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED"}`, or before you point a
frontend hosted elsewhere at a somewhere.cloud project.

The same origin policy applies to every project. There is no opt-out. The policy is enforced when the request reaches the project, so
existing apps do not need a new deploy for it.

## Your own origins are allowed by construction — nothing to configure

While the platform is serving your project on a host, that host's origin is
your project's own origin. There is no row to write and nothing to turn on:

- your **production** project URL, `https://<subdomain>.somewhere.site`
- every **verified custom domain** attached to the project
- your **private preview** URL

A brand-new project has an empty allowlist and its own frontend still works.
If you are calling your API from a page the platform served for that same
project, the allowlist is not your problem — read "Diagnose a 403" below.

The one nuance: a preview origin is admitted while the preview host is being
served, and a production origin while production is being served. It is not a
cross-environment grant, so a page on your production host calling your
preview host is a third-party call and needs the allowlist.

## The allowlist is for THIRD-PARTY origins only

Configure an origin when the page making the call is **not** served by this
project — a frontend you host elsewhere, a marketing site on another
domain, a local dev server on `http://localhost:5173`, or another
somewhere.cloud project.

Manage the list with `somewhere project allowed-origins`. Your own origins
are never listed.

```bash
# Read the current list first — set replaces it wholesale.
somewhere project allowed-origins list --project my-app

# Replace the FULL list. Include everything you want kept.
somewhere project allowed-origins set https://app.example.com http://localhost:5173 --project my-app

# Allow no other origins; the project's own addresses stay trusted.
somewhere project allowed-origins set --clear --project my-app
```

`--project` defaults to the linked project.

The response returns the configured `allowed_origins`. There is no
`cors_mode` setting or response field; sending that obsolete selector to a
project update or to `project_allowed_origins_set` is rejected.

Over MCP the same tools are `project_allowed_origins_get` and
`project_allowed_origins_set`. `project_id` accepts the UUID, subdomain or slug; use the resolved
`project_id` the response echoes in follow-up calls.

Rules the platform enforces on each entry:

- An **exact origin**: scheme + host + optional port. No path, query,
  fragment, credentials, or wildcards — `https://app.example.com/` and
