  `https://*.example.com` are both rejected with `VALIDATION_ERROR`.
- `https` only, except `http://localhost` and `http://127.0.0.1`.
- Matching is **byte-exact**. A different subdomain, a different port, and a
  trailing slash are each a different origin and must be listed on their own.
- At most 50 origins per project.
- Reading the list is open to any project member; changing it is the project
  **owner or a platform admin** only, and every change is audited.

## What is refused, and what reaches your function

The check covers requests to your functions (`/api/*`), the managed data
and files endpoints (`/__sw/data`, `/__sw/files`) and live list connections
(`/__sw/live/subscribe`). It is about
**credentials**, not about blocking traffic:

| Request | Outcome |
|---|---|
| No `Origin` header (server-to-server, `curl`, a mobile app) | Reaches your function. CORS is a browser mechanism; a non-browser caller is unaffected. A `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` authenticated by a session cookie gets `400 ORIGIN_REQUIRED` when your function reads its user: send the app's `Origin`, or use `Authorization: Bearer`. |
| Approved origin (own or configured) | Reaches your function. The platform adds the CORS response headers, including `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`. |
| Approved origin, `OPTIONS` preflight | Answered by the platform with `204` and those headers. You never write preflight boilerplate. |
| Unapproved origin, **no** `Cookie` and **no** `Authorization`, method `GET`/`HEAD`/`POST` | Reaches your function, with **no** platform CORS headers. Whether the browser may read the result is decided by the headers your own handler sets. |
| Unapproved origin carrying `Cookie` or `Authorization` | Refused with `403 {"ok":false,"error":"ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED"}` before your code runs. |
| Unapproved origin, preflight advertising a method other than `GET`/`HEAD`/`POST`, or `Authorization`/`Cookie` in `Access-Control-Request-Headers` | Same `403`. The preflight is announcing a credentialed follow-up. |

So a deliberately public, credentialless API stays possible: set your own
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (without `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`)
in the handler's response. When your handler sets its own
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, that header wins and the platform layers
nothing on top.

## Diagnose a 403 ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED

1. Read the exact `Origin` header the browser sent — the DevTools Network
   tab shows it on the failing request. That string, byte for byte, is what
   has to match.
2. Is it a host the platform serves for **this** project (production URL,
   verified custom domain, this project's preview)? Then it is already
   allowed, and the failure is something else: a stale bookmark on an old
   subdomain, a call aimed at a different project, or a custom domain that is
   attached but not yet verified. Check with
   `somewhere call project_get '{"project_id":"my-app"}'` and
   `somewhere call domain_list '{"project_id":"my-app"}'`.
3. Otherwise it is a third-party origin: add it with
   `project_allowed_origins_set`, sending the full list.
4. Not from a browser at all? Then `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED` means something is
   forwarding a foreign `Origin` header along with a cookie or bearer token.
   With `Authorization: Bearer`, drop the `Origin` header — bearer calls are
   not origin-checked. With a session cookie, a write still needs an
   `Origin` (`400 ORIGIN_REQUIRED` without one): send this project's own
   origin, or switch to `Authorization: Bearer` (`docs({ topic: 'auth-client' })`).

Related: `security-model`, `auth-client`, `troubleshooting`.

pages.title: Design System — Read before generating UI
pages.body:
Decide how the app looks before you build features, then build every screen from that decision. The React starter from `somewhere init` gives you the pieces: design tokens in `src/styles/tokens.css`, shared classes in `src/styles/app.css`, and ready components in `src/ui/`. Choose a visual idea that fits your audience, record it in `DESIGN.md`, and set the starter's colors and fonts to match. Build one screen with its loading, empty and error states before adding features. Reuse those tokens and components on the next screen so the app keeps the same look. Deploy the raw source to check the result on a phone; the platform compiles it for you. ## Decide the look first Write the decision down in a short `DESIGN.md` at the project root, before the first feature. Keep it to a few lines your agent can reread every session: - **Audience** — who uses the app and where (a nurse between shifts, a collector browsing at night). - **One distinctive idea** — something specific enough to recognize. "Library card: cream paper, oxblood accent, serif headings" works; "clean and modern" describes every app. - **Palette, type and layout** — the token values you chose and why. - **Components** — which starter components you use as they are, and what you add. ```md # DESIGN.md — reading list Audience: readers keeping a shelf of books to read next, mostly on a phone. Idea: a library card — cream paper, an oxblood accent, a serif display face. Palette: --color-bg #f6f0e4, --color-accent #7a1f2b; neutrals stay warm. Type: Iowan Old Style for headings, Avenir Next for body text. Layout: one centered column; each book is a .panel row. Components: AppShell and AuthCard as shipped; EmptyState for an empty shelf. ``` Point to it from the starter's `AGENTS.md` so every session reads it. A root `.md` file stays on your machine: `somewhere deploy` publishes it only if your app references it or you opt it in with `somewhere deploy --include DESIGN.md` (or a `!DESIGN.md` line in `.somewhereignore`). ## Start from the starter | File | What it holds | |---|---| | `src/styles/tokens.css` | The design values, as custom properties on `:root`, with a light block and a dark block. | | `src/styles/app.css` | The classes the kit renders and the shared ones (`.panel`, `.muted`, `.hint`, `.error`), all reading the tokens. | | `src/ui/` | The UI kit: `Button`, `TextField`, `SelectField`, `TextareaField`, `CheckboxField`, `FormRow`, `Card`, `Table`, `Stat`, `Badge`, `Tabs`, `Dialog`, `Notice`, `Skeleton`, `Stack`, `Grid`, `Inline`, `PageHeader`; plus `AppShell` (the frame), `AuthCard` (sign-in) and `feedback.tsx` (`Alert`, `EmptyState`). | | `src/pages/HomePage.tsx` | A worked example of the kit: a header with the one main action, a stat row, a table in a card, a dialog form. Copy its shape. | Set your design in `tokens.css` first; the starter's classes and components read it. Reuse them before writing new ones, and have new components read the same tokens, so a new screen carries the look instead of restating it. ## Build with the kit The starter is a small design system, and pages built with it look finished; pages built around it look like a form from 2009. The rules that keep a page inside the system: - Every control is a kit component. A bare ``, `` with the browser's grey box and square arrow: it is not a `SelectField`. ## Add to the sign-in page `AuthCard` has two slots: `providers` above the email form and `children` below it. Social sign-in buttons go in `providers`, which `SIGN_IN_PROVIDERS` in `src/config.ts` already fills; a magic-link form or a terms line goes in `children`. Nothing is added as a sibling of the card: its two-column grid holds exactly the intro and the form, and a third child lands in its own row. `APP_NAME` and `APP_TAGLINE` in `src/config.ts` set the page's words. ## CSS variable convention (theme-correct by default) Components read colors, type, spacing and radii from the tokens, never from hardcoded values: ```tsx

Saved

``` The starter's tokens: | Tokens | Use | |---|---| | `--color-bg`, `--color-surface`, `--color-surface-2` | Page background, panels and inputs, a subtle second surface | | `--color-text`, `--color-muted` | Body text, secondary text | | `--color-border`, `--color-border-strong` | Dividers, input borders | | `--color-accent`, `--color-accent-hover`, `--color-accent-soft`, `--color-on-accent` | Primary actions, their hover, a tint, and the text on them | | `--color-danger`, `--color-focus` | Errors, the keyboard focus ring | | `--color-success`, `--color-warning`, `--color-info` (+ `-soft`) | Tones for `Badge`, `Notice` and `Stat` details, never for buttons | | `--font-display`, `--font-body`, `--font-mono` | Headings, everything else, codes and IDs | | `--text-xs` … `--text-2xl`, `--text-display` | Type sizes | | `--space-1` … `--space-16` | Spacing in steps of 4px | | `--radius-control`, `--radius-panel`, `--radius-pill` | Inputs and buttons, panels, badges | | `--shadow-sm`, `--shadow-md`, `--shadow-lg` | Cards, panels, dialogs | | `--control-height`, `--content-width` | The 44px control height, the page column | Pick one accent and let everything else stay quiet: tinted neutrals for background and surface, with the surface distinct from the background. When you need a value the set lacks, add a token to `tokens.css` and use it, so the next change happens in one place. The starter ships both modes: `tokens.css` holds the light values on `:root` and the dark values in a `prefers-color-scheme: dark` block, so a colour you change is changed in both. Keep the font, spacing and radius tokens shared. For the library-card idea, cream paper and an oxblood accent, the colour part of the file looks like this: ```css :root { color-scheme: light dark; --color-bg: #f6f0e4; --color-surface: #fffcf5; --color-text: #221c17; --color-muted: #6b5f53; --color-border: #918170; --color-accent: #7a1f2b; --color-on-accent: #fffcf5; --color-danger: #a63c12; --color-focus: #7a1f2b; } @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { --color-bg: #1b1714; --color-surface: #26201b; --color-text: #f1e8da; --color-muted: #b8aa98; --color-border: #80705f; --color-accent: #e3a1a6; --color-on-accent: #2a0c10; --color-danger: #f4a06a; --color-focus: #e3a1a6; } } ``` The page switches with the device setting, so there is no toggle to build. `color-scheme` lets the browser draw scrollbars and form controls to match. In both modes, body text, secondary text, links and errors keep at least 4.5:1 contrast on the page and on panels, and button text keeps it on the accent. The starter's classes follow these tokens; check any component that sets its own colors. ## Font pairing — defaults that work The starter uses local font stacks, so text renders immediately with no font download. Pair one display face with one body face, and choose the pairing to fit your distinctive idea: - **Precise** — the system sans for both. The starter's default: `--font-body: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif` with `--font-display: var(--font-body)`, `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on figures and `--font-mono` for codes and IDs. Suits dashboards and tools, and falls back well on every platform. - **Editorial** — serif headings over the same sans: set `--font-display: "Iowan Old Style", "Palatino Linotype", Palatino, Georgia, serif`. - **Friendly** — a rounded display face (`ui-rounded, "SF Pro Rounded", system-ui, sans-serif`) over the system sans. Suits consumer and family apps. Local stacks are the working default. To use a font you chose deliberately, add its `.woff2` to the project, declare it with `@font-face` in `tokens.css`, and name it first in `--font-display` or `--font-body`, keeping the local stack as the fallback. Setting fonts through these two tokens keeps the choice in one place. ## Layout - One centered content column on phones; switch to a grid from about `768px` when the content has two real columns. - Space with the `--space-*` tokens rather than freehand pixel values. ## Animation - Keep hover and press feedback short: transitions on color and shadow around 150ms. - Wrap motion in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`. ## The edit→deploy→verify loop Build each feature on the design: write the screen with the starter components and token classes, then deploy and check it. Read the live source, make the smallest coherent edit, run the relevant local check, deploy once, and verify the public `.somewhere.site` URL. The default workflow has no staging or private-preview step. ## Read the live tokens back `project_design_tokens({ project_id })` returns the palette, fonts, spacing and radii found in the authored CSS of the project's active release (from a shell: `somewhere call project_design_tokens '{"project_id":"my-app"}'`). Use it to check what shipped, or to hand a visual editor the current values. ## One theme across projects Projects in a group can share a theme. The group stores design tokens as a JSON object, written by an owner or editor with `PUT /v1/groups/:id/tokens` `{ "tokens": { "color-accent": "#7a1f2b" } }` and read back with `group_get`. Keys may omit the leading `--`. Member sites receive them as custom properties on `:root` on later page loads, with no redeploy. A project's own declarations take precedence: a token defined in its `tokens.css` overrides the group value. To let a member follow the group, leave that token out of the member's `tokens.css`. The full group model is in `project-groups` → `the-shared-theme`. ## Self-check before `somewhere deploy` 1. Search the components for hex colors and raw font names; each should be a token. 2. Search the pages for bare ``, `

pages.title: Pricing
pages.body:
Bandwidth is included on every plan. We do not meter it or bill for it.
Fair use applies: this covers normal traffic to your app's pages, functions and files.

Database, auth, functions, files, email and custom domains are included on every plan. Projects and deploys are unlimited. Paid plans add capacity and features.

Prices are in USD per month. Database and file storage allowances are totals across your account.

| Plan | Monthly price | Database storage | File storage | Auth users | Transactional emails / month |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Free | $0 | 500 MB | 5 GB | 1,000 | 4,500 |
| Builder | $25 | 10 GB | 100 GB | Unlimited | 50,000 |
| Pro | $50 | 25 GB | 250 GB | Unlimited | 100,000 |
| Scale | $100 | 50 GB | 1 TB | Unlimited | 250,000 |
| Enterprise | Custom | Custom | Custom | Custom | Custom |

### Plan allowances for file storage and outbound email

On Free, reaching a limit stops new writes or sends until the next period or an upgrade. On paid plans, allowances are not hard stops: we warn you and your app keeps running, with no overage charges. Nothing is deleted, and nothing is charged without your say-so.

Free file storage has no reset period. Deleting files yourself frees space. Technical limits and AI have separate rules. For paid AI, add to your prepaid balance. Automatic top-up applies only if you turn it on.

Enterprise: contact us.

See [what happens at each limit](https://somewhere.cloud/pricing.txt) for details.

Managed data grows with your app; the platform handles storage. Your account allowance covers the total across projects. Authentication emails are quota-exempt; abuse protection still applies.

### Included allowances

- **Free:** 10 scheduled jobs per project, minimum interval 5 minutes; 10 MB per upload; 10 browser sessions; managed AI included. Transactional email also has a 150 per-day limit.
- **Builder:** 100 scheduled jobs per project, minimum interval 1 minutes; 250 MB per upload; 10 browser sessions; managed AI included.
- **Pro:** 100 scheduled jobs per project, minimum interval 1 minutes; 250 MB per upload; 10 browser sessions; managed AI included.
- **Scale:** 100 scheduled jobs per project, minimum interval 1 minutes; 250 MB per upload; 10 browser sessions; managed AI included.

Payments through Stripe Connect have a 0.5% platform fee in addition to Stripe processing fees. Managed AI uses published model rates; see [AI billing](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/billing.txt).

This table is generated from [the public pricing API](https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/pricing) when the docs are published. Read that endpoint for live values, or [compare plans](https://somewhere.cloud/pricing).

pages.title: Plans & Pricing
pages.body:
(Building YOUR OWN app's plans + feature-gating for your users? That's a
different thing — see `docs({ topic: 'sw.billing' })`. This topic is what
somewhere.cloud charges you.)

Pricing is DB-driven (the tier_plans table) and served live at
/v1/pricing — always fetch that for the current numbers rather than
hardcoding them. Every tier includes unlimited projects and deploys.
Bandwidth is included on every plan. We do not meter it or bill for it. Fair use applies: this covers normal traffic to your app's pages, functions and files. Custom domains are free on every tier.

Payments: charges settle to your connected account, minus Stripe's standard
processing fee and a 0.5% platform fee (each checkout response includes
`fee_percent` so you can account for it). Managed AI uses the same all-in
catalog rates on every tier. Every plan includes a managed-AI allowance that
renews each month on Free and each billing period on paid plans. Included/default calls never spend prepaid
balance automatically; explicit paid-model selection on Free uses prepaid
only, while eligible paid-plan calls use the allowance first and then prepaid.
Published request and model limits still apply.

## Balance and included AI
`GET /v1/billing/balance` keeps the prepaid balance fields at the top level
and reports the plan inclusion separately as `included_ai`:

```text
included_ai: {
  scope: "account"
  period_start: number | null
  period_end: number | null
  allowance_microdollars, spent_microdollars, reserved_microdollars,
  available_microdollars: number
  allowance_dollars, spent_dollars, reserved_dollars, available_dollars: number
}
```

Period values are Unix epoch milliseconds, or null. `spent` is settled use;
`reserved` is outstanding included-allowance holds and must not be counted as
spent. Included `available` is clamped at zero. It is distinct from the
top-level prepaid `balance`, `pending` and `available` values.

## The tiers
Five tiers — Free, Builder, Pro, Scale, Enterprise. Fetch /v1/pricing for the
live prices and per-tier caps (files, database, email, realtime publishes,
upload size, uptime-check frequency). They differ along two axes:

- **Core platform plus plan capabilities.** Every tier includes functions,
  database, auth, outbound email, AI, payments, files, live updates, one-shot
  jobs, customer cron schedules, builds, and deploys. Higher tiers raise caps
  and shorten the minimum schedule interval; Builder and higher add recurring
  smoke checks. See /v1/pricing for the current
  numbers and capability flags.
- **Service level.** Free uses its included AI allowance and request limits.
  Every plan can request a review. Paid plans get a longer report. Eligible paid
  plans also review when a preview is promoted. Pro adds office hours.
  Scale adds priority support. Enterprise adds custom limits, contracts, SLA, and
  invoicing.

## The "unlimited" caveat
Advertised "unlimited" (e.g. database rows / auth users on higher tiers)
means a high SAFETY cap, never literally uncapped — to protect shared
infrastructure. Row/user counts are metered with warnings before any cap;
the platform never silently blacks out a live app at a limit.

## Check your plan / upgrade
Your plan covers your account. See it under [Plan and billing](https://somewhere.cloud/app/account/billing).
Upgrade there, or create a platform subscription checkout directly:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/billing/checkout \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SOMEWHERE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"plan":"builder"}'
```

The JSON body has exactly one field, `plan`, whose value is `builder`,
`pro`, or `scale`. This platform upgrade does not take a Stripe Price ID.

Read the [current plans and prices](https://somewhere.cloud/pricing.txt) or query

pages.title: You own your domain
pages.body:
When you buy a domain through somewhere.cloud, it is registered in **your name** from the moment of purchase. The owner of record is you — not us.

## What that means

- **You are the legal owner.** The registration lists your name and email as the registrant. Somewhere HQ, Inc. appears only as the operational contact, which is what lets us handle DNS, SSL, and renewals for you.
- **Privacy protection.** On purchase the platform turns on the registrar's free privacy protection, which keeps your name and email out of public domain lookups on endings that support it.
- **Your address stays private too.** We don't ask for a postal address when you buy; the record uses our company address on your behalf.

## Price

You pay the registrar's price with no markup. The first year can be a registrar promotion priced below later years; the purchase page and the search show the price of each later year.

## Taking your domain elsewhere

You can keep the domain here or move it:

1. **Keep it here (default).** We manage DNS, SSL, and renewal. Nothing to do.
2. **Move it to your own Name.com account.** Free, from 5 days after registration. Name.com is the registrar of every domain bought here.
3. **Transfer to any other registrar.** Standard transfer with an authorization code, from 60 days after registration: the [ICANN transfer rule](https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/name-holder-faqs-2017-10-10-en) lets a registrar refuse a transfer in a domain's first 60 days, and Name.com locks every new registration for those 60 days. Country endings such as .co.uk and .de follow their own registry's rules.

To start option 2 or 3, email support@somewhere.cloud from your account email and name the domain. No exit fees, no retention hoops.

## Renewals

Each year the platform charges the registrar's renewal price at that time, with no markup, and then renews the domain. If the charge does not go through, you are emailed and the domain is not renewed. Automatic renewal can be turned off for a domain at any time.

## Domains you bought elsewhere

Connecting a domain you already own (from any registrar) never changes its ownership — it stays in your account at your registrar; we only serve traffic for it.

pages.title: sw.logs — Application Logging (inside deployed functions)
Analytics — Track Events, Query Aggregates
pages.body:
Answer product questions such as "how many people who start onboarding finish
it?" Record `onboarding_started` and `onboarding_completed` from your functions
with `sw.analytics.track`. Events go to the platform's event store, outside
your app database, so there is no table to create. Compare the daily counts
with two MCP calls:

```text
analytics_query({ project_id: "my-app", event: "onboarding_started", group_by: "day" })
analytics_query({ project_id: "my-app", event: "onboarding_completed", group_by: "day" })
```

Each returns `{ rows: [{ bucket: "2026-09-02", count: 31 }, …], count, group_by: "day" }`,
newest day first. Convert each count with `Number(row.count)`, then divide
completed by started for each day to get the completion rate. Page views are
counted on the server with no script in your pages, and kept apart from
events (**Page views** below).

## Record an event from your app

Copy the checked handler in `browser` → `count-what-users-do`. It requires a
signed-in user, accepts only the event names you list, and returns the track
result. Add `onboarding_started` and `onboarding_completed` to the event
names it accepts, and call it at each step.

`sw.analytics.track(event, { properties?, page?, referrer?, user_agent? })`
waits for the platform and returns one of:

- `{ recorded: true, event, user_id, attribution }`
- `{ recorded: false, reason }`, where `reason` is `consent_pending`,
  `consent_declined` or `consent_unavailable` when the project requires
  visitor consent (**Consent** below)

Not recording is a normal result, not an error. When recording is allowed, an
invalid event or a platform failure throws.

The platform sets the attribution. When the request comes from a verified
signed-in user, `user_id` is their id and `attribution` is `"app_user"`;
otherwise the event belongs to the project (`user_id: null`,
`attribution: "project"`). Identity fields in the options are ignored, so a
caller cannot claim to be someone else.

Name events as stable snake_case verbs (`onboarding_completed`,
`checkout_started`) and keep names short. `properties` is a JSON object of
labels you can read back on raw rows. Queries count events; they do not sum or
average property values. An event name or `properties` over the size limit
returns `VALIDATION_ERROR` naming the limit.

## analytics_query({ project_id, event?, from?, to?, group_by?, limit? })

| `group_by` | Each row | Order |
|---|---|---|
| `"day"` | `{ bucket: "2026-09-02", count }` | newest first |
| `"hour"` | `{ bucket: "2026-09-02T14:00:00Z", count }` | newest first |
| `"event"` | `{ event, count }` | most frequent first |
| `"user"` | `{ user_id, count }`, signed-in users only | most active first |
| omitted | `{ timestamp, event, user_id, properties, page }` | newest first |

Omit `event` to count every event. `from` and `to` take an ISO-8601 date or a
unix-ms number and include their own instant, so `to: "2026-09-02"` stops at
the start of that day (UTC). `limit` caps the rows; the tool's input schema
gives the default and maximum. A day or hour with no events has no row, so match rows by
`bucket` when you compare two events. The result is
`{ rows, count, group_by }`.

Inside a function, `sw.analytics.query({ event, group_by: "day" })` returns the
same result. Query results are project-wide: anyone with access to the project
can read them, including properties and user ids on raw rows. Read them from
MCP or run `somewhere call analytics_query '{…}'`.
Do not add a public endpoint that forwards browser input into a query or
returns its rows.

## analytics_track({ project_id, event, user_id?, properties?, page?, referrer?, user_agent? })

From a developer session, `analytics_track` records a project-level event as
you, for example after a migration or a pricing change:

```text
analytics_track({ project_id: "my-app", event: "pricing_changed", properties: "{\"version\":3}" })
```

It needs editor access. It has no visitor, so it carries no user attribution,
and the platform ignores a `user_id` argument. It cannot carry a visitor's
consent choice: when consent mode is required, it returns `recorded: false`
with `consent_pending`. Use it for project events your policy allows, not as a
stand-in for a visitor's opt-in.

## Page views

Successful HTML page loads on your site are counted on the server, with no
script in your pages. Asset requests, `/api/` routes, known bots and the
preview (`-dev`) address are not counted, and consent mode applies the same
way. Page views are separate from your events, so `analytics_query` leaves
them out. Read totals, top pages and referrers with a developer key:

```text
GET /v1/projects/<project-id>/analytics/pageviews?days=30
```

`days` is `7` (the default), `30` or `90`; page views are kept for about three months.

## Common patterns

- **Funnel:** one event per step, then one `group_by: "day"` query per step,
  as in the opening example.
- **What happens most:** `analytics_query({ project_id, group_by: "event" })`.
- **Most active signed-in users:**
  `analytics_query({ project_id, group_by: "user", limit: 20 })`.
- **Check recent events while building:** omit `group_by` and set a small
  `limit` to see raw rows.

## Consent

An app whose code calls `sw.analytics.track` gets `mode: "auto"` (below) at
its next deploy, unless it already has a consent setting of its own. The deploy
answer says so in `consent_prompt` and in a line of `privacy_lines`; tell your
human: "Visitors in the EU and UK will see a small analytics choice on your
app." A running app is never changed between deploys. To keep the prompt off,
set `analytics_consent: { mode: "off", policy_version: "1" }` through
`project_update`; that choice is kept at later deploys.

Without `sw.analytics.track`, events and page views are recorded without a
consent prompt. If the app asks visitors for consent before counting them, set
`analytics_consent: { mode: "required", policy_version: "v1" }` through
`project_update`. The platform then records only when the incoming request carries
the visitor's original acceptance of that exact policy version. The choice is
read from the platform's own consent cookie on the original request; your code
cannot supply or change it.

With `mode: "auto"` the platform decides per visitor and shows its own small
prompt, so the app needs no banner. Visitors in the EU, EEA, UK and
Switzerland are asked first, with "no" as easy as "yes"; elsewhere events are
recorded. A browser that sends Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track counts
as "no" everywhere, with no prompt. Page views stay anonymous and are counted
without a prompt, except with those browser signals. The visitor's country is
read per request and never stored. Tell your human when you turn this on:
"Visitors in the EU and UK will see a small analytics choice on your app."

Without a matching acceptance, `track` returns `recorded: false` with
`consent_pending` or `consent_declined`. If the policy cannot be read or is
malformed, nothing is recorded and the reason is `consent_unavailable`. The
banner, revoking a choice and the consent endpoint are in `deploy` →
`optional-analytics-consent`. Consent mode covers the platform's page views
and `sw.analytics` events; anything else your app collects is outside it.

## What NOT to do

- Don't count events in your app database. Events go to the platform's event
  store, and `analytics_query` counts them without a table or a write on
  your database.
- Don't write logs through analytics; use `sw.logs`. Analytics is for counting.
- Keep personal data such as names and emails out of event names and
  `properties`: everyone who can query the project sees them. Signed-in
  attribution already links events to the user's id.
- Don't expect sums or averages. Track a distinct event for each outcome, and
  keep amounts in your database.
- Don't send a user id to attribute events; the platform derives it.

Related: `browser` → `count-what-users-do`, `deploy` →
`optional-analytics-consent`, `sw.logs`.

pages.title: Tasks — shared context for work
pages.body:
sw.tasks keeps direction, working rules, current work and delivery evidence in
the same project. An agent can read what matters, follow related work and leave
the next agent a current summary. `description` holds the intent;
`status_note` holds what is true now; comments hold evidence.

Start a board scan with `tasks_list`:

```json
{"project_id":"my-app","view":"board","limit":50,"include_superseded":false}
```

Work rows contain the title, type, status, health, waiting state and current
note, without descriptions or comments. `page` reports the total, ordering and
next cursor. `tasks_overview` adds a short view of direction, SOPs, recorded
priorities, active work and shipping. `project_id` accepts a project ID or slug;
`default` selects the shared organization board for callers with access.

Filter by an exact label with `label`. For work tagged `needs-review` and
assigned to `alex`, pass both filters to `tasks_list` or run
`somewhere tasks list -p my-app --assignee alex --label needs-review`.
The REST equivalent is `GET /v1/tasks?project_id=my-app&assignee=alex&label=needs-review`.
A label search without `assignee` checks up to the 1,000 most recently added
tasks. When older tasks were skipped, `page.partial` is true and
`page.candidate_note` explains how to narrow the search.

Create a piece of work with `tasks_create`:

```json
{"project_id":"my-app","title":"Verify the welcome email","status":"in_progress","status_note":"The email is implemented; checking signup and retry behavior next."}
```

Use the returned ID as `task_id` in `tasks_update`. Record progress by replacing
the note, and attach receipts as a comment in the same call:

```json
{"project_id":"my-app","task_id":"<returned task ID>","status_note":"Signup and retries pass; ready for the copy decision.","waiting_on":"product_decision","comment":"Two test signups received the message once. Retrying delivery produced no duplicate."}
```

The status note stays separate from the comment. Earlier field values remain
in activity history, so updating the summary retains the previous state.

## Current state and waiting

`status` applies to work records only. It is `backlog`, `open`, `in_progress`, `blocked`, `needs_review`, `done`
or `archived`. `priority` is `low`, `normal`, `high` or `urgent`.
`health` records `on_track`, `at_risk` or `off_track` independently of status.
`assignee` identifies who owns the work.

`waiting_on` records `human`, `product_decision` or `external`. Put the action
or decision needed in `status_note`; clear the wait with `null` or an empty
string when it is resolved. A wait does not change the assignee or status.
Closing through an ordinary status update clears an omitted wait.

## Ask the person for something

When only the person can do the next thing (create an account, approve a
charge, press a button elsewhere, decide), record it in one call. An ask said
only in chat is lost; a recorded one shows in their dashboard under "Waiting
for you", with your steps and who asked.

```json
{"project_id":"my-app","title":"Create a GitHub sign-in app for my-app","waiting_on":"human","status_note":"1. Open github.com/settings/developers and press New OAuth App.\n2. Set the callback address to https://my-app.somewhere.cloud/auth/github/callback.\n3. Press Register application, then press Done here.","description":"Sign in with GitHub needs a client id only the account owner can create.","author":"Claude Code"}
```

`title` is what is needed, in one line. `status_note` is the steps: numbered,
one per line, plain words, exact addresses. `description` is why. `author` is
the name you go by; the platform records how you were signed in beside it, as
`asked_by`. `waiting_on` is `human` for an action, `product_decision` for a
choice. `tasks_update` takes the same fields on an existing task. Never ask for
a secret in the reply (collaborators and agents can read it); `env_request`
collects secrets.

Keep the list true. When you no longer need something from the person, withdraw
the ask: clear `waiting_on` with a one-line `status_note` saying why. When the
need has changed, replace it in one call: create the new ask with `supersedes`
set to the old task's id (or set `superseded_by` on the old task). The old ask
leaves their list at once and the new one says it replaces an earlier request.
Closing or archiving the task removes it too. Nothing leaves the list by age.
Posting something for the person is the moment to tidy what is already waiting:
the write's answer lists their other open asks in the project under
`suggestions` (`still_waiting`), oldest first.

The person answers with Done, I can't do this or This is no longer needed, and
an optional note, in the dashboard or through any agent they ask. That clears
`waiting_on` and makes `status_note` the answer: `Done.`, `Not doing this.` or
`No longer needed.`, then their note. Read it
with `tasks_get` or a board scan, continue, and write the new state to
`status_note`. A comment on the task, or closing it, is read the same way.

`tasks_list` with `waiting: "me"` lists what is waiting for the signed-in person across their
projects (HTTP `GET /v1/account/waiting`). Use `next_cursor` as `cursor` to continue.
`limit` is the number of projects per call and defaults to 25. Larger limits are
reduced to 25. The response includes tasks from readable projects, and
`unread_projects` names any projects that could not be read. Retry one by
passing its `project_id`. Each project's list is kept for up to ten minutes and read again after a call
once it is a minute old, so a new item shows on the call after that one; with `project_id`
it reads that project at once. An answer given through Somewhere shows at once. `answered`
lists what was answered and by which credential (`answered_by`).
Answer for them with `tasks_update` (`answer`: `done`, `cannot` or `not_needed`, and `note`;
HTTP `POST /v1/tasks/<id>/answer`). Never answer `done` unless the person did
it or told you to.

The board defaults to unfinished records. Human and product-decision waits,
review work and blocked work sort before routine work, then priority and
creation time decide the order. A status filter can include closed work;
`sort: "updated"` or `"created"` selects recency instead. `waiting_on: "human"`
with `view: "board"` returns the human-input queue. `type`, `area`, `assignee` and `parent_id` narrow
the same read. Board rows show their type so guidance is distinguishable from work.

On the shared organization board, founder assignee aliases resolve to `founder`.
`founder-decision` also sets a product-decision wait on unfinished work,
replacing any previous wait unless `waiting_on` is supplied in the same write.
Customer-project assignees keep their own values.

## Direction, links and supersession

`tasks_overview` reads direction and work together. `memory_search` searches
durable guidance; `memory_save` records it. Direction types are `vision`, `philosophy`, `decision`, `directive`, `sop`,
`principle`, `policy` and `stance` (case and surrounding
whitespace do not matter). They are relevant until explicitly replaced, regardless
of historical status. Current payloads omit their `status` and `completed_at`.
Supplying a status for direction is refused, including in bulk updates.
`include_archived` includes archived work only; `include_superseded: true` includes
replaced records. Ordinary `tasks_list` shows relevant direction; `include_superseded: false`
excludes replaced records.

For a focused memory read: `memory_search({ project_id: "my-app", q: "welcome email" })`.

Set `parent_id` for a sub-task. `tasks_update` accepts `relationship`, for
example `{"type":"implements","task_id":"<SOP ID>"}`, to connect work to its
guidance. `tasks_get` returns linked guidance; `view: "relationships"` pages
related records and replacement pointers without their discussion bodies.
Links carry context; the agent decides which guidance applies.

Set `superseded_by` on the older record to its replacement ID. A `supersedes`
relationship points from replacement to older record. Both forms are honored
in current memory and the overview. A direction replacement counts only while its
named record exists. A dangling link does not hide direction. Reads with
`include_superseded: true` report broken target IDs in `dangling_replacement_ids`
on each affected direction record; reads never clear those links. Old records remain readable. Guidance
revisions preserve earlier text; a task's `guidance_context` can record the
revision used or a scoped exception. Retrieve that source with `tasks_get`
before recording its revision ID.

## Archive, supersede or delete

Direction is never archived or closed: name its replacement with `superseded_by`
or a `supersedes` link. Bulk deletion refuses each direction ID and continues with
work. An owner may delete a mistaken direction record by full ID with a reason,
unless direction names it as a replacement; change that link first.

Archive and supersede keep work history: an archived or replaced record stays
readable and searchable, so anyone can see how the work got here. Use them for
anything that was real, even if it was abandoned or replaced.

Delete is only for records that should never have existed: a duplicate, a
mistake, wrong direction. `tasks_delete` takes a required `reason`. The task,
its comments, activity and links leave lists, search, history, counts, memory
and other tasks' relationships on the next read; children are detached and replacement
pointers cleared.

```json
{"project_id":"my-app","task_id":"<task ID>","reason":"Duplicate of <other task ID>"}
```

For 30 days `tasks_restore` brings it all back, including comments and links. It
takes the full task ID; a prefix is refused. Without `task_id` it lists deleted tasks with who deleted them, why, and
`purge_at`. Trash is purged after the 30-day recovery period. Links to tasks that no
longer exist, or that would now form a cycle, are not restored and are listed in
`not_restored`. For direction, a missing, conflicting or unpreservable replacement
link refuses the whole restore, naming its target IDs. Nothing is restored and
no replacement link is cleared.

Only the board owner can delete or restore, through their own account sign-in:
the dashboard, the CLI (`somewhere tasks delete|restore|deleted`) or an agent
signed in with that account. Collaborators, deployed functions, project-limited
CLI sessions and scope-limited keys get `TASK_DELETE_FORBIDDEN`.

## Types

Types are labels for retrieval; custom labels are supported.

vision — why the organization exists.
philosophy — a belief guiding trade-offs, including why it matters.
directive — a rule or instruction, including what it supersedes.
decision — a steer from the person who owns the project: their words, what it changes, what it replaces, the work it governs.
sop — how to carry out a recurring job.
spec — what to build and its acceptance criteria.
roadmap — direction and outcomes for work ahead.
epic — a larger outcome grouping related tasks.
task — a concrete piece of current work.
bug — behavior that needs correction.
report — an observation, incident or customer finding.
principle — a reusable rule for making decisions.
learning — a lesson supported by experience or evidence.
supplier — facts about an external service or supplier.
content — a draft or plan for published material.
policy — a standing rule governing operations.
stance — a position on a subject and its reasoning.
When the person who owns the project changes direction, parks or picks something, or overrules a plan, record it as a decision the same day, quoting them.

## Read only the detail needed

`tasks_get` returns current state and history counts. `view: "history"` with
`kind: "comments"` or `"activity"` returns newest entries first.
`view: "field"` expands a field named in `omitted`; its `content` is JSON text.
For saved guidance text, history supports `revisions` and `reviews`.

For continuation, repeat the filters and view with `page.next_cursor` as
`cursor`. Expand one page at a time. Task-list ordering is live: edits can move
rows between pages; restart for a fresh queue. `truncated_fields` on board rows
and `omitted` on detailed reads name content available through field expansion.
`view: "full"` requests complete fields and history.

## Closing work

Close with `tasks_update`, using the real outcome and verification evidence:

```json
{"project_id":"my-app","task_id":"<task ID>","status":"done","status_note":"The welcome email is live and signup is verified.","resolution_note":"Delivered the welcome email and retry fix in release v12. Verified two signups and a repeated delivery; each account received one message."}
```

`resolution_note` is saved as a comment and included in configured resolution
notifications. `shipped_in` records a release tag; tasks requiring deployment
evidence use `deployment_project_id` and `deployment_version` to link a
verified deployment. Release mentions trigger a closure-review suggestion;
they do not close the task.

Write responses also suggest missing current-state notes, similar guidance
and recently copied evidence. Supersession and closure remain explicit writes.
Comment appends are not retry-safe: after an uncertain response, inspect history
before retrying.

## From a deployed function

The same records are available through `sw.tasks`. `listPage` returns both
rows and continuation metadata; `get` takes the same view options:

```ts
const board = await sw.tasks.listPage({ view: 'board', limit: 50 });
const task = board.data[0];
if (task) {
  const current = await sw.tasks.get(task.id, { view: 'current' });
}
```

The no-options runtime `get` and `list` return full records. Bounded reads use
an explicit view. `sw.tasks.update(id, fields)` sets state;
`sw.tasks.comment(id, body)` appends evidence. Deployed functions cannot delete
tasks: `sw.tasks.delete` is refused with `TASK_DELETE_FORBIDDEN`.

## Notifications

Task mutations publish on the project's signed system channel. Optional email
and webhook settings use `tasks_settings_update` or `sw.tasks.settings.update`.
If the settings tool is outside the default surface, `catalog({ load: "tasks" })` loads it.
The returned `webhook_secret` signs `X-Somewhere-Signature`; save it when setting
the webhook. The header is `t=<milliseconds>,v1=<hex>`, where hex is HMAC-SHA256
over `<milliseconds>.<raw body>` using `webhook_secret`. Verify the raw bytes
before parsing. Settings reads do not return the secret. An empty `webhook_url`
clears the webhook and its secret.

## Deletion and recovery

Deletion is gone from normal task reads on the next read; restorable for 30 days; purged after. Other tasks retain their history. Deletion removes attachment references, never the underlying files. Raw database dumps are exact copies and may include trash until purge.

`tasks_delete` accepts one full `task_id` (a prefix is refused) or up to 200 full `task_ids`, with `project_id` and a required `reason`. Bulk deletion returns one result per ID; each ID succeeds or is refused on its own, so one refusal does not undo the others. It uses the same owner authority and protection as single deletion. Tasks referenced as guidance by live tasks cannot be deleted; the refusal names the referencing tasks.

pages.title: Recent behaviour changes
pages.body:
## How we handle breaking changes

### Our principle

We keep your app running as the platform evolves. If a platform change affects
it, we tell you first, give you time to respond, and prepare a fix with
instructions for applying it. Safety is the exception: protections may take
effect immediately, but we still ask for your approval before changing your
code to address the safety issue.

### Where we're heading

We intend to introduce compatibility dates, so each app can keep the platform
behavior it was built against until you choose to adopt newer behavior, subject
to safety protections. This is our direction, not a feature available today or
a promised launch date.

### Compatibility notice periods

Compatibility notice periods are at least 7 days
for active Free owners and 30 days for paid apps. Free apps are never paused for
idleness; we pause one only if a platform change would break it and its owner
has had no login or deploy for 30 days, with notice and a prepared fix, while
paid apps are never paused because of a platform change.

## Change log

Dated platform behaviour changes, newest first. One entry per change: what
changed, what it means for code you already deployed, and the topic that carries
the full contract. Affected owners receive an email and a project notice;
this log records what changed.

Each entry names a topic. That topic, not this line, is the current contract;
the entry records when and why it changed.

CLI releases are listed in the CLI's own `CHANGELOG.md`, shipped in the
`@somewhere-cloud/cli` package. A project stays on the CLI version it records
until `somewhere upgrade`, which prints the entries between that version and
the new one.

Before you update an app for a change, check what it is running:

- `somewhere status` shows the active release, and
  `project_deploys({ project_id })` lists the deploy history.
- In an empty folder, `somewhere pull` downloads the live source with local typecheck files, and
  `somewhere typecheck` runs `tsc --noEmit` over it.
- Compare the `@somewhere-cloud/sdk` version in the app's `package.json` with
  the current 0.14.1 listed in `sdks`.
- `somewhere deploy-check` compiles your changed source on the server
  without deploying it.

Then read the named topic for the new contract. If a documented contract
looks wrong, file it with `support_ticket({ message })`.

- **2026-11-19 — the old inbox is removed.** `sw.inbox`, the `/v1/inbox` API
  and the `inbox_*` tools are gone: `/v1/inbox` answers 410 and reading
  `sw.inbox` in a function throws. Received mail is on the mail API
  (`/v1/mail`). `docs({ topic: 'domains' })`.
- **2026-10-31 — a `sw.endpoint` handler that reads `body` without a
  `body` schema is refused at deploy.** Without a schema `body` is always
  `null`, so what the caller sent was dropped. 400 `ENDPOINT_BODY_UNDECLARED`
  names the file and line; declare the fields, or read `request` yourself.
  Endpoints already deployed keep running. `docs({ topic: 'sw.endpoint' })`

- **2026-10-31 — a bare `id()` keeps a table's existing integer ids.** Source
  that says `id()` over a table that already has integer ids redeploys
  unchanged, with no change to the table or its ids.
  New tables still get a random text key. `docs({ topic: 'declared-data' })`

- **2026-10-21 — `somewhere test-users` signs local Playwright and
  agent-browser in as test users (CLI 0.37.63 or later).** `prepare` writes a
  standard storageState per actor, `address` and `inbox` test real signup,
  and `cleanup` removes the users it prepared; app data they created is kept.
  `docs({ topic: 'browser' })`.
- **2026-10-21 — magic-link and invite sign-ins complete in the browser.**
  `sw.auth.verifyOtp` returns `expires_at`, as login and signup do. A function deployed before 18:33 UTC keeps the earlier
  runtime until it is deployed again. `docs({ topic: 'sw.auth' })`.
- **2026-10-21 — `sw.inbox` `list()` and `threads()` take `cursor`.** Pass the
  previous `next_cursor` with the same filters to read the next page. A function
  deployed before 12:32 UTC keeps the earlier runtime until it is deployed again.
  (Removed 2026-11-19.)
- **2026-10-21 — browser and `verify` actions keep `frame` (CLI 0.37.58 or
  later).** A `"frame"` on an action runs it inside that iframe.
  `docs({ topic: 'browser' })`.
- **2026-10-21 — inbox message and thread lists page with a cursor.**
  `inbox_list` and `inbox_threads` (`GET /v1/inbox`, `GET /v1/inbox/threads`)
  return `next_cursor`; pass it back as `cursor` with the same filters until it
  is `null`. `inbox_threads` returns `{ threads, next_cursor }`.
  (Removed 2026-11-19.)
- **2026-10-21 — `docs` summaries carry the topic's content, not mostly its
  index.** A summary fills its existing size budget with whole sections, marked
  `(shown above)` in its section list, so one call usually answers; `--full`
  and `--section` are unchanged. `docs({ topic: 'cli' })`.
- **2026-10-21 — new starters ignore the generated `__somewhere_*.d.ts` files
  (CLI 0.37.47 or later).** `typecheck`, `dev` and `deploy` rebuild them from
  `db/schema.ts`; an older project can add both names to `.gitignore`.
  `docs({ topic: 'cli' })`.
- **2026-10-21 — a fixed browser or `verify` wait over 45 seconds is refused.**
  The error names the step: split a longer pause into several waits of at most
  45000 ms, or wait for a condition. When an absent element fails
  `visible: false`, or `count: 0` together with `text`, the error
  says to use `count: 0` alone. `docs({ topic: 'browser' })`.
- **2026-10-21 — `verify` creates its own test users and can run users at the
  same time (CLI 0.37.46 or later).** An actor `{ "test_user": true }` gets a
  verified test user for the run, and `verify` asks the platform to delete it
  when the run ends unless you pass `--keep-test-users`. A
  `{ "parallel": [...] }` item runs 2–3 users' segments at once, for realtime
  checks. `docs({ topic: 'browser' })`.
- **2026-10-21 — a magic-link request for something that is not an email address
  answers 400.** It answers `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` under the same address
  rule as sign-up, before anything is stored. `docs({ topic: 'sw.auth' })`.
- **2026-10-20 — browser and `verify` `auth: { user_id }` signs in managed test
  users only.** A seeded session for an ordinary app user answers
  `AUTH_INVALID_CREDS`; sign real accounts in through your app's UI. Create
  managed test users with
  `somewhere api POST /v1/auth/test-users -d '{"project_id":"<project>","count":2}'`,
  or use `test_user` actors (entry above). `docs({ topic: 'browser' })`.
- **2026-10-20 — app users' files are private by default.** A signed-in
  `sw.fs` call reaches only a declared file collection's files (as its rules
  allow), public files, and files that user already owns; anything else answers
  403 `FILE_ACCESS_DENIED` (writes) or 404 (reads). Files a function keeps for
  a user use `sw.fs.server` after the function's own check.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.fs' })`

- **2026-10-20 — browser and `verify` reports say where the time went.** Each
  report includes `timing`: admission wait, browser start or reuse, page setup,
  first navigation, actions and total. `docs({ topic: 'browser' })`

- **2026-10-20 — `email_verified` is a boolean in the access token and
  `/me`.** Nothing to change unless your code compared it to `1`.

- **2026-10-20 — email verification, magic links and app invites work on
  per-app sign-in stores.** On apps that sign users in through the per-app
  sign-in store (new apps since 2026-10-19, and existing apps after their
  sign-in migration), sign-up mail carries a verification code, and group
  joins that need a verified email accept those users.
  Nothing to change in your code. `docs({ topic: 'sw.auth' })`

- **2026-10-20 — notifications, managed email and push reach these apps' users
  again.** On apps that sign users in through the per-app sign-in store (new
  apps since 2026-10-19, and existing apps after their sign-in migration),
  notification sends were refused with `APP_USER_NOT_FOUND`, notification reads
  with `AUTH_REQUIRED`, and managed-sender `sw.email` sends with 422
  `MANAGED_SENDER_RECIPIENT_NOT_A_USER`. Nothing to change in your code.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.notifications' })`

- **2026-10-24 — sign-in identity and billing are separate.** Auth users no
  longer carry `plan`, `plan_status` or `entitlements`. Read billing
  explicitly from an authenticated function. React `useEntitlements` and
  `Gate` take a billing observation; `PricingTable` takes `currentPlan`.
  Missing observations are not free plans. `docs({ topic: 'sw.billing' })`

- **2026-10-20 — password sign-in limits are per source and per account.** Up
  to 600 sign-in attempts a minute per source and 30 a minute per account; 10
  consecutive wrong passwords lock the account for 15 minutes. Refusals are 429
  `RATE_LIMITED` with `retry_after_ms`. Nothing to change in your code.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.auth', section: 'automatic-password-sign-in-protection' })`

- **2026-10-19 — browser and `verify` limits are the same on every plan.** Up
  to 10 runs at once per account, no daily run count, and a 50 browser-hour
  daily abuse limit. A refusal says which limit applied and when it resets.
  `docs({ topic: 'browser' })`

- **2026-10-19 — writes report `live_delivery`.** A write that affects a live
  view returns `{ delivery: 'queued' }` (watchers refetch just after the
  response) or `{ delivery: 'resync_required' }`. Neither means the write
  failed: never retry a committed write because of it.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.db' })`

- **2026-10-19 — test-inbox messages include `verification_code`.** A test
  user can be signed up and verified without parsing email HTML.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.email' })`

- **2026-10-18 — group owners can delete a group, and owners and admins can
  add an existing user directly.** `sw.groups.delete(request, groupId)` and
  `sw.groups.add(request, groupId, userId, role)`; invites still cover people
  who aren't users yet. `docs({ topic: 'sw.groups' })`

- **2026-10-18 — a bare `id()` is a random text key on new tables.** Use
  `id({ uuid: false })` for an integer key. A live integer table whose source
  says bare `id()` is refused at deploy with the one-line fix, and foreign keys
  must match the parent's key type. `docs({ topic: 'declared-data' })`

- **2026-10-18 — `db_browse` reads managed tables.** Raw dump and query cover
  only the raw database and point to `db_browse` for managed rows.

- **2026-10-18 — jobs: 100 at once on every plan, and cron runs don't use job
  slots.** Up to 100 jobs queued, scheduled or running per account on every
  plan; job creation allows 600 calls a minute per account owner.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.jobs' })`

- **2026-10-18 — a job's `timeout_seconds` is its deadline.** A job that
  times out fails with `JOB_TIMEOUT` and is not sent again. In functions
  deployed after this change, the platform refuses new covered `sw.*` calls
  from a handler once its job has ended; work already accepted can finish, and
  the exact limits are in `sw.jobs`. Write handlers so a later run can pick up
  safely. `docs({ topic: 'sw.jobs' })`

- **2026-10-18 — once-a-minute crons fire every minute.** They had been
  firing about every other minute. Nothing to change in your code.

- **2026-10-17 — a `sw.endpoint` written without `auth` is refused at
  deploy.** 400 `ENDPOINT_AUTH_OMITTED` names the file and line; write
  `auth: 'none'` for an endpoint that is public on purpose. Endpoints already
  deployed keep running. `docs({ topic: 'sw.endpoint' })`

- **2026-10-17 — the in-app notification inbox works on new projects.** Each
  user keeps their newest 1,000 notifications for up to 90 days.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.notifications' })` Clarified 2026-10-20: from 2026-10-19
  to 2026-10-20, on apps that sign users in through the per-app sign-in store
  (new apps since 2026-10-19, and existing apps after their sign-in migration),
  sends were refused with `APP_USER_NOT_FOUND`; fixed on 2026-10-20 (entry
  above).

- **2026-10-17 — rate-limit windows reset when they end.** Steady traffic is no
  longer refused after hours of use. Nothing to change in your code.

- **2026-10-17 — find users by email from server code.**
  `sw.auth.server.listUsers({ emails })` looks up users by exact address.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.auth', section: 'member-contacts' })`

- **2026-10-11 — previews for signed-in accounts on every plan.** Signed-in
  Free accounts include `somewhere preview` (private hosted previews,
  promote, and the separate preview database), so every plan has it;
  anonymous accounts cannot create previews. Nothing was removed from any plan.
  Capacity per plan: `docs({ topic: 'dev-environments' })`.
- **2026-09-20 — eligible public pages and assets on your own host are served
  before the routing check, not after it.** On a project host or a custom
  domain, a `GET` or `HEAD` for a page, a compiled asset or a public file
  — answered from a route that location resolved recently — is served while
  the routing check runs behind the response. For up to 60 seconds after a
  deploy, a location that missed the update can still answer with the previous
  release; past that window, and whenever there is no recent route to go on,
  the request is exact, and a failed check never extends the window. Requests
  that are not plain `GET`/`HEAD`, preview and development addresses, group
  and platform-overlay surfaces, and the platform's own
  addresses resolve the route before answering, as before. Nothing to change in
  your code. `docs({ topic: 'speed' })`.
- **2026-09-19 — public reads may be served from a shared copy; a declared
  write drops it.** On a table declaring `client.publicRead`, a `list`,
  `get` or related-record page requested with no session, no visitor
  cookie and no `Authorization` may be answered from a shared copy kept
  close to readers. A committed declared write or transaction to that table
  invalidates the copy asynchronously. Allow up to
  120 seconds from when the database produced it
  for every anonymous reader to see an edit, deletion or withdrawal. Reads carrying any
  identity, and every owner, member and private read, are unchanged and
  exact. Developer SQL writes are not declared operations and are picked up
  only when the copy expires. `docs({ topic: 'declared-data' })`.
- **2026-09-19 — composed aggregates.** `sw.db.aggregate` and
  `sw.db.server.aggregate` compose count / sum / avg / min / max with
  `groupBy`, `where`, `has`, `having`, `order` and `limit`,
  with the caller's row permissions in the same WHERE. The generated browser
  client gains `aggregate` on every table with a `read` grant, over
  readable fields only; grouped calls return at most 100 groups and report
  `has_more`. Nothing existing changes. `docs({ topic: 'sw.db' })`.
- **2026-09-19 — `belongsTo` relations.** `relations: { project:
  belongsTo('projects', 'project_id') }` on the table that holds the key is
  the inverse of `hasMany`. In functions, `include: ['project']` nests
  the single parent row, or `null` when the parent is missing or not
  readable by the caller; `has: { project: { … } }` filters by it. The
  browser client adds no method; read a parent with `get`.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.db' })`.
- **2026-09-06 — the outbound guard refuses literal blocked targets.** A request that reaches the platform's outbound guard with a
  non-public address or internal hostname, embedded `user:password`, a
  non-HTTP scheme, or a port other than 80, 443 or 1024 and above gets a 403
  with `x-sw-outbound-error` before it leaves. Requests to public hosts are
  unchanged, and the runtime's own checks still run first. Preview functions
  still cannot fetch at all (`DRAFT_EGRESS_DENIED`).
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.fetch' })`.
- **2026-09-02 — local dev reaches your project's database and files on
  every plan.** Running `somewhere dev` on your own machine reads and writes
  the project's own database and files on Free and Builder as well as Pro and
  Scale. Nothing to enable, no setup step, and it is the same database and the
  same files the deployed app uses — a project with a published release behaves
  like one that has never been deployed, so local writes are production writes.
  No current plan returns `LOCAL_DEV_DB_NOT_ENABLED`. Preview (`somewhere
  preview`, private previews, promote, the dev/prod split and its separate
  database) is a different product, on every plan since 2026-10-11. `docs({ topic: 'local-dev' })`.
- **2026-09-02 — whole numbers wider than a JSON number travel as strings, in
  both directions.** A whole number above `9007199254740991` written as a JSON
  number in a request body — `db_query` / `db_batch` parameters, a structured
  write's values, an `api` body — is rounded by JSON itself before the platform
  ever sees it. Those requests are refused before anything is written, with
  `NUMBER_PRECISION_LOST` naming the field, the digits you sent and the number
  that arrived. Send such a value as a string (`"9223372036854775807"`): that is
  the same exact form a read returns, so a value read out of the database writes
  straight back. `sw.db.insert` / `sw.db.update` accept that string on a
  declared `integer` column. A dump emits such a value as a bare numeric
  literal, so a restore produces a whole number again. Whole numbers up to `9007199254740991`, decimals, and any larger whole number
  a JSON number carries exactly are written as sent.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.db' })`.
- **2026-09-02 — structured writes return 64-bit whole numbers intact.**
  `sw.db.insert`, `sw.db.update` and `sw.db.remove` project their affected row
  through the same exact-decimal-string cast reads already use, so a write that
  touches a row holding a 64-bit id (a Snowflake id, an imported `bigint`)
  returns normally instead of reporting `DATABASE_VALUE_TOO_LARGE` after the
  write succeeded. On a SQL-mode project raw `sw.db.query` is never rewritten, so
  cast the column yourself in your own `RETURNING` clause.
  `docs({ topic: 'sw.db' })`.
- **2026-09-02 — cron has a plan minimum fire interval.** Creating or editing a
  schedule tighter than the plan allows is refused with
  `CRON_SCHEDULE_TOO_FREQUENT`; existing schedules are not re-checked and keep
  running unchanged. Read the plan's interval from `cron_list({ project_id })`.
  `docs({ topic: 'cron' })`.
- **2026-09-01 — empty AI completions say whose problem they are.**
  `/v1/ai/complete` still answers `MODEL_EMPTY_RESPONSE` when a model produces
  no text, and the status splits the class: HTTP 422 `retry: false` when the
  request is yours to fix, with the cause, stop reason, and token counts in
  `data`; HTTP 502 `retry: true` only on a genuine provider failure worth
  retrying — 5xx is theirs, 4xx is yours. `docs({ topic: 'sw.ai' })`.

## Where the rest of the history lives

This log carries behaviour changes, not the release feed. Per-project deploy
history is `project_deploys`; what a specific deploy changed is
`project_diff_versions`. If a documented contract looks wrong, report it with
`support_ticket({ message })`; the team replies on that ticket
(`docs({ topic: 'feedback' })`).

Related: `troubleshooting`, `guarantees`, `feedback`.

pages.title: Platform Feedback — Bug? Doc gap? Tell us.
pages.body:
Send platform bugs, unclear documentation and feature requests with
`support_ticket`. Include what you tried, what you expected and what
happened. You can attach the project and structured context so the team
can investigate without asking you to repeat the basics.

## Submit

```ts
const t = await support_ticket({
  message: "I need to reorder project groups in the dashboard. Is there a supported way to do that?",
  project_id: "my-app",                 // optional
  context: { area: "dashboard", action: "reorder groups" },  // optional
});
// → { ticket_id: "pfb_<ticket-id>", status: "open", created_at: 1715000000000 }
```

Our team is alerted immediately with your message and ticket
id. They reply on the ticket — and **when they do, you get an email**
at the address on your account. No polling required.

## Read back

Use these if you want to check before the email lands:

- `support_ticket({ ticket_id })` — one ticket, full
  detail including the response.
- `support_ticket({ status?, limit? })` — every ticket
  you've filed (most recent first), with status and response inline
  (omit `message` and `ticket_id` to list).

## Shape returned by status / list

A single-ticket read returns this ticket object inside the response
`data` field:

```json
{
  "ticket_id": "pfb_<ticket-id>",
  "user_id": "<your user id>",
  "email": "you@example.com",
  "project_id": null,
  "message": "your original report",
  "context": null,
  "status": "resolved",
  "response": "This is fixed and live. No action needed.",
  "responder": null,
  "parent_id": null,
  "created_at": 1715000000000,
  "updated_at": 1715000360000,
  "resolved_at": 1715000360000
}
```

`status` is `open`, `investigating` or `resolved`. `response` is
`null` until the team answers, and `resolved_at` is `null` until the ticket is
resolved. `responder` is `null` unless you are platform staff. A list
returns `tickets` with the same fields except `context`, named `id` and
`responder_email` instead of `ticket_id` and `responder`.

## What "good" looks like

A useful ticket gives the platform team three things in 4–5 lines:

1. **What you tried** — exact endpoint or MCP tool + the args.
2. **What you expected** — based on what doc or precedent.
3. **What happened** — the raw response or error code, not a paraphrase.

For an error report, include the command or tool call and the returned
error code. For a feature request, describe the job you want to finish and
where the current workflow stops. Remove passwords, API keys and private
customer data from the example.

## When to use which

- **Stuck on architecture** → `advisor({ question })`.
- **The platform itself is broken or unclear** → `support_ticket`.
- **You think the docs are wrong** → `support_ticket`. Include the topic,
  the example you followed and what happened so we can correct the shared
  documentation used by the website, CLI and MCP.

## What the team does with it

The team investigates the report and records its answer on the ticket.
The response explains the fix, a workaround, or the information needed
to continue. For a documentation correction, include the topic and the
example so the update reaches the shared website, CLI and MCP docs.

pages.title: Speed
pages.body:
Paint the screen first, start independent reads together, and measure the
requests your visitor waits for. Somewhere compiles your source, delivers
static assets close to visitors, and batches production reads started together:

```ts
const [posts, tags] = await Promise.all([
  sw.db.from('posts', { where: { published: true }, order: [['created_at', 'desc']], limit: 20 }),
  sw.db.from('tags'),
]);
```

In production, these independent reads share a database round trip. Preview
and development runs send each read separately. Awaiting the first before
starting the second adds another trip. Keep dependent work sequential; use
`sw.db.tx` when several writes must succeed or fail together.

Measure cold and warm loads in the regions your visitors use. The sections
below explain page delivery, data reads, and the tools for finding slow work.

## Pages and assets

Deployed source is compiled for you. The browser bundle is minified, ships no
source maps, and declares its chunks up front so they load alongside the page
instead of after it. Compiled assets are content-addressed: a browser and the
edge can both hold one indefinitely, and a deploy produces new addresses rather
than changing old ones.

On your project host and on a custom domain, an ELIGIBLE public request — a
`GET` or `HEAD` for a page, a compiled asset or a public file, answered from
a route this location has already resolved recently — runs the routing check
behind the response instead of in front of it. The trade is bounded and
deliberate: for up to 60 seconds after a deploy, a location that missed the
update can still answer with the previous release. Past that window, and
whenever this location has no recent route to go on, the request is exact.

Not every request takes that path, and none of them are slower for it: anything
that is not a plain `GET`/`HEAD`, a preview or development address, a
group or platform-overlay surface, and the platform's own addresses
all resolve the route before answering. Those confirm the
routing decision first, which is a different guarantee from being instantly
consistent everywhere — a deploy still propagates.

Separately from routing: eligible static pages and single-page app routes can
reuse the release's stored HTML. The shared copy contains only the base page.
User-specific prefetched data is added afterwards for each request, using that
request's identity and the current release's function. That personalized
response is private and must not be cached. Preview, development, grouped and
overlay views keep their existing serving path.

## Choosing whether to use shared copies

Control shared copies of pages, static assets and eligible public-data
responses through `PATCH /v1/projects/:id`. Set `edge_cache_disabled: true` to
turn shared caching off. Set it to `false` to restore the default. This uses the existing project editor
permission. The saved boolean is returned by the project API.

Turning shared caching off starts clearing existing copies; it is not an instant global
flush. Copies can remain for up to about an hour if clearing fails. Browser
copies already downloaded are separate and are not removed by this setting.
Authenticated page data still uses the requesting visitor's identity; this
switch does not grant access to private data.

## Deploy performance hints

A deploy can return a small number of warnings about absolute stylesheet
references, large images referenced by source, or repeated awaited raw SQL
calls. Each names the source location and the bytes or calls observed, with
an action to consider. These are warnings, never deploy refusals or measured
latency claims. The scan is bounded: it flags recognizable shapes and does not
inspect every possible execution path. For visitor performance, with or
without warnings, measure the real page's cold and warm loads and its request
waterfall.

## Server-rendered pages and the SPA

A function can return HTML rendered on the server. Declare a root
`[...path].ts` route for document paths, including `/`, `/articles/example`
and `/sitemap.xml`. This is explicit Request/Response code, not automatic
framework rendering or deploy-time pre-rendering. See `functions` →
`server-rendered-pages-alongside-the-spa` for a complete route.

Keep the SPA shell in `index.html`. The catch-all can decline `/` with
`Response.json({ error: 'FUNCTION_NOT_FOUND' }, { status: 404 })`; the
platform then serves the normal static/SPA path at the same URL. An HTML 404
from the function remains a 404. A database read before returning HTML adds
its latency to the first paint; use server rendering when the initial document
needs that content, and browser fetching for data that can arrive afterwards.

## Page data with the document

This is opt-in. It runs only for a release whose own JavaScript reads
`window.__PREFETCH`; the starter and the SDK do not read it. For such a
release, a page request carrying a session cookie or bearer token makes the
platform try the matching `/api/<path>` function with those same
credentials. The function verifies the caller and decides what data to
return. This applies to `GET` requests for page paths other than `/` and
`/api/*` when the project has functions.

A `200` JSON answer is added as `window.__PREFETCH`, with
`window.__PREFETCH_PATH` naming its source. The headers and body share a
1-second deadline and a 100 KiB body
limit. A missing route, error, invalid JSON, or exceeded limit leaves the
original page unchanged. Check for the global and fetch normally when absent.

The personalized response is private and cannot be stored in shared caches.
The platform stores only the base HTML and adds this data for each request.

## What a database call costs

Your function runs close to the visitor, and reaching the database is a
network round trip. Writes reach the database primary; eligible reads may be
served closer to the reader. Either way, sequential database calls can still
incur separate round trips — and a round trip carries a BATCH of statements,
not one statement, so statements your handler sends together share one while
statements it awaits one after another each pay their own.

For an ordinary indexed read of a modest number of rows, the crossing is
usually the larger share of the time and the distance to the database is the
term that moves it most. That is not universal — a wide scan, a big sort, an
unindexed filter or an aggregate over a large table can spend more time in the
query engine than on the wire, and no amount of batching helps with that. The
two problems look identical from the outside and have opposite fixes, so
measure (last section) before deciding which one you have.

The habit that follows: count the ROUND TRIPS a handler makes, then check
whether any single statement is doing too much work.

Composed calls — `sw.db.from` / `count` / `aggregate` / `insert` /
`update` / `remove` / `tx` — run on the project's own database connection.
That is the ordinary path and the fast one. Start there.

## Reads issued together travel together

The `Promise.all` example above starts both reads before awaiting either.
Production reads through the project database connection are batched automatically;
preview and development reads are sent separately. Each awaited write is its
own trip; `sw.db.tx([...])` sends its steps in one atomic request, one
`insert` step per row (`recipe-csv-import`). Raw `batch` never writes
declared tables.

## Dependent reads: bound the number of round trips

The expensive shape is a read per row — fetch 50 tasks, then fetch each task's
project. Declaring the relationship replaces that with a fixed cost:

```ts
// a declared belongsTo relation
const tasks = await sw.db.from('tasks', { include: ['project'], limit: 50 });
```

`include` reads the root rows, then reads the related rows in bounded
batches rather than one query per row. The number of database round trips
grows with the relations you include and with the number of key batches, not
with the rows themselves. It is the fix for the read-per-row loop, not a way to
reach one round trip, and it is deliberately not a single snapshot.

`sw.db.aggregate` genuinely is one statement, and it is the right answer
whenever you were about to read rows only to count, total or group them:

```ts
const byStatus = await sw.db.aggregate('orders', { count: true, groupBy: ['status'] });
```

`include`, `has` and `sw.db.aggregate` all carry the caller's row
permissions into the question the platform composes; `docs({ topic: 'sw.db' })`
has their full contracts. When a read genuinely cannot be expressed this way it
stays sequential. That is a correct program, just a slower one.

## What raw server SQL costs

On a project with a declared schema, ordinary `sw.db.query` and
`sw.db.batch` are refused. The escape hatch is `sw.db.server.query` /
`sw.db.server.batch`. They also do not apply declared row permissions —
authorize the caller yourself before calling them.

Where the extra cost comes from: a declared structured operation can run on
the project's own database connection, while an explicit server statement goes
as a separate platform request that then reaches the database through the
provider's authorized read-only API. That is more network requests per
statement, and more requests can add latency. How much, and whether it matters
for a given statement, depends on your workload and where things sit — so
measure your own app rather than budgeting from a figure.

So, in order:

1. Try to express it as a composed call. An `include`, a `has` filter or an
   `aggregate` usually covers what the raw read was for, on the faster route
   and with permissions already applied.
2. If you do need raw reads and they are independent of each other, send them
   in ONE call rather than awaiting several:

```ts
// Server authority reads ACROSS users. Authorize the caller first — the
// platform applies no row permissions to these statements.
const actor = await sw.auth.fromRequest(req);
if (!actor || actor.role !== 'admin') return new Response('Forbidden', { status: 403 });

const since = new Date(Date.now() - 7 * 86_400_000).toISOString();   // last 7 days
const [recent, totals] = await sw.db.server.batch([
  { sql: 'SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE created_at > ?', params: [since] },
  { sql: 'SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY status' },
]);
// One result per statement, in order; rows are on .data
// recent.data -> [{ id, email }, ...]   totals.data -> [{ status, n }, ...]
```

Dependent raw reads stay sequential, for the same reason dependent composed
reads do.

## Writes, permissions, and freshness

Three different guarantees get confused with each other. Keeping them apart is
most of what you need:

**Access checks remain enforced.** Session revocation checks read current
authority. Structured queries apply declared row permissions; policy shapes
that depend on mutable membership or parent authority retain their
primary-read requirements. Identity-bearing requests bypass the shared
public-result cache. Ordinary row reads still follow the consistency rules
below.

**Declared constraints and the conditions in an atomic write are checked when
it commits.** Express balances, inventory and limits with those operations:
reading a value and later writing a replacement does not prevent concurrent
lost updates. The response to a write describes what committed.

**Reading your own write is a carried position, not magic.** Your database may
answer a read from a copy kept nearer the reader, which can be slightly behind.
To make that safe, a response from your function publishes the position it
