reached — as an `x-sw-d1-bookmark` response header, and for browsers as a
short-lived host-only cookie — and the next request presenting that position is
answered at or after it. So a browser that just wrote through your app sees its
own write on its next call. The conditions are worth knowing, because they are
where the guarantee ends: the carried position is short-lived (about a minute),
it belongs to that one client, and a DIFFERENT client, a later visit, or a
request that never carried it can be answered from a copy that is slightly
behind. This is another reason a read-then-write pair is the wrong shape for a
balance or a seat count: put the condition in the write.

**Public data is the one deliberate trade.** Anonymous reads of data you
explicitly declared public may be answered from a shared copy kept near
readers; a committed declared write drops that copy, and a copy that was missed
expires on its own. `docs({ topic: 'declared-data' })` carries that contract in
full — read it before building on public data that can be withdrawn.

## Files

A public file is served from a nearby copy once it has been fetched there. A
file reached through a signed link is cacheable only by the browser holding
that link, for as long as the link is valid, and is fetched from storage
otherwise.

## Measure your own app

A function's clock advances across awaited work, so `Date.now()` around an
awaited database call measures that call's round trip honestly. The same
measurement around work that never awaits anything reads 0 — that is a property
of the runtime clock, not a sign the work was free.

```ts
const started = Date.now();
const posts = await sw.db.from('posts', { limit: 20 });
sw.logs.info('posts read', { ms: Date.now() - started, rows: posts.data.length });
```

Read the result back with `project_logs`, which also reports each request's
own duration. Compare warm requests with warm requests: the first request into
a freshly deployed release does one-time work the next one does not, so it
belongs to its own cohort and is not the number to plan against.

Related: `sw.db`, `declared-data`, `database-engine`, `deploy`,
`sw.logs`.

## Image and font caching

Import images and fonts from source, or reference them with CSS `url()`, to
ship them at content-hashed `/_compiled/` addresses. PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF,
SVG, ICO, WOFF, WOFF2, TTF and OTF assets use the same
`public, max-age=31536000, immutable` policy as compiled scripts and styles.
Changing an asset changes its address; HTML references to emitted assets are
rewritten too.

Fixed-name media from `public/` or `static/` has a bounded policy:
`public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=60`, with an ETag. A changed file
can remain cached for at most two minutes. This policy requires source-folder
provenance from a new deployment; older deployments retain revalidation. It
does not apply to HTML, API responses or authenticated views. Deploy and
deploy-check name static-folder images or fonts of at least 32 KiB and suggest
importing them from source for a permanent address.

Project public configuration is inlined before module execution on ordinary
HTML document requests. The external no-store script remains a fallback; it
is not a shared cache across projects.

Use `deploy-check` to check imported media and static-folder cache notices
before publishing. It leaves the current app version unchanged.

pages.title: Common Mistakes — Things real users have hit
pages.body:
**STOP.** Before writing any code, check if the platform already
handles it. Eight rules cover most of the wasted-time tickets:

- ❌ Don't build a `messages` or `conversations` table for chat
  history → use `conversation_id` on `sw.ai.chat()`. The platform
  loads, persists, and truncates history for you.
- ❌ Don't write `getCookie()` / token-parsing helpers →
  `sw.auth.fromRequest(req)` reads cookie + Bearer header and returns
  the validated user (or null) in one call.
- ❌ Don't write visitor-session management → declare `owner({ visitors: true })`
  on the table; the platform issues the visitor session and moves its rows to
  the account on sign-in. If the move would conflict with the account's rows or
  cannot be confirmed, the rows stay with the visitor session the sign-in replaced
  (`declared-data` → `visitors`).
- ❌ Don't hand-roll Stripe webhook handling — see the `payments` topic
  for the supported flow.
- ❌ Don't deploy a single-file change via MCP `project_deploy` — a full
  deploy replaces the project's static files with the ones you send (functions
  you omit stay live unless you pass `replace_functions: true`). Use
  `project_patch` for a single file or the `somewhere deploy` CLI for a
  full deploy.
- ❌ Don't wrap `sw.*` in blind retry loops → a thrown `sw.*` error
  carries its `code` and `status`; when present, `retry` says whether
  trying again can help and `retry_after_ms` says when. Follow them. Never
  repeat a write whose outcome is unknown until you have checked whether it
  happened.
- ❌ Don't call `https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/...` from inside a
  deployed function → use `sw.*` (same authenticated runtime surface,
  no developer-key or hand-built platform request).
- ❌ Don't set env vars for platform services (`SOMEWHERE_API_KEY`,
  database URLs, etc.) → `sw.*` is already authenticated. Env vars
  are for YOUR external services (e.g. a payment provider, an SMS API,
  your own AI key, etc).

The rest of this topic is the *long* list of failure modes from real
support tickets. Skim once.

## 1. Calling api.somewhere.cloud from inside a deployed function

**Wrong:**
```typescript
// inside a deployed function
const res = await fetch('https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/db/query', {
  headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer smt_...' },
  ...
})
```

**Right:**
```typescript
const res = await sw.db.from('contacts', { limit: 50 })   // res.data is the rows
```

Inside a deployed function, `sw.*` reaches the platform with the
function’s own credentials — no API key to manage. Use the REST surface
(`api.somewhere.cloud`) from trusted developer tools, CI and external
servers. Browser app features use the starter’s cookie session and the
generated data and file clients.

## 2. Using project_deploy when you meant project_patch

`project_deploy` **replaces** the project's static files. If you pass
`{ files: { "index.html": "..." } }`, every other static file is deleted.
Functions you omit stay live; `replace_functions: true` removes them.
`scope: 'functions'` leaves static files untouched, and `scope: 'static'`
leaves functions untouched (`deploy` →
`projectdeploy-replaces-files-preserves-omitted-functions-by-default`).

For a single-file edit, use `project_patch`.
`{ path, content }` rewrites the file, and
`{ path, find, replace }` does a server-side substring swap (~200
bytes on the wire). The platform auto-routes the path to static or
function. Use a `files` map to write several whole files in one patch,
or `edits` for ordered substring replacements across files. Each patch names
the release it edits as `base_release_id`: the `active_release_id` from
`project_export` (`deploy` → `projectpatch-incremental`).

## 3. Putting tokens or JWTs in URLs

Don't do this:
```text
https://my-app.somewhere.site/dashboard?token=eyJhbGc...
```

Tokens in query strings end up in:
- Browser history
- Server access logs
- HTTP referrer headers when the page links out
- Anyone watching over your shoulder

Use cookies (httpOnly, secure, sameSite) or the `Authorization: Bearer`
header. The auth flows the platform ships with already do this — only
break the pattern if you have a very specific reason.

## 4. Putting smt_ keys in browser-accessible code

The `smt_` developer key is admin. It can read every project, deploy
code, change env vars. If it leaks (committed to GitHub, embedded in
JavaScript bundle, dropped in browser localStorage) someone can take
over the account.

Use the smt_ key only in trusted developer tools:
- Your local terminal and the CLI
- CI/CD secrets
- Administrative server code you run for developer operations

App features inside a deployed function use `sw.*`, which is already
authenticated.

For browser sign-in, keep the starter’s auth route and cookie session
(docs({ topic: 'auth-client' })). The platform stores the session in an
HttpOnly cookie; your UI does not need to parse or store a token.

## 5. Reasoning models with too-low max_tokens

Reasoning models (models that enable reasoning) think first, then answer. The `<thinking>`
block consumes tokens. If `max_tokens` is too small, the model burns
its budget on reasoning and returns no answer at all —
`MODEL_EMPTY_RESPONSE` at HTTP 422, `retry: false`, with the stop
reason and token counts in `data`. Raise the budget; do not retry and
do not switch model.

**Wrong:** `max_tokens: 500` for a reasoning model.
**Right:** `max_tokens: 4000` minimum, `8000+` is safer.

For non-reasoning models (Claude and Luna) 500 is fine.

## 6. sw.fs.write camelCase vs snake_case

The `sw.fs.write` binding accepts both `contentType` (camelCase) and
`content_type` (snake_case) for the MIME type. Other fields are
camelCase only. Pick one style per project for consistency, but the
platform tolerates either on this option.

```typescript
// api/weekly-report.ts — POST generates a report on the server
export default async (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext): Promise<Response> => {
  if (req.method !== 'POST') return new Response('Method not allowed', { status: 405, headers: { Allow: 'POST' } })
  const user = await sw.auth.requireUser(req)
  const csv = 'period,total\nweekly,42\n'
  const path = '/reports/' + user.id + '/weekly.csv'
  await sw.fs.server.write(path, csv, {
    contentType: 'text/csv'  // or content_type — both work
  })
  return Response.json({ path })
}
```

## 7. "My deploy didn't update the live site"

A successful production deploy or patch publishes an immutable release
and makes it active; a dry run only checks the proposed change. If the live site
looks stale, it's almost always one of:

- Browser or CDN cache. Hard-reload (Cmd-Shift-R), or check with
  `curl -sI https://{subdomain}.somewhere.site`.
- The deploy hit a different project than you think (wrong
  `project_id`).
- A location that has not picked up the new release yet; how long it can
  serve the previous one is in `speed` → `pages-and-assets`.

## 8. Auth emails not arriving

The platform sends auth emails (signup confirmation, password reset)
from `noreply@somewhere.cloud` by default. That domain is not on your
project — it's the platform's. Some email providers flag it as
suspicious because the sending domain doesn't match your app's domain.

Fix: [verify a sender domain](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.email.txt#your-own-sender-domain). Once verified, auth emails go out from `noreply@yourdomain.com`.

## 9. A changed env var is not visible yet

Check the save response's `requires_deploy` field. An existing project
needs one ordinary raw-source production deploy before live env updates
work. New projects are ready after their first deploy. Once the save response
says `requires_deploy: false`, production `sw.env.MY_KEY` reads inside
the handler use the current value on new requests within 60
seconds, without another deploy. Public browser values, including one made private or
deleted, reach new page loads in the same window; reload an already open page. A preview keeps its captured values until you
create a new preview snapshot.

## 10. Libraries that need a different import or setup

Most npm packages work as they are: declare them in `package.json` and the
platform bundles them on deploy. Your pages carry no Content-Security-Policy
unless your app adds one, so browser libraries that use `eval` or blob workers
load normally. These are the cases that need a change:

| Library or need | Where | Use this |
|---|---|---|
| Node built-ins | Function | Import every built-in with the `node:` prefix: `import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'`. A bare `'crypto'`, `'fs'` or `'path'` fails to build. |
| A package with no `exports` field and no root `index.js` (pdf-lib) | Function | Import its ESM file directly: `import { PDFDocument } from 'pdf-lib/dist/pdf-lib.esm.js'`. A plain `'pdf-lib'` import fails to build. |
| Native modules: sharp, canvas, native bcrypt | Function | They cannot load. Serve resized images through `sw.image.resize` URLs; verify bcrypt hashes with `sw.crypto.bcrypt.verify`; draw in the browser, or print HTML with `sw.render.pdf`. |
| WebAssembly | Function | A `.wasm` import does not build in a function. Run WebAssembly in the browser. |
| ffmpeg | Both | A function bundles JavaScript only, so the ffmpeg binary is not available. Use ffmpeg.wasm in the browser with its single-thread core (`@ffmpeg/core`); pages are not cross-origin isolated, so the multi-thread core has no `SharedArrayBuffer`. |
| PDF.js, react-pdf | Browser | Set `pdfjs.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc` to a CDN URL at `pdfjs.version`, or copy `pdf.worker.min.mjs` into `public/`. The compiler does not rewrite `new URL('…', import.meta.url)` or `?url` / `?worker` imports (`recipe-pdfs`). |
| lottie-web | Browser | Works, full build included. `lottie-web/build/player/lottie_light` is the smaller build when you need no expressions. |

pages.title: Troubleshooting — Common errors and what to do
pages.body:
Start from what the platform recorded, then apply the fix for that error below. Read the newest errors first: `project_logs({ project_id, level: 'error', limit: 20 })` from an MCP client, or `somewhere errors` in the project folder. An uncaught function exception shows its code (`FUNCTION_ERROR`), the route, and a `stack` that names the file and line in your code. If a page or route is missing, `deploy_status({ project_id })` shows the active release and version that is serving. For what a visitor's browser saw — failed requests, console errors and the rendered page — use `browser` → `read-what-happened`. Then find the error code in the sections below; each gives the cause and the fix. `troubleshooting` → `how-to-read-your-error-logs` has the full log format. Use the returned `hint` for the next step; `all-api-errors-include-a-hint-field` explains that field. To rule out a platform problem, read the live status: `curl https://somewhere.cloud/status.txt` lists every component (sites, functions, app databases, sign-in, file storage, AI, payments, email API, deploys, API and MCP, and the somewhere.cloud website) with its state (Operational or Disrupted), when it was last checked, what it covers, and whether a check failed in the period on record (up to seven days). A component whose latest check is late shows its last known state, and a single failed check is re-run before a component shows Disrupted; the feed has no pending or unknown state. The same data is at https://somewhere.cloud/status and, as JSON, at https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/status. ## "FUNCTION_NOT_FOUND" or 404 on a /api/* route The function file isn't deployed, or the route doesn't match. Check: 1. Did you actually deploy the function? `deploy_status({ project_id })` lists deployed functions. 2. Does the file path match the URL? `api/users/[id].ts` serves `/api/users/123`. `api/users.ts` serves `/api/users`. 3. Was the deploy actually successful? Re-run `project_deploy` and check the response — every deploy goes live; if the route still 404s, the function isn't in the bundle. ## "API key is invalid" inside sw.* calls Inside a deployed function, `sw.*` calls authenticate with the project's own key. Read the error first: a thrown `sw.*` error carries `code` and `status`. - `AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE` (503) is temporary. Retry after `retry_after_ms`. - `INVALID_API_KEY` (401): confirm the call runs in the project and release you expect (`somewhere status`, or `deploy_status({ project_id })`), then read `somewhere errors` and `somewhere logs` for the failing path. If it persists on the current release, send the code, project id and release id with `support_ticket`. Don't copy a developer key or CLI session into source or environment variables to work around it. ## "AI_SPEND_CAP_REACHED" The project reached its monthly AI spend cap (HTTP 429). Your code is not at fault: every AI call from the project is refused until the month turns (UTC), and the rest of the app keeps working. `data` shows the cap, the spend so far and when it resets. Fix: if the spend is expected, the project owner raises the cap with `PATCH /v1/projects/{id}` `{ "ai_spend_cap_cents": }` (MCP `project_update`), or turns it off with `null`. The prepaid balance still bounds spend. Details: docs({ topic: 'sw.ai' }). The cap is per-project, not per-account, and it is not divided among your app's users: to stop one user spending the project's allowance, add `rateLimit` to that endpoint (`docs({ topic: 'sw.endpoint' })`) or use `sw.rateLimit`. ## Auth emails (signup, password reset) not arriving Two common causes: **Sender not verified** — Without `from`, mail goes from your app's own `somewhere.site` address, and auth emails from `noreply@somewhere.cloud`. Some inboxes flag this as suspicious. Follow the [sender domain setup](https://somewhere.cloud/docs/sw.email.txt#your-own-sender-domain) to send auth emails from your own domain. **A send failed** — Sign-in links and email verification codes report a failed send to the caller with an error code, for example `EMAIL_SUPPRESSED` (422), `EMAIL_PROJECT_PAUSED` (503), or `EMAIL_SEND_FAILED` / `EMAIL_DELIVERY_UNKNOWN` (502). A 202 response marked pending means the send is not confirmed yet. The password-reset email and the welcome email after sign-up (unless `auth_welcome_email` is false) are sent in the background: the request succeeds even when the send fails, and a reset request always gets the same answer, so it never reveals whether an account exists. To check those two, use an account at `@.test.somewhere.site` and read its mail with `somewhere email test-inbox
`. In a function, `sw.email.send` throws on failure; the error's `code` and `status` say why. ## A deploy failure that needs no change from you Some deploy failures come from the platform's build, not from your source. The live version stays as it was. Don't rename or move files for these: - `COMPILED_ASSET_COLLISION`: The compiler produced an asset whose filename already belongs to different bytes. Use the failure reference to investigate the compiled asset. No source change is required. - `POSTVERIFY_MISMATCH`: The deploy did not complete because the served version did not match the release being verified. The project deploy logs record the recovery outcome; no source change is required. Platform support requests are accepted at POST /v1/platform-feedback. - `DEPLOY_COMPILE_TIMEOUT`: The platform compiler exceeded its time limit while preparing this deploy. Your live version is unchanged. An immediate repeat of the same request meets the same time limit. Exact pinned dependency versions in package.json, rather than latest ranges, shorten the install for a raw-source deploy. When the versions are already pinned, platform support requests that include the failure reference are accepted at POST /v1/platform-feedback. The failed deploy's reference is in `project_deploy_log({ project_id })`. Report it with that reference through `support_ticket({ message })`. ## "Site not loading after deploy" Every `project_deploy` and `project_patch` writes to the live serving slot. If the live site still shows the old version, it's almost always cache: 1. **Browser cache.** Hard reload (Cmd-Shift-R) or open the URL in a private window. 2. **Edge cache.** `curl -sI https://{subdomain}.somewhere.site/` shows the response headers. Where present, `X-Somewhere-Edge-Cache` reports a platform cache hit or miss. `Cache-Control` describes what the browser may cache; it does not tell you whether the platform reused stored bytes. 3. **Wrong project.** Confirm the `project_id` matches the subdomain you're hitting. If a deploy genuinely failed silently, `deploy_status({ project_id })` returns the most recent timestamp — older than your last deploy means the deploy errored. ## Managed-mode raw SQL errors The project has a deployed `db/schema.ts`, so it is in managed mode. On an older shared database, ordinary `sw.db.query` / `sw.db.batch` fail before transport with `MANAGED_RAW_SQL_REQUIRES_SERVER_AUTHORITY`, including in job, queue, and cron handlers; with a separate SQL database they run there and never see declared tables. Explicit `sw.db.server.query` / `sw.db.server.batch` reads run as written after your function authorizes the caller. A raw write through them reaches only a separate SQL database, never declared tables; on an older shared database it fails with `MANAGED_RAW_WRITE_FORBIDDEN`. Fix: write with `sw.db.insert` / `sw.db.update` / `sw.db.remove` (the table needs a declared intent), or run the statement with developer authority (`db_query` / `db_batch` / `db_migrate`), which is unaffected. There is no flag that switches the project back to SQL mode; the owner-approved managed exit is the one path. Full contract: `docs({ topic: 'sw.db' })`, "Managed mode". ## "AUTH_REQUIRED" from sw.db.from / insert / count on an owner() table The table is user-owned, so the platform scopes it to a principal, and this request had none: there is no signed-in user, and this table does not declare `owner({ visitors: true })`, which is the declaration that accepts a stable anonymous visitor identity. Inspect the table in `db_scope_list`; its `owner_principal` summary describes both declaration forms. Fix: send the request signed in (same-origin session cookie, or `Authorization: Bearer `); or, after the handler independently checks that this caller is allowed to read across users, use the deliberate server-side cross-user mode `{ asServer: true }` with `sw.db.from` / `sw.db.count` for that exceptional operation. For anonymous-owned rows, declare `owner({ visitors: true })` and use the generated browser client; do not replace declared ownership with a hand-written visitor key. ## "REALTIME_RETIRED" (410) or "CHANNEL_FORBIDDEN" (403) The platform does not offer caller-named channels. This is not a configuration problem and there is no flag to turn them on. Fix: for browser live updates declare a live view — `sw.rooms.live(name, sw.db.from(...))` + `watchLive`. Developer tooling can subscribe to the reserved platform system channels with `events_subscribe_project` or `events_subscribe_user`. See `docs({ topic: 'live' })`. ## "payload is required" from sw.push.send `sw.push.send` takes ONE object with the notification nested inside it: `sw.push.send({ payload: { title, body }, user_id })`. The two-argument `send(payload, options)` form is not accepted. ## Schema changes with explicit SQL Schema changes outside `db/schema.ts` go through `db_migrate` with explicit SQL: it takes an automatic named bookmark before production-targeted statements and applies them atomically, exactly as written (the platform does not analyze raw migration SQL). In-place restore is unavailable. Save a copy before migration with `db_dump` or `POST /v1/db/dump`. Access rules are set in `db/schema.ts` and take effect on deploy. ## "DOMAIN_NOT_VERIFIED" on a custom domain This code comes from receiving-mail setup, not from serving the site: a mail address names a host that is not a receiving host with inbound mail on for this project. Attach the claimed domain to the project, run `domain_enable_email({ id })`, then register the address again on its `receiving_host` (the domain, or reply. when it has its own mail provider). A domain that does not serve the site yet is a separate check: 1. Claimed domain: `domain_check_ns({ id })` shows `claim_status`. `pending_ns` means the registrar does not yet show the two nameservers from `domain_claim`; compare them with `dig +short NS `. 2. DNS-record domain: `domain_verify({ project_id, domain })` returns `cname_ok`, `txt_ok` and `next_step`, which names the record that is missing or wrong. The TXT record is `_somewhere-verify.`; check it with `dig +short TXT _somewhere-verify.`. 3. Two TXT records on that name: delete the old one. ## A claimed domain is active but does not resolve `domain_owned` shows `claim_status: "active"` and `zone_status: "active"`, but `dig ` returns NXDOMAIN or no answer: the domain's platform records are incomplete. Repair them with: domain_publish({ id }) It sets the apex and `www` records and the routing again and returns any `failures`. It is idempotent and never changes the domain's mail records. ## "API_KEY is invalid" from sw.ai With a dedicated provider key stored for the project (`somewhere ai keys set --project ` or `POST /v1/ai/provider-keys`), each completion that selects that provider reads its current key. After you rotate the key at the provider, store the new one the same way; the next matching completion uses it, with no redeploy. A key the provider rejects returns `UPSTREAM_AUTH_FAILED`. Without a dedicated key, `sw.ai` uses platform-managed credentials, which never reach your deployed code, so a redeploy does not change the result. Send the error code with `support_ticket`. ## An existing hosted workspace shows "Disconnected code=4001" The workspace machine is on an outdated agent version. The platform restart-loops it until either the image gets fixed or the machine is replaced. Fix is on our side. If you hit this, submit a `support_ticket` with your `project_id` and the error text — it's not user-fixable. ## "Origin not allowed" when calling from a custom subdomain The project's CORS allowlist doesn't include the origin you're calling from. By default the platform allows the project's own `*.somewhere.site` URL plus any verified custom domains for the project. Fix: add the exact origin to the project's allowlist. From the CLI/MCP, read it with `project_allowed_origins_get` and set the full list with `project_allowed_origins_set` (owner or platform admin only), e.g. `somewhere call project_allowed_origins_set '{"project_id":"my-app","allowed_origins":["https://app.example.com"]}'`. Each entry is an exact origin — scheme + host + optional port, no path or wildcards. Server-to-server callers can use the `smt_` key. ## End-users see "Something went wrong" on my live site When the deployed function throws or crashes during a page load, the platform serves a branded fallback page so visitors never see a raw infrastructure error or JSON blob. It looks like: > # Something went wrong > The app ran into a problem. Try again in a moment. Three things to know: 1. **The crash is in your function — read the stack trace.** Every uncaught exception is captured to your project's logs with the full stack: ``` project_logs({ project_id, level: 'error', limit: 20 }) ``` Each row has `data.stack`, `data.path`, `data.method`, `data.route`, and `data.request_id` (the `cf-ray` you can correlate with deeper logs if you contact support). 2. **The fallback only triggers for page loads.** `/api/*` requests still return JSON to JS callers — your client error handling stays the same. The branded page only appears when a *page* request itself fails. 3. **You can customize the page.** Upload a `_error.html` file (or `_error/index.html`) in your project. If present, the platform serves that on any unhandled error instead of the default. Plain static HTML — no templating, no function dispatch needed. ## `somewhere test`: "the browser could not read its own files" (macOS) On a Mac, when the project is on an external drive and the command is started by an app that cannot show the macOS permission prompt, macOS refuses the browser the volume it is on (Chromium: "icudtl.dat not found", "GPU process isn't usable"): give that app access to removable volumes (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Files and Folders), or start the command as `node node_modules/@somewhere-cloud/cli/bin/somewhere.js test`. ## How to read your error logs Read application errors and record your own error messages: - **MCP**: `project_logs({ project_id, level: 'error', limit: 50 })` returns the most recent error rows in JSON. Add `search: '/api/checkout'` to match message text, `source: 'function'` to select a source, or `trace_id` to follow one distributed request. - **From inside a function**: `sw.logs.error(message, data)` writes a row with source='server'. Use this for known-bad branches your code handles deliberately. What you'll see for an uncaught function exception: ```json { "level": "error", "source": "server", "message": "FUNCTION_ERROR: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')", "data": { "code": "FUNCTION_ERROR", "stack": "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined...\n at handler (api/users.ts:14:18)\n ...", "request_id": "8f3c1d2a4b5e6789-LHR", "method": "POST", "path": "/api/users", "route": "/api/users", "slot": "prod" }, "created_at": 1715551234567 } ``` The `stack` field is the single most useful field for debugging — it tells you the exact file + line in your code where the throw originated. `CONTEXT_BUILD_FAILED` means the function's project context could not be assembled before the handler ran. Page-dispatch failures (the function could not start or timed out) show up with `FUNCTION_DISPATCH_FAILED`; a runtime that fails before it can answer reports `FUNCTION_RUNTIME_FAILED` (docs({ topic: 'limits' })); an uncaught handler exception is `FUNCTION_ERROR`. Match `data.request_id` to the response's `x-request-id` when tracing one request. The platform records the error separately from serving the fallback page. Write the HTML with `fs_write` or include it in your next deploy: ```html

my-app is down

back in a sec

``` The default page is the right call most of the time — only override when your app's design needs a matching aesthetic. ## Find a crashed function's stack When a function throws, the caller gets 500 `FUNCTION_ERROR` with a neutral `message` ("Function handler threw an error."), a `request_id`, a 32-character `trace_id` (also the `X-Trace-Id` header) and a `hint` for the developer naming that trace. With CLI 0.37.69 or later, read that one request: ```bash # Set TRACE_ID to the trace_id from the error response. somewhere logs --trace "$TRACE_ID" ``` It shows the request's lines with the recorded stack, file and line. Logs show your thrown message exactly as you wrote it, so keep secrets and personal data out of error messages. `somewhere support packet --trace ` builds a repro packet for that request locally; it leaves out the message, the stack and the request body, and uploads nothing. ## Words for errors: GET /v1/error-words `GET /v1/error-words` (no key needed) returns words for common error codes from one catalogue: `{ words: { CODE: { person, next } } }`. Look up the `error` code of any platform error answer: show `person` to a person as it is instead of writing your own wording, and use `next` as the agent's next step. The answer's own `message` stays the detailed explanation. ## All API errors include a hint field Every JSON error from the platform now ships with a `hint` field that names the most relevant `docs` topic. Read the hint instead of guessing what to call next: ```json { "ok": false, "error": "STALE_RELEASE_BASE", "message": "This deploy was prepared from release rel_previous, but release rel_current is live now, so nothing was changed. An earlier attempt (for example one that timed out) may already have completed; the project's status and source show whether it did. Otherwise the change applies on top of the current source.", "data": { "base_release_id": "rel_previous", "active_release_id": "rel_current" }, "hint": "Usage details: docs({ topic: 'deploy' }). Platform bug reports: support_ticket({ message }) returns a ticket_id, and support_ticket({ ticket_id }) returns its response. Advisor: somewhere advisor \" — \" (or advisor({ question }) over MCP) explains this error from its code." } ``` Every hint ends with that same advisor line. Put what you were doing and the error code in the question — the advisor answers best with the code in hand. The line appears only in API error responses for you and your agent; the error pages and function errors your app's visitors see never include it. If a hint looks misleading, send `support_ticket({ message })` — you'll get a ticket_id you can check with `support_ticket({ ticket_id })`. A failed MCP tool call that reached the platform also carries `_repro`, a `somewhere.repro/1` packet built only from typed, validated fields, each when present: the code, outcome, HTTP status, operation (the tool name), request, trace and project ids, the platform's retry verdict and `retry_after_ms`, and the location of an invalid field. Its `omitted` list names what it leaves out (the message, arguments, tokens, SQL and more), and `recipe` describes reproducing the same call shape on a disposable test project. Nothing is sent automatically: review it, and if it shows a platform bug, pass it as `context` to `support_ticket({ message, context })`. An error raised before the call reaches the platform, such as an unknown project name, has no packet. From the CLI (0.37.65 or later), `somewhere support packet` builds the same kind of packet for the last failed command, locally, and also records the command and how long it ran; `--out ` writes it as a private file, and nothing is uploaded.

pages.title: File tools — project-wide search, glob, diff and integrity check
pages.body:
These tools look across every file a project stores. They're for you and your
coding agent while developing, not for app code.

- **Search, glob and diff** are the developer tools `fs_search`, `fs_glob`
  and `fs_diff`. The same operations are on `sw.fs.dev` in developer
  `run_code`.
- **The integrity check** is only the developer tool `fs_integrity_check`.
  `run_code` can't call it.

From a terminal, `somewhere call <tool> '<json>'` runs any of these tools;
a full MCP connection calls them directly.

A deployed function never has these tools, whether it handles a request, a
cron, a queue message or a job: `sw.fs.dev` is undefined there, and
`sw.fs.search`, `sw.fs.glob` and `sw.fs.diff` throw `FS_DEV_ONLY` (400). For
each user's own files, use `recipe-file-uploads`. Ordinary file calls,
`sw.fs.replace` included, are in `sw.fs`.

## Who can use them

- The tools act with your developer login: the CLI, a full MCP connection or
  an `smt_` key. The integrity check accepts nothing else and answers 403
  `FORBIDDEN` to other callers, `run_code` included.
- `run_code` runs your script with the project's own authority, not your
  developer key. Project environment values (`sw.env`) are omitted unless you
  pass `include_env: true`.
- `sw.fs.dev` acts on the whole project and ignores any app user.
- Use these through developer tools. Never put a developer key in browser code.

## Search, glob and diff

```bash
# Every Markdown page under /content, paths only:
somewhere call fs_glob '{"project_id":"my-app","pattern":"/content/**/*.md"}'

# Pages that mention invoices; limit 20 is this example's choice:
somewhere call fs_search '{"project_id":"my-app","path":"/content/","query":"invoice","limit":20}'
```

- **`fs_glob`** — `{ project_id, pattern, limit? }`. It reads paths only, not
  contents, and supports `*`, `**`, `?` and `{a,b}`. A pattern can have up to
  500 characters, including the leading `/` (added
  when omitted). `*` and `?` stay within one path segment; `**` can cross
  `/`, including in the middle of a segment. `**/` matches zero or more
  nonempty directory segments. Braces can nest and expand into at most
  64 plain patterns, each within the same character
  limit. A larger expansion is refused with a validation error naming the
  limit, never truncated. Backslash escapes `{`, `}` and backslash; an
  unmatched brace stays literal. Brackets such as `[ab]` and other regex
  punctuation are literal, not character classes or regular expressions.
  Paths longer than 4,096 characters are refused by
  glob matching. `limit` defaults to
  500 (5,000 at most). The answer is
  `{ pattern, total, truncated, matches }`, and each match is
  `{ path, size_bytes, content_type, version, updated_at }`.
- **`fs_search`** — `{ project_id, query, path?, limit?, max_files? }`. It
  searches text files, judged by content type or extension, under `path`
  (default `/`). A query can have up to 500
  characters. `limit` defaults to 50
  (500 at most). The answer is
  `{ query, path, mode, total_matches, truncated, results }`.
  - `mode: 'fts5'` uses the project's index. It matches each run of ASCII
    letters and digits in the query as the start of a word, ignoring case,
    and returns the best matches as `{ path, snippet }`. Each write indexes
    the first 1,048,576 characters of a text file. When the index is
    built for files already stored, files over 1,048,576 bytes are
    skipped.
  - `mode: 'scan'` is used when the index is not ready or falls back, and in development
    environments. It's a literal, case-sensitive match, line by line, over at
    most `max_files` files (500 by default,
    2,000 at most), and it skips files over
    1,048,576 bytes. Each result is
    `{ path, line, snippet, before, after }`, and the answer adds
    `files_scanned`. A production scan schedules index backfill.
  - 503 `FILE_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE` means the index needs recovery; search
    again later.
- **`fs_diff`** — `{ project_id, path, version? }`. It compares the current
  text file with its previous version, or with the `version` you name, and
  returns `{ path, from_version, to_version, changed_lines, diff }`.
  `NOT_FOUND` means there's no earlier version, and `DIFF_TOO_LARGE` means a
  side has more than 2,000 lines.

`truncated: true` means the answer reached `limit`, so there may be more. A
`limit` or `max_files` above its maximum is lowered to it; a longer query or
pattern is refused.

In `run_code`, the same operations are
`sw.fs.dev.glob(pattern, { limit? })`,
`sw.fs.dev.search({ query, path?, limit?, max_files? })` and
`sw.fs.dev.diff(path, { version? })`, with the same answers.

## Integrity check: orphan file records

Reading a file whose stored bytes are missing answers `NOT_FOUND` and removes
that file's record. Its version records stay. To check a whole project, for
example after an incident, start read-only:

```bash
somewhere call fs_integrity_check '{"project_id":"my-app"}'
```

The answer is `{ scanned, orphan_files, orphan_versions, auto_clean,
cleaned, next_cursor }`. Each orphan file is `{ id, path, storage_key }`;
each orphan version is `{ id, file_id, version, storage_key }`. One call
checks up to `limit` files (1,000 by default,
5,000 at most). Pass `next_cursor` back as `cursor` until
it's `null`.

Removing records is a separate, explicit choice. After reviewing the list,
repeat the call with `"auto_clean": true`. That call deletes the orphan
records it finds, together with their version records, and reports the counts
in `cleaned`. The deletion can't be undone; the stored bytes were already
gone. Over HTTP, the same call is `POST /v1/fs/{project_id}/integrity-check`
with a developer credential.

pages.title: Discovered API surface
pages.body:
# Discovered API surface

Use this index to find an operation, then open its focused guide for a working example. Inside a deployed function, use the `sw.*` bindings: the platform supplies their project credentials. In a server integration or CI job, call the REST routes with a developer key; keep that key out of browser code. Connected coding agents use the matching MCP tools.

Read one family with `docs({ topic: "api-surface", section: "runtime-bindings" })`. For app data, start with `declared-data`; for sign-in, `sw.auth`; for uploads, `declared-files`. Each guide shows the access rules and request shapes for that feature.

Generated from the live runtime and route registrations. This page is the catch-all discovery index for public primitives; the focused topic pages remain the best starting point for examples and workflows.

## Behavioral primitives discovered from source

- **Database batch atomicity refusal** - `sw.db.batch` refuses to run when it cannot assemble an atomic batch and throws `DB_BATCH_NOT_ATOMIC` instead of falling back to sequential writes.
- **File conditional write** - `sw.fs.write(path, body, { ifMatch })` sends `If-Match`; stale versions throw `FS_VERSION_CONFLICT` with the current version so editors can re-read instead of clobbering concurrent writes.
- **Queue dead-letter inspection** - `GET /v1/queue/dead-letters` lists queue messages that exhausted their retries, scoped by `project_id` when supplied or by the caller otherwise.

pages.title: somewhere.cloud vs Supabase — honest comparison
pages.body:
## When to use somewhere.cloud

✓ **You want one platform for the whole backend.** Database + auth + files
  + email + payments + AI + cron + background jobs all behind one API and one bill.
  Supabase covers database + auth + storage + edge functions; you still
  wire Stripe, Resend, Inngest, Pinecone, OpenAI yourself.
✓ **You're shipping fast** — typically AI-built apps from Claude Code or
  Cursor. The MCP server gives the coding agent tools to deploy,
  query, and configure without leaving the chat.
✓ **Payments built in.** Stripe Connect is wired for you — no separate
  Stripe/billing integration to stand up. Supabase doesn't offer this.
✓ **Predictable pricing.** Flat monthly tiers — current ladder at /v1/pricing.
  No per-MAU jumps or project caps. Bandwidth is included on every plan. We do not meter it or bill for it. Fair use applies: this covers normal traffic to your app's pages, functions and files.

## When to use Supabase

✗ **Heavy Postgres dependency you want managed FOR you.** pgvector tuning,
  PostGIS, listen/notify, or an extension we don't substitute for. Worth
  knowing before you decide: you can attach your own PostgreSQL database here
  instead of leaving — any plan, Free included, your provider account and your
  bill (`docs({ topic: 'postgres' })`). What Supabase gives you that an
  attachment does not is Postgres managed as a product, with their console,
  their backups and their support behind it.
✗ **Existing Supabase project with momentum.** No reason to migrate
  for migration's sake.
✗ **One very large relational database you resize yourself.** Each project
  has its own managed SQL database. Managed data grows with your app:
  Somewhere handles storage as it grows, measured across your account under
  your plan, rather than through a self-serve resize. File contents, platform logs, analytics and
  search vectors are stored separately. Attach PostgreSQL when the relational
  workload needs it. Moving existing managed tables and their access rules is
  separate migration work, not an automatic result of attaching a database.
✗ **Self-host requirement.** Supabase is open-source and you can
  self-host the whole thing. We are not self-hostable.
✗ **You want Postgres-native client libraries.** PostgREST, postgrest-js,
  the broader Postgres tooling ecosystem. An attached database here speaks to
  the provider's official driver, not to PostgREST.

## What's roughly equivalent

| Need                | somewhere.cloud              | Supabase                  |
|---|---|---|
| Database            | `sw.db` (full SQL)        | `supabase.from()` (Postgres) |
| Real PostgreSQL     | attach your own, `sw.postgres` | built in, managed by them |
| Auth                | `sw.auth` (Google, magic link) | `supabase.auth` |
| Storage             | `sw.fs` (no egress fees)  | `supabase.storage` (S3) |
| Row-level security  | `sw.db.from/insert/update` (auto-scoped) | Postgres RLS policies |
| Database change events | developer-side `db_webhook_*` tools | Postgres replication |
| Vector search       | `sw.search` (built-in)     | pgvector (add-on) |
| Edge functions      | every `api/*` file         | `/functions/v1/*` |
| Email send/receive  | `sw.email` + mail API      | not included — wire Resend |
| Payments            | `sw.payments`              | not included — wire Stripe |
| AI                  | `sw.ai` (multi-provider proxy) | not included — wire OpenAI |
| Background jobs     | `sw.jobs` / `sw.cron` | not included — wire Inngest |
| Pricing             | flat tiers — see /v1/pricing | $25/mo Pro + usage |

## Migration paths

→ **somewhere.cloud → Supabase**: `db_dump` → load into a database file →
  `pgloader` that file into Postgres. Application data comes out in full.
  Password export is not available, so users set a password in the new
  app; `db_dump` and `auth_users_list` never return password hashes.
  See `migration.txt` for the same portability contract.
→ **Supabase → somewhere.cloud**: today this is a per-piece migration, and
  each piece is its own move — there is no one-shot import, and copying a
  database would not carry auth, files or functions with it. Steps:
  `pg_dump` → import via `db_migrate` +
  `db_import_csv` per table. Auth users: importing users with their
  passwords is not available, so each user creates their account again
  with the same email. `auth_users_list` is a READ tool and cannot create
  users.

Related: `portability`, `database-engine`, `pricing-comparison`.

pages.title: somewhere.cloud vs Vercel — honest comparison
pages.body:
## Framework and backend responsibilities

Next.js is an application framework; Vercel is a hosting platform optimized for
running it. A Next.js application can integrate managed database, auth, files,
email, payments, AI, and job providers. The application team chooses those
providers and owns their credentials, SDKs, migrations, authorization policies,
webhooks, and cross-service diagnostics.

somewhere.cloud hosts static or client-rendered React/Vite frontends and server
functions, and includes those backend capabilities behind one project contract.
It applies declared database permissions, generates the typed data client, and
connects deploy diagnostics to the same project. The application still owns its
business rules and the content it publishes.

## When to use somewhere.cloud

✓ **You want backend included, not added on.** Database, auth, storage,
  email, payments, AI — all behind one API. Vercel gives you hosting +
  serverless functions; you still need Supabase / Neon / Clerk / Resend
  / Stripe / OpenAI / Inngest / Pinecone.
✓ **AI-built apps shipped from a chat client.** The MCP server lets
  Claude / Cursor deploy, query, and configure end-to-end. Vercel CLI
  is the equivalent for the hosting half, but the backend half lives
  in 7 different dashboards.
✓ **Predictable pricing on bandwidth and MAUs.** Vercel meters bandwidth
  ($40/TB after 1 TB on Pro), function invocations, and Edge Middleware
  invocations. Bandwidth is included on every plan. We do not meter it or bill for it. Fair use applies: this covers normal traffic to your app's pages, functions and files.
✓ **One bill for the whole stack.** A flat monthly tier (see /v1/pricing)
  covers everything. A typical Vercel + Supabase + Clerk + Resend stack runs
  ~$170/mo before usage.

## When to use Vercel

✗ **You're shipping a Next.js app with ISR / SSR / app router.** Next.js
  is Vercel-native; SSR, ISR, on-demand revalidation, image optimization,
  middleware all work best there.
✗ **Existing team workflow.** GitHub-PR previews per branch, preview
  environment URLs, the Vercel deploy bot in your PRs. We have CLI
  deploys + dashboard previews, but not the same per-PR ergonomics.
✗ **Edge runtime + edge config + ISR cache.** If your app's whole
  identity is the edge-rendering story, Vercel's primitives are deeper
  than ours (we expose less of the edge-cache machinery directly).
✗ **You don't want any backend.** A pure static site with a few API
  routes that hit external services is what Vercel is best at. We're
  optimized for "needs a database + users."

## Rendering and SEO responsibilities

Next.js can render route output statically, from cached server work, or for a
request. Its App Router also provides metadata APIs and file conventions for
`sitemap.xml`, `robots.txt`, icons, and social images. The application chooses
the rendering and cache behavior and supplies the actual metadata and content.

somewhere.cloud does not execute Next.js SSR, ISR, or App Router code. It compiles
raw React/Vite source, serves deployed HTML and assets, and runs `api/*` server
functions. For crawler-facing route content, deploy a separate HTML page for
that route or generate the HTML before deployment. A client-router-only path
shares the entry HTML and is not a separate crawler document. Deployment
screenshots are preview evidence, not rendered HTML for crawlers.

Edit titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, Open Graph tags, and other metadata
in the deployed HTML. If the project does not provide `sitemap.xml` or
`robots.txt`, the platform generates fallbacks; the sitemap enumerates only
deployed HTML pages. A custom file overrides its generated counterpart. Search
Console registration and ownership verification remain application work.

Next.js references: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/partial-prerendering
and https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/metadata-and-og-images

## What's roughly equivalent

| Need              | somewhere.cloud            | Vercel + …                |
|---|---|---|
| Static hosting    | every project, all tiers  | Vercel Hobby / Pro |
| Server functions  | `api/*` files             | `/api/*` Vercel functions |
| Database          | `sw.db` (built-in)        | Vercel Postgres / Neon / Supabase |
| Auth              | `sw.auth` (built-in)      | Clerk / Auth.js / NextAuth |
| File storage      | `sw.fs` (built-in)        | Vercel Blob / S3 / R2 |
| Email send        | `sw.email` (built-in)     | Resend / SendGrid |
| Payments          | `sw.payments` (built-in)  | Stripe (you wire it) |
| AI                | `sw.ai` (built-in)        | OpenAI SDK (you wire it) |
| Background jobs   | `sw.jobs` / cron           | Vercel Cron / Inngest / QStash |
| Bandwidth         | [Current bandwidth and fair use](https://somewhere.cloud/pricing.txt) | 1 TB free, $40/TB |
| MAU pricing       | none                       | depends on auth provider |
| Pricing           | flat tiers — see /v1/pricing | $20 Pro + add-ons |

## Migration paths

→ **somewhere.cloud → Vercel**: code is standard JS/TS. Replace `sw.*`
  bindings with direct service calls (Neon for DB, S3 for files, Resend
  for email, Stripe SDK for payments). `db_dump` → load into a database file
  → `pgloader` that file into Neon Postgres.
→ **Vercel → somewhere.cloud**: adapt your route handlers to the Somewhere
  function contract and use the starter's auth integration. For a managed
  database, declare tables and access rules in `db/schema.ts`, then use
  the documented structured `sw.db` operations. Managed mode refuses
  ordinary raw `sw.db.query`; replacing a database import is not enough.
  See `declared-data` and `sw.db` for the schema, operation and return
  contracts before moving data or changing queries.

Related: `portability`, `pricing-comparison`, `vs-supabase`.

pages.title: Account tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## connector-link-email

Save the current connector session's work to a recoverable account. This requires an email address supplied by the user and sends that address a one-click verification link. Nothing is merged or unlocked until the human clicks: before verification the email remains unverified; afterward the account is saved, or the session is merged into an existing account for that email. Returns { sent: true }. Repeated calls are rate-limited and become a no-op once the account is saved.
