Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## ai-complete

Call a platform AI model for a project. ai_catalog lists current models and prices; docs({topic:"sw.ai"}) explains the full contract.

With neither provider nor model, the call uses free gpt-6-luna: 10 requests/minute and 200/day per project owner on every plan, 8,192 estimated input tokens including system/tools/history, and at most 1,024 output tokens. Standard service, reasoning disabled, 20-second provider deadline including the body. No paid fallback, BYOK charge, or automatic paid repair.

Explicit provider/model selection uses that model's normal billing path, including explicitly selecting gpt-6-luna. Included workers-ai models retain their separate limits. ai_catalog lists the valid model IDs.

messages is a JSON-stringified array of {role,content}. For text use result.text; result.content contains text/tool_use blocks. With response_schema, the result carries result.parsed and result.parse_error. Paid OpenAI/Anthropic responses may report pending cost: unknown is not zero, and repeating a successful model call does not settle accounting.

Tool-capable models accept Anthropic-shaped tool definitions and tool_result messages. A caller-chosen conversation_id together with subject_type and subject_id retains history under that scope; that caller key continues the conversation on later ai_complete calls. ai_conversation_list, ai_conversation_delete, and ai_conversation_fork take the same scope. Later turns send only new messages. History works across supported providers. Free-default overflow truncates history for the request and never runs paid summarization. For larger conversations and explicit paid compaction read docs({topic:"sw.ai"}).

Structured output: pass response_schema as a JSON-stringified JSON Schema, without caller tools or streaming.

## ai-conversation-list

List the saved AI conversations for one subject, or fetch one with its messages. subject_type and subject_id are required so conversation history never falls back to a project-wide view. Without conversation_id it lists (most-recently-updated first; each row includes id, created_at, updated_at, message_count, summarized_message_count, and summary_updated_at). With conversation_id it fetches that single conversation — returns its summary (rolling text from compaction:"summarize", null otherwise), summary_updated_at, and the message log in chronological order. By default a fetch returns only live (non-summarized) messages, matching what the model sees on the next call; include_summarized:true also returns rows folded into the summary.

## ai-conversation-fork

Branch one subject-owned AI conversation under a new id without losing the original. subject_type and subject_id are required and rechecked against the source row. It backs "regenerate from this point" or "what if I asked differently" UIs. up_to_message_id (the numeric id from ai_conversation_list messages[]) truncates the copy at that message inclusive; omitted, the full history is copied. Returns 404 if the source is missing or belongs to another subject, 409 if the new id is already in use.

## ai-embed

Need custom semantic similarity, clustering, or recommendation math? ai_embed turns text into vectors you control. For a managed FAQ/catalog/RAG index, search_upsert is the managed path — it embeds and indexes content for you. Returns an array of float vectors. Free via provider:"workers-ai" (bge-base-en-v1.5, bge-large-en-v1.5, bge-small-en-v1.5, qwen3-embedding-0.6b, embeddinggemma-300m). It accepts one string or up to 100 strings. No activation required for free models. Rate limits: Free tier 10/min and 200/day; Builder tier 200/min and 10,000/day.

## ai-transcribe

**Accepting voice notes, meeting recordings, interviews, or audio uploads?** `ai_transcribe` turns audio into text from base64 bytes or a public URL, returning the transcription, duration, and cost.

Rates by plan at /v1/pricing. Activation required: `ai_transcribe`.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "audio_url": "https://my-saas.somewhere.site/uploads/recording.mp3"
}
// Returns: { "text": "Hello, this is a test recording...", "duration_seconds": 45, "cost": { "total": "$0.000394" } }
```

## ai-tts

Synthesize speech from text. Returns audio bytes as base64, or saves to a storage path.

Without `model`, the free default voice is used — no activation, no bill, nothing to choose.

- `inworld-tts-2-flash` (default) — free: 166 English voices by name (default Ashley; e.g. Dennis, Olivia, Duncan). A Kokoro voice id maps to a similar voice. Up to 2,000 chars per call. `word_timings: true` also returns per-word start/end seconds.
- `hexgrad/Kokoro-82M` — free: 28 English voices by id (default af_bella). Up to 8,000 chars.
- `ResembleAI/chatterbox-turbo` — free: one built-in voice (no `voice` argument). Up to 8,000 chars.

All are free within fair-use limits; ai_catalog lists every voice. A voice whose provider is down returns VOICE_UNAVAILABLE; nothing is substituted.

Activation required: `ai_tts`.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "voice": "Ashley",
  "text": "Welcome to our app! Let's get started.",
  "storage": "/audio/welcome.mp3"
}
// Returns: { "storage_path": "/audio/welcome.mp3", "size_bytes": 40320, "cost": { "total": "$0.00" } }
```

## ai-generate-image

**Need a hero, product image, social card, thumbnail, or draft visual?** `ai_generate_image` creates it from a text prompt without wiring a separate image provider. Returns image bytes (base64) or a stored path plus cost.

Two managed models, priced in `ai_catalog`. Which model: omit `model` for fast, low-cost drafts (`@cf/black-forest-labs/flux-1-schnell`, fixed 1024×1024, billed per tile and step); `gpt-image-2.5-flare` suits final assets, legible text, UI mockups or a transparent background (reserves balance up front; a successful call uses reported token usage capped at that reservation, or the calculator estimate when usage is missing). Failed GPT Image calls return the reservation; an unconfirmed return is reported as `settlement: 'unconfirmed'`. Earlier retired managed models are refused with a message naming the default. For any other model, bring your own provider: store the vendor's key as a project secret and call the vendor from your own function; there is no managed AI charge on that path (the vendor bills you directly; your function's ordinary platform usage still applies).

**Inline rendering:** Pass `inline: true` to get the image as an MCP image content block alongside the JSON result. An MCP client that supports image content blocks can render it directly. Default `inline: false` keeps the response lightweight (base64 only when not stored).

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "prompt": "A minimalist logo for a fitness app, clean lines, blue and white",
  "inline": true
}
```

## ai-catalog

List every AI model the platform offers — feature, model id, provider, pricing string, and whether it's free for Builders. Paid-model rates vary by plan and are listed at /v1/pricing. It lists what is available before a model is chosen for `ai_complete`, `ai_tts`, `ai_generate_image`, or embeddings.

Read-only. No activation needed.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{}
// Returns: { "free_tier": { ... }, "markup_rate": 0.05, "models": [{ "feature": "tts", "model": "hexgrad/Kokoro-82M", "provider": "deepinfra", ... }, ...] }
```

## ai-usage

Return this month's AI spend broken down by feature (transcribe, tts, generate_image, complete). Read-only; no charges.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{}
// Returns: { "complete": { "calls": 142, "cost": "$0.23" }, "tts": { "calls": 12, "cost": "$0.003" }, ... }
```

pages.title: Analytics tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## analytics-track

**Building anything with users?** `analytics_track` gives the app per-event product analytics with one call. Track the moment a user signs up, starts checkout, purchases, publishes, or completes another product action; `analytics_query` returns it within seconds. Up to 20 numeric properties are automatically aggregatable (sum/avg).

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "event": "purchase_completed",
  "user_id": "u_alice",
  "properties": { "amount": 49.99, "plan": "pro", "source": "landing_page" }
}
```

## analytics-query

Query product analytics. Filter by event name and time range; group by hour, day, event, or user. Returns aggregated counts and numeric sums.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "event": "purchase_completed",
  "from": "2026-04-01",
  "to": "2026-04-20",
  "group_by": "day"
}
// Returns: [{ "date": "2026-04-01", "count": 12, "sum_amount": 587.88 }, ...]
```

pages.title: Api tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## api

Call platform /v1 endpoints that do not have a dedicated MCP tool yet. Dedicated tools cover common operations; this tool covers the remaining and newly added endpoints. `catalog` lists existing tools and `docs({ topic })` documents endpoint shape.

Each request is explicit and inspectable: `calls` is a flat array of independent `{ method, path, body? }` items. A single invocation runs up to 10 calls, each still endpoint-auth and quota gated. Data from one call is not inserted into another; data-dependent chains run across separate tool calls. `path` must be a platform `/v1/...` path, not a full URL.

Write calls require `confirm:true` by default. `GET` and `HEAD` run without confirm; `POST /v1/ai/complete` and `POST /v1/ai/embed` are the only read-shaped write routes currently allowlisted. Without confirmation the tool returns the exact calls it would run and asks you to re-call with `confirm:true`. Calls run with the caller's own auth and the same permission checks as dedicated tools.

## api-read

Read Somewhere platform API endpoints in a batch of up to 10 independent GET/HEAD requests. Paths and response shapes follow the Somewhere REST API reference: https://somewhere.cloud/docs.txt. Returns one result per request in input order. No write methods or request bodies are accepted. On the directory connector, AI routes (model calls and stored AI conversations) are unavailable.

## api-write

Create, update, or delete platform data through up to 10 independent POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE requests. Requests are not a transaction; some may succeed when others fail. Paths and request bodies follow the Somewhere REST API reference: https://somewhere.cloud/docs.txt. AI media generation, financial transfers, credential creation, and domain purchases are unavailable. On the directory connector, AI routes (model calls and stored AI conversations) are unavailable.

pages.title: Artifacts tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## artifact-publish

Publish a project file as an immutable ARTIFACT — a durable, addressable snapshot with typed metadata, so another agent (or a human) can consume exactly these bytes later without you re-describing the file through a context window.

A file path is mutable: a later write replaces the bytes and old versions get trimmed. Publishing freezes "the file at /specs/plan.md right now" into a fact — the bytes are copied to the artifact's own storage and the row records who produced it. It never changes; a new version is a new artifact whose `supersedes` points at the old one.

Returns `{ id, uri, ... }` where `uri` is `sw://{project}/artifact/{id}`, a stable reference for a later reader. They call `artifact_get` on it and see the title + summary + schema (enough to decide read-or-skip) and, on request, the exact frozen bytes.

Publishes an EXISTING file — it is written first (fs_write / fs_upload), then published.

**Example:**
```json
{
  "project_id": "acme",
  "path": "/specs/checkout.md",
  "title": "Checkout redesign spec",
  "summary": "Final 2-step checkout spec; supersedes the v1 draft; ready to implement.",
  "schema": "sw.design-doc@1",
  "agent": "cursor"
}
```

## artifact-get

Fetch a published artifact by its id or `sw://…` URI — metadata + provenance by default, or the exact immutable bytes with `include_content: true`.

This is the consume side of a handoff: another agent published a file and handed you `sw://{project}/artifact/{id}`. You get the title, summary, schema, size, and who produced it (`agent` + `derived_from`/`supersedes`) — enough to decide read-or-skip WITHOUT the producer re-describing it. `include_content: true` also returns the frozen bytes (text is inlined; the bytes are the exact ones from publish time, even if the source file has since changed).

Resolves across projects: any principal with access to the artifact's OWN project can fetch it, which raw file paths can never do.

**Example:** `{ "id": "sw://acme/artifact/art_9f2c…" }` or `{ "id": "art_9f2c…", "include_content": true }`

pages.title: Auth tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## account

Which somewhere.cloud account is this session connected as? Takes no arguments and reads only the caller's own account.

It answers "who am I connected as" without a guessed route or an identity inferred from the project list.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{}
// Returns: { "id": "u_abc", "email": "alice@example.com", "name": "Alice",
//            "anonymous": false, "email_verified": true, "tier": "builder",
//            "summary": "Connected as Alice (alice@example.com). The email address is verified." }
```

This is the DEVELOPER ACCOUNT holding the projects. For the end user of a customer's app, `auth_me` with that user's app token answers instead.

## auth-signup

Register user, create account, new user, sign up, onboard user — sign up a new end user for your app. Returns registration and user metadata; credentials are omitted from MCP output. This result cannot sign an agent in from a transcript. Sign-in goes through the app’s normal secure sign-in flow. Passwords are securely hashed. Intended for server-side code, not browser code.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "email": "alice@example.com", "password": "<password>" }
// Returns registration and user metadata without authentication credentials.
```

## auth-login

Sign in user, authenticate, login user, password check, end-user login — log in an existing end user of your app. Returns user profile, authentication token, and session token.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "email": "alice@example.com", "password": "<password>" }
// Returns: { "user": { "id": "u_abc", "email": "alice@example.com" }, "token": "eyJ...", "session_token": "st_...", "refresh_token": "rt_..." }
```

## auth-me

Get the current end user's profile from their authentication token.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "app_token": "eyJ..." }
// Returns: { "id": "u_abc", "email": "alice@example.com", "email_verified": true, "display_name": "Alice" }
```

## auth-google-url

Get a Google OAuth URL for end-user login. Redirect users to this URL to start the OAuth flow. After login, the platform redirects back to redirect_uri with a short-lived authorization code in the query string (`?code=...`). The JWT is never put in the URL — your backend exchanges the code for the JWT via POST /v1/auth/google/exchange (smt_ key required, server-side only), or via `sw.auth.googleExchange({ code })` from inside a deployed function. Codes are single-use and expire after 60 seconds. docs({ topic: 'sw.auth' }) documents the full flow.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "redirect_uri": "https://my-saas.somewhere.site/auth/callback" }
// Returns: { "url": "https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/auth/google?project_id=...&redirect_uri=..." }
```

## auth-users-list

List end-user accounts of your app — the people who signed up via auth_signup. Distinct from `project_list` (your own projects). Returns id, email, display_name, email_verified, created_at, last_login_at. Paginated by created_at descending.

## app-role-grant

Give an app user an app-wide role declared in db/schema.ts (`appRoles`, e.g. staff) with your developer key, so every `appRole()` rule on your tables applies to them at once. Name the person by user_id or by the exact address they signed up with; the address does not have to be verified (you vouch for the person; `emailDomain` roles stay verified-only). No claim, no app-admin promotion and no endpoint of your own are needed: this is how the first staff member is seeded. Idempotent: a role already held answers already_granted:true. Refused: an address nobody signed up with (USER_NOT_FOUND), a banned account (TARGET_INELIGIBLE), a role the live schema does not declare (ROLE_UNKNOWN), a project that has not deployed a schema with appRoles (POLICY_UNAVAILABLE). An app admin can still grant and revoke the same roles from inside the app with sw.groups.appRoles.

## app-role-list

List who holds which app-wide role (db/schema.ts `appRoles`) in a project: every grant, or one user's (user_id or email), or one role's. Each item carries user_id, email, email_verified, role, granted_by ('developer' for a grant made with the developer key, otherwise the app admin or delegating user's id) and created_at. The answer also names the roles the live schema declares. Keyset pages: pass next_cursor back as cursor.

## auth-reset-password

Consume a password-reset token (from the email link) and set a new password. Token is single-use. After success, all existing sessions for the user are invalidated.

**Example:**

```json
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "token": "rst_abc123", "new_password": "<credential>" }
```

## auth-verify-email

Verify the 6-digit code that was emailed to the user. On success, `email_verified` is set to true. After 5 wrong attempts the code is wiped and a new one is needed.

**Example:**

```json
{ "app_token": "eyJ...", "code": "482917" }
```

## auth-send-magic-link

Email a one-shot sign-in link to a user (passwordless / OTP). Auto-creates the user if they don't exist yet — same call covers sign-in and sign-up.

The link expires in 15 minutes and can only be used once. Token verification goes through `auth_verify_magic_link` (or `sw.auth.verifyOtp({ token })` from a deployed function).

**Example:**

```json
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "email": "alex@example.com", "redirect_uri": "https://my-saas.somewhere.site/auth/callback" }
```

## auth-mfa-enroll

Turn on email sign-in codes for the signed-in app user (the app's policy must be 'optional' or 'required'). Mails a code to their verified address and answers { challenge_id, delivery, expires_in }; confirm with auth_mfa_verify. Already on: { enrolled: true }.

## auth-refresh

Exchange a refresh token for a fresh (access_token, refresh_token) pair. Refresh tokens rotate — the old one is invalidated. Access tokens last 1 minute; refresh tokens last 30 days. Intended for server code, not browser code.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "refresh_token": "<refresh_token>" }
// Returns: { "token": "eyJ...new", "refresh_token": "<refresh_token>" }
```

## auth-cli-pair

Mint a short-lived `smt_` API key for ephemeral environments (hosted coding environments, sandboxes, containers). `somewhere auth set` takes the returned key through standard input or the command environment as `SOMEWHERE_TOKEN`. The CLI verifies and stores it, so the session can use the CLI without a browser login. Positional tokens are refused; the key does not belong in command arguments or chat.

Returns: `{ id, key: "smt_...", prefix, name, kind: "cli_pair", expires_at, ttl_seconds }`. Key auto-expires in 24h; the next session takes a new key. No refresh token is returned here: the pairing response omits the long-lived refresh credential. `somewhere auth login` gives a CLI session that renews itself; it stores its credentials directly in the CLI config.

For a shell without CLI credentials. The CLI is the scoped package `@somewhere-cloud/cli` (`npm i -g @somewhere-cloud/cli`). After pairing, first-class CLI commands cover routine work and `somewhere call <tool> '<json>'` covers the complete platform tool catalog. Without a shell, the MCP tools are the path.

Security note: scoped to the same user as the caller. Auditable as kind='cli_pair' separately from your main developer key, so a stolen ephemeral token is revocable on its own.

**Example flow (run once per session):**

```text
1. Call auth_cli_pair() → { key: "smt_...", expires_at: "..." }
2. Set SOMEWHERE_TOKEN to the returned key in the command environment.
3. Run: somewhere auth set   // reads SOMEWHERE_TOKEN
4. Run: somewhere whoami     // confirms identity
5. somewhere deploy          // deploy raw source
```

## auth-cli-pair-connector

Create a short-lived (24-hour) API key that links the somewhere CLI in a shell environment to this account; the CLI then performs the same operations as this connector. Returns the key, its prefix and its expiry. The key is recorded as its own CLI pairing key, revocable separately, and no refresh credential is returned. The CLI reads the key from standard input or the SOMEWHERE_TOKEN environment variable through `somewhere auth set`. No operation on this connector requires it. In a terminal, the CLI reads deployment files from disk in one command without placing their contents in conversation tool arguments; for a typical app that keeps tens of thousands of tokens out of the conversation.

## auth-templates-list

List the three platform-issued email templates for a project: `password_reset`, `email_verification`, and `welcome`. Returns the live subject + HTML, whether it's a custom override or the default, and the default values inline.

pages.title: Browser tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments. ## browser SEE, inspect, DRIVE and CAPTURE any web page — your app's EYES for perception, a VERIFY harness for QA, AND the one way to turn a page into a picture or a PDF. One call returns a structured health SIGNAL (console errors, page errors, failed network requests), not a raw image to vision-parse; a bad step or wrong shape hands back a correcting error. Capture a page or HTML snippet in the format you need: a full-page **webp** of a logged-in view saved to a path you choose, or a **PDF invoice**, out of the same call. **One tool, several outputs** — `capture: { "as": "png" | "jpeg" | "webp" | "pdf" }`. Printing is an output format, not a different operation: ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "url": "https://my-saas.somewhere.site/pricing", "capture": { "as": "webp", "full_page": true }, "storage": "/renders/pricing.webp" } ``` ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "html": "

Invoice #1234

Total: $49.99

", "capture": { "as": "pdf", "paper": "A4" }, "storage": "/invoices/inv-1234.pdf" } ``` **See below the first screen, and watch it move.** The default screenshot is the first screen only (the viewport). `capture: { "full_page": true }` captures the whole scrollable page; the `frames` action watches a page over a few seconds and returns ONE labelled contact sheet plus measured change: ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "capture": { "full_page": true } } ``` ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "actions": [ { "click": "#open-menu" }, { "frames": { "count": 6, "interval_ms": 150, "selector": "#menu" } } ] } ``` `frames` takes 2–12 screenshots at fixed geometry, `(count - 1) × interval_ms` at most 10000 ms, and reports `steps[].value.motion` (`from_ms`, `to_ms`, `changed_ratio` between consecutive frames, measured times) and `visual_change_detected`, worded as "visual change detected in the sampled region" — sampled pixels neither prove an animation runs nor that none does. With `selector` the region is that element's box at the first frame, held fixed, and `element_box` reports how the element itself moved; when it moved, `visual_change_detected` is true and the summary says by how much, even if it left the region before the next capture. Captures in the hosted browser are spaced by their measured times (`frames[].at_ms`), not the requested `interval_ms`: each takes a few hundred milliseconds, so a 200 ms request can come back 400–700 ms apart. Directly after a click it samples at once, so a short transition is caught. An incomplete capture (deadline, element gone, navigation) fails the step with `complete: false` and its captured count; it never reports "no change". The sheet comes back inline (re-encoded to fit) and, with a project, stored like a screenshot. **Modes:** - **EYES (perception)** — NO `project_id`, any public `url` (e.g. `{ "url": "https://example.com" }`): look at / inspect / screenshot ANY page. Ephemeral output — the screenshot returns **inline** (auto-downscaled to fit) by default; `store:true` gives a short-TTL signed scratch URL (`screenshots[].scratch_url`, never durable project storage). No-actions inspect includes the bounded clickable-element map. An explicit `include` list selects sections; `include:["network","dom"]` adds the full network table and the map. No auth, no origin-lock — any public URL. - **VERIFY (project QA)** — `project_id`: drive + assert the deployed app of that project. `actions` clicks / fills / asserts a flow, and `auth:{ "user_id": "…" }` runs it as a logged-in user (1h audited impersonation), and screenshots store durably to the project filesystem (`screenshots[].fs_path`). Origin-locked — a `url` must be on the project's own origin. Same engine and the same signals-first report either way. Each completed page run also returns one `accessibility_layout` line for WCAG AA text contrast, horizontal overflow, and tap targets below the 24×24px WCAG 2.2 AA minimum (24–44px is listed as a note). Those findings are advisory and never change `passed`. - **Without `actions`** → a health snapshot by default: console errors, page errors, failed network requests (the 4xx/5xx + dropped calls — the real signal), the rendered page text (`rendered_text` — grep-able structured text beats a screenshot ~80% of the time), `final_url`, a small screenshot, and a bounded interactive-element map (`dom_outline` + testid handles). An explicit `include` list selects optional sections: `include:["network","dom"]` retains the map and adds the full per-request `network` table + redirect chain; `include:[]` omits both. This is the quick "what does my app look like and is it healthy" call (it replaces a standalone screenshot). That page screenshot comes back **inline as an MCP image content block by default** (it renders directly in the conversation) while its file path stays in the output as the durable artifact; `inline:false` skips the inline image and keeps only the path. An oversized capture on a tall/heavy page is auto-downscaled to fit inline — a no-`project_id` call still returns a real image in one shot. - **`actions`** → the same concise action-sequence JSON as the CLI: `{click}`, `{fill,value}`, `{upload,file,name?}`, `{select,value}`, `{wait}`, `{expect}`, `{screenshot}`, `{frames}`, `{eval}`, and `{goto}` (a path on the app, e.g. `{goto:"/club"}`). Every item reports ok/fail with a reason, and the first failure stops the sequence. - Existing expanded `steps` remain accepted for older callers; new flows use the shared `actions` shape above. - **`url` with NO `project_id`** → capture/inspection of ANY public third-party page (e.g. `{ "url": "https://example.com" }`), not just your own app. (When you DO pass `project_id`, `url` is scoped to that project's origin.) The screenshot comes back inline by default; `store:true` instead returns a short-lived, auto-expiring signed URL to the full-res image (`screenshots[].scratch_url`) — handy for a big external capture you'd rather link than inline. It's kept in an ephemeral scratch store and never touches project storage. - **`html`** → a raw HTML snippet rendered straight to an image (e.g. an OG card). No page navigation, no steps; returns the image inline, or the stored file path when `storage` is set. - **`extract:"markdown"`** (or `include:["markdown"]`) → the page as clean MARKDOWN (headings, links, lists, main content) in the `markdown` field, instead of vision-parsing the screenshot. The cheapest way to actually read a page's content. (The plain rendered text is always in `rendered_text`.) - **`session_id`** → ONE live browser page kept alive ACROSS calls (persistent session). Navigate in call 1; in call 2 (same session_id) wait for a 20s stream and screenshot the SAME page — cookies, current URL, and the in-flight stream all survive. The call returns `session_id` + `session_expires_at`; a reconnect skips the initial navigation (the page is where you left it — a `goto` step moves). Sessions are yours only, capped per developer, and idle out after 5 min (10 min hard cap); a failed step keeps the session, and an expired one restarts signed out and says so (`session_note`). Omitted, it is the default fresh-per-call browser (cache-safe — a session is only for cross-call state). **With a shell:** `somewhere browser` covers navigation, waits, evaluation, screenshots, and flow steps. This MCP tool covers clients without a shell, and cases where an inline image or result is more useful. It checks what a UI looks like AND whether it works — clicks land, the form submits, the modal opens — and to catch the 500-ing API call a screenshot alone would hide. (run_code proves a function's backend; `browser` proves the rendered UI.) Signals come FIRST: `passed` reflects step outcomes only — console_errors / page_errors / failed_requests matter too (a 500 shows there even when every step "passes"). Elements are targeted by selector rather than pixel coordinates. **Shared action-sequence JSON** (preferred; the CLI's `--actions` file uses this exact array): Example transcript or fragment ```text "actions": [ { "fill": "#email", "value": "a@b.co" }, { "upload": "#avatar", "file": "data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo=", "name": "avatar.png" }, { "select": "#plan", "value": "pro" }, { "click": "button[type=submit]" }, { "wait": ".dashboard" }, { "expect": { "selector": ".welcome", "text": "Hi", "visible": true, "count": 1 } }, { "screenshot": "after" }, { "eval": "document.title" } ] ``` Files over the 10 MB inline limit come from project files via `{ "upload": "#video", "fs_path": "/uploads/big.mp4" }` (optional `name`, `type`; up to 50 MB per call, streamed into the page). `wait` is a CSS selector string or a millisecond number. `expect` requires a selector and at least one of `text` (substring), `visible` (boolean), or `count` (exact non-negative integer); conditions may be combined. A failed action stops the sequence and names its zero-based action index. Native `alert`/`confirm`/`prompt`/`beforeunload` dialogs are dismissed by default and listed in the report's `dialogs`. `{ "dialog": "accept" }` (with `"text"` for a prompt) right before the action that opens one accepts it; the answer applies to the next dialog only. Expanded `steps` remain runtime-compatible for older callers, but are not a second authoring contract. `actions` is the form for new flows. A failed action aborts the run while preserving console, network, and screenshot state. **Examples:** Example transcript or fragment ```text // See + inspect — screenshot, signals, and the clickable-element map, no actions: { "project_id": "my-saas" } ``` Example transcript or fragment ```text // Drive a logged-in flow as a specific user (impersonation, 1h, audited): { "project_id": "my-saas", "auth": { "user_id": "usr_123" }, "actions": [ { "wait": "h1" }, { "expect": { "selector": "h1", "text": "Welcome" } } ] } ``` ## browser-connector Inspect or screenshot an external public URL without project authority. Actions, steps, eval, authentication, session seeding, and persistent sessions require project_id, and their navigation stays on an authorized origin owned by that project. Owned apps may load their normal external assets and APIs under backend policy. Interactive operations can change application data. Returns page, console, network, and screenshot evidence. ## site-verify Runs one browser flow across desktop and phone viewports and returns one structured verdict: every named step, page/console/network health, expected request outcomes, both screenshot paths or URLs, and a non-blocking accessibility/layout line per viewport covering WCAG AA text contrast, horizontal overflow, and tap targets below the 24×24px WCAG 2.2 AA minimum (24–44px is listed as a note). Authenticated or seeded flows require project_id and a project-owned origin. An absent action list produces a load/health/two-screenshot check. Each viewport uses a fresh browser that closes inside the call, including on failure. ## site-verify-connector Inspect or screenshot an external public URL at desktop and phone sizes without project authority. Actions, eval, authentication, and session seeds require project_id, and their navigation stays on an authorized origin owned by that project. Owned apps may load their normal external assets and APIs under backend policy. Returns step results, page errors, network outcomes, and screenshots; interactive operations can change application data.

pages.title: Code tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## run-code

Run a short script once, server-side, against a project's own bindings — get the result + console logs back in one call. It replaces a throwaway debug endpoint or dozens of tool calls when inspecting data, trying a query variant, or running a one-off transformation.

`code` is an ES module whose default async function receives `sw` (the same database / files / search / ai bindings a deployed function gets) and returns a JSON-serializable value:

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "code": "export default async function (sw) { const { data } = await sw.db.server.from('notes', { limit: 1 }); return data; }"
}
```

Application tables are declared in db/schema.ts. sw.db.from reads them with caller-scoped access, and sw.db.server.from reads them once the caller is authorized for server access. The corresponding structured methods, such as sw.db.server.insert, change them. Raw query and batch go to the separate raw SQL database on current projects. The script entry point above is for `run_code`. A JSON route in api/ is export default sw.endpoint({ auth, handler }) with auth set explicitly. TypeScript infers the handler inputs and sw context. auth: 'none' marks a deliberately public route.

Runs with the project's OWN authority, not your developer key: no env secrets unless you pass `include_env: true`, no admin, no cross-project access, and outbound fetch is limited to public hosts. Returns `{ result, logs, duration_ms, error? }`. `result` is capped at 256KB (truncated with a notice past that). `logs` keeps at most 100 entries. Each log message is cut at 64KB with a `[truncated: …]` marker at its end. All logs together stop at 4MB, followed by one final `[logs truncated: …]` entry. `logs_truncated: true` is set when entries were dropped by either limit (not when a single message is cut). `error.message` and `error.stack` are each cut at 64KB. A returned `session` over 64KB is not stored and the call answers `SESSION_TOO_LARGE`. `timeout_ms` defaults to 10000, max 30000.

**Threading state across calls (opt-in):** pass a stable `session_id` to carry explicit JSON state between runs. The saved JSON is exposed to your script as a read-only `sw.session`; a returned `{ session: {...} }` object saves state for the next call (it is stored under that `session_id`, separately from `result`). Absent `session_id` = stateless, byte-identical to a normal run. This is explicit data you thread by id — NOT live-variable/closure persistence.

## run-code-connector

Execute a short ES-module script against one project’s live bindings and return JSON plus console logs. The default async function receives sw. Writes persist; the script is temporary. Optional session_id preserves explicit returned JSON between runs. include_env exposes project secrets only when true. Platform AI media generation and financial transfers are unavailable in connector runs. Runtime API reference: https://somewhere.cloud/docs.txt.

pages.title: Connect tool reference
Cron tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## cron-create

Create a scheduled trigger. Schedule is a 5-field cron expression (`minute hour dom month dow`). It uses UTC by default; an IANA `timezone` such as `America/Los_Angeles` gives local wall-clock scheduling with daylight-saving changes handled automatically. Each fire dispatches a job to your handler (at-least-once delivery, so handlers are idempotent). Missed fires during platform downtime are NOT replayed.

**Common patterns:**

| Pattern | Schedule |
|---------|----------|
| Every 15 minutes | `*/15 * * * *` |
| Daily at 08:00 UTC | `0 8 * * *` |
| Every 6 hours | `0 */6 * * *` |
| Weekly Monday midnight | `0 0 * * 1` |

**Minimum interval.** Your plan sets the smallest gap allowed between two
fires. `cron_list({ project_id })` reports it as
`policy.min_interval_minutes`, alongside `policy.max_per_project`. A
schedule tighter than the floor is refused with
`CRON_SCHEDULE_TOO_FREQUENT` and the message names both intervals.
Schedules that already exist are never re-checked — they keep firing on the
cadence they were created with.

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "name": "daily-digest",
  "schedule": "0 8 * * *",
  "handler": "https://my-saas.somewhere.site/api/cron/daily-digest",
  "payload": { "type": "digest" }
}
```

## cron-list

List cron triggers for a project (or all your projects). Each row includes timezone, last_run_at, last_run_status, last_run_job_id, bounded last_error_code/last_error diagnostics, and next_run_at. A task that has never run returns null for every last-run field. job_get with last_run_job_id returns full bounded attempt history. Passing project_id also returns `policy` — the project owner's plan name, the smallest interval a new or edited schedule may have, and how many scheduled tasks the project may hold.

## cron-run

Run an existing scheduled task once now through the same job handler used by scheduled fires. This does not change its schedule. The run is recorded in job history with trigger `manual`. With preview_session_id and preview_id, the task's handler path and payload run once in that exact open preview instead (its code, data, files and mail; one attempt, at most 270 s); the production schedule is only read and never changes.

## cron-update

Update a cron trigger's schedule, IANA timezone, handler, payload, display name, or enabled state. Sending a new `schedule` or `timezone` recomputes the next fire and re-checks the plan minimum (see cron_list `policy`); every other edit, including resuming a paused task, leaves an existing schedule alone.

pages.title: Db tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## db-describe

Schema inspection, list tables, show schema, table structure, columns, types — describe the project database. With no table argument, lists visible managed and raw table names with table_planes metadata. Omitted plane prefers a declared managed table; plane:"raw" inspects a same-name raw table. With a table name, returns its column names, types, constraints, and row count.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
// List all tables:
{ "project_id": "my-saas" }

// Describe one table:
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "table": "users" }
// Returns: [{ "name": "id", "type": "TEXT", "pk": true }, { "name": "email", "type": "TEXT", "notnull": true }, ...]
```

## db-query

SQL query, run SQL, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, execute SQL against the project database — the read/write-ROWS entry point. A documented Postgres-flavored syntax subset is translated; the default database keeps its own expression, typing, comparison, and ordering semantics. For example, division by zero returns NULL rather than throwing. The database is created on first use, but tables are not — new projects declare them in `db/schema.ts` and deploy raw source; db_migrate is for SQL-mode projects. Raw SQL reaches the project's raw SQL database only; on a project that keeps its tables in the managed database, rows are read with db_browse (plane: "managed"), schema with db_describe, and writes go through sw.db in functions.

Schema changes (CREATE / ALTER / DROP) belong in `db/schema.ts` plus deploy for managed projects, or db_migrate for SQL-mode projects, not here, and not inline in a deployed function's handler: runtime DDL runs on every request, isn't versioned, and hides new tables from the platform's per-user data protections (a table with an owner_id/user_id column is cross-user readable until it's scoped). db_query is for the rows.

Every successful query returns `{ data: [], count: N, changes: N, last_row_id: X }`: `data` contains returned rows, `count` counts those rows, and `changes` counts affected rows. A write without RETURNING has empty `data` and a zero `count` even when it changes rows. `last_row_id` is a number, an exact decimal integer string when the ID exceeds JavaScript’s safe integer range, or null; other transport metadata may also be present.

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "sql": "SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20",
  "params": [1704067200]
}
```

The database has a 30-second hard query ceiling. `timeout_ms` bounds how long this call waits (default 30000, max 30000) and returns QUERY_TIMEOUT; it does not promise cancellation of work already accepted by the database.

## db-batch

Run multiple SQL statements as a single atomic transaction. Every statement commits together, or none do — a single failure rolls the entire batch back. Suited to any logical operation that spans more than one write (account deletion across multiple tables, moving money between rows, denormalized counters). Max 1000 statements per call.

Each statement returns its own `{ rows, count, changes, last_row_id }` in `results[i]` matching the order you passed in.

**Example (account deletion):**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "statements": [
    { "sql": "UPDATE accounts SET status = 'deleted' WHERE id = ?", "params": ["u_abc"] },
    { "sql": "DELETE FROM sessions WHERE user_id = ?",            "params": ["u_abc"] },
    { "sql": "DELETE FROM posts WHERE author_id = ?",             "params": ["u_abc"] }
  ]
}
```

## db-migrate

Run explicit SQL schema migrations for SQL-mode projects. New projects use declared data: define tables and access rules in `db/schema.ts` and deploy raw source; db_migrate does not create their tables. docs({ topic: 'declared-data', section: 'declare-a-table-and-use-it' }) has a complete example. Managed projects refuse DDL with SCHEMA_LOCKED and apply no SQL.

For SQL-mode projects, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX and DROP are supported; multiple statements may be separated by `;`. Explicit preview targeting changes only that preview database. Developer-only — app-user JWTs are rejected.

## db-migrate-connector

Run a SQL schema migration for a SQL-mode project. New projects declare tables in db/schema.ts and deploy raw source; docs declared-data, section declare-a-table-and-use-it, has the example. Managed-project DDL is refused without applying SQL.

## db-import

Bring an existing database table under schema management — introspect a table you already have and GENERATE its `db/schema.ts` entry so a deploy can manage it. Read-only: it proposes an entry you paste into db/schema.ts and deploy; the deploy is what adopts the table (never a hidden change).

The generated entry preserves the table's shape faithfully — column types, single-column primary key, indexes, unique constraints, auto-timestamp defaults, and (for a per-user table) its owner column as `owner({ column })`. A composite primary key, a view, a triggered table, or a column type the managed schema can't represent is refused with a plain fix-it. A column whose stored values don't match its declared type is loosened and reported, never silently changed.

`with` imports several related tables at once so a foreign key between them can be represented.

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "table": "products"
}
```

## db-import-csv

Import CSV data into a database table. If the table doesn't exist and `create_table` is true, it will be created with column types inferred from the data (INTEGER / REAL / TEXT). Headers in the CSV become column names.

Inline CSV strings are capped at 5 MB. Larger files are uploaded to `/v1/fs` first and passed by filepath.
The import saves rows in batches. If a batch fails, the error gives the number of rows already imported and the CSV line to resume from. Keep the header and import only the remaining rows. If the error says a write could not be confirmed, check the table before trying again.

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "table": "products",
  "csv": "name,price\nWidget,9.99\nGadget,19.99",
  "create_table": true
}
```

## db-browse

Browse rows in a database table with pagination, sorting, and filtering. Inspects data without writing SQL.

Filters use the same operators as db_query: `eq`, `neq`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `like`, `ilike`, `is`, `not`.

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "table": "users",
  "limit": 10,
  "order_by": "created_at",
  "order": "desc",
  "filters": [{ "column": "email_verified", "op": "eq", "value": true }]
}
```

## db-export

Export a database table as CSV. Returns the CSV content as a string. Filters export a subset (same shape as db_browse). Capped at 100,000 rows — filters cover larger tables.

**Example:**

```json
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "table": "users" }
```

## db-dump

Full SQL dump of the project's database — schema (CREATE TABLE / INDEX / TRIGGER) + every row as INSERT statements. The output is standard SQL you can pipe into any SQL database client to restore, or migrate to Postgres via `pgloader`.

Returns the raw .sql file as a string. One call gives you the complete raw SQL database's schema and rows to take anywhere. A project that keeps its tables in the managed database has no raw SQL database to dump (RAW_DATABASE_NOT_READY); its managed rows are read with db_browse (plane: "managed") and their schema and row counts with db_describe.

Table access declarations and sensitive-column marks are platform policy, not SQL. Their labels travel as comment lines in the SQL preamble and, parsed, as `excluded_security_policy.policies` (labels only, never applied by a SQL restore); a warning appears only when the list is non-empty. `policies: []` on a successful capture means no table-access declarations were found in this capture — it does not establish that access is safe or preserve your application's authorization, and member join definitions and handler authorization are outside that list. After restoring, redeploy `db/schema.ts` (access rules are set there and take effect on deploy), then verify with `db_scope_list`.

`excluded_security_policy.capture` (v1) is the capture receipt, carrying identity, hashes and times only: canonical `project_id` and `database_id` (the top-level `project_id` echoes your reference), `sql_sha256` / `schema_sha256` / `policy_sha256`, and `policy_observed_at`, `data_observation_started_at`, `data_observation_completed_at`, `binding_checked_at`. The hashes detect changed bytes against metadata you retain; they are not a signature, not provenance, and not a cross-store snapshot. Matching binding checks before and after mean the same project, owner and database were observed; they do not exclude a change in between. When capture metadata is present but malformed, or its SQL or policy hash does not match, this tool returns `DUMP_INTEGRITY_UNCONFIRMED` (502) and no SQL. An absent `capture` (an older API during a rolling release) means no capture-integrity evidence; the informational policy labels may still be present.

Refusals, never a partial file: `DATABASE_NOT_INITIALIZED` (409 — the dump never creates a database), `DUMP_SOURCE_CHANGED` (409), `DUMP_SCHEMA_CHANGED` (409), `DUMP_POLICY_INVALID` (422), `DUMP_UNSUPPORTED_SCHEMA` (422), `DUMP_ROW_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (413, above 1,000,000 rows in a table — no truncation and no streaming export; narrow with `db_export_csv` filters), `DUMP_CAPTURE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (413), `DUMP_POLICY_UNAVAILABLE` (503), `DUMP_CAPTURE_UNCONFIRMED` (503), `DUMP_SCHEMA_UNAVAILABLE` (503), `PROJECT_ACCESS_DENIED` (403).

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas" }
// Returns the full .sql as text — write it to disk and you're portable.
```

## db-scope-list

List the table scopes a project has on record (`scopes`: recorded declarations, which a deploy that did not complete can leave behind) beside `live_rules`, the rules the live version actually serves, plus tables that LOOK like per-user data (a user_id/owner_id-style column) with no scope on record. An entry in `unscoped_user_tables` is a finding to inspect under the table's actual access contract, not a verdict: on a managed project the contract is the table's declaration in `db/schema.ts` (and structured queries on an undeclared table are refused, not run unscoped); on a SQL-mode project it is the previously recorded declaration, and raw SQL in server functions is unscoped by design. Developer-only.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas" }
// Returns: { "scopes": [{ "table": "bookings", "owner_column": "user_id", "intent": "scoped", ... }], "unscoped_user_tables": [{ "table": "notes", "owner_column": "user_id" }] }
```

## db-explain-access

Explain whether one app user of your project may read, update or delete one existing row of a declared table right now, and which declared rule link decides it. For a table declared with `allOf(gate, who)`, `create` is also explained, for a new row in the named row's group: create authority comes from the gate's create roles alone. The answer comes from the same access rules and active release the app enforces, read live. It names declared tables and columns only, never row values or other users' memberships. Developer-only; the project must be one you can edit.

Reasons: ROW_NOT_FOUND, SUBJECT_NOT_ELIGIBLE (no such signed-up, unbanned user in this project), PARENT_MISSING, NOT_OWNER, NOT_A_MEMBER, NOT_OWNER_OR_MEMBER, NOT_OWNER_OR_GROUP_MEMBER, NOT_OWNER_OR_GROUP_ROLE, NOT_OWNER_OR_APP_ROLE, OWNER_NOT_A_MEMBER (owns an anyOf(owner(), member()|group()) row but is no longer in its group: team rows belong to the team), OPERATION_NOT_GRANTED, GROUP_ROLE_NOT_ALLOWED, APP_ROLE_NOT_HELD, GROUP_POLICY_CHANGED, and for allOf GATE_DENIED (the gate refused: not a current member, or no role for the operation) or WHO_DENIED (a current member who is not the row's owner, nor allowed by the who slot's role). If the access check cannot run, the answer is AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE (retry), never a denial.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-trips", "table": "expenses", "id": 42, "operation": "update", "user": "usr_123" }
// Returns: { "allowed": false, "chain": [{ "table": "expenses", "rule": "parent", "via": "trip_id" }, { "table": "trips", "rule": "group" }], "reason": { "code": "GROUP_ROLE_NOT_ALLOWED", "table": "trips", ... } }
```

## db-bookmark-create

Record a named marker around a database migration. It is operational evidence, not an undo point: in-place database restore is unavailable. db_dump or db_export creates a recoverable copy. Reusing a label overwrites the previous marker.

**Example:**

```json
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "label": "before-migration-v3" }
```

## db-webhook-set

Register an HTTPS endpoint to receive database change notifications for this project. Fires after a successful INSERT / UPDATE / UPSERT / DELETE through db_query — one POST per mutation, no row contents.

The first call generates a per-project secret you'll see in the response (`secret`). Subsequent calls update the URL or event filter and return the same secret. The incoming `X-Somewhere-Signature: t={ms},v1={hex}` header verifies by recomputing `HMAC-SHA256(secret, "{ms}." + rawBody)`.

**Example:**

```json
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "url": "https://example.com/db-hook", "events": ["insert", "update"] }
```

## postgres-status

Read the project's attached Postgres database without changing it. Never returns a key or connection string.

- `view: "attachment"` (default): connection state plus `credentials` — `{ stored, separated, migration_role, runtime_role, login_verified_at, privileges_verified_at, setup_role, setup_started_at, revision, generation, verified_now: false }`. Timestamps record the last successful check; they do not prove the current database state.
- `view: "migrations"` + `target`: the migration ledger, `{ target, migrations: [{ name, checksum, state: "applying" | "applied" | "failed", applied_at }] }`. `applying` means the outcome is unresolved and blocks later migrations.
- `view: "preview"`: the project's preview database, or an error when none has been created.

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app", "view": "migrations", "target": "production" }
```

## postgres-migrate

Apply ONE native PostgreSQL migration file to the attached database. Owner only; requires separated credentials (`postgres_credentials_separate`).

The SQL is run exactly as given — never split or rewritten — inside a transaction the platform opens, so it must not contain BEGIN, COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Maximum 1 MB. The ledger stores a SHA-256 checksum per name:
- same name + same SQL already applied → returns the recorded receipt, runs nothing;
- same name + different SQL already applied → refused (`POSTGRES_MIGRATION_CHANGED`), so changed SQL takes a new name;
- a failed file was rolled back and may be corrected and applied again;
- an unresolved outcome (`POSTGRES_MIGRATION_UNCERTAIN`) blocks every later migration until the database is inspected.

Files apply one call at a time in version order, stopping at the first error. Migrations never run on deploy. Returns `{ target, migration: { name, checksum, state, applied_at } }`.

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app", "target": "preview", "name": "0002_add_orders", "sql": "CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint PRIMARY KEY);" }
```

## postgres-preview

Create, reset or delete the project's one preview database. Owner only. Production is never changed.

- `create`: copies production data into an isolated branch in the customer's own provider account. A preview never falls back to production. Published app draft execution does not yet bind this database; creating the branch alone does not make it available to published previews.
- `reset`: replaces the preview's data with a fresh copy of production.
- `delete`: removes the preview database.

Reset and delete lose the preview's data and affect an already-deployed preview at once, until it is redeployed. `postgres_status` `view: "preview"` returns the current state.

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app", "action": "create" }
```

## postgres-credentials-separate

Give deployed functions their own limited database role, keeping the attached role for migrations only. Owner only; required before `postgres_migrate`. Calling it again after setup rechecks the stored runtime login and privileges.

The status timestamps record the last successful check, not continuous verification. Takes effect on the next deploy: releases already deployed keep their old credentials until redeployed or until the credential is rotated in the provider account. An interrupted setup remains pending for owner recovery and does not start a second role. Never returns a key or connection string.

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app" }
```

## postgres-copy

Copy the project's Somewhere database into a NEW private schema of its attached Postgres database (a database attached or created through the connected provider account). Owner only; requires separated credentials (`postgres_credentials_separate`). The Somewhere database and the running app are not changed, and nothing is switched over.

Faithful copies only: values are exact, and keys, unique rules, foreign keys, NOT NULL, defaults and identity sequences are recreated. A CHECK rule, trigger, view, non-binary collation, unsupported default, or a reference to a table that is not copied (app users, platform tables) refuses the copy with the exact item and what to change — nothing is silently dropped. App users, sessions and other platform tables are never copied; access rules are listed, not translated.

- `action: "prepare"` (writes nothing): reads one snapshot and returns the plan — tables with the destination type per column, keys, foreign keys, `fidelity`, `excluded`, `access_rules_not_copied`, `performance_indexes_not_recreated` (speed-only indexes), `refusals` and `limits`. Any refusal → 422 `POSTGRES_COPY_UNSUPPORTED`. Optional `schema`: the new schema name.
- `action: "copy"` + `plan` (the `plan` object prepare returned): one transaction creates the schema, tables and rows, recreates keys and identity sequences, verifies every table's row count and value digest inside the destination, and stores a receipt. Refused with `POSTGRES_COPY_PLAN_STALE` if the attachment, its credentials or the source schema changed since prepare. Retrying a committed plan returns its receipt (`already_copied: true`). `POSTGRES_COPY_OUTCOME_UNCERTAIN` means the connection dropped while committing; status is the first read.
- `action: "status"` + `schema` + `copy_id`: `committed` (with receipt), `in_progress`, `not_found` or `conflict`.

No other role (including the app's runtime role) is granted access to the new schema; additional access requires an explicit grant. Limits: 64 tables, 20,000 rows, 4 MiB of values, 60 seconds.

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app", "action": "prepare" }
```

## rooms-get

Read a room: the shared state people are working on together for one database row, its version, and who is in it now. A room belongs to one row of a table that declares `rooms` in its schema. When nobody is in the room, it returns the state last saved to the row. To find rooms, list the table's rows.

Returns `{ state, version, people: [{ id, user, info }] }`.

```json
{ "project_id": "my-app", "table": "games", "id": "g_123" }
```

pages.title: Domains tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## domain-add

Add a custom domain to your project. Returns the DNS targets you need to configure at your registrar.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "domain": "app.yourcompany.com" }
// Returns: { "domain": "app.yourcompany.com", "cname_target": "proxy.somewhere.tech", "verified": false, "verification_txt_name": "_somewhere-verify.app.yourcompany.com", "verification_txt_value": "smt-verify-...", "dns_records": [{ "type": "CNAME", "host": "app", "full_name": "app.yourcompany.com", "value": "proxy.somewhere.tech" }, { "type": "TXT", "host": "_somewhere-verify.app", "full_name": "_somewhere-verify.app.yourcompany.com", "value": "smt-verify-..." }], "instructions": "..." }
```

Each record in `dns_records` has `host` (the name most DNS hosts expect, relative to the registrable domain), `full_name` and `purpose`. A bare domain (example.com itself) with DNS at another company is answered `400 BARE_DOMAIN_NEEDS_CLAIM_OR_WWW` and no records: claim it (`domain_claim`, its nameservers move here) or add www.example.com and forward the bare name to it at the DNS company. Adding the same domain to the same project again returns its real `verified` state. `409 DOMAIN_TAKEN` carries `data.reason` (`own_app`, `own_claim`, `deleted_app`, `other_account`) and the next call in its message.

## domain-verify

Check if a custom domain's DNS is configured correctly. `next_step` is a plain sentence naming the missing or wrong record (CNAME or TXT) with its name and expected value; `cname_ok` and `txt_ok` say the same per record, and `dns_records` lists both records. `parent_zone_in_account` is set when the registrable domain is a domain this account claimed here: attach that claim with a host instead of adding records. Each `dns_records` entry carries `in_place`. A bare domain gets no records: its next_step names the two ways it works (claim it, or connect www and forward the bare name).

## domain-check

Check if a domain is available for purchase and get the price, or find available domain names for a word.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "domain": "acmedash.com" }
// Returns: { "available": true, "price": "$12.00/year" }
```

With `search: true` (or a word with no dot as `domain`), it searches priced endings for the word, excluding internationalized endings, and returns available names with their first-year price (`price`, `price_cents`), renewal price when known (`renewal_price_cents`) and a `premium` mark, cheapest first after an exact match. Prices are the registrar's, with no markup. A first year can be a promotional price; `renewal_price_cents` is the registrar's price for each later year. `max_price` (dollars) keeps only names at or under it; `sort` is `price` (default) or `name`. At most 60 names come back; `more_available` counts the rest and `next_cursor` (passed back as `cursor`) gives the next 60. A name whose price did not come back has `price_status: "unknown"` and is still available.

If `partial` is true, checks are still running. Repeat shortly for the finished search. Once it finishes, `unanswered` lists the names whose availability could not be checked and `unanswered_count` gives their count.

```json
{ "domain": "somewhere", "search": true, "max_price": 40 }
```

## domain-check-connector

Check availability and pricing for an exact domain name, or use search: true or a single word to find available names across priced endings. Search suggestions exclude internationalized endings. Use max_price (dollars) and sort (price or name) to narrow the results. Prices are the registrar's, with no markup. The renewal_price_cents field gives the price for each later year. If partial is true, repeat shortly for the finished search. Once it finishes, unanswered lists the names whose availability could not be checked and unanswered_count gives their count.

## domain-buy

Preview a domain purchase and get a secure checkout link.

`domain_buy` takes project_id + domain. The platform returns the price and a `dashboard_checkout_url`. The price is quoted verbatim, and the secure checkout link is where payment completes.

Customer purchases cannot be completed through another MCP tool. The user completes payment through the checkout link, and registration begins only after that payment settles.

The price is the registrar's first-year price with no markup. Each later year costs the registrar's renewal price at that time, also with no markup, which can be higher than the first year.

Purchase connects the domain to the app with no DNS steps. A bought domain is set up as a claim: its DNS is hosted here, and it serves the bare name and www over HTTPS, usually within 30 minutes of payment. Receiving email stays off until `domain_enable_email`.

The domain is registered **in the buyer's name**. It can move to another registrar from 60 days after registration (the ICANN transfer rule), or to the buyer's own Name.com account from 5 days after; details: https://somewhere.cloud/docs/domain-ownership

**Example:**

```json
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "domain": "acmedash.com" }
```

The response will be an error of type `PURCHASE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` carrying the price and checkout URL, e.g. `{ "ok": false, "error": "PURCHASE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED", "domain": "acmedash.com", "price": "$17/year", "dashboard_checkout_url": "https://somewhere.cloud/app/<project id>/buy/acmedash.com" }`. This response is a checkout handoff: payment completes at the `dashboard_checkout_url`.

## domain-claim

Claim a domain you already own by delegating its nameservers to us. The platform creates a dedicated zone, returns the nameserver pair to paste at your registrar, and starts polling for propagation. Once the zone goes active you can attach the domain to any project (and re-attach later without re-claiming).

This is the recommended path for any domain you control — it covers apex (`example.com`), `www`, and any subdomain in one move, and unlocks receiving mail on the same domain.

Claims belong to your account, not to a project. Project deletion is not the cleanup path for an unattached or pending claim. `domain_remove({ domain: "example.com" })` removes one from the account (including a claim created for a temporary test), ahead of deleting the project.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "domain": "example.com" }
// Returns: { "id": "...", "nameservers": ["<assigned-ns1>", "<assigned-ns2>"], "claim_status": "pending_ns", "instructions": [...] }
// The actual nameserver hostnames are assigned by the platform and returned by this call.
```

After a nameserver update at the registrar, `domain_check_ns` (or the hourly poll) flips `claim_status` to `active`. `domain_attach` then binds it to a project.

## domain-attach

Bind a claimed (active) domain to one of your projects. `host` picks the entry point — `apex` (`example.com`), `www` (`www.example.com`), or a single subdomain label like `app` (→ `app.example.com`).

A domain attached to another project is refused (`DOMAIN_ATTACHED_ELSEWHERE`, naming that project); `domain_detach` there first, then attach here, with no re-verification. `domain_detach` frees the binding without unclaiming.

**Example:**

```json
{ "id": "dom_...", "project_id": "my-saas", "host": "apex" }
```

## domain-publish

Recovery action for a claimed domain that isn't resolving. Re-asserts the apex + www records and the platform routing — idempotent, so safe to run any time. It applies when `domain_owned` shows `claim_status: active` and `zone_status: active` but `dig <domain>` returns NXDOMAIN or empty answers. `domain_claim` already runs this once; this is the manual unstick path for the rare case where the initial publish had a partial failure.

`domain_publish` never changes the domain's mail records.

pages.title: Email tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments. ## email-send **Adding a welcome, receipt, status, or alert email to an app?** `email_send` sends one transactional email to one recipient on every plan. Without `from`, the platform-managed sender is used immediately; the project name appears as the sender label. `from` selects a verified sender domain of the app. Domains bought through us or connected with our nameservers are set up automatically; a domain hosted elsewhere is verified once in Settings → Domains. A caller cannot explicitly name a platform domain. The platform-managed sender is transactional-only. A verified sender domain carries the branding of the app itself and its marketing email. Outbound transactional email is available on Free, Builder, Pro, Scale, and Enterprise. The plan's email allowance and send rate limit apply either way; current limits are at /v1/pricing. It takes `html` or `text` (or both). `reply_to` is optional. **Example:** ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "to": "alice@example.com", "subject": "Your order shipped", "html": "

Tracking number: ABC123

" } ``` ## email-status Look up the safe delivery timeline for an email previously sent by a project or issued by the platform for that project's app auth. It takes the tracking_id (same as the id returned from email_send or an authorized project workflow). Returns origin, source, auth_purpose when recorded, every lifecycle event — sent, delivered, opened, clicked, bounced, complained — in order, and event_counts. Message bodies, auth codes, credential links, and provider payloads are not returned. Historical rows without trusted sent provenance report origin/source as unknown. An opened event can come from an image proxy or automated scanner as well as a person, so it is an image-fetch event; reading and sign-in are separate actions. Missing events mean unknown, and this tool does not imply that open tracking is active. **Example:** Example transcript or fragment ```text { "id": "1234-abcd-..." } // Returns: { "current_status": "delivered", "events": [{ "event_type": "sent", ... }, { "event_type": "delivered", ... }] } ``` ## email-events-list List recent project mail and platform-issued app auth mail recorded for an authorized project. Each row includes origin, source, auth_purpose when recorded, latest delivery status (sent / delivered / opened / clicked / bounced / complained / delivery_delayed), and event_counts. Historical rows without trusted sent provenance report origin/source as unknown. The timeline supports delivery diagnostics: an opened event can come from an image proxy or automated scanner as well as a person, so it is an image-fetch event; reading and sign-in are separate actions; missing events mean unknown, and this tool does not imply that open tracking is active. email_status({ id: tracking_id }) has a specific message's safe timeline. ## email-bounces-list Deduplicated list of recipient addresses that have bounced or complained (spam-marked) in a project. It supports scrubbing a mailing list before sending — repeated sends to a dead address are the most common email problem. Returns one row per address with last_status, last_at, and occurrences. Window defaults to 30 days (max 365). A send loop skips any address that appears here. ## email-reputation Is this project's email paused for a high bounce or spam-report rate? Every project sends through the platform's shared sender, so a project whose rolling 24-hour bounce or spam-report rate crosses the published line is paused automatically: its sends (auth email included) answer EMAIL_PROJECT_PAUSED until the rate recovers, then resume on their own. Returns { state: 'healthy'|'paused', reason, paused_at, resumed_at, window: { hours, sent, bounced, complained, bounce_rate, complaint_rate }, thresholds }. email_bounces_list shows which addresses caused it. ## email-test-inbox Read rendered messages sent to one address in a project's controlled test inbox: auth email and the project's own `sw.email.send` to that address (which returns status `captured`). Passwordless sign-in tests use an address shaped like `robot@.test.somewhere.site`. These messages are stored instead of being delivered, and each row includes `magic_link` when the auth template supplied one and `verification_code` when the message carries a code (email verification, sign-in code). Real recipient mail never appears here. The live app and every preview share this one inbox: each row says who sent it in `environment` ("production" or "preview") and `preview_session_id`. ## managed-email-send Compose one managed email and send it to either an explicit recipient list or a saved contact segment. A segment is `{ "tag": "..." }` or `{ "all": true }`. Every recipient gets a distinct idempotency claim derived from `idempotency_key`, so retrying the same batch does not send duplicates. The result reports every recipient as sent, suppressed, preference-blocked, failed, or queued for a rate-limited later minute. Marketing email requires `topic` and the project's `marketing_postal_address` (set it with `project_update`; it is printed in the footer); recipient preferences, suppression, and the unsubscribe footer are enforced by the managed email sender. It takes `html` or `text` (or both).

pages.title: Env tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## env

Environment variables, secrets, config and integration keys. It sets with project_id, key and value; deletes with key and delete:true; lists with project_id only. Values are encrypted and omitted from list results. New values are private for server functions by default. A VITE_ or REACT_APP_ prefix alone never publishes a value. Publishing a browser value requires a prefixed name and public:true. Recognized secret credentials, including test credentials, cannot be marked public. Server functions read sw.env.NAME. Browser code reads import.meta.env.VITE_NAME or process.env.REACT_APP_NAME only for explicitly public values. A private browser reference refuses compilation. Provider and purpose are optional descriptive labels, not access controls. After the project adopts live config on a deploy, saves reach new ordinary requests within 60 seconds, usually in a few seconds. Cron and new background deliveries see changes within 5 seconds. Public browser values reach new page loads within 60 seconds. Previews keep the config they captured. List and save responses contain exact references and effective visibility, never values. A project's combined environment values have a 5,120 byte limit.

## env-request

Secure secret entry — get a link where the user types an API key or other secret (Stripe, OpenAI, Twilio) on Somewhere. The value goes from the user's browser straight into the project's encrypted environment; it is never sent to, stored by, or returned from this tool, so secrets stay out of the conversation.

Returns `{ status: "pending", url, request, expires_at }` — the link works for 30 minutes and only for a signed-in editor of the project. When the key already has a value it returns `{ status: "set", server_reference: "sw.env.KEY" }` and no link; `replace: true` returns a link that replaces it. `handoff_status({ request })` reports progress. Functions read the value as `sw.env.KEY`.

**Example:**

```json
{ "project_id": "my-shop", "key": "STRIPE_SECRET_KEY", "purpose": "Charge customers at checkout" }
```
