pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## group-create

Create, organize, groups — create a project group to organize related projects under one group with shared members and one shared design theme; the caller becomes the group owner. Owners and editors can manage membership, invites and the shared theme, and delete the group. Project ownership and billing stay with each project’s owner.

Returns the new group: `{ id, owner_id, name, description, created_at, updated_at, role: "owner", project_count: 0 }`.

**Example:**

```json
{ "name": "marketing-apps", "description": "All public-facing marketing projects" }
```

## group-get

Group detail, inspect group — get full detail for a group: the group fields plus `projects: [{ id, name, subdomain, status }]`, `members: [{ user_id, role }]`, and `design_tokens` (the shared theme object, `{}` until one is saved). 403 FORBIDDEN if you are not a member. Owners and editors can manage membership, invites and the shared theme, and delete the group. Project ownership and billing stay with each project’s owner.

**Example:**

```json
{ "group_id": "grp_abc123" }
```

## group-delete

Delete a group — available to any group member. Removes the group, its membership and theme; projects in the group are DETACHED, never deleted. Errors: FORBIDDEN (403, no group membership). Owners and editors can manage membership, invites and the shared theme, and delete the group. Project ownership and billing stay with each project’s owner.

**Example:**

```json
{ "group_id": "grp_abc123" }
```

## group-add-project

Add project to group, organize project — put a project you can edit into a group you belong to. A project belongs to AT MOST ONE group — if it's already in another, returns 409 GROUP_CONFLICT and you must group_remove_project from the old group first. Returns `{ added: true, group_id, project_id }`. Owners and editors can manage membership, invites and the shared theme, and delete the group. Project ownership and billing stay with each project’s owner.

**Example:**

```json
{ "group_id": "grp_abc123", "project_id": "e4f2a1b0-..." }
```

## group-remove-project

Remove project from group, detach project — pull a project out of a group. Allowed for any group member or anyone with editor access to the project. 404 NOT_IN_GROUP if the project isn't in that group. Returns `{ removed: true, group_id, project_id }`. Owners and editors can manage membership, invites and the shared theme, and delete the group. Project ownership and billing stay with each project’s owner.

**Example:**

```json
{ "group_id": "grp_abc123", "project_id": "e4f2a1b0-..." }
```

## group-invite-list

List pending group invites, view invites — Any group member can list open invites for a group (not yet accepted, not expired). Returns `{ invites: [{ email, role, invited_at, expires_at }] }`.

**Example:**

```json
{ "group_id": "grp_abc123" }
```

## group-invite-accept

Accept a group invitation, join group — accept a pending invite using the token from the invite email (`cinv_...`). The CALLER's signed-in account must be the invited email address, with a verified email. On success the caller becomes a group member with the invited role. Returns `{ accepted: true, group_id }`. Errors: EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED (403, caller's email isn't verified), INVITE_INVALID (404, bad/unknown token), INVITE_USED (409, already accepted), INVITE_EXPIRED (410, past the 7-day window), INVITE_WRONG_ACCOUNT (403, caller is signed in as a different email than was invited), GROUP_NOT_FOUND (404, group was deleted since the invite was sent).

**Example:**

```json
{ "group_id": "grp_abc123", "token": "cinv_a1b2c3..." }
```

## group-invite-revoke

Revoke group invite, cancel invite — Any group member can revoke a PENDING invite by email (an accepted invite is membership, not an invite — the members list is in group_get). Returns `{ revoked: true }`. 404 NOT_FOUND if there's no pending invite for that email in this group.

**Example:**

```json
{ "group_id": "grp_abc123", "email": "teammate@example.com" }
```

pages.title: Help tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## catalog

The caller-visible index of available tools. Three reference surfaces have distinct effects: **catalog** lists which tools exist; **docs({ topic })** returns the static contract for one surface; **advisor({ question })** can answer open-ended questions from an authorized live project's state.

catalog returns the directory / table of contents / manifest for every tool available to this caller on the active surface, grouped by category with a one-line summary per group: `{ categories: { project: { summary, tools: [...] }, db: { summary, tools: [...] }, ... } }`. Categories cover projects, deploys, database, files, env vars, end-user auth, email (out + inbox), AI (chat + media), jobs, cron, queue, logs, errors, usage, feedback, domains, search, web scraping, push, rate limiting, telegram, analytics, captcha, payments, live updates, render, stock photos, and platform help.

**Search:** `search` finds a tool by keyword or exact name — e.g. `catalog({ search: "auth_signup" })`, `catalog({ search: "upload url" })`. Returns matching tools + their group + how to load each. Most tools are not in the default surface, so an empty default tool-search is not evidence that a tool is unavailable.

**Lazy-load:** `load` returns FULL tool definitions for one or more groups instead of the index — `catalog({ load: "auth" })`, `catalog({ load: "db,fs" })`, or `load: "all"`. A group-scoped connection (`?groups=db,fs` on the MCP URL, or the `Mcp-Tool-Groups` header) limits a session to the tools it needs.

## advisor-start

Answers how to build or diagnose something from the current public platform contracts. It takes the question and the facts for the Advisor to use. It cannot read your projects, account, files or earlier conversations, fetch URLs, or call tools, and its answer is advice, not executed actions.

The question is recorded with your account. Depending on platform configuration the call either sends the question to the model provider and returns the advice, or saves a durable run and returns its run_id without starting inference; in that case advisor_resume with that run_id starts the inference.

## docs

The static manual for one platform surface at a time. Returns signatures, examples, common patterns, failure modes, and exact behavior for deploy, sw.db, sw.auth, files, payments, and other primitives. The tool list names verbs; docs defines their contracts.

This is the static manual; `advisor({ question })` provides tailored advice from supplied facts, and `catalog` lists available tools.

Returns a bounded summary by default: the read-first sections plus an id index of every section. The first line reports `view` and `complete=true|false`. `section` returns one section, and `detail: "full"` the complete topic.

Core topics include adopt, analytics, api-surface, app-mcp, architecture-patterns, auth-client, billing, browser, calendar, changes, cli, common-mistakes, connect-agent, cors, cron, database-engine, declared-data, declared-files, deploy, deploy-intelligence, design-system, dev-environments, domain-ownership, domains, feedback, file-tools, functions, getting-started, github, google-calendar, guarantees, handled-for-you, inspect, limits, live, live-data, local-dev, migration-supabase, payments, portability, postgres, pricing, pricing-comparison, project-groups, projects, recipe-ai-agent, recipe-ai-features, recipe-ai-receipts, recipe-background-jobs, recipe-booking, recipe-csv-import, recipe-ecommerce, recipe-email, recipe-escalation, recipe-file-uploads, recipe-import-app, recipe-login, recipe-multi-chat, recipe-paid-api, recipe-pdfs, recipe-push-notifications, recipe-seo, recipe-signed-in-app, render, rooms, sdk, sdks, search, security-model, setup, smoke, speed, sql-compatibility, sw.agent, sw.ai, sw.auth, sw.billing, sw.db, sw.email, sw.endpoint, sw.env, sw.fetch, sw.fs, sw.groups, sw.image, sw.jobs, sw.logs, sw.mail, sw.notifications, sw.push, sw.rateLimit, sw.web, tasks, test, troubleshooting, typed-functions, verify-before-deploy, vs-supabase, vs-vercel. Aliases such as fetch/http/outbound and ctx.* names also resolve. Unknown topics return the current canonical list, including tool reference topics. Example: `{ "topic": "sw.fetch" }`, then `{ "topic": "sw.fetch", "section": "<id>" }`.

## errors

Why is my app broken, exceptions, stack traces, failures, recent errors, crash reports, debugging. One trace_id returns the complete ordered parent/child operation waterfall plus its correlated logs, errors, deploy failures, and journey events. No project lookup is required for that one-id path. Without a trace id, project_id returns the last 24h of failures from that project's functions. Each row carries `kind`: "exception" means nobody chose the outcome (an uncaught throw, or a 5xx) and "refusal" means a handler answered 4xx on purpose — a 401 from your own auth gate is a refusal, not a bug, and `kind` separates the two.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "limit": 20 }
// Returns: [{ "timestamp": "2026-04-20T...", "path": "/api/users/signup", "status": 500, "message": "UNIQUE constraint failed: users.email" }, ...]
```

pages.title: Payments tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## payments-onboard

Start Stripe Connect onboarding for the developer (per-account, not per-project — onboard once and every project you own uses the same connected account). `mode` picks which account: `live` (the default) returns a URL the developer visits to set up identity, bank, and tax info for live charges, which then settle to their connected account with Stripe's standard processing fee deducted; `test` sets up a test-mode connected account (no real charges). The response carries the current platform fee so the onboarding UI can show it.

**Building starts without this.** Test-mode checkouts work immediately — payments_checkout in dev mode runs on the platform's own Stripe test account (no Connect destination, no fee) until you onboard, so card 4242 4242 4242 4242 succeeds with no setup. Test onboarding is only for exercising your own connected test account.

A test response is `{ mode: 'test', test_only: true, charges_enabled, checkout_ready, onboarding_url, expires_at }`. When the test account is already ready, `onboarding_url` and `expires_at` are null and there is nothing to visit; otherwise visit the URL to finish it.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "mode": "test", "return_url": "https://my-app.somewhere.site/done", "refresh_url": "https://my-app.somewhere.site/retry" }
// Returns: { "mode": "test", "test_only": true, "checkout_ready": false, "onboarding_url": "https://connect.stripe.com/setup/...", "expires_at": "..." }
```

## payments-status

Get the caller's Stripe Connect status: connected, onboarded, charges_enabled, payouts_enabled, details_submitted. Per-account (not per-project). refresh=true forces a live Stripe API lookup (otherwise returns the last-cached DB state).

## payments-checkout

Create a Stripe Checkout Session for a project. Once the project owner has onboarded, funds settle to their connected account; the response's fee_percent is the platform fee on the session (current rate at /v1/pricing) and Stripe's standard processing fee also applies. Before onboarding, env='dev' checkouts run on the platform's own Stripe test account with no Connect destination — the response includes is_stand_in: true and platform_fee_cents: 0 so card 4242 4242 4242 4242 succeeds end-to-end. env='prod' returns 412 until the owner finishes onboarding. Supports mode='payment' | 'subscription'.

Three payment bases (exactly one per call): line_items (ad-hoc), quote_id (a stored quote from a payments quote — server supplies the amount; one-time only, and may compose with calendar_hold_token + booking_id for an atomic booking checkout), or plan (a catalog plan slug — the <PricingTable>/sw.billing subscribe path).

Plan tracking: a developer may pass metadata={"app_user_id":"<id>","plan":"<slug>"}; app functions use sw.payments.checkoutForUser for their verified signed-in user. The platform binds the user, price, payment account and test/live mode before checkout, then verifies the payment before granting the selected plan. Live subscriptions keep access during payment retries and lose it when unpaid, paused, canceled or expired. Test purchases are recorded separately and never unlock live access; auth and billing readers currently show live access only. Redeploy older apps normally to enable the runtime user proof. Historical or unmatched payments require reconciliation; metadata alone never grants a plan.

## payments-transactions

List recent charges on the project owner's connected account. Returns Stripe's native cursor pagination — `starting_after` set to the previous response's `next_cursor` fetches the next page. Default page size 20, max 100. env=prod lists live-mode charges; default env=dev lists test-mode.

## payments-portal

Create a Stripe Billing Portal session for an app user. The platform resolves the stored Stripe customer for `app_user_id` server-side; raw Stripe customer ids are not accepted by this tool. Returns a short-lived URL to redirect to.

## payments-events

Paginated feed of Stripe webhook events the platform received for this project (from the payments_events ledger). It can drive an in-product activity feed or confirm webhook reception during integration. The webhook handler is idempotent — duplicate Stripe redeliveries appear once.

pages.title: Project tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments. ## project-list My projects, my apps, my sites, my deployments, account inventory, dashboard overview — show every project I own or collaborate on. Each row includes `is_owner` so you can tell which is which. **Compact + paginated by default** to keep the payload small: returns up to **50** projects with the core fields (id, name, subdomain, status, tags, created_at, last_deployed_at, latest_screenshot_url, favicon_url, is_owner). The render fields are included in this one response; screenshot/favicon URLs are null until their live-release asset exists. When more exist, the response ends with a note telling you the total and how to page. To narrow or expand: pass `q` (substring filter on name/subdomain), `tag` (organization label filter; multiple values combine with AND), `limit`/`offset` (paging), or `fields:"full"` for the complete record per row. **Example:** Example transcript or fragment ```text // project_list({ q: "saas", limit: 50 }) returns: [ { "id": "p_abc123", "name": "My SaaS", "subdomain": "my-saas", "status": "deployed", "last_deployed_at": "2026-04-01T...", "latest_screenshot_url": "https://api.somewhere.cloud/v1/deploy-screenshots/p_abc123/v7-desktop.png?exp=...&sig=...", "favicon_url": "https://my-saas.somewhere.site/favicon.ico", "tags": ["marketing"], "is_owner": true }, { "id": "p_xyz789", "name": "Jen's App", "subdomain": "jen-app", "status": "draft", "last_deployed_at": null, "latest_screenshot_url": null, "favicon_url": null, "tags": [], "is_owner": false } ] ``` Shared projects: you can deploy, edit files, run db migrations, send email, and use AI — all billed to the project owner. You cannot delete, transfer, change env var values, or manage billing/spend caps on shared projects. ## project-privacy-facts Read what the platform knows about this app's personal data. From the active release's source: declared owner tables, file collections, outside domains. From the platform: who signs in and how, whether the app sends email, takes payments or uses AI (and which providers), its analytics consent mode, the cookies the platform sets, how long things are kept, and the outside services that handle its users' data. Use it to write or check the app's privacy page. Facts only; no source or row contents. ## project-notice-mark-read Mark a somewhere platform notice read for you, so its reminders stop. This replaces any earlier read or snooze record you set for the notice. It changes only your notice delivery; it never resolves the underlying project issue or grants any capability. It takes the project_id and notice_id supplied with the notice. ## project-notice-snooze Pause a somewhere platform notice's reminders for you for 1–720 whole hours (default 24). This replaces any earlier read or snooze record you set for the notice, so a notice you had marked read becomes unread when the snooze ends. It changes only your notice delivery; it never resolves the underlying project issue or grants any capability. ## project-get Project details, app info, project record, settings, metadata — fetch one project by id, subdomain, or `"default"`. Returns the full project record. When the project's editors have saved context (see `project_context`), it is included as `project_context`: instructions, design principles and note topics, labelled as project data. Includes a source overview of the active release when available. **Example:** Example transcript or fragment ```text { "project_id": "my-saas" } // or { "project_id": "default" } ``` ## project-set-tags Set freeform organization tags on a project. Tags are labels for finding/filtering projects only; they have zero runtime, auth, routing, billing, deploy, or group meaning. Tags normalize to lowercase `a-z0-9-`, max 32 characters each, max 10 per project. This replaces the full tag set with the normalized unique list and returns the saved tags. ## project-allowed-origins-get Read a project's cross-origin allowlist (CORS allowed_origins) — the exact browser origins permitted to make credentialed cross-origin requests to the project's API. Returns `allowed_origins` (the configured OTHER origins). Every project uses the same origin policy; a project always trusts its own origins (its `.somewhere.site` subdomain and verified custom domains), which are automatic and NOT listed here. Shows the allowlist for review before a change with `project_allowed_origins_set`. ## project-allowed-origins-set Set a project's cross-origin allowlist (CORS allowed_origins) — the exact browser origins permitted to make credentialed cross-origin requests to the project's API. This is the first-class way to fix a "cross-origin request blocked" / CORS error for a separate frontend origin from the CLI/MCP instead of the dashboard. Owner-or-platform-admin only, and every change is audited. Replaces the FULL allowlist with the list you pass; [] clears it. Each entry must be an exact origin — scheme + host + optional port, no path/query/fragment and no wildcards (e.g. `https://app.example.com`, or `http://localhost:5173` for local development). Matching is byte-exact: a subdomain or a different port is a different origin and must be listed explicitly. You never need to list the project's own `.somewhere.site` origin or its verified custom domains — those are always trusted. **Example:** ```json { "project_id": "my-app", "allowed_origins": ["https://app.example.com", "http://localhost:5173"] } ``` ## project-create Create a new project / app / website / site — initialize a project with a subdomain to start building and hosting it. This is the first step for any new app: a web app, API, backend, landing page, SaaS, or full-stack site. The project starts with the same starter `somewhere init` writes — a React + TypeScript app with sign-up, sign-in and sign-out, styled views and design tokens (`src/styles/tokens.css`) — deployed as its first release; when `data.starter.status` is `deployed` it is live at `https://{subdomain}.somewhere.site`. The call waits up to 120 seconds for that deploy. `starter.status` is `deployed`, `preview`, `failed` (the deploy was refused; `starter.error` says why) or `unknown` (no answer in time, or an answer without a release). For `failed` and `unknown`, `starter.recovery` lists the checks to run and the exact `project_deploy` call (or the equivalent `somewhere init` command) that ships the same starter. If a project_create response is lost, the project may exist: look for it with `project_get` or `project_list` (by subdomain) before creating again. Repeating the call returns `SUBDOMAIN_TAKEN`, and a new name makes a second project. `data.starter` lists the deployed files and returns the starter's `agent_contract` (its AGENTS.md), `readme` (the file map) and `skills` index; deploys do not publish those files, so they arrive here. `project_patch` edits the starter. `starter: "auth,private-data"` adds per-user notes backed by `db/schema.ts`; `starter: "none"` creates an empty project. New projects use declared data: tables and access rules live in `db/schema.ts`, deployed as raw source. Pages use the generated `somewhere:data` client for normal data, and a function only for a write the grant cannot express: docs({ topic: 'declared-data', section: 'declare-a-table-and-use-it' }), then docs({ topic: 'recipe-signed-in-app' }) for a public form that files a row for an owner. The subdomain must be unique platform-wide and cannot use reserved names (api, admin, www, etc.). Projects and deploys are unlimited on all tiers. **Example:** Example transcript or fragment ```text { "name": "Acme Dashboard", "subdomain": "acme-dash", "description": "Internal team dashboard" } // Returns: { "data": { "id": "…", "url": "https://acme-dash.somewhere.site", "starter": { "status": "deployed", … } } } ``` ## project-delete Request deletion of a project. **Two-step flow.** Step 1 — `project_delete` takes just the project_id. The platform returns a 6-digit confirmation code that expires after 10 minutes. No project state changes before the code is confirmed. Step 2 — Human authorization is required before calling `project_delete_confirm` with the same project_id and code. Confirmation immediately takes the project and its hostnames offline, blocks new project effects, frees its custom domains and email sending setup at once (domains claimed or bought stay in the account, unattached), retains its database, files, functions, and environment variables for 30 days, and schedules permanent erasure after that retention period. Recovery during the retention period requires support and does not bring back domain connections or sending setup. **Example:** ```json { "project_id": "my-saas" } ``` The response is a SUCCESS carrying the code and a machine-readable status, e.g. `{ "ok": true, "status": "needs_confirmation", "confirmation_code": "482917", "code": "482917", "next_call": { "tool": "project_delete_confirm", ... } }` — minting the code is this step's whole job, so it is never an error. The response carries `confirmation_code` (`code` is the same value, kept for existing callers). The response carries no `error_code` and no `canonical_error`, so branching on those stays a reliable failure test. ## project-rename Rename a project or update its description. This changes the display name only: the project's web address (subdomain) is set when the project is created and does not change. **Example:** ```json { "project_id": "p_abc123", "name": "Acme Portal v2", "description": "Updated customer portal" } ``` ## project-update Update a project's name, description, function placement, optional analytics consent policy, monthly AI spend cap, which emails app-user signup sends, or the postal address printed in its marketing email footer. **Example:** ```json { "project_id": "p_abc123", "placement": "near-data" } ``` **AI spend cap (owner only):** `{ "project_id": "p_abc123", "ai_spend_cap_cents": 5000 }` sets this project's monthly AI spend cap to $50. `null` turns the cap off for this project (the prepaid balance still limits spend); `"plan"` goes back to the plan's cap. The current cap, this month's spend and every change are in `project_get` → `ai_spend_cap`. **Marketing postal address:** `{ "project_id": "p_abc123", "marketing_postal_address": "1 Main St, Springfield, IL 62701, USA" }`. Marketing email (category `marketing`) is refused with MARKETING_POSTAL_ADDRESS_REQUIRED until this is set; it is printed in the footer of every marketing email. `null` clears it. ## project-deploy Deploy / ship / host / push / release your app — upload raw source (HTML, CSS, JS, server functions) to a project and put it in production at `https://{subdomain}.somewhere.site`. The platform compiles your code; you deploy source, not a build. **If you can run a shell, LEAD WITH the CLI: `somewhere deploy` reads files straight from disk (no inline JSON payload) and is the faster path. The CLI installs with `npm i -g @somewhere-cloud/cli && somewhere auth login` (shares MCP auth). This MCP tool is the inline fallback — for agents without shell access, small projects, or when the CLI isn't available.** **For UPDATES to an existing project, `project_patch` with `find`/`replace` ships surgical edits in ~200 bytes instead of resending every file. `project_deploy` is for the FIRST deploy of a new project, or for replacing the whole tree.** **Large or binary files are referenced, not pasted.** Instead of being inlined into `files`, a big asset (or base64 bytes) goes to project file storage first with `fs_write` and is referenced by storage path via `file_refs` (text files) or `binary_file_refs` (images, fonts, other binaries). The platform resolves the referenced content server-side at deploy time, so a big tree ships without a giant inline payload. Inline `files`/`functions` keep working and can be mixed with refs in the same deploy. Deploys your app. The result lands at `https://{subdomain}.somewhere.site` and on any verified custom domain — every deploy reaches production. ⚠️ **Omitted items are NOT all treated the same.** Static **`files`** are full-replacement: anything you omit from `files` is deleted (`scope:"functions"` leaves static untouched). **`functions`** are **merge-preserved by default**: a function already in production but omitted from this call is KEPT, not deleted — so you can ship a backend-only change without resending the frontend, and `project_patch`-only functions survive a later full deploy. `replace_functions:true` makes a deploy delete functions it no longer ships. (Env vars, database, and uploaded `fs` files are never affected.) Use `dry_run:true` to inspect exactly what will be added / removed / modified before anything is written. **`project_patch` with a `files` map changes several files of an existing project without resending the rest: files not listed are kept.** Server-side functions are the core — handler code goes in the **`functions`** map (keyed by path, e.g. `"api/hello.ts"`) and becomes routable at `/api/...` on your production URL. The **`files`** map is for STATIC assets only (HTML, CSS, client-side JS, images). **Handler code (`api/*`, `_lib/*`, root `[id].ts` routes) belongs in `functions`, not `files`** — a static asset never routes, so `/api/*` would just serve the app's HTML. (A handler-shaped path found in `files` is moved into `functions` with a warning.) A JSON route in api/ is export default sw.endpoint({ auth, handler }) with auth set explicitly. TypeScript infers the handler inputs and sw context. auth: 'none' marks a deliberately public route. ```ts export default sw.endpoint({ auth: 'none', handler: async () => ({ ok: true }) }); ``` Application tables are declared in db/schema.ts. sw.db.from reads them with caller-scoped access, and sw.db.server.from reads them once the caller is authorized for server access. The corresponding structured methods, such as sw.db.server.insert, change them. Raw query and batch go to the separate raw SQL database on current projects. Functions run directly on the platform with access to `sw.db` (database), `sw.fs` (file storage), `sw.email` (send email), `sw.ai` (AI models), `sw.env` (environment variables), `sw.jobs` (background jobs), `sw.queue`, and `sw.logs`. `sw.db` uses the function's authenticated project binding, so application code does not send a developer API key or construct a platform HTTP request. First-use activation, placement, transport, scheduling, and engine work can still contribute to latency. `sw.db.batch([{sql, params}, ...])` runs multiple statements as one atomic transaction; any failure rolls every statement back. (`ctx` is an alias — same object, both names work.) **Source base (required on every live deploy).** Pass `base_release_id`: the `active_release_id` from the `project_export` read your source came from, or `null` when the project has no source yet. The base is the one that came with the edited source; a newer id read just before deploying is not a valid base. A missing base returns 400 `BASE_REQUIRED` and nothing changes; a base that is no longer live returns 409 `STALE_RELEASE_BASE` with `data.changed_files`. Recovery is a re-export, the change re-applied to the new source, and a deploy with the new base. `force:true` deliberately replaces the live source; it still fails if another deploy lands while yours builds. **Projects without releases** use `base_version` from your last deploy/export response instead. If the project changed elsewhere, deploy returns 409 `STALE_BASE` with `data.changed_files`, `data.last_change_source`, and `data.last_change_at`; review `project_diff_versions` before choosing `force:true`. **Deploy counter on projects without releases.** The numeric `expected_version` field applies only to projects without releases. For released projects send the observed `active_release_id` as `base_release_id`. The success response always includes the new `version`. When available, it may also include `_runtime_key_summary`, a plain-language note on whether the runtime key for this deploy was narrowed to least-privilege scopes or fell back to blanket access. **Example:** ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "files": { "index.html": "

Hello

" }, "functions": { "api/hello.ts": "export default sw.endpoint({ auth: 'none', handler: async () => ({ ok: true }) });" } } ``` Handler code goes in `functions`; static assets (here, `index.html`) go in `files`. The default workflow has one environment: read production source, check, deploy once, then verify the public production URL. `somewhere preview` is an optional advanced capability; preview inputs apply when a preview is explicitly requested and the account has hosted preview access (every plan includes it for signed-in accounts). ## project-deploy-connector Deploy raw application source to a Somewhere project and publish it at its live URL. The platform compiles the source and applies a declared db/schema.ts. Pass pages in files and server routes in functions. A JSON route in api/ is export default sw.endpoint({ auth, handler }) with auth set explicitly. TypeScript infers the handler inputs and sw context. auth: 'none' marks a deliberately public route. For an existing app, first read its live source with project_export, then use project_patch to update selected files. A full deploy replaces the source. The deployment API contract is at https://somewhere.cloud/docs.txt. ## project-patch Edit / change / update / modify / fix / tweak files in a deployed project — **edit one or several deployed files in place** with a find/replace, an ordered `edits` array of many find/replaces across files, a full-file rewrite, or a `files` map of several full-file writes in one atomic patch. Suited to visual-editor iteration and any quick code change. Unchanged files are preserved; only what you send is touched. Static changes reach production in ~1 second; function changes in 2–4 seconds. For an existing project this touches only the files sent; `project_deploy` replaces the static file tree, so unchanged static files must be sent again. `project_deploy` is for the first deploy of a brand-new project. The source comes from `project_export`. Its `active_release_id` is the `base_release_id` of the patch, including on dry runs. This required release anchor identifies the exact source you edited; `base_version` is an additional optional conflict check. **Three modes — same tool.** **1. Find / replace (token-optimal, preferred for small edits):** pass `path` + `find` + `replace`. The platform reads the current file, replaces every occurrence of `find` with `replace`, and writes it back. ~200 bytes on the wire instead of re-sending the whole file. ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "base_release_id": "", "path": "index.html", "find": "

Pricing

", "replace": "

Plans & pricing

" } ``` If `find` doesn't match the file, you get a 400 `FIND_NOT_FOUND` with a head/tail snippet. When a sufficiently similar region exists, `data.closest_match` also includes its offset, text and 0–1 `confidence`; unrelated text may have no close match. A corrected patch uses the exact text from a current `project_export` and that export's release anchor. **2. Ordered edits (many small changes in one patch):** pass `edits`, an array of `{ "path", "find", "replace", "expect"? }`, instead of top-level path/find/replace. Edits apply in order to the source of `base_release_id` (a later edit to the same file sees the earlier ones), across any number of files, and publish as ONE patch. If any edit does not match, nothing is published: the error is `FIND_NOT_FOUND` with zero-based `data.edit_index`. `expect: n` requires exactly n non-overlapping matches, else `FIND_COUNT_MISMATCH` with `data.edit_index`, `data.path`, `data.expected` and `data.actual`. At most 200 edits per call. A path is edited, written whole (`files`), or deleted (`delete_files`) in one patch, never two of these; other paths combine freely. ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "base_release_id": "", "edits": [ { "path": "src/App.tsx", "find": "const TITLE = 'Old'", "replace": "const TITLE = 'New'", "expect": 1 }, { "path": "src/App.tsx", "find": "
", "replace": "
" }, { "path": "styles.css", "find": "color: red", "replace": "color: teal" } ] } ``` Unified diffs are not a patch format: ordered exact replacements plus whole-file `files` writes cover the same changes without a second parser. Whole local trees deploy with `somewhere deploy`; `somewhere call project_patch --file args.json` sends a large argument object from a file. **3. Full content (rewriting the file):** pass `path` + `content`. The new bytes replace the file entirely. ```json { "project_id": "my-saas", "base_release_id": "", "path": "styles.css", "content": "body { background: black }" } ``` Path auto-routes: `api/*`, `_lib/*`, and root `[id].ts` paths go to functions; everything else (HTML, CSS, SVG, JSON, etc.) to static. Binary assets (images, fonts) use the matching binary surface — `content` and `find`/`replace` do not carry raw bytes. **Delete:** `delete_files` is an array of paths. Works for static files and functions; missing paths are silently ignored. A rename or atomic replace combines one `path` + `content` write (or the one-entry `files` alias) with `delete_files` in the same call: the new file and removals publish as one patch transaction. **Source base.** For a released project, take `active_release_id` from the export you edited and send it as `base_release_id`. If production changed, the platform returns `STALE_RELEASE_BASE`. For an unreleased project with existing source, `base_version` identifies the source version the patch is based on. **Preview first (optional):** pass `dry_run: true` to get a per-file unified diff of what the patch WOULD change (`data.diffs`), plus added/modified/removed lists — nothing is written and the version doesn't change. The same call without `dry_run` applies it. **Safety net — what IS and is NOT checked.** After any patch goes live, the after-deploy check loads the home page in a browser and reports a blank page or one that throws as a warning (`access_check` in `project_deploy_log`). A blank page is never rolled back automatically: when the previous version worked, `access_check.go_back` names it, and `project_rollback({ project_id, version })` with that version puts it back, or a patch that fixes the cause replaces it. A **function-only patch** (`api/*`, `_lib/*`, root `[id].ts`) gets one extra check. After a function patch the response carries a best-effort `function_health` field — `{ checked, status, ok }` from one GET of a patched route. `function_health.ok === false` means the route returned a 5xx (e.g. a missing import → 500): your edit shipped but is broken in production. If `function_health.checked === false` the route couldn't be probed (no concrete route, or it was unreachable) — it was NOT verified, so confirm it yourself. A clean build is NOT a working function; only `function_health.ok === true` (or your own request to the route) confirms it runs. For a risky edit, `dry_run:true` and `project_check` come first, then one patch, verified on the public production URL. `project_rollback` restores the previous production version if needed. Patches reach production immediately at `https://{subdomain}.somewhere.site`. The success response includes the new `version`, a `next_step`, `function_errors` (build failures) and, for function patches, `function_health` (runtime 5xx). Preview is advanced and must not be selected unless the user explicitly says the account is enabled. ## project-patch-connector Read the current source with project_export, then use this tool to update selected files. Supports full file contents, find/replace edits (one, or an ordered edits array across files published as one patch), and explicit file deletion. Production file changes go live. A JSON route in api/ is export default sw.endpoint({ auth, handler }) with auth set explicitly. TypeScript infers the handler inputs and sw context. auth: 'none' marks a deliberately public route. The note_version option edits a deploy note without publishing. The patch contract is at https://somewhere.cloud/docs.txt. ## project-check **About to deploy source you edited? A pre-deploy check.** `project_check` typechecks / compiles / lints WITHOUT deploying — a fast green/red so you fix everything before you ship, instead of deploy→error→fix→redeploy. Runs the SAME compile gate a real deploy runs, against the source you pass in, and returns structured errors with `file:line` — but writes NOTHING (no version change, nothing goes live). A green here means the deploy's compile step will pass too. Catches the deploy-fatal classes: **syntax errors** in your function code and inline `

pages.title: Push tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## push-vapid-key

**Building notifications that must arrive after the app tab closes?** The flow starts with the VAPID public key of the project, which the browser passes to `PushManager.subscribe({ applicationServerKey })`. The key is auto-generated and stable for the project's lifetime.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas" }
// Returns: { "vapid_public_key": "BN..." }
```

## push-subscribe

**Register your own browser as a developer device** for operator alerts, after it returns a `PushManager.subscribe()` result. Developer devices carry no app-user id; reach them with `push_send with audience set to developer`. App users register their own browsers from a signed-in session (`somewhere:push` `enablePush()` or `sw.push.subscribe` in a function), never through this tool. Idempotent on (project_id, endpoint).

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "subscription": { "endpoint": "https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/...", "keys": { "p256dh": "...", "auth": "..." } },
  "label": "My laptop"
}
```

## push-unsubscribe

**When a user disables notifications or a browser subscription is replaced,** remove the old subscription by endpoint. The operation is idempotent.

**Example:**

```json
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "endpoint": "https://fcm.googleapis.com/..." }
```

## push-send

**Need an alert to reach a user even when the app tab is closed?** `push_send` sends a web push notification to one device, one app-user's devices, your developer devices, or the whole project.

Recipient targeting (exactly one; a missing, null or empty target is refused):
- `user_id`: every device that signed-in app user registered.
- `subscription_id` or `endpoint`: one device. Sending again sends another notification.
- `audience: 'developer'`: devices registered with `push_subscribe`.
- `audience: 'all'`: every device in the project (refused whole above 500).

`payload` may be a JSON object (recommended — your service worker parses it) or a string. Subscriptions that the push provider reports as gone (404/410) are auto-deleted. Inside a deployed function the equivalent call is `sw.push.send({ payload, user_id })` — one object, payload nested; there is no second options argument.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "user_id": "u_alice",
  "payload": { "title": "New message", "body": "From Bob", "url": "/inbox/123" }
}
// Returns: { "sent": 1, "failed": 0, "gone": 0, "captured": 0, "recipients": 1, "history_recorded": true, "devices": [{ "subscription_id": "psub_...", "device_label": "Chrome on Android", "outcome": "sent", "http_status": 201, ... }] }
```

## push-deliveries

**Why didn't a notification arrive?** Read per-device push history, newest first: each send's device, outcome (`sent`, `failed` with the HTTP status and a reason, `gone` when the browser revoked the device, `captured` for a test inbox device), title, URL and time. Test-inbox deliveries include the full payload, so a hosted browser can prove a user was notified. Returns the last seven days.

**Example:**

Example transcript or fragment

```text
{ "project_id": "my-saas", "user_id": "usr_123", "limit": 10 }
// Returns: { "deliveries": [{ "device_label": "Chrome on Android", "outcome": "failed", "http_status": 403, "error": "The push service refused the signing key (403). Re-subscribe this device.", "title": "New message", "created_at": "..." }] }
```

pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments. ## security-sitekey Get the CAPTCHA site key to embed in your frontend HTML. This is safe to expose publicly — it identifies the widget, not the user. **Example:** Example transcript or fragment ```text {} // Returns: { "sitekey": "0x..." } ``` **Usage in HTML:** ```html
``` ## security-review On-demand LLM security review of a project's deployed functions. Returns a structured Markdown report — findings (one per real risk), severity, and a fix. Every plan can request a review. Paid plans get a longer report. Eligible paid plans also review when a preview is promoted. All plans use the same review model and minimal reasoning; only the report length limit differs. Advisory only — never blocks anything. The deploy path never blocks on a pattern scan; it surfaces hits as warnings, and this tool is how you get the deep dive. project_id is required (returns VALIDATION_ERROR if omitted). Backend failures are distinguishable, so a retry is never wasted on a persistent failure: a transient outage returns UPSTREAM_DOWN / UPSTREAM_RATE_LIMITED (retryable), while a persistent platform problem returns UPSTREAM_ERROR / CONFIG_ERROR (not retryable — a retry loop does not clear it). **Example:** Example transcript or fragment ```text { "project_id": "my-saas" } // Returns: { "findings": "## Findings\n### Auth bypass at api/checkout.ts ...\n...", "review_depth": "standard", "tier_unlocks_deep_review": false, ... } ```

pages.title: Smoke tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## site-check-status

Get the latest smoke-test run for a project plus a short history. Smoke runs are auto-wired — homepage and any attached custom domains are probed every ~20 min and after every deploy. Status is "pass" / "fail" / "partial". Each run includes per-target details (URL, HTTP code, duration).

## site-check

Trigger an on-demand site check for a project. Usually returns the finished run with per-target details within ~10s; if probes are still executing it returns { run: { id, status: "running" } } — site_check_status has the result a moment later. It answers "is it back yet" after a fix, and serves as a post-deploy check.

To run part of the live app's after-deploy check, pass `check: "access"`, `check: "crawl"`, or the path of one saved check, such as `check: "checks/add-note.json"`. Pass the returned `run_id` as `check_run_id` with the same project to read the result. It reports `scope: "partial"`, `checked_parts`, and `not_checked`. Starting and reading a targeted run both require editor access.

## smoke-config-get

Read the per-project smoke configuration. Returns enabled (false if opted out), test_auth_flow (auto-detected), test_user_email (the designated test user for authed checks), alert_cooldown_seconds, last_alert_at, and any developer-defined extra checks.

pages.title: Tasks tool reference
pages.body:
Use the section for the tool and connection in the current workflow. Each tool’s input schema defines the accepted arguments.

## tasks-create

Create a task in a project. Tasks are per-project tickets — useful for bugs, todos, or end-user-filed feedback inside your app. Tasks live in the project's own database.

**Example:**

```json
{
  "project_id": "my-saas",
  "title": "Fix login redirect",
  "description": "After OAuth, users land on /home instead of /dashboard.",
  "priority": "high",
  "labels": ["bug", "auth"]
}
```

## tasks-bulk-update

Apply the same field changes to many tasks in one call (cap 100 per call). One request → one batch DB write per target + one activity-log row per changed field. Failures are returned per-task so partial errors do not roll back the whole batch.

## tasks-overview

Start with a bounded project brief: vision, SOPs, recorded priorities, work underway, blockers and completed work with release links. Uses existing records, no model ranking. Two records per section; a focused section returns up to five. Counts, ordering and continuation are explicit. Reviewed guidance is distinguished from newer drafts. Excerpts are partial; tasks_get has the source and linked guidance. Closed tasks without a release link are not presented as shipped.

## tasks-list

Read tasks. view=board returns a board scan: 50 concise current-state rows by default, no descriptions/comments. Other reads default to a small task page (10, bounded response). The same filters with page.next_cursor as cursor continue; pages are not concatenated automatically. Task ordering is live keyset: edits to sort/filter fields may skip or repeat rows; a new read starts a fresh queue. Fields in omitted are partial; tasks_get view=field expands them. detail=full explicitly permits unbounded descriptions. task_id reads one current task; tasks_get covers history/field options. review_for_closure reports its source candidate limit. tasks_overview covers project direction and work; tasks_summary gives counts and memory_search durable guidance. waiting="me" is a separate read: what is waiting for the signed-in person, everything agents have asked that person to do across all their projects, most urgent first, 25 projects per call (next_cursor continues as cursor). This is how an agent finds out what the person still has to do. Each item has its task id, project_id and project_name, the title, the steps as written (steps) and as a list (step_list), the reason (why), who asked (asked_by) and when (asked_at); answered lists what was answered and through which credential (answered_by). An agent may walk the person through an item’s steps. An item is answered with tasks_update: answer "done" or "cannot", with an optional note; "done" is only for an item the person did or asked to have marked done.

## tasks-get

Read current task state by default, bounded to about 12,000 JSON characters, with history counts and expansion instructions. view=relationships pages explicit links and parent/replacement-field links, current target state and supersession pointers; task_id leads to the target. Missing targets and partial pointers are explicit. view=history pages comments, activity, guidance revisions or review records (kind), newest first with stable ID ties; default 5. view=field expands an omitted top-level field as bounded JSON-text chunks; a history field also takes kind and event_id. The same read options with next_cursor as cursor continue. History uses a keyset and initial rowid/time upper bounds; appends do not restart it, deletions disappear, and edited bodies are live. Membership is not frozen: deletion followed by a same-timestamp insert can admit a new event on a later page. Field chunks reject changed content with CURSOR_STALE; a new field read returns the current content. view=full explicitly requests the unbounded compatibility response with all comments/activity ordered oldest first (created_at ASC, id ASC). Prefix task IDs work when unique.

## tasks-summary

At-a-glance ticket counts for a project with ZERO rows returned — total plus counts grouped by status, priority, area, and assignee, plus a stale count (in_progress tasks untouched beyond stale_days). It returns a dashboard number ("urgent: 3, high: 28, blocked: 5") instead of listing every task; it scales to thousands of tickets. tasks_list returns the rows themselves.

## tasks-update

Update a task's fields, append a comment, or upload and attach authorized file references. `comment` adds a comment without changing other fields. Status transitions to 'done' automatically stamp completed_at. **Closing a task (status: 'done') takes a `resolution_note`** — it's persisted as a comment AND included in the resolution email/webhook so the reporter knows what was done. Omitting it when transitioning to done returns a non-blocking `suggestions` entry asking for a resolution note.

**Progress belongs in `status_note` (and `health`), not a comment per step.** The three fields have distinct jobs: `description` is the living document (intent and contract, rewritten as the truth changes), `status_note` is the current state (overwritten each update, so one read tells you where things stand), and comments are append-only EVIDENCE — commit hashes, verification output, links. Appending status as comments is what makes a long-lived task unreadable: the thread renders oldest-first, so a reader meets the superseded version before the live one. Overwriting `status_note` loses nothing; the old value is kept in the activity log.

## tasks-comment-add

Append a comment to a task without changing its fields. Each comment is a new entry; it is announced to the project's configured task webhook and notification email when those are set. Progress is recorded in tasks_update status_note, and a task closes through tasks_update with status 'done' and resolution_note.

## tasks-attachment-upload

Upload native files and append them to a task's attachments. Each file is stored privately under /tasks/{task_id}/attachments/<name>; a file with the same name as an earlier attachment on that task replaces the stored file (its previous version stays in file history). The saved paths are returned. The change is announced to the project's configured task webhook and notification email when those are set. tasks_update with attachments replaces the attachment list itself.

## tasks-relationship-remove

Delete one explicit relationship from a task by its relationship id, as listed in the task's relationships. A parent link set through parent_id is removed by clearing parent_id with tasks_update instead. The deletion cannot be undone except by adding the relationship again.

## tasks-delete

Delete a task that should never have existed (a duplicate, a mistake, wrong direction). Gone from normal task reads on the next read; restorable for 30 days; purged after. Other tasks keep their history; attachment files remain. Raw database dumps may include trash until purge. Only the board owner's account can delete; anything else gets TASK_DELETE_FORBIDDEN. To keep a record as history, archive it or set superseded_by instead.

## tasks-settings-update

Configure where task events are delivered. webhook_url receives signed POSTs (X-Somewhere-Signature: t=<ms>,v1=<hmac-sha256-hex>) and/or notify_email receives emails. An empty string clears a field. The first time webhook_url is set, the response includes webhook_secret exactly once — it is stored server-side to verify the signature.

## memory-search

Search a bounded page of the org's memory before building, when unsure about a past call, or when the user references something not in context. The same filters with page.next_cursor as cursor continue the page; pages are not drained automatically. Expand omitted fields with tasks_get view=field.

## tasks-list-connector

Read a bounded page of project tasks. The same filters with next_cursor continue the list. Omitted fields can be retrieved separately; sorting and filters reflect live edits. With waiting set to me, the read is instead what is waiting for the signed-in person across their projects: what agents have asked that person to do, with the steps, the reason, who asked and when, and what was answered and through which credential. It is how an agent finds out what the person still has to do, and an agent may walk the person through the steps. tasks_update answers an item (done or cannot, with a note); done is only for an item the person did or asked to have marked done.

Get account usage totals, owned-project count, limits, and aggregate database/file storage with no arguments. Project AI calls and costs exclude Advisor calls, which are accounted separately. pages.title: API quick reference
pages.body:
## How Somewhere works

Somewhere is the backend for apps your agent builds. One project gives your app
its web address, server functions, one SQL database, sign-in, files, email, AI
and background work. Write React and TypeScript, then run `somewhere deploy`.
The platform compiles your source and serves the app and its functions together.

Somewhere runs on Cloudflare. Functions run on Workers, each project has its own
D1 database, files are stored in R2, and Durable Objects coordinate real-time
channels and releases. Replicas and limits: `docs({ topic: 'database-engine' })`.

A starter has these parts:

| Part | Source | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| App | `src/`, `index.html` | The interface and browser routes. |
| Functions | `api/` | Server code: `api/notes.ts` answers `/api/notes`. Every handler receives `sw`, bound to the project. |
| Data | `db/schema.ts` | Optional: tables, columns and access rules, applied on deploy. The default starter has none. |
| Auth | `api/auth/[...path].ts`, `src/auth/` | Working sign-in and session hooks to extend. |

The default starter includes sign-in screens; minimal includes the SDK and auth
route, while bare omits both. Browser
sessions use Secure, HttpOnly cookies. Normal owner-table operations get the
user from the verified session and scope rows to that user. A table's `client`
block chooses which operations and columns the browser may use.

Your functions decide who may perform privileged actions. Check the caller
before using server authority, sending an email or charging a card. Keep
secrets in `sw.env`, read them inside handlers, and make repeated effects safe
with a stable operation identity. Deploy raw source from the app root; the
platform handles compilation.
Expose a browser value only with `public: true` and a `VITE_` or
`REACT_APP_` name; visitors can read it.

Your data and code are yours: `somewhere pull` returns the source, `somewhere db dump`
the raw SQL database as one `.sql` file and `db_export` one table as CSV, and a
project can attach PostgreSQL in your own Neon account. Managed-database tables
are not in the dump or CSV export yet; `docs({ topic: 'portability' })` lists each path's limits.

Start with **Start an app**, **Data**, **Auth**, **Functions** and **Env vars
and secrets**. Each primitive opens with one working path and links to deeper
sections. Recipes contain complete jobs and live outside this short reading
path. The index below lists every topic, including specialized capabilities.

Use `somewhere docs <topic>` or MCP `docs({ topic })`. To load one section,
use `somewhere docs <topic> --section <id>` or `docs({ topic, section })`.
Use an explicit full view for the complete reference. Recipe first calls
already return the whole recipe.

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED CAPABILITY INDEX -->

## Getting started — build, deploy, verify

Ask before destructive or paid actions unless the user already authorized them.

To change an existing app, start with `somewhere pull <app>` in a fresh folder.
In a connector without a terminal, read its live source with `project_export`.

For a new app, `somewhere init --name <slug>` writes React + TypeScript. Signed out: local only;
signed in: also creates and links a project.
Default: sign-in UI; minimal: SDK/auth route; bare: neither. `init --catalog --json`: modules.
`npx -y @somewhere-cloud/cli@latest deploy` publishes raw source: signed out, a temporary URL, claim link
and expiry; linked, your account project. On a hosted VM, `somewhere login` uses browser approval and keeps you signed in.
Cron needs a claimed project. The test inbox works on temporary projects.
Start auth/data/cron with `somewhere docs recipe-signed-in-app --full`.

After edits: `somewhere typecheck` and focused local/browser tests. Publish:
1. `somewhere deploy` (do not build first). Deploy
   checks compilation, schema and secrets; `somewhere deploy-check` runs them without publishing
   (diagnosis, review, `--run /api/x`).
2. Run `somewhere verify` on the final journey (`--flow flow.json`). Sign test users up
   in-app at `*.test.somewhere.site`; more: `actors` + `journey` (`somewhere docs browser`).
   In your own Playwright script: `page.setDefaultTimeout(5_000)`, never a fixed sleep (wait for
   the thing itself), stop at the first failure and print `page.url()` and the visible error
   text, and after a fix rerun only the checks that failed (`somewhere docs test`).
3. Inspect: `somewhere browser`; diagnose: `somewhere logs --tail 10`, `somewhere errors`.
4. Test mail: `somewhere email test-inbox <addr>` includes `verification_code`.
   Don't retest sign-in or `sw.db.from` scoping; test each table's scope, auth before `sw.db.server`/raw SQL, bad input and journeys.

Routes: `index.html` loads `src/main.tsx`; unmatched extensionless paths
(`/signin`) serve it. Route the app by `location.pathname`.
`api/notes/[id].ts` is `/api/notes/:id`; `_`-prefixed names are import-only
helpers. Avoid names differing only in case.

With auth enabled, `api/auth/[...path].ts` is
`export { somewhereAuth as default } from '@somewhere-cloud/sdk/server'`; pages
use `createSomewhereAuth()` from `@somewhere-cloud/sdk/auth` (client and React hooks:
`somewhere docs auth-client --section react-auth-state`). `auth.signUp({ email, password,
displayName? })` / `auth.signIn({ email, password })` return the user or throw
with the message. Use the starter's `useAuthState()` gate. Render private UI only
after the session is confirmed. Keep the pending view and the retry view.
Browser tests wait for the expected screen. If your SDK publishes
`data-sw-auth` on `<html>`, first wait for the expected sign-in state there.
Sign-up sets `email_verified: false`; unverified users pass
`auth: 'required'`. `sw.auth.requireUser(req)` returns `{ id, email,
role, email_verified, … }` or throws 401 `AUTH_REQUIRED`;
`sw.auth.fromRequest(req)` returns it or `null`.

Functions: JSON endpoints use `sw.endpoint({ auth, body, rateLimit, handler:
async ({ body, user, params }, sw) => value })`; set `auth` (`'required'`,
`'optional'`, `'none'`) or deploy refuses it. Webhooks and streaming use a bare `export default async
function (req: Request, sw: SomewhereRuntimeContext)` returning a `Response`.
Params: `params.id` there, `sw.params.id` bare.

Data: `id()` is a random text key on new tables (reference with `text()`); integer-id tables keep integers. The starter's `id({ uuid: false })` is deliberate.
Declare tables in `db/schema.ts`; pages use `somewhere:data`
(`data.notes.list()`, `.create()`, `.update(id, …)`) without API files.
Its wire is same-origin `POST /__sw/data` (`somewhere docs declared-data --section
calling-the-data-endpoint-directly`); app hosts serve no `/v1/…` API.
Use `owner()` for personal rows, `group()` for invited teams, `appRole()`
for app-wide roles, `anyOf()` for owner or a role, `allOf()` for members-only rows.
Sharing your own rows with specific people: `anyOf(owner(), grant())`
(`somewhere docs declared-data --section per-owner-sharing`).
Booking/help desk: `somewhere docs sw.db --section provider-or-booker-and-owner-or-staff-recipes`.
Keep fitting scopes when an exceptional write needs `sw.db.server.tx`.
`shared()` gives signed-in reads and creator-only writes. `client` sets browser
columns. `publicRead: { where }` admits visitors and may cache anonymous reads
for up to 120 seconds. For fresh pages, use `sw.db.server.from` in a page handler
with a publication filter, public columns and `Cache-Control: no-store`. Public-profile enquiries use
`client.intake` (`somewhere docs declared-data`). Keep scopes and grants;
functions handle authorized exceptional writes and side effects. Declare the
body schema (a missing or mistyped field is a 400); `handle` below is a
public address its owner claimed:

```ts
export default sw.endpoint({
  auth: 'none',
  body: { handle: 'string', title: 'string', from_email: 'email' },
  handler: async ({ body }, sw) => {
    const title = body.title.trim();
    if (!title || title.length > 200 || /[\r\n]/.test(title)) return Response.json({ error: 'bad title' }, { status: 400 });
    const { data: [profile] } = await sw.db.server.from('profiles', { where: { handle: body.handle }, limit: 1 });
    if (!profile) return Response.json({ error: 'unknown handle' }, { status: 404 });
    await sw.db.server.insert('entries', { user_id: profile.user_id, owner_email: profile.owner_email,
      title, from_email: body.from_email, created_ms: Date.now() });
  },
});
```

Use the looked-up owner, never the body. Rate limits/alerts: `recipe-signed-in-app`.
Use `serverOnly()` only when every operation needs a function's own access check.
Structured queries: `sw.db.from` / `insert` / `update` / `remove` return `{ data: rows[], count,
changes }`; `where: { a: 1, b: { in: ids }, c: { gte: 2 }, d: null }` (one
operator per column). Raw SQL uses a separate raw database, never managed tables.
For cross-user managed work, authorize the caller and use `sw.db.server.from` /
`insert` / `update` / `remove`; keep `owner()`/`group()`. Parallel reads: `Promise.all`.

Unique pair: `unique: [['org_id','email']]` in table options.

Test schedules now: `somewhere cron run <id> --wait`. Do not wait for it to fire.

### Release privacy facts

`GET /v1/projects/:id/privacy` returns `{ release_id, privacy_facts, privacy_lines }`.
Read access is the same as project deploy history. `project_privacy_facts` reads this record;
`somewhere privacy` prints its lines. A successful source deploy includes the same record
and lines. Only declared owner table names, file collection names, domains and flags are
stored with the release. Source references do not cover requests built while the app runs.
Unavailable source signals or older releases say the facts are unavailable.
A missing privacy/policy name warns only when a declared owner table, file collection,
AI reference or outside domain was found, and names those signals. This is a guess from
file and route names. Sign-in settings and executed email/payment/AI usage are not included.
